Why: with a database adapter present, Auth.js runs a linking step it previously skipped. It asks storage "which account owns this Google identity", and we have nowhere to answer from — there is no table tying a provider's id to an account, and adding one would need a schema wave for a column nothing else would read. So the answer is always "unknown", and Auth.js's default response to an unknown identity whose address already has an account is to **refuse the sign-in**. Without this flag, every existing Google user would be locked out the moment email sign-in shipped.

The flag's name warns about a real risk and it is worth naming: if an identity provider hands over an address it never checked, matching on that address hands over the account. The guard is what removes it — Google states whether it verified the address, and a stated "no" is now refused. A *missing* statement is deliberately not treated as a "no", because a provider that simply omits the claim would otherwise lock every user out, which is a worse failure than the one being prevented and would arrive silently.

What this is not: a change of policy. Sign-in has resolved accounts by lowercased email since `T1.1` — `provisionAccount` looks the address up and creates it if absent, whatever provider carried it — and the unique index on `accounts.email` is the same statement in the schema. The flag makes the library agree with what the app already did.
Nearest spec: main §4.1 — "standard email + OAuth (Google) signup", silent on identity linking.
Class (filled by audit):

## 2026-09-02 — T-EMAIL — A sign-in link lasts fifteen minutes
Decision: `SIGN_IN_LINK_MAX_AGE_SECONDS = 15 * 60`. Auth.js's default is 24 hours.
Why: the link is a bearer credential — whoever holds the message holds the account until it lapses — and it sits in a mailbox, which is forwarded, archived, synced to phones and scanned by corporate filters. Fifteen minutes is comfortably more than mail delivery takes and short enough that a message found later is inert. The day-long default is a convenience setting on a credential, which is the wrong trade for a tool that manages somebody's storefront.
**This is a number the founder may want to move**, and moving it is one constant plus the "expires in N minutes" line in the email, which is generated from it. Ten minutes is defensible; an hour is defensible if support finds people are being timed out. Nothing in the specs states a figure.
Nearest spec: main §4.1 — silent on link lifetime.
Class (filled by audit):

## 2026-09-02 — T-EMAIL — The sign-in email goes straight through the email wrapper, not through the notification queue
Decision: the magic-link email is sent by calling the `EmailProvider` wrapper directly. It writes no `email_sends` row and takes no `dedupe_key`. The send is made idempotent on the link itself: the vendor's idempotency header carries a hash of that one link's secret.
Why: the queue's row is `(account_id, type, dedupe_key)` and `account_id` is required — but the person asking for a sign-in link may have no account, which is the entire point of the link. Dedupe would also be actively wrong here. Every other email in this product is a notification that must not go twice; a sign-in link is the opposite — asking for a second one because the first is stale *must* send a second email, so a dedupe key on a notification type would suppress exactly the send the user just asked for. Keying on the link instead gives the property that is actually wanted: a retry of one send cannot deliver twice, and a new link is a new email.
Invariant 25 is satisfied — the send goes through the one instrumented wrapper, and Auth.js's own bundled email provider (which speaks SMTP through Nodemailer) is deliberately not used. Invariant 26's uniqueness constraint is about `email_sends`, and this send is not one.
**Flagged for the integrator:** `T8.2` (lane G) is building the email pipeline in parallel and owns `packages/core/email`. If that card decides sign-in mail should be queued after all, this is the one send that would have to change, and it would need the account-less case solving first.
Nearest spec: tech §1.4 (email pipeline, `email_sends`), §1.5 (suppression — "account-security email" is exempt, and a sign-in link is that). Neither contemplates mail to a non-account.
Class (filled by audit):

## 2026-09-02 — T-EMAIL — The sign-in email's words live with the sign-in code, not in the UI string file
Decision: the four sentences of the magic-link email are written in `apps/web/app/api/auth/_lib/signInEmail.ts`, not added to `packages/ui/strings/en.json`.
Why: CLAUDE.md says copy lives in `packages/ui/strings/*.json` only, and this departs from it knowingly rather than quietly. That file is a screen dictionary owned by the frontend lane; nothing in the repo sends an email with words in it yet; and the card that builds the email pipeline (`T8.2`) is choosing where template copy lives *tonight*. Putting email copy into a screen's dictionary now would pre-empt that choice inside a file another lane is editing, and would have to be undone.
**This wants a ruling.** Once `T8.2` lands, either email copy joins the UI dictionary — and these four strings move — or emails get their own home and this file follows it. Neither is decided here.
Nearest spec: main Appendix A lists no sign-in email copy; tech §1.4 says templates are versioned in the repo but does not say where the words go.

## 2026-09-02 — T-EMAIL — A new OAuth signup is recorded as `oauth` rather than `google` in the funnel
Decision: the `provider` property on `signup_completed` reads `email` or `oauth`. It previously read `google` for Google signups.
Why: with the adapter in place, the account row for a brand-new user is created inside the adapter's `createUser`, and Auth.js does not tell it which provider is signing in — only whether the address has just been verified, which distinguishes a link signup from an OAuth one and nothing finer. The distinction the founder decision actually turns on is preserved ("does email sign-in bring signups Google was losing us"), and there is exactly one OAuth provider, so `oauth` and `google` currently name the same set. Recovering the exact provider name would mean firing the event from a later callback and threading "was this a create" through to it — more moving parts than the property is worth today.
Consequence: a PostHog breakdown of `signup_completed` by provider will show `google` before this change and `oauth` after, for the same route in. Worth knowing before reading that chart across the boundary.
Nearest spec: main §14.7 (funnel events) — names the events, not their properties.

## 2026-09-02 — T-EMAIL — FLAGGED, not fixed: the sign-in screen's Google button cannot work, and the same defect would have hit the email form
Decision: not fixed here. Recorded, because it is one line away from my card and in another lane's directory.
Why: `packages/ui/src/public/SignIn.tsx` posts a form to `/api/auth/signin/google` carrying a `callbackUrl` and nothing else. Auth.js rejects any sign-in POST that does not carry the anti-forgery token it hands out at `GET /api/auth/csrf` — verified in the library's own request dispatcher, and I hit it while writing this card's tests, which have to fetch that token before they can ask for a link. So the button on our sign-in screen returns an error rather than starting a sign-in. The screen belongs to the frontend lane and its copy file (`packages/ui/strings/en.json`) is being edited tonight, so this is surfaced rather than resolved.
Consequence for the founder decision that email sign-in ships in v1: **the capability is built and reachable at Auth.js's own page (`/api/auth/signin`), but our branded `/signin` screen still offers only Google, and that button is broken.** Adding the email field is a small frontend change — an input named `email`, a hidden `csrfToken` fetched first, posting to `/api/auth/signin/email` — plus two or three new strings, and it fixes the Google button in the same edit. It is not done, and until it is, no merchant reaches email sign-in from the product.
Nearest spec: ui §1 (sign-in screen); main §4.1.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — Nine steps on the server become seven rows on the screen, and three of them collapse into one
Decision: the setup progress list shows the seven rows the UI spec names. The server reports nine steps, and `catalog_sync`, `distill` and `family_group` are drawn as the single row "Reading your store". A row's state is worked out from all its steps: any failure wins, then anything running, then all-skipped, then all-finished; a row two-thirds through reads as active rather than done.
Why: the nine exist because fetching a catalogue, reducing each product to a fact sheet and grouping those products into families fail, retry and resume independently — that is a property of the work, not something to show a merchant, who would read three indistinguishable technical names as the product stalling. The spec names seven labels and the response schema names nine steps; neither says how they line up, so the mapping was a choice. The precedence order is the load-bearing part: had "anything succeeded" been tested before "anything running", a row would flicker to done between two of its own jobs.
Nearest spec: ui §3.2 — the seven labels; main §6.3–6.4 and the ingestion status schema — the nine steps.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — Two opposite screens share one domain state, and the connection tells them apart
Decision: `domains.state = awaiting_shopify_auth` renders the blocking connect card when `connections.shopify` is `none`, and the "your connection was lost" parked card when it is `broken`.
Why: the spec describes these as separate screens (§3.3 and §3.5) but the state machine gives them one state — a store that has never connected and a working store whose token was revoked both sit in `awaiting_shopify_auth`. They want opposite words: one is a step in setting up, the other is an account that stopped, with history that stays readable. The connection field is the only thing in the account response that separates them. **This puts a requirement on the backend:** revocation must set the connection to `broken` rather than back to `none`, or a working merchant is shown the first-run screen. Registered in the screen contract.
Nearest spec: ui §3.3, §3.5; main §6.2 — "the account drops back to `awaiting_shopify_auth` with a reconnect banner".

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — The first scan's progress lines are named, not ticked, because nothing reports the scan's progress
Decision: the "Finding your growth opportunities…" card lists the five stages the design canvas names, all rendered as work in flight. No stage is shown as finished. The card polls `GET /api/opportunities` every five seconds and moves the merchant on when `lastScanAt` stops being null. A `stageStates` prop is where a real feed plugs in.
Why: the spec says the sub-lines mirror `signal_runs` over the same kind of stream as the ingestion stepper. The frozen API contract has no route for that — 55 routes, none of them a scan-progress read or stream — and this lane may not add one. Two ways to fill the gap were available: tick the stages on a timer, or name them without ticking. A timer would be a fabricated progress bar on the one screen whose whole job is to earn trust before the product has produced anything, so it was rejected. What is lost is the sense of movement; what is kept is that nothing on screen is untrue. **This needs a route** — a `signal_runs` status/stream pair shaped like the ingestion one — before §3.8 is actually satisfied.
Nearest spec: ui §3.8 — "sub-lines that reflect `signal_runs` progress … SSE-driven like the stepper"; main §6.9.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — Language and country are validated fields rather than dropdowns, because nothing defines the options
Decision: the confirmation screen's language and country are text inputs holding short codes, validated to the shape the confirm request requires (language at least two characters, country exactly two, upper-cased as typed). "Confirm profile" stays disabled until the description, language and country all hold something.
Why: the spec calls for dropdowns, and a dropdown needs a list. No document names one, no endpoint serves one, and the set that actually matters is whichever locales the paid search vendor accepts as parameters — which lives in another lane's package. Inventing a list here would be inventing product data, and a wrong entry in it quietly sends every later search lookup to the wrong market. Validating the shape gets the same guarantee the confirm request itself asks for; swapping in a select is one component when a list exists.
Nearest spec: ui §3.7 item 1 — "language + country dropdowns"; main §6.5 — the persona produces the codes.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — Three places where the design canvas and the specs disagree, each resolved towards the spec
Decision: **The parked card's sentence.** The canvas renders "…contact us for a custom solution." and the canonical copy table ends "…or join the waitlist." The canonical string is used whole. **The waitlist capture itself is not built:** §3.4 asks for one and no route accepts an email address, so the card offers the contact link alone. **"Try a different domain"**, which the canvas offers on the same card, is not built either: §3.4 says the state persists until support intervenes, with no self-serve exit in v1. **"Save and finish later"** on the confirmation screen is not built: nothing persists a partial edit — the only write is confirming — so the button would silently discard what it appeared to save.
Why: `docs/design/README.md` makes the spec the source of truth for behaviour and copy and asks for disagreements to be stated rather than picked. Each of these is the canvas offering a control the product has nowhere to send.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — The competitor suggestion line was reworded away from the spec's example, to keep a count off a denominator
Decision: a suggested competitor reads "ranks alongside you in 8 top searches" rather than the spec's illustrative "appears in 8 of your top queries".
Why: the constitution forbids rendering a count against a denominator anywhere the merchant can see, and the existing copy test enforces it by refusing any sentence of the shape "{n} of …". The spec's phrasing is an example in parentheses rather than a pinned string, and the meaning is unchanged — the number is how many of the store's own top searches this domain turned up in. Rewording was preferred to loosening the test, because the test is the only thing standing between the product and "3 of 30".

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — The competitor cap appears a third time, in the screen, and enforces nothing
Decision: `MAX_COMPETITORS = 5` lives in `packages/ui`. It disables the two add controls and fills their tooltip; it is not a check.
Why: the cap is already enforced twice, in the API and by a database trigger, which is what the invariant requires and what makes it true regardless of what any screen does. A screen that let the merchant type a sixth and then showed them a refusal would be worse to use for no extra safety. The number is not a scoring threshold, so it does not belong in `packages/rules`; it is a product limit stated in the spec's prose.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — A blocklisted competitor is recognised from the refusal, not from a code, and the override is offered back
Decision: adding a competitor treats a 409 carrying `competitor_is_own_domain` or `competitor_limit_reached` as those two specific messages, and any other refusal of a well-formed domain as the marketplace blocklist — which is shown as a warning with an "Add anyway" button that retries with `overrideBlocklist: true`.
Why: the request schema has the override flag, so the blocklist refusal is meant to be overridable, but the conflict-code enum has no entry for it — the two named codes are the only ones the contract gives this route. Guessing a code that does not exist would break the moment one is added; treating "refused, and not one of the two we know" as the overridable case behaves correctly today and degrades to a slightly generic warning if the route ever refuses for a third reason.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — Best sellers reorder by dragging or by arrow keys, and the revenue figures are a band rather than an amount
Decision: each row is draggable and its handle is a button that answers ArrowUp and ArrowDown. The row shows the source badge and, where the response carries one, the revenue band — not a currency amount or a unit count.
Why: the spec asks for drag to reorder; an ordering control that only answers a mouse is unusable from a keyboard or a phone, and the ranking it sets is what the persona and the seed keywords are drawn from, so it is not optional detail. The keys are the same control, not a second one. On the figures: §3.7 asks for "90d revenue/qty badges", and the profile response carries `revenueBand` and no numbers at all — showing a number would mean inventing one.
Nearest spec: ui §3.7 item 2; the profile response schema — `topProductSchema`.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — Reporting a wrong grouping sends the merchant's words to support and three facts to analytics
Decision: a new browser event, `family_grouping_reported`, carrying the family's id, its member count and which signal grouped it. What the merchant typed goes only to `POST /api/products/families/report`.
Why: the spec names this event. The three properties are what makes a report useful in aggregate — whether we merge too eagerly, and which grouping signal does it — and each fits a kind the property table allows. The merchant's text does not: it is free prose about their own catalogue, and there is deliberately no kind that could hold it.
Nearest spec: ui §3.7 item 5 — "support/feedback record + PostHog event `family_grouping_reported`"; main §14.7 — events carry ids and aggregates only.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — The one-time explainer is dismissed per browser, because nothing stores a dismissal
Decision: the strip explaining the four action types remembers being dismissed in the browser's own storage, under `sortiva.activationExplainerDismissed`.
Why: the spec says it appears once and is dismissible for good. "For good" needs somewhere per account to keep it, and neither the settings response nor any route has a field for one — and this card may not add a column. The cost of the browser-local version is that a merchant who signs in on a second device sees the strip once more; the cost of the alternative is a schema change nobody asked for.
Nearest spec: ui §3.8 — "a one-time explainer strip … dismissible".

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — Onboarding fills the dashboard, and stops at the edge of the screen another card owns
Decision: `/dashboard` renders every stage of setting a store up and, once that is over, an empty marked slot. `/opportunities` renders the activation header — the count and the one-time explainer — above an empty marked slot for the list.
Why: the spec is explicit that the dashboard is the container and there is no wizard route, so the states had to live here. Both steady-state screens belong to later cards, and building either would be building somebody else's card badly. The slots are empty elements with a name rather than placeholder copy, so the card that fills one deletes a div rather than untangling a stand-in.
Nearest spec: ui §3 opening — "The dashboard is the container for all onboarding states"; ui §4 and §5 — the two screens that follow.

## 2026-09-02 — T9.3 — Contradiction, not resolved here: Google sends a merchant to Settings in the middle of onboarding
Decision: recorded rather than changed. `apps/web/app/api/gsc/_lib/config.ts` returns the merchant to `/settings/connections?gsc=granted` after Google's consent screen. During onboarding the Search Console step and its property picker are part of the progress list on the dashboard, so a merchant who connects mid-setup is dropped out of setup onto a settings screen that does not exist yet.
Why not fixed: that file belongs to Lane C. The dashboard already reads `?gsc=granted` and shows the property picker when it sees it, so the screen works the moment the return address points back at it during onboarding. Two shapes of fix, both someone else's call: carry the origin through the OAuth state, or return to the dashboard whenever the domain is not yet confirmed.
Nearest spec: ui §3.6 — the picker is a step in the stepper; main §12.2 — the property picker mechanics.
## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — The change stream lives in the webhook table, and the account travels in the row

Decision: `CatalogEvents` — the frozen seam that tells the content inventory and the drift rules what a merchant changed — is backed by `webhook_events`, the existing table for "something arrived, deal with it later". Two kinds of row sit there now, told apart by topic: a **receipt** keyed on Shopify's own delivery id, and a **change** keyed on a fingerprint of the change itself. `webhook_events` has no account column, so the account id travels inside the row's JSON payload and the per-store read filters on it.

Why: the stream has to be durable, per-store, ordered and de-duplicable, and no table for it exists. Adding one is a migration, which a feature card may not do. Of the tables that do exist, this is the only one whose purpose matches. The cost, stated plainly: reading one store's changes cannot use an index on the account, so it is a scan over rows arriving in the last thirty days (the retention sweep prunes at thirty days). At v1 volumes — a webhook is a merchant editing something — that is small. **If it stops being small, the fix is a column in the next schema wave, not a second table.**

Alternative rejected: deriving the stream from the `products` table's own timestamps. It cannot represent a deletion, because a deleted product's row is what would have to be missing, and it cannot represent a blog post or a static page at all.

Nearest spec: main §13 (`webhook_events`), §14.3.8 (process from the table, never from the body); build plan §4 (`CatalogEvents` frozen).


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — A change is identified by what changed and when, not by which producer found it

Decision: a change row's key is `catalog_change/<account>:<kind>:<entity>:<the merchant's own edit time>`. Recording is insert-or-ignore.

Why: two things produce changes — a webhook we processed, and the nightly re-read that catches the webhooks Shopify dropped. Both see the same edit. Keying on the edit rather than on the delivery makes the second one a no-op by construction, which is what makes "run the sweep twice and it converges" true rather than merely usually true. It is also what stops a store that never changes accumulating change rows for ever, with every consumer downstream re-reading pages that did not move.

Consequence: a change with no edit time of its own — a deletion — is stamped with the sweep's own clock, so a store left with a deleted product records one removal per sweep. The consumers collapse that (a page removed twice is removed once), and the alternative, a key with no time in it at all, would make a deleted-then-recreated product invisible the second time.

Nearest spec: main §14.3.8 (the sweep is idempotent by construction), §14.1 (webhooks plus reconciliation, never webhooks alone).


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — A product's fingerprint covers its words, not its price or its stock

Decision: `products.checksum` is computed over the title, description, handle, type, vendor, tags, status, variant names and codes, and image addresses. It deliberately excludes prices and stock levels. Price and availability changes are detected separately, by comparing the stored `variants` against the arriving ones.

Why: the same column has two readers with opposite needs. The drift sweep wants to know "did anything change"; distillation (`T2.3`) re-runs when this moves, and a model call per product is the most expensive thing onboarding does. A merchant running a weekend sale changes every price in the shop, and a checksum covering prices would buy a fresh distillation of the entire catalogue for an event that changed no words. main §14.3.2 says the distillation key is "the product's `updated_at` + **body** checksum", which this follows.

The three kinds of change are reported separately into the stream (`product_updated`, `price_changed`, `availability_changed`), which is what lets the content inventory ignore the two that cannot move a page's words — the decision `T3.2` already took.

Nearest spec: main §14.3.2 (the distillation key), §14.1 (drift triggers); DECISIONS 2026-09-02 `T3.2`.


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — Test orders and cancelled orders are not sales

Decision: an order flagged as one of Shopify's own test orders, or one carrying a cancellation, is dropped when the orders are read. It contributes to neither the best-seller ranking nor the landing-page takings.

Why: main §6.2 says to aggregate order line items over the trailing ninety days and does not say which orders count. Both defaults are wrong in a visible way. Shopify's test orders are placed with a test gateway while a merchant is setting their shop up, and counting them means a brand-new store's "best sellers" are whatever the owner bought from themselves — the first thing they would see, and obviously wrong. A cancelled order is not a purchase, and counting it inflates the revenue figure the ranking is sorted by.

Risk accepted: a refunded order still counts, because a refund is a separate record we do not read. Correcting that means reading refunds, which is more order data for a marginal improvement to a ranking; it is worth revisiting if a merchant disputes their best-seller list.

Nearest spec: main §6.2 — "aggregate order line items over the trailing 90 days"; silent on which orders qualify.


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — A landing page is kept as a path with its query string removed

Decision: `landing_revenue_daily.landing_url` holds the path a buyer arrived on — `/collections/trail-shoes` — and never the query string Shopify recorded with it.

Why: two reasons, and either alone would be enough. The query carries campaign parameters and advertising click ids, which are per-visitor and belong to the shopper rather than to the shop; keeping them would put visitor-scoped identifiers in a table whose whole purpose is that it holds none. And a page reached through five campaigns would otherwise be five rows meaning the same thing, which makes the aggregate useless for the one question it exists to answer.

Nearest spec: main §17.3 (`landing_site` aggregated per day per landing URL, aggregates only), §14.6.


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — An order's day is the store's own day, taken from Shopify's stamp verbatim

Decision: the day an order is counted under is the first ten characters of Shopify's `created_at`, not a date computed by converting that timestamp.

Why: Shopify stamps orders with the store's own UTC offset. A sale at 23:30 in a New Zealand shop is the previous day in UTC, so converting would move every evening's takings into the day before and a merchant comparing our numbers with their own Shopify report would find them disagreeing. Reading the characters Shopify already wrote gives the merchant's day with no timezone table and no persona dependency — which matters because the persona, where the store's timezone eventually lives, is built two steps *after* this one.

Nearest spec: main §17.3 (per day per landing URL), §9.4 (per-account clocks); neither says whose day.


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — The catalogue sync's idempotency key is the store plus the day

Decision: `catalog_sync`'s `input_version` is the shop handle and the current date. A redelivery on the same day returns the stored answer without reading the store; the next night is genuinely different work.

Why: main §14.3.2 specifies "the Shopify shop ID + a monotonically increasing sync generation number", and no column holds a generation number — adding one is a schema wave. The date is a generation number that increments once a day and needs no storage. What it costs: two syncs on the same day are one, so a merchant who reconnects after a failed first attempt on the same day gets the stored answer rather than a fresh read. That is the right answer when the first attempt succeeded and the wrong one if a re-read is genuinely wanted the same day; the nightly reconciliation covers the gap within a day, and a deliberate re-sync path would need its own input version rather than a weaker key.

Nearest spec: main §14.3.2 — names a generation number this schema does not have.


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — A product the store stopped listing keeps its row; the removal is reported, not acted on

Decision: when the nightly re-read finds a product Shopify no longer lists, a `product_deleted` change is recorded and the `products` row is left exactly where it is. Nothing is deleted and nothing is marked.

Why: the row is the only record that the product ever existed, and the drift rules (`T5.3`) need precisely that — an article recommending a discontinued product has to be repairable, which means knowing what it pointed at. Deleting the row would cascade the product's fact sheet away and leave every reference to it dangling with no way to explain itself. Marking it needs a column, which is a schema wave. This mirrors the decision `T3.2` took for deleted store pages, and inherits its open question: **what should eventually happen to the row is for the founder or the integrator to settle before the drift card ships.**

How "no longer listed" is decided: the sweep stamps every product it sees with the moment its walk began, so anything still carrying an older stamp was not shown to us. Asked that way rather than by accumulating ids, so a walk spread over several runs still gets the right answer.

Nearest spec: main §14.1 (product deleted → flag referencing articles); silent on the catalogue row itself.


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — There is no request cache on the Shopify reads, deliberately

Decision: invariant 20 requires billable reads and model calls to be cached at request level and written before processing. The catalogue sync and the sweep have no such cache.

Why: the invariant exists to stop us paying twice for one answer — a crash after the vendor responded but before we finished with the response. Shopify Admin reads are not billed; main §14.3.6 classifies them as "pure read: freely retryable, no protection needed beyond backoff". Caching them would add a table write per page for no saving and would make a re-read return stale data during a sweep whose entire purpose is freshness. What *is* protected is the request budget, by the page cursor: a resumed walk does not re-spend the pages it already read, which is the equivalent scarce resource here.

Recorded because a reader checking invariant 20 against this card will find nothing and should find the reason rather than a gap.

Nearest spec: main §14.3.6 (external side-effects by class); invariant 20.


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — The receiver keeps the store's name beside the body, because the header has nowhere else to go

Decision: a stored Shopify delivery's `payload` is `{ shop_handle, body }` rather than the body alone.

Why: Shopify names the store in the `X-Shopify-Shop-Domain` header, not in the body, and `webhook_events` has no column for it. The drain has to answer "whose store is this" without the request still being open, so the name has to survive the response. This card is the first writer of Shopify rows in that table, so nothing else reads the old shape. A column is a schema wave.

Nearest spec: main §14.3.8 (process from the table, never from the request body); main §13 (`webhook_events`).


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — `shop/redact` is recorded and answered; the purge itself is not built here

Decision: of the three mandatory privacy webhooks, `customers/redact` and `customers/data_request` are fully answered — logged, and answered "no customer data held", which is true by construction because order ingestion keeps no customer field. `shop/redact` is verified, recorded and logged, and **no store data is erased by this card**.

Why: erasing a store's data within thirty days is account-lifecycle work (main §14.6): it spans billing, tokens, the domain claim's grace window and every table an account owns, and belongs to whoever builds account deletion. Building half of it here would leave two places that delete a store, one of them incomplete. **Flagged for the integrator: `shop/redact` currently has a receiver and no consequence. Some card must own the purge before launch, and none does today.**

Nearest spec: main §14.6 — the three mandatory topics and what each must do.


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — The rate limit lives inside the one Admin client, so every caller inherits it

Decision: the one-request-a-second budget is enforced inside `ShopifyAdminClient`, per store, and the process holds a single instance of that client. A 429 pauses the whole store for exactly the `Retry-After` Shopify sent.

Why: the budget Shopify enforces is per store, not per caller. Two things read a store on the same night — this card's catalogue sync and the content inventory (`T3.2`) — and a limiter per call site would let each believe it was alone and together earn the rate limiting the pacing exists to avoid. Putting it in the client also means the inventory lane inherits pacing it did not have, with no change to its code. **Visible consequence for Lane C: their nightly walk is now paced. It was not before.**

Nearest spec: main §14.4 — "background sync budgeted at 1 req/s ... honor `Retry-After` exactly".


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — Files touched outside Lane B's directories

Decision: this card writes into five files no lane owns, listed so the integrator expects them. `packages/db/src/repositories/catalog.ts` and `catalog-events.ts` (new) plus one line in `repositories/index.ts` — repositories, not migrations. `packages/jobs/src/chaos/harness.ts` gains one entry in its scenario list and one import, which is what that file's own comment says T2.2 will do. `apps/web/instrumentation.ts` registers the two new task handlers, beside the ones already there. `apps/web/app/api/webhooks/shopify/[topic]/` is new; the path is the one the frozen route table already names, and `apps/web/app/api/webhooks/` is not in any lane's ownership list (Lane A owns `webhooks/stripe` specifically).

Why: build plan §3 marks `instrumentation.ts` and the chaos harness as integrator-resolved rather than union-merged, and a merge that silently drops half of either is worse than a conflict.

Nearest spec: build plan §3 ("Files no lane owns"), §4 (the frozen route table).


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — The stub report no longer lists the change stream, and a T2.1 test changed meaning

Decision: two small edits outside this card's own files. `scripts/stub-report.mjs` no longer constructs `StubCatalogEvents`, because that seam is filled — the product runs on the real change stream now, and a report that still listed it would fail the M2 exit gate for a gap that no longer exists. The double itself is untouched and tests still use it. And one assertion in `T2.1`'s onboarding test changed: it said "the next step belongs to a later card, so the run correctly stops", and that later card is this one, so a store with permission granted now carries straight on into reading its catalogue and stops at distillation instead.

Why recorded: the second is a behaviour change to something another card wrote, and a reviewer seeing an edited assertion should find the reason here rather than guess at one.

Nearest spec: build plan §4 (a consumer's tests re-run against the real implementation once the producer lands).


## 2026-09-02 — T2.2 — No dev-store evidence: the store reads are proved against an in-memory Shopify

Decision: this card's Shopify behaviour is proved against stand-ins — an in-memory store that pages the way Shopify pages, and, for the rate limiter and the `Link`-header cursor, a real HTTP server standing in for Shopify. There are still no Partner credentials.

Why: the same posture `T2.1` recorded and four earlier cards took with Stripe, Turnstile, Anthropic and PostHog. What a stand-in cannot prove: that Shopify's real cursor format, `Retry-After` behaviour, order and product field shapes, and webhook headers behave as assumed; and that the field lists we send are accepted. **This card must be re-run against a Partner dev store before launch, and it is now the largest single piece of outstanding real-vendor evidence in the build.**

Nearest spec: build plan §6 `T2.2` done-when; `docs/founder-decisions.md` A1.


## 2026-09-02 — T8.0 — A Shopify store is held by its live connection only, so losing one releases the store
Decision: `shopify_conns.shop_handle` is unique among rows where `invalidated_at IS NULL`, instead of unique across every row that ever existed. The abandoned row is kept, not deleted. Because two rows may now carry one handle, `findAccountByShopHandle` — the "whose store is this" lookup an incoming Shopify webhook depends on — now asks for the live row; it previously relied on the unconditional index to make its answer single, and would otherwise have been free to answer with the abandoned account and route an uninstall to a merchant who no longer has that store.
Why: the old index made a lost connection a permanent lock. A merchant who uninstalled us, or deleted their account and came back later under a new one, could never reconnect the same store: the leftover row still owned the handle and no path in the product cleared it, so the attempt died on a database constraint the merchant could do nothing about. Recommended in these words by audit `T0.3` ("makes the release real at the database level ... the version that survives a sweep job failing to run") and by the `T1.4` entry of 2026-09-01, and collected into this wave by the integrator. Risk considered and accepted: another account can now connect a store whose connection is dead, including while the original merchant is still being asked to reconnect. Connecting requires completing Shopify's own install on that store, so only someone with real admin rights there can do it — the exposure is narrower than the failure it replaces. Note for the record that "defence in depth", the phrase the `T1.4` entry uses, describes it wrongly: a partial unique index permits strictly more rows than an unconditional one, so this is a deliberate relaxation, not an extra guard.
Nearest spec: main §14.4 (a rejected token moves the account to `awaiting_shopify_auth`) and §6.2 — both describe losing a connection, neither says whether the store stays reserved afterwards.

## 2026-09-02 — T8.0 — `domains.release_after` does not become a partial unique index; the wave stops and asks instead
Decision: the domain claim's uniqueness is left exactly as it is — unconditional on `domain_normalized` — and the matching change recommended alongside the Shopify one is **not** made in this wave. Deferred to the founder or the integrator, not declined.
Why: the two look symmetrical and are not. Making the domain index partial on `release_after IS NULL` frees the domain the instant the column is set, which is the moment the account is deleted — and main §14.6 sets that column precisely to hold the domain for seven days first, "so a squatter cannot take it the same hour". Postgres index predicates must be immutable, so the deadline itself cannot go in the predicate; there is no version of this index that both survives the release sweep never running *and* keeps the grace window. Three further consequences, none of which this card can take alone: the claim path would have to start reading the deadline it deliberately ignores today (`T1.4`, 2026-09-01), which is a file in another lane's directory pinned by a test asserting the opposite; two rows could then exist for one domain, one lingering and one live, so every lookup by domain would have to disambiguate; and unlike a Shopify connection, claiming a domain has no external gate — anyone can type it — so the grace window is the only thing standing between a deleted account and a squatter. The open question is put in the session report in plain terms.
Nearest spec: main §14.6 (7-day grace), §2/§5 (one account per domain); invariant 1.

## 2026-09-02 — T8.0 — Marking a store page as deleted is not built; the wave stops on the shape of it
Decision: no column is added for "this page is gone" in this wave. The inventory — one row per web address the store publishes — still keeps a row for a page the merchant has deleted, with nothing recording that it is gone, exactly as `T3.2` left it.
Why: `T3.2`'s entry of 2026-09-02 asks for this and ends "This needs the founder or the integrator to settle before the existing-target check ships in `T3.5`", and the integrator's collection for this wave repeats that the shape — a nullable timestamp saying when the page went, or a state column naming which of several conditions the row is in — leaks into what `T3.5` reads. `CLAUDE.md` prime directive 3 makes an interface another lane consumes a stop-and-ask, not a lane's choice. What stays broken until it is settled, unchanged from `T3.2`: `T3.5` would recommend improving a page that no longer exists. Nothing new breaks by waiting; `T8.1` and `T8.2`, this lane's next two cards, do not read the inventory at all.
Nearest spec: main §12.3 — specifies the inventory sync and its checksum, silent on removal.

## 2026-09-02 — T8.0 — The rest of the wave's collected list is closed without a migration, and "retention bookkeeping" has no outstanding item
Decision: schema wave 4 ships one index change and nothing else. Everything else the integrator collected is recorded here as closed rather than left ambiguous. **Already built, re-checked against the migrations rather than the journal:** `verification_tokens` and the completed-work ledger `idempotency_ledger` (both `0004_wave2b.sql`, the ledger's write-once trigger in `0005_wave2b_guards.sql`); and every table `T8.1` and `T8.2` need — `notifications`, `email_sends`, `email_suppressions`, `notification_prefs`. **Declined earlier on substantive grounds and not revived:** a "price unknown" marker on spend events, and an account column on the completed-work ledger. **Conditional on cards nobody has written, so not requested:** the detected store name as a queryable column, a measured-or-defaulted marker on the click-through curve, stored cluster-share tables, and a per-episode marker for the Shopify connect reminder. **Retention:** tech §1.7's rules — notifications pruned at 90 days, `email_sends` kept 12 months — are sweep behaviour for `T8.3`, and both tables already carry the timestamp a sweep reads, so the card's "retention bookkeeping" scope line has no column behind it.
Why: the card's done-when is "every schema-tagged DECISIONS entry is resolved or explicitly deferred", and an entry nobody closed reads the same as an entry nobody found. Note for the spec keepers: the card also says to read "`DECISIONS.md` (class-b entries tagged `schema`)" and **no such tagging exists** — the `Class (filled by audit):` line is empty almost everywhere. The card text should be corrected to point at the collected list instead.
Nearest spec: tech §1.3, §1.7 — the card's own citations; both are satisfied by existing tables.
## 2026-09-02 — T-START — Re-claiming a domain asks for the run again, and the job key is what stops a second one
Decision: the claim queues the "move this store's onboarding along" job on both successful paths — the real claim, and the merchant who submits their own domain a second time (which the code answers as `already_yours`). It is not queued on any refusal. What prevents two jobs is the queue's own de-duplication: the job is filed under a key derived from the account (`ingestion_dispatch:<account id>`), so a second ask lands on the first job rather than stacking behind it.
Why: the card's done-when is "re-running the claim does not queue a second job for the same run", and a merchant re-pasting their address *is* the re-run — the first one committed, so the second is answered as "already yours". Reading that done-when as "only queue on the first claim" would make it trivially true and prove nothing. Queueing on both is also the more useful behaviour: a merchant who sees nothing happen and pastes their address again gets the pipeline nudged, without anyone touching the database. It cannot duplicate work — the steps are claimed by guarded updates and the completed-work ledger returns the stored result — so the worst case of an extra nudge is a worker finding nothing to do.
Alternative rejected: keying the job on the *run* rather than the account. The run id is derived from the domain, so it would behave identically today; the account is what every other queue in the codebase keys on, and it is also the thing a second, unrelated request to move onboarding (the OAuth callback, a sweep) would key on — so keying on the account is what makes those collapse together too.
Nearest spec: main §5 step 3 — "claiming enqueues the deep ingestion job", silent on repeat claims; main §14.3.1–14.3.2.

## 2026-09-02 — T-START — The queue call is a separate file, and the claim calls it directly rather than through an injected port
Decision: `packages/jobs/src/ingestion/queue.ts` is a new file holding the task name and `enqueueIngestionDispatch`, importing only drizzle — matching the Search Console and inventory queues, which were split the same way. The claim calls it directly, rather than taking it as a function it can be handed (which is how the Search Console connect flow does it).
Why: two reasons for the split file, one for the direct call. The dispatcher itself imports the Shopify steps, the LLM wrapper and the threshold config; a request that imported it to queue one job would pull a file-reading config loader into a bundle with no filesystem, and the build would fail while every test passed — this has already happened once (`T-BOOT`). And the property this card has to demonstrate is that the claim and the queued job commit together, which only the real queue in a real transaction can show; an injected stand-in would prove the claim calls *something*, which is not the guarantee. So the test installs the queue's own tables and inspects them.
Nearest spec: CLAUDE.md code-structure rules — file placement is convention, not spec.

## 2026-09-02 — T-START — The queue's tables are a start-up prerequisite, and two test suites now create them themselves
Decision: the claim's transaction writes into the queue's tables, which are created by the worker at start-up and **not** by our own migrations. `apps/web/app/api/domain/_lib/domain.test.ts` and `funnel.test.ts` now install them in their setup, via a new shared helper (`packages/jobs/src/runtime/testing.ts`). Their test cases are unchanged.
Why: the worker runs inside the web server's own process and installs those tables before the server can answer a request, so in production the prerequisite is met by the time any claim arrives — and a route already queues work this way (finishing a Search Console connection). **The consequence to know about:** a database that no worker has ever started against has no queue in it, and a claim against such a database now fails rather than silently claiming without starting anything. That is the safe direction — a claim that quietly starts nothing is the bug this card exists to fix — but it means `WORKER_ENABLED=false` against a fresh database (local screen work) breaks the claim, where before it merely stalled it. Adding the queue's tables to our own migrations would remove the hole; that is a migration, which this card may not write.
Alternative rejected: catching the "no such schema" error and letting the claim commit anyway. That reintroduces exactly the failure this card removes, and hides it.
Nearest spec: tech §2 — silent on who installs the queue's schema.
## 2026-09-02 — T-ANALYTICS — What stops store content reaching analytics is the shape a property is allowed to have, not a list of banned words
Decision: each browser event's property table now says, for every property, *what kind of thing it may hold* — an identifier, an enumerated name we chose, a count, or a yes/no — and that table exists at run time rather than only in the type system. Everything a screen reports is filtered through it: a property the event does not declare is dropped, and a declared property holding the wrong kind of thing is dropped too. There is deliberately no kind for text.
Why: an open audit finding (`docs/audits/false-confidence.md`, finding 9) records that the server-side wrapper redacts secrets and lets an article title, an article body and a prompt straight through, and that the rule's only enforcement was a doc comment. The founder's decision that browsers talk to the vendor directly removes the last place our code could inspect an outgoing event, so the check had to move into the definitions. Two candidate designs: a list of property *names* that are allowed, or a rule about the *values*. The name list alone is defeated by anyone adding a name; the value rule alone lets an undeclared field through. Both are in, and the value rule is the one that carries the guarantee: identifiers and enumerated names must be under sixty-four characters with no whitespace, so a headline, a paragraph or a prompt is not expressible under any property name at all.
One case the shape rule does not catch on its own: a vendor access token is short and has no spaces, so it looks exactly like an identifier. The same secret matcher the server-side wrapper already uses rejects it here. It is **rejected rather than redacted** — an id that is really a token is a bug, and an event carrying `[redacted]` where an opportunity id should be is worse than an event missing the property.
What this does *not* claim: a future card could still add a property called `article_title` and give it the enum kind, and a one-word title would pass. Two things bite if it tries — a test refuses any property whose name contains `title`, `body`, `text`, `prompt`, `token` and a dozen similar words, and the value rule rejects anything with a space in it — but neither is a proof. The real protection against that is that adding a property is a visible edit to one table rather than a field appearing at a call site.
Nearest spec: main §14.7 ("events carry ids and aggregates only — never product content, article text, prompts") — it states the rule and says nothing about how it is held.

## 2026-09-02 — T-ANALYTICS — Session replay is off everywhere, and every view has to say whether it renders a merchant's store
Decision: nothing is recorded. The vendor library starts with recording disabled, no code anywhere turns it on, and a list in `packages/ui/src/analytics/replay.ts` records for every view whether it renders a merchant's store data. A view that does can never be recorded whatever else is configured, and a view nobody has classified counts as store data.
Why: session replay saves a film of the page and plays it back to us later, so a replay of a merchant's screen is a copy of their catalogue sitting on a vendor's server. The card requires this to be provable rather than configured, and the honest proof needs three parts, because each alone is weak: the start-up options (which a later edit could change), the per-view answer (which is only as good as the list), and the list being complete (which nothing but a test can keep true). A test walks the app's routes and fails naming any view that is not classified — proved by adding an unclassified screen and watching it fail — and a second test tries to switch replay on for a store-data view and shows it stays off.
Judgement call worth knowing about: `/`, the public landing page, is classified as **store data**. It is the one public page that renders a shop's products — the preview card shows what was read from whichever address the visitor typed. That shop is a stranger's rather than a customer's, which is exactly why recording it would be worse rather than better.
The list is empty of enabled views and no card has asked for replay, so today this fences off something nobody has switched on. That is the point: the day someone asks for it on a marketing page, the store screens are already out of reach rather than needing to be remembered.
Nearest spec: main §14.7 privacy note — "Turn off PostHog session replay on any view that renders store data, or mask it." It does not say how "off" is held true over time.

## 2026-09-02 — T-ANALYTICS — Everything the vendor's browser library does by itself is switched off
Decision: the library starts with autocapture, page-view capture, page-leave capture, performance capture, rage-click detection and surveys all disabled, and creates a person record only for someone who has signed in. The only events that exist are the ten a screen can report.
Why: **autocapture is the setting that would defeat the property table.** Left on, the library records every click along with the text of whatever was clicked — and on a product list or a draft article, that text is the merchant's store. Every guard in the event definitions would be beside the point. Page views are off for a different reason: the funnel is already emitted server-side as the work happens (`preview_requested`, `signup_completed`, and the rest), so a browser-side copy would leave the funnel's numbers depending on which of the two you counted, which is the specific thing the card asks not to happen. Surveys and rage clicks are vendor features nobody asked for that put things on a merchant's screen we did not write.
Consequence for later cards: a screen needing a new event adds it to the property table. There is no autocapture safety net catching it in the meantime, deliberately.
Nearest spec: main §14.7 — the taxonomy is a closed list of named events; nothing in it is captured automatically.

## 2026-09-02 — T-ANALYTICS — Only the authenticated screens report from the browser; the public funnel is untouched
Decision: the reporting provider is mounted in the authenticated layout (`apps/web/app/(app)/layout.tsx`) and nowhere else. The landing page, the plan page and the sign-in page load no analytics library at all.
Why: `T9.2` already established that every step of the public funnel is recorded where the work happens, so there is nothing for a browser to add there. Mounting nothing is a stronger guarantee than mounting something configured not to duplicate — no library, no events, no possibility of a second copy of the funnel. It also keeps a vendor script off the page a stranger lands on.
Consequence: `useUiAnalytics()` on a public screen returns the do-nothing default, which is correct rather than broken. A card that later wants a genuinely browser-only public event mounts the provider there and classifies the view; `/` is already classified as store data, so it would arrive with replay already fenced off.
Nearest spec: main §14.7 (server-side capture); ui §11 (browser-only events). The two disagree, and `T9.1` recorded that; this decision is where the disagreement is resolved for the public half.

## 2026-09-02 — T-ANALYTICS — The browser's key is its own environment variable, even though it holds the same value as the server's
Decision: a new variable, `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY`, holds the analytics project's key for the page. `POSTHOG_API_KEY` — the same value, in practice — stays server-only.
Why: the project key is public by design; that is what makes reporting from a browser possible at all. But one variable read in both places means the day somebody puts a different kind of key in `POSTHOG_API_KEY`, it is written into every page with no code change and no test failing. Two variables cost one line in `.env.example` and make "this one goes to the browser" a property of the name.
Nearest spec: none. tech §2 covers deployment configuration and names no variables.

## 2026-09-02 — T-ANALYTICS — The mock-fixture fields these screens now depend on
Decision: registered in `packages/ui/src/fixtures/screen-contract.ts` — `GET /api/account` must carry `accountId` and `domain.normalized`.
Why: the account id is who the analytics vendor is told is using the product and the normalised domain is the group every cost and usage question is asked by; they are the same two the server-side events already carry, so a click on a screen and a job on a queue land on one story rather than two. Both are already in the response schema and in the mock fixture; nothing new is asked of the backend. The shell's own view of the account (`ShellAccount`) gained them as **optional** fields, because nothing rendered needs either: an account response without them draws exactly the same screen and simply reports nothing.
The one requirement on whoever fills this in for real: `domain.normalized` must be the *claimed* domain and never a host a visitor typed into the preview, or a stranger's browsing would be attributed to a real store — the same rule the server-side attribution already enforces by having no field for it.

## 2026-09-02 — T3.4 — A store's own middle page is the yardstick, measured across pages rather than across searches
Decision: "the store median" that three of the four Search-Console signals compare against is the middle value of **what each page was shown for in the window, totalled across every search**, counted only over pages the store's own inventory holds and that Google showed at least once. Decay uses the same shape over clicks in its earlier window. A page's own total is what gets compared against that middle, not the slice of it belonging to the one search the signal is about.
Why: the specs use "store median" four times and never say the median of what. Two readings were available and they behave differently. Across page-and-search pairs it would be a much smaller number, so nearly every page would clear it and the floor would stop doing its job. Across pages is what §9.6.2 means where it does define the term — "median clicks/impressions across its rated **articles**" — and what §9.6.5 means by "impressions ≥ store median" for a refresh candidate, and it is a sentence a merchant could be told: half your pages are shown more often than this one. Comparing a page's total against a median of page totals also keeps both sides of the comparison the same kind of number, which the mixed reading would not. Pages the inventory does not hold are excluded from the middle rather than counted, because a page we cannot act on should not move the bar for the pages we can — and they are counted and returned instead of dropped, so a mismatch between the URL Google reports and the one the store gave us surfaces as a number rather than as signals quietly going missing.
Nearest spec: main §7.3 (striking distance, low CTR, decay rows), §9.6.2, §9.6.5 — none defines the population.

## 2026-09-02 — T3.4 — One piece of work per page, not one per phrasing
Decision: striking distance and low CTR produce at most one detection per page. Where several search intents on the same page clear the same test, the page keeps the intent it is shown for most often, and the number of others travels with it as evidence (`other_qualifying_clusters`).
Why: two forces point the same way. A collection can sit just off page one for a dozen wordings of one thing, and a merchant's list showing that as twelve items would bury everything else — it is one job, improve the collection. And the database only allows one: the open-opportunity index is unique on account, signal type and entity, so two detections on the same page could not both survive; whichever was written last would silently replace the other, in whatever order the rows happened to come out. Ties break on the head search's text so the same data always produces the same card. The cost is a fact rather than a guess: if a page is off page one for two genuinely different intents wanting different work, only the busier one is surfaced, and the count on the card says the other exists.
Nearest spec: main §7.3 ("Page × query-cluster"), §7.9 (dedupe on `(account_id, signal_type, entity_ref)`), main §13 `opportunities`.

## 2026-09-02 — T3.4 — Nothing stores whether a page was decaying last week, so the detector is handed that and reports what has not been confirmed yet
Decision: decay's "the decline must hold across two consecutive weekly runs" is implemented as an input — how many earlier consecutive weekly runs already found this page decaying — and the detector returns two lists: confirmed decays, and **provisional** ones seen for the first time. Provisional decays are not opportunities and the merchant never sees them.
Why: the rule is about history across runs and this card builds pure functions, so the count has to come from somewhere the card does not own. Nothing holds it today. Two homes are possible and both belong to `T3.7`, the card that runs the weekly scan: the count can live in the evidence of the open decay row, which needs no new column but means writing a row before the decline is confirmed; or it needs a small table of weekly observations, which is a migration and therefore a schema-wave card. **Neither is decided here.** What is decided is that the detector never guesses: with no history handed in, a decaying page comes back provisional and firing is impossible, which is the safe direction — a single bad month around a holiday, an outage or one of Google's experiments cannot reach the merchant. The consequence to accept: until `T3.7` supplies the history, content decay produces nothing at all.
Nearest spec: main §7.3 (decay row — "trend must hold across ≥ 2 consecutive weekly evaluations"), §7.5 (weekly scan), main §13 — no table holds this.

## 2026-09-02 — T3.4 — Cannibalization cannot validate today, because nothing writes what job a page is doing
Decision: the same-intent half of cannibalization's validation reads `store_pages.intent_class`. Where any competing page's intent class is unknown — which is every page in every store right now — the candidate is returned **unvalidated with the reason**, never as a finding and never dropped. Same for two pages whose intent classes differ.
Why: main §7.3 makes this validation mandatory ("Not treated as an error until validated: same intent class for both URLs *and* …"), and guessing it is the one thing this signal must not do: the work it leads to is consolidating pages, and consolidating a buying guide into a how-to because we assumed they were the same thing destroys something that was working. So unknown fails closed. **The consequence is that this P0 signal produces nothing on any real store until something populates that column.** `store_pages.intent_class` exists in the schema from wave 2 and no code writes it — `T3.2` built the inventory and left the column null by design, and no card in the plan claims it. `query_clusters.intent_class` is equally empty. Whoever picks this up should note that the intent class wanted here is the *page's*, not the search's, and the natural producers are the inventory sync (Lane C) or the persona/families work (Lane B). Flagged rather than fixed: classifying pages is a feature nobody asked this card for.
Nearest spec: main §7.3 (cannibalization row), §13 `store_pages.intent_class`; build plan T3.4 — requires the validation, names no producer for the input.

## 2026-09-02 — T3.4 — Worked example 5's fixture states the alternation and does not contain it; the test supplies it and the shared fixture is left alone
Decision: the acceptance fixture for example 5 spreads each URL's 28-day totals evenly across every day, so the leading URL never changes and the "alternate" the example describes is not in the data. The cannibalization test re-arranges the *same totals* into weeks so the leader does change, and asserts the re-arrangement against the fixture's own numbers before detecting anything. `packages/core/src/fixtures/scenarios.ts` is not changed.

The evidence the detector reports is still the example's — 3,000 / 2,400 / 1,800 impressions at positions 8.2 / 9.6 / 12.4 — because only the split across weeks moved. **For the integrator:** the fixture would be better with weekly variation in it, and adding it is a small change to `window28`; it belongs to whoever next owns that file, not to a lane building on top of it.

## 2026-09-02 — T3.4 — A page Search Console reports that the inventory does not hold produces nothing, and is counted
Decision: every detector filters to pages present in `store_pages`, and returns the addresses it had to skip. Trailing slashes and `#fragments` are normalised away before matching; query strings are not.
Why: an opportunity is a piece of work on a page, and a page we hold nothing about is one nobody can do the work on — the recommendation stages need its title, its body and its headings. But silently dropping is how the two spellings of a URL (what Google shows in a results page, what the storefront calls it) turn into a signal that stops being found with nothing to notice. Counting and returning them makes the mismatch a number the scan can log. Query strings are deliberately kept distinct because on a storefront they usually *are* a different page — a filtered collection, page two of a listing — and merging them would pool pages that rank separately.

## 2026-09-02 — T3.4 — Five more numbers into `packages/rules`, because §7.3 states them in words and the config had no key for them
Decision: `signals.config.yaml` gains five values, all marked UNSIGNED. Striking distance gets `impressions_store_median_multiple_min: 1` and content decay gets `baseline_clicks_store_median_multiple_min: 1` — the "impressions ≥ store median" and "baseline clicks ≥ store median" halves of their rules, which existed as English and as nothing else. Cannibalization gets the three numbers its validation half needs: `leader_changes_min: 1` (how many times the page Google leads with has to change across the window's weeks before that counts as the pages alternating), `baseline_offset_weeks: 12` (how far back the "before" comparison reaches) and `aggregate_loss_clicks_ratio_max: 1.0` (this window's clicks as a fraction of that earlier window, below which the search counts as having lost ground).
Why: invariant 9 says no threshold literal lives outside `packages/rules`, and a number the spec expresses as "≥ store median" is still a number — written in code as a bare comparison it would be a `1` nobody could find or change. Two of the five are the spec's own values restated (the median multiples, and the twelve weeks decay already uses). The other two had to be invented because the spec asks for a test and gives no size: "the leading URL flips week-over-week" does not say how many flips, and "aggregate performance loss vs. the 12-week baseline" does not say how much loss. **`aggregate_loss_clicks_ratio_max: 1.0` is deliberately a no-op bound** — at 1.0 any decline at all counts, which is the literal reading. It is set that way rather than at some invented figure so that the looseness is visible in the file and can be tightened in one edit instead of found in code. It matters less than it looks: it is one branch of an OR, behind a gate that already requires two of the store's own pages each holding a fifth of the same search within the top thirty.
Nearest spec: main §7.3 (striking distance, low CTR, decay and cannibalization rows), §7.10 (every number in §7.3 lives in the config layer).
