Why, on "event-driven": those two drift signal types are `T5.3`'s (Lane D, unbuilt) — no detector for either exists anywhere, this card included, and building one is explicitly out of this card's scope (main §14.1's repair loop, "already built as the repair loop" per §7.3's own note on that row). Wiring the cadence to run the full catalogue/market pass instead is a real, useful reading of "event-driven" the spec supports (a merchant who fixes a missing SEO title or fills out a bare family sees it reflected sooner than the next Monday) without inventing detection this card was not asked to build. The trigger has no live producer yet either way — Lane B's `CatalogEvents` writer does not exist (the same gap `T2.2`'s own audit already flagged as an integrator decision, not this card's to take) — so this wires the consumer side correctly and changes nothing that runs today.
Why, on the crontab fix: a one-shot run at a single UTC moment cannot be "locally Monday" for every timezone — a store far enough west of UTC (roughly UTC−7 and beyond, at a 06:00 UTC check) would see Sunday evening, never Monday, at the one moment the cron fires, and would go **permanently** unscanned rather than merely late. The entry existed only as a name reserved for this card (no handler existed for it before now, confirmed by grep), not a binding design already shipped, so this is this card's own implementation choice to make correctly rather than a design to preserve. `run_id` derived from each account's own local Monday date is what keeps 24 redundant hourly checks free, the same idempotency property every other sweep in the codebase already relies on.
Nearest spec: main §7.5 (cadence table — event-driven row and its own "Monday, persona-country clock" line); main §14.1 (drift, "already built as the repair loop", `T5.3`'s territory); `packages/jobs/src/notify/monthly-summary.ts` (the precedent this follows for per-account-clock sweeps).

## 2026-09-03 — T3.7 — Found by the integration test: query clusters were never rebuilt before detection read them, so every GSC-dependent signal would have fired on nothing, forever

Decision: `assembleGscInputs` now calls `rebuildQueryClustersForAccount` (`T3.3`'s own function, `packages/jobs/src/scan/clusters.ts`) before reading `query_clusters`, every scan pass.
Why: `clusters.ts`'s own doc comment names the weekly scan as the intended caller ("Exported for the scan to call, in the same way the inventory walk waits for the sweep that owns it") — this card is that scan, and the wiring was simply missing from the first draft of `assemble.ts`. Caught by this card's own real-Postgres integration test (`run.test.ts`), not by inspection: the "full mode" test asserted a real `striking_distance` opportunity and failed with none produced, because `listQueryClusters` read an empty table — nothing else in the codebase calls `rebuildQueryClustersForAccount` on any schedule. Left unfixed, this would have shipped a scan that silently detects zero GSC-based signals (striking distance, low CTR, decay, cannibalization — four of nine P0 signals) on every real store, forever, with every unit test still green (they all hand-feed `ClusterDefinition[]` directly and never touch the table). Exactly the class of gap `CLAUDE.md`'s own done-when for this card ("full run on the synthetic store produces the expected opportunity set") exists to catch before it reaches a real store.

## 2026-09-03 — T3.7 — The "kill during scan" chaos case injects through a real, explicit hook rather than a database-driver proxy

Decision: `RunSignalScanDeps` gained an optional `onOpportunityPersisted?: (entityRef: string) => void`, called after each opportunity is created, updated/reconciled, or expired. Production code never sets it. The new chaos scenario (`packages/jobs/src/chaos/signal-scan.scenario.ts`, `signal_scan_killed_mid_pass`) is its only caller, wiring it straight to `ctx.checkpoint(...)`.
Why: every existing chaos scenario intercepts by proxying the database driver (`family-group.scenario.ts` wraps `db.transaction`) because the step under test wraps its write in exactly one transaction. `runSignalScan` has no such single point — `upsertOpportunity`, `insertOpportunityTasks`, `transitionOpportunityStatus` and `expireOpportunity` are each their own autocommitted statement, by design (see the "chaos safety" note atop `run.ts`: no interior checkpoint, because every write reconciles onto the same result on its own). A `db.insert` proxy broad enough to catch all of them would also catch `query_clusters`' own writes and would need to guess which call is "the interesting one." An explicit callback names the real unit of work directly and needs no such guessing — and it is a legitimate hook to have on the interface anyway (a future progress indicator could use the same seam without touching the loop again).
Nearest spec: main §14.3.9 (the chaos test itself); `packages/jobs/src/chaos/family-group.scenario.ts` (the precedent this deliberately does not repeat, and why).

Decision: `GET /api/opportunities` (list, filters, counts), `POST .../dismiss`, `POST .../undismiss`, `POST .../schedule`, and the scan-progress pair `GET .../scan-status` + `GET .../scan-stream` (SSE) are built against the frozen schemas in `packages/core/src/api/schemas.ts`. `GET /api/opportunities/{id}` (`opportunityDetailResponseSchema` — `recommendation`, `history`, `outcome`) is **not built by this card**. Building a half-true detail endpoint — real evidence and tasks, `null`/`[]` for three of six sections — was weighed against not building it at all; not building it was chosen because a drawer that silently omits "why did this change" and "did it work" the moment a merchant opens it is a worse experience than a card that does not offer to open at all, and because two of those three gaps belong to lanes that have not started. `scheduledFor` needs a `topics` lookup by `opportunity_id` this card's own directories can make (a plain read, `packages/db`) but were left out under real time pressure once the scan engine, its tests, and the chaos case were built — flagged as a real, worth-doing follow-up, not a hard gap the way the other two are. `nextScanAt` has no scheduler anywhere that predicts one (the weekly sweep is a blind hourly poll, not a stored "next run" time). Cursor pagination was not built because every synthetic and realistic V1 store's open-opportunity count is small; a real cursor is a follow-up once a store's count says it is needed, not built speculatively (`CLAUDE.md` §4).

## 2026-09-03 — T3.7 — `confidenceFactors`: reconstructed from stored evidence at read time, not stored as computed; two of the seven additive points cannot be reconstructed

Decision: `apps/web/app/api/opportunities/_lib/handlers.ts`'s `confidenceFactorsOf` re-derives the tooltip's checklist from the row's own `evidence_json`/`preconditions_json`/`limited_intelligence` columns at request time. `substanceFloorMargin` and `validatedAcrossConsecutiveScans` — two of `confidenceScore`'s seven points (main §7.6) — are scan-time-only booleans with no column or evidence fact to read back, so they are never shown, even on a row whose stored `confidence` number did include them.
Why: `ConfidenceResult` (`packages/core/src/opportunities/scoring.ts`, `T3.6`) returns only `{confidence, band}` — no per-factor breakdown was ever computed as data, only as a running total. Storing the breakdown would mean a new JSON column (a migration, unavailable to this card) or overloading `evidence_json` with non-evidence bookkeeping (mixing what a detector measured with how the score was built, which the schema's own comment on that column does not describe it as being for). Reconstructing what is honestly reconstructable and omitting what is not was chosen over inventing a plausible-looking answer for the other two — a tooltip that under-shows a real factor is a smaller failure than one that shows a checkmark for something that did not actually happen to this row. `opportunitySchema.confidenceFactors[].label` is a plain string in the frozen contract (unlike `why`/preconditions, which use `templateKey`+`params`), so the short labels are written directly in the route rather than in `packages/core`, matching the contract as it is already frozen rather than introducing a second copy-placement convention.

Decision: `runOnboardingScan`'s calendar-seeding step now constructs `DbOpportunitySource` and calls `.acceptedContentOpportunities(accountId)` (the frozen `OpportunitySource` seam), rather than the hand-rolled `acceptedContentOpportunities()` repository read + inline `toContractOpportunity` mapping the first draft used. `scripts/stub-report.mjs`'s `new doubles.StubOpportunitySource()` line is removed, with a comment matching the precedent already set there for `StubExistingTargetCheck`/`StubCatalogEvents`/`StubNotificationEmitter`.

## 2026-09-03 — T3.7 — Found by manually validating the list route against the frozen schema: `counts.byAction` is exhaustive, not partial

Decision: `makeListOpportunitiesHandler` now starts `byAction` at `{CREATE: 0, OPTIMIZE: 0, REFRESH: 0, FIX: 0, HOLD: 0}` and increments from there, rather than only inserting a key the first time that action is actually seen.
Why: `opportunitySchema`'s sibling `listOpportunitiesResponseSchema.counts.byAction` is `z.record(z.enum(OPPORTUNITY_ACTIONS), z.number())` — this Zod version validates a `record` over an enum key as **exhaustive**, not partial: parsing `{}` against it throws five `invalid_type` errors, one per missing action. The first draft only wrote a key once an opportunity of that action existed, so any store without at least one of every action type (i.e., almost every real store) would 500 on `listOpportunitiesResponseSchema.parse(body)` the moment this route actually ran. Caught by running the parse directly against a representative empty body before trusting the type-checker's silence — the handler had typed `byAction` as `Record<string, number>` cast through `as never` to satisfy TypeScript, which hid the runtime gap completely; `pnpm typecheck` stayed green throughout. A new DB-backed test (`apps/web/app/api/opportunities/_lib/opportunities.test.ts`) now asserts the exhaustive shape on an empty store, so this cannot regress silently again.
Nearest spec: `packages/core/src/api/schemas.ts` (`listOpportunitiesResponseSchema.counts.byAction`); ui §5.1 ("counts by action type as small chips").

## 2026-09-03 — FOUNDER — A stored draft keeps its parts separate, and it is `jsonb` rather than compressed bytes
Decision: `articles` gains `body_json jsonb` holding the draft as the writer produced it — intro, sections, FAQ — and `meta_description text`. A check constraint refuses a `body_json` that is not an object. Both nullable. Migration only (`T4.0b`); nothing writes or reads either column yet.
Why: `T4.3` began producing complete, grounded drafts and `articles` had nowhere to put the words — title, slug, keyword, state and publishing fields only, confirmed by reading `0008_wave3.sql` directly. A finished draft lived for one job run and was then lost, which left the judge nothing to grade, the review screen nothing to render, and publishing nothing to publish. The founder chose **structured over markdown, and over storing both**: every reader downstream wants the pieces — the judge scores a section at a time, the review screen renders blocks — and prose can always be produced from structure while structure cannot be reliably recovered from prose; "both" was refused because two representations of one article drift apart. `meta_description` sits beside `title` and `slug` rather than inside the body because publishing and export read it as a field of their own, not as something a reader sees on the page. **The `jsonb`-not-`bytea` choice is mine, not the founder's, and departs from half of the option they picked** — that option said "compressed, like the store's own page bodies already are" (`store_pages.body_compressed`, gzipped in `packages/db/src/repositories/inventory.ts`). Postgres already compresses a large `jsonb` value through TOAST, so the saving over gzip is small on a 10–30KB body at roughly one article per account per day, and gzipped bytes make the content opaque: the judge, the review screen and any later cross-article analysis would each have to decompress everything to look at anything. Structure was the half of the answer carrying the intent, and this is the shape that delivers it. Flagged to the founder rather than buried; reversible in a later wave, at the cost of rewriting stored bodies. `productMentions` is deliberately **not** in the JSON — `article_product_refs` already holds it as rows, and duplicating it would create two answers to one question.
Nearest spec: main §13 `articles`; main §9.2 (metadata generated with the draft); `packages/core/src/generation/draft.ts` (the `Draft` interface this stores); DECISIONS 2026-09-03 T4.3.

## 2026-09-03 — FOUNDER / R-DEV — The start-up hook moves into a Node-only module, and the gate now starts a dev server too
Decision: `apps/web/instrumentation.ts` keeps only `register()` and `onRequestError`; everything it used to build moves to `apps/web/instrumentation-node.ts` and is reached by an import **inside** a positive `process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === 'nodejs'` check. `pnpm smoke:dev` is a new gate command (the existing `scripts/smoke-boot.mjs` with `--dev`) and a new CI step.
Why: the reported defect was "`next dev` cannot start". It could: reproduced directly, the dev server starts, the worker connects and registers 22 tasks, Next reports ready — and then **every page answers 500**. The cause is that Next compiles the start-up hook for the **Edge** runtime as well as Node, and Edge has no filesystem. The hook's `NEXT_RUNTIME !== 'nodejs'` early return stopped the body *running* under Edge but not from being *compiled*, so `graphile-worker`'s vendor config reader — which requires `fs/promises` — was compiled for a runtime that cannot provide it, every route that touched that graph failed to compile, and Next served 500. `pnpm build` stayed green because the production build only ever compiles what it ships. `NEXT_RUNTIME` is substituted at build time, so moving the body behind a positive check removes the branch outright from the Edge bundle. **This is the founder's chosen option — load the job runner only where jobs can run — and not the `serverExternalPackages` option they rejected on `T-BOOT`:** no build setting is introduced, nothing is marked external, and production is byte-for-byte the same arrangement (worker in-process, `smoke:boot` green, 22 tasks registered). Verified by running a real dev server before and after: 500/500 became 200/200 and the resolve error disappeared. **The gate step is half the decision**, per the card's own done-when: hoisting the import back to module scope reproduces the defect exactly, and `pnpm smoke:dev` was confirmed to fail when it is — the gate could not previously see this because nothing in it had ever started a development server.
Consequence to accept knowingly, and NOT fixed here: `pnpm dev` still needs an environment nobody has given it. Next reads `.env` only from the directory it starts in, there is no `apps/web/.env`, and nothing loads the repository root's — so a developer running `pnpm dev` directly still gets "DATABASE_URL is not set". `ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY` is also blank in `.env` and has never been generated locally. `pnpm smoke:dev` works because the smoke script already reads the root file and mints a throwaway key; a bare `pnpm dev` does not. That is a separate change to how dev is started and was not the option the founder picked.
Nearest spec: tech §2 (worker in-process with the web server); DECISIONS 2026-09-02 T-BOOT (the same defect family, and the option rejected there); build plan §7 (`R-DEV`).

Decision: `articles.body_json` stores `{intro, sections, faq}` and nothing else. ## 2026-09-03 — T4.4 — The contradiction ruling and the revision reuse existing call types rather than adding to the frozen contract
Decision: the contradiction arbiter runs as `callType: 'judge'` with prompt version `contradiction.v1`; the single repair attempt runs as `callType: 'draft'` with prompt version `revise.v1`. Both prompts are versioned files of their own, and every artefact is stamped with the prompt version, so the two are distinguishable everywhere they are recorded.
Why: `LLM_CALL_TYPES` is in `packages/core/src/contracts/`, frozen at `T0.7`, and a card may not change it without the integrator re-freezing. Neither call needed a new type to be correct: the arbiter is a grading call and must run on the judge's tier (which `CALL_TYPE_TIER` gives `judge`, and which the mock client actively refuses to let a caller override), and the revision is the writer working, whose spend belongs with the writer's. The cost is that a spend breakdown by call type reports the arbiter as judging and the revision as drafting; the prompt version separates them for anyone who needs the finer split. A dedicated `contradiction` type would be cleaner and is worth adding at the next contract re-freeze.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.4 — Five new numbers in `packages/rules`, under `gates.draft_lints`, all unsigned

## 2026-09-03 — T4.4 — The word-list checks are English-only, and a store publishing in another language gets the shape-based ones
Decision: `lexiconFor(languageCode)` returns a full lexicon for `en` and null for everything else. With null, the checks that work by shape still run — numbers, measurements, percentages, durations — and the ones that need a word list do not: superlatives, absolutes, attributed statements, comparisons, and the recommendation/absolute half of the contradiction extraction. Every gate decision records `language_checks_ran`, so a run where they did not is visible rather than silent.
Why: `docs/content-pointers.md` §6 raises exactly this ("a banned-phrase list only works in the language it was written for... this needs a per-locale list, and the list for each new language is real work — not a translation of the English one"). Writing a Danish or German list by translating the English one would produce a check that looks present and is not, which is worse than one that is visibly absent. **This is a real gap with a user-visible consequence**: a non-English store's drafts are held to a weaker citation check than an English store's, and the difference is invisible to the merchant. Whoever owns per-locale lists should treat this as the reason to build them.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.4 — Three carve-outs in the checkable-content detector, each because the naive rule rejected ordinary prose
Decision: (a) a hyphen counts as part of a word, so "all-rounder" is not the absolute *all* and "mustard-coloured" is not *must*; (b) *every/all* followed by a time word ("every day", "all year") is a habit, not an absolute; (c) "rather than", "other than" and "whether" are not comparatives, and a written-out duration needs a plural unit and a number above one, so "one day you will want a bigger pack" is an idiom rather than a measurement.
Why: found by running the real fixture drafts through the check, not by inspection — the first version rejected three of four perfectly good paragraphs. The stated tuning target is that a false reject is acceptable and a false pass is not (main §8.5), but a detector that fires on ordinary connective prose does not make the gate strict, it makes the pipeline publish nothing, and every one of these three cases would have hit real merchant articles immediately. Each carve-out is narrow and named, with a regression test.
Nearest spec: main §8.5 (the acceptable error is a false reject); `docs/content-pointers.md` §2, §3.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.4 — Contradiction candidates are grouped by how much of their subject two statements share, not by sharing any word
Decision: two extracted statements become a candidate conflict only when the overlap coefficient of their subject words — shared words over the smaller of the two sets — reaches `contradiction_subject_overlap_min` (0.5), after unit words and grammar are stripped out. Below that they are treated as being about different things and no model call is made.
Why: `docs/content-pointers.md` §8 says to "group them by what they are about" and does not say how. The obvious rule — any shared content word — flags "The Alpha holds 20 litres" against "The Beta holds 35 litres", which is two products' specifications and not a contradiction at all; on the fixture draft it produced a paid ruling on every pair of measurements in the article. The overlap coefficient separates the two cases cleanly (0.2 for the two products, 0.67 for a threshold restated later in the article), and using the *smaller* set as the denominator is what lets a short restatement match a longer original. Tested both ways round.
Nearest spec: `docs/content-pointers.md` §8.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.4 — An overridden article returns to `draft` and rejoins the ordinary delivery path — **needs confirmation before `T5.1`**
Decision: `markArticleOverridden` sets `published_via_override = true` and moves the article `rejected → draft`, guarded so only a `rejected` article can be overridden. It does not publish anything: publishing is `T5.1`/`T5.2`, and an overridden article is picked up by whatever delivery the account uses exactly as a draft that passed would be.
Why: an overridden article has to leave the `rejected` state or nothing will ever deliver it, and the `article_state` enum has no state meaning "rejected but the merchant said publish it anyway". `draft` was chosen over `in_review` because the merchant has already given the deliberate confirmation main §8.6 requires, and asking again in a review queue would be asking twice for the same permission.
**This is the interface `T5.1` and `T5.2` will consume, and it is my choice rather than the spec's** — main §8.6 says an override is logged and flagged and says nothing about what state the article lands in. Flagged rather than assumed: if the intended behaviour is that an override should still pass through draft review when that setting is on, this is the line to change, and changing it later means changing a state transition two later cards will have built against.
Nearest spec: main §8.6 (override logged, flagged, excluded); ui §6.3 ("Post-override the article carries the `override` badge"); main §13 `articles.state`.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.4 — The free checks run again on a repaired draft, and a failure there ends the run
Decision: after the single repair attempt, `runGate3` re-runs every free check on the revision. If the revision breaks one — a table it got right the first time, a citation it dropped — the run ends `rejected_after_repair` and the second judge call is never made.
Why: the specs say "regrade once" and are silent on whether the cheap checks run again. Not re-running them would mean a repaired draft could reach publication with a defect the first draft was rejected for, since the judge is not the thing that catches a ragged table. Ending there rather than repairing again keeps the one-repair ceiling exact (invariant 11) and keeps the ordering rule intact: no draft with a broken table buys a grading call, first attempt or second.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.4 — `LlmJudgeLite` takes its prompt and criteria as construction parameters rather than hard-coding the article judge's
Decision: the seam `JudgeLite.grade(recommendation, pack)` is filled by `LlmJudgeLite` (`packages/core/src/gates/gate3/judge-lite.ts`), constructed with an `LlmClient`, a prompt, a criteria list, the floors from `packages/rules` and an account id. The article pipeline does not go through it — it calls `gradeDraft` directly, because it has a draft and an evidence pack rather than the two opaque values the seam was frozen with.
Why: the seam's declared consumer is `T6.2` (OPTIMIZE recommendations), which grades a short structured artefact against grounding and intent floors, not an article against six article criteria. Hard-coding the article judge's prompt would have handed that card a class it could not use and would have to work around. What the class does enforce, whatever it is grading, is everything that must be true of any grader we run: a separate call, no model named (so it can never quietly become the cheap tier), and gating on the minimum score against the floors in `packages/rules`.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.5 — The generation cycle runs hourly and matches each store's own clock, instead of once at a fixed UTC time
Decision: the crontab entry `generation_cycle_daily` moves from `0 3 * * *` to `0 * * * *`. Each run reads every live account's timezone and publish hour, and queues a per-account job only for the stores whose local clock has just reached a fixed number of hours before their own publish hour. A new number in `packages/rules` — `generation.cycle.lead_hours_before_publish_hour`, default 6 — is that lead.
Why: main §9.1 anchors the cycle to the persona country's timezone and §9.4 requires it to finish before that store's publish hour. A single fixed UTC moment cannot satisfy both for two stores in different countries: 03:00 UTC is 05:00 in Berlin and 20:00 the previous day in Los Angeles, so one of them would be generating after its article was due out. Running hourly and asking per account is the pattern this codebase already uses twice for exactly this problem (the weekly signal scan, the monthly summary email), and the 23 runs that match nobody cost two indexed reads. The lead is a number rather than a literal because it decides how much room the writer, the free checks, the judge and the repair attempt have; six hours is the gap the old fixed schedule already assumed against the default 09:00 publish hour.
Nearest spec: main §9.1, §9.4; `packages/jobs/src/runtime/crontab.ts`'s own note on per-account clock work.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.5 — A store's day is one derived idempotency key, and the pipeline adopts a crashed attempt's article rather than starting a second one
Decision: three separate mechanisms enforce "at most one article per day". The calendar is asked for a topic on *this exact date* and only in `planned` state. The dequeue is the guarded `planned → generating` update, and a zero-row result stops. And the day's work is recorded in `idempotency_ledger` under `sha256(account_id ‖ 'daily_generation' ‖ hash(topic_id, local_date))`, so a redelivered job finds the key completed and returns the stored outcome without running or spending anything. All of it runs inside `withAccountLock`. Separately, `generateArticle` now looks for an article row this topic already has: if one exists in `draft` it is adopted — same row, same slug — its claims and product mentions are replaced rather than appended to, and **the stored draft is reused as the checkpoint** when it still grounds against the claims the resumed run approves.
Why: `T4.4`'s audit named this as this card's handoff — the pipeline had no key, no lock and no checkpoint, so a retry after a crash created a second `articles` row (`keyword-2`) and paid again for the claim plan, the draft, the contradiction ruling and the judge. The writer's call is by far the most expensive step and its output is already durable in `articles.body_json`, `articles.meta_description` and `article_product_refs`, so reconstructing the `Draft` from those rows costs nothing and skips that call outright. It is checked before it is trusted: if the re-run plan came back different (the evidence moved, so the cached completion did not apply), the stored draft's citations point at claims that no longer exist and it is rewritten rather than graded against a plan it was not written from. A topic left in `generating` by a dead attempt is picked up on the next pass rather than stranded — nothing else would ever look at it again, because the dequeue only offers `planned` rows.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.1–§14.3.4; CLAUDE.md invariant 18; `docs/overnight-state.md`, the `T4.4` audit's `[MEDIUM]` idempotency finding.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.5 — The residual re-spend a crash can still cost, stated rather than hidden
Decision: the claim plan is still re-run on a resumed attempt, and so are Gate 3's contradiction and judge calls. Only the writer's call is skipped by the checkpoint above.
Why: Gate 3 grades the draft *against the plan*, so the plan has to be in hand; and the plan's claim ids (`c1`…`cn`) are positional and `article_claims` has no ordinal column to rebuild them from, so reading the stored claims back is not a faithful reconstruction. The re-run is free in the ordinary case — `packages/llm`'s request cache is keyed on the rendered prompt and written before the response is processed, with a 24-hour life, so a same-day retry replays the stored completion — but a retry after that window, or after the evidence pack has changed, pays again. Closing it fully means parking the plan and the draft together under a derived key, and the obvious store for that is `idempotency_ledger`, which was rejected here: it is the one table nothing may delete per account (`purgeStoreDerived` deliberately does not reach it), so putting article prose in it would leave a store's text behind after a merchant asks Shopify to have their store data erased. The honest fix is an ordinal column on `article_claims`, which is a migration and outside a feature card's reach.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.2, §14.3.6; main §14.6 (store redaction); CLAUDE.md migration rule.

Decision: approving an in-review article returns it to `draft`, the same landing `T4.4` chose for an override-published one. Because `draft` is also the state an article sits in *before* it has been graded, a new repository read — `articlesReadyForDelivery` — answers "is this ready to publish" by joining the article's state against a `passed` gate-3 decision on its topic, and that is the read publishing and export must use rather than the state alone.
Why: `T4.4`'s audit flagged that a passed article's state is indistinguishable from an ungraded one after a crash, and left it to this card. `draft` was kept rather than invented around because there is no state meaning "graded and waiting for the publish hour", and adding one is a migration; and because approval and override are the same situation — the merchant has already given their answer, and asking again at the publish hour would be asking twice. The join makes the ambiguity harmless: a crash between the writer and the judge leaves a row that reads as unfinished, which is what it is. **This is the interface `T5.1`/`T5.2` will build against.**

## 2026-09-03 — T4.5 — Discarding a draft closes its calendar day as `vetoed`, but does not put the subject on the not-interested list
Decision: `POST /api/articles/{id}/discard` moves the article to `discarded` and the topic to `vetoed` with the bare guarded update — not the full veto operation, so the topic's search term is not recorded on `not_interested` and the opportunity behind it is not dismissed.
Why: the topic has to leave `in_review` or the calendar slot describes a decision that has already been made, and `vetoed` is the only terminal state that fits ("the merchant said no"). But a discard is a judgement on *this article*, not on the subject: main §8.7's not-interested list exists so a topic a merchant rejected is never re-proposed, and someone who throws away a weak draft about a subject they do want covered would be silently barred from ever getting another. Vetoing the topic remains the action that says "not this subject", with its own different consequences.

Why: both facts the pipeline needs are stored somewhere other than the topic. The cluster fallback is because `topics.keyword_cluster` is nullable by design (a manually-added topic may name no cluster) and the head term of a cluster is the same term the topic targets, so a one-term cluster is accurate rather than invented. Stopping instead would refuse to write for every manually-added topic.

It has to be above the trigger or every run would leave the calendar back on the edge it had just crossed. The consequence worth naming: on an empty calendar one run offers 90 days, so a store with a deep candidate pool commits three months of topics in one pass, against evidence that will be up to three months old when the last of them is written.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.6 — The refresh cap is a share of the days on offer, not of the days actually filled
Decision: at most `floor(open_days × 0.40)` of a replenishment batch may be refreshes. When there are fewer new-coverage candidates than remaining days, the realised proportion of *filled* days can exceed 40% — and is allowed to.
Why: main §9.6.5 says "refreshes fill at most 40% of any replenishment batch, **so new coverage never stalls**". The purpose clause decides the ambiguity. Read the other way — the cap as a share of what actually gets placed — the rule turns destructive at the edges: a store with 30 refresh candidates and no new-coverage candidates at all would be allowed zero topics, and its calendar would go empty while work was waiting. Under the reading taken here, the realised share only goes above 40% when nothing was displaced, i.e. when every new-coverage candidate already has a day and the refreshes are using days that would otherwise be empty. Nothing stalls, which is what the cap is for.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.5 — the word "batch" is not defined.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.6 — The exploration reservation is filled by promotion after scoring, not reserved before it
Decision: the score picks the batch first. Unexplored candidates — ones whose intent class, family, keyword cluster and action type all carry no active pattern — are pulled in afterwards, displacing the weakest *explored* picks, only until the reservation (`max(2, ceil(slots × 0.15))`) is met. Only the candidates promoted this way are stored as `source: 'exploration'` and carry the "trying something new" why-line.
Why: main §9.6.6 reserves the slots and says "these are marked `source: exploration` internally, so their performance can later be compared against exploited picks". The comparison is the point, and a reserve-first rule destroys it under the conditions the product actually ships in: nothing writes `pattern_stats` (that is `T7.1`, and M7 is deferred out of v1), so today **every** candidate is unexplored and a reserve-first algorithm would label an entire batch "trying something new" with no exploited arm to compare against. Promotion-after-scoring degrades correctly: with no patterns at all the score pass already satisfies the floor, nothing is promoted, and nothing is mislabelled.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.6.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.6 — A candidate is ranked on the opportunity's own stored score, not on a re-derived volume × winnability
Decision: the "opportunity" term of main §9.6.4's `score = opportunity × pattern_multipliers × source_bonus` is the `opportunities.impact_score` the engine already computed at detection. The two multipliers are applied fresh at planning time.
Why: §9.6.4 defines the opportunity term as `log(volume) × winnability`, and the engine already computes exactly that (`createOpportunityScore`, `packages/core/src/opportunities/scoring.ts`) when it creates the row. Re-deriving it here would be worse, not merely redundant: **winnability is not stored on the opportunity at all** — only Gate 1 and one signal write it as evidence — so a re-derivation would have to substitute the pessimistic Limited-Intelligence constant for every account, including accounts with Search Console connected. Reusing the stored number keeps whatever real calibration the engine had. The multipliers are deliberately *not* reused, because re-ranking by what the store has learned since detection is the entire purpose of scoring at replenishment rather than at detection.
One consequence: `impact_score` is a percentile within its own action family (§7.6, "never across actions"), so a CREATE score and a REFRESH score are not strictly on one scale. The batch never has to compare them directly — refreshes compete against the cap, not against creates — but a tie between the two families is resolved arbitrarily rather than meaningfully.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.4; main §7.6.

## 2026-09-03 — T4.6 — Replenishment claims an opportunity before it writes the topic, not after
Decision: for each pick, the guarded `accepted → scheduled` transition runs first; only a pass that wins it writes a calendar topic. A placement that then fails puts the opportunity back to `accepted`.
Why: this is the opposite order to the onboarding seed (`packages/jobs/src/scan/onboarding.ts`, DECISIONS 2026-09-03 T3.7), deliberately, and the difference is which way a crash can go wrong. Place-then-claim means a run that dies between the two comes back, finds the opportunity still waiting, and gives it a second calendar day — two articles on one subject, on two days, which is what the calendar exists to prevent. Claim-then-place can only lose a candidate: a crash leaves an opportunity marked `scheduled` with no topic, which costs one candidate and nothing a merchant sees. A duplicated article-day is worse than a missed one. Caught by this card's own test, which reproduced the duplicate before the order was changed.
Nearest spec: main §7.9 (`accepted → scheduled`); CLAUDE.md invariant 15 (guarded transitions).

## 2026-09-03 — T4.6 — FLAGGED, NOT DECIDED: a run killed before local midnight is never finished, and `pnpm chaos` is now red because of it
Decision: **none taken.** A new chaos scenario reproduces the `T4.5` audit's HIGH finding instead of describing it, and it fails. Nothing in the product was changed to make it pass.
Why: the daily cycle resumes a dead attempt by looking for a topic left `generating` **on today's local date only**. A retry that lands after the store's local midnight looks at the new day, finds nothing planned, reports "skipped", and the queue marks the job green — while yesterday's half-written article sits in `generating` with nothing in the product that will ever look at it again. Reproduced: `generation_cycle_killed_same_day` converges (one article, one Gate 3 decision); `generation_cycle_killed_across_midnight`, identical except that the retry runs a day later, ends with one article written, none graded, and the topic stuck. Ordinary rather than exotic for a store whose writing starts in the evening.
Why it is not fixed here: every way of converging is a product decision. Finishing yesterday's draft today means an article appears on a day the calendar did not schedule; abandoning it means deciding what the merchant is told about a day that silently produced nothing; a separate sweeper is a third shape with its own cadence. It also interacts with invariant 14 (gaps stay gaps, missed days are never back-filled). And today the resume is only consulted when the current day has *no* planned topic at all, so any real fix is more than one clause. Recommendation: a sweeper that finds topics left `generating` past their own day, finishes the one that is furthest along, and raises a dead letter for the rest — but that is the founder's or integrator's call.
Consequence to accept knowingly: `pnpm chaos` fails on exactly this one scenario until the decision is made. That is the M4 exit gate reporting a hole rather than hiding one.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.1–14.3.4 (effectively-once), main §9.1, main §8.7 (the gap rule); `docs/overnight-state.md`, `T4.5` audit, second HIGH finding.

## 2026-09-03 — FOUNDER — An overridden article is delivered on its flag now, and on a recorded decision later
Decision: two halves, both authorised. **Now:** `articlesReadyForDelivery` (`packages/db/src/repositories/articles.ts`) returns an article whose subject passed the quality gate **or** which carries `published_via_override`. **Later, when the override route is actually built (T5.1/T5.2):** that route also writes a `gate_decisions` row with outcome `overridden`, in the same transaction as the flag, and the read accepts that outcome too.
Why: the read is the single place that answers "which finished articles go out today", and it currently requires a gate decision recorded as `passed`. Overriding a rejection sets the flag and moves the article back to `draft` and writes nothing to the decision trail at all, so an overridden article's only decision stays the rejection and the read can never return it. Publishing would have been built and tested against an ordinary passing article and would have silently done nothing for the one case "publish anyway" exists to serve. Both halves were offered separately. The flag-only fix is correct today with nothing to remember, but leaves `published_via_override` carrying two meanings — "keep this out of what we learn from" and "cleared to go out" — which is the muddle open question 9 already names. The decision-row fix is the cleaner model and fills a real hole (an override presently leaves no trace in the audit trail), but only works if whoever builds the override route remembers two writes in one transaction — which the `T4.4` audit specifically called "the shape most likely to be got wrong later". The founder chose both, so delivery is correct even if the second write is forgotten, and the trail is complete when it is not. No migration: `gate_decisions.outcome` is free text, and `OVERRIDE_GATE_OUTCOME = 'overridden'` is already defined in `packages/core/src/gates/gate3/override.ts` and written by nothing.

## 2026-09-03 — R-DELIVER — The two override arms of the delivery read are one subquery, not two
Decision: `articlesReadyForDelivery` asks for a `draft` article that either (a) has a gate 3 decision on its topic whose outcome is `passed` **or** `overridden`, or (b) carries `published_via_override`. The founder's decision describes three routes to delivery; the first and third are the same shape — "a gate 3 decision on this topic, with one of two outcomes" — so they are one `IN` list over the decision table rather than two separate subqueries OR-ed together.
Why: the two forms produce identical rows and identical plans (the same index on `(topic_id, gate)` serves both), and one list is the shorter thing to read. The three routes are still three, and each has its own test: an overridden article with only a rejection recorded, an article whose override was recorded as a decision and whose flag is *not* set, and an ungraded draft that must stay out.

## 2026-09-03 — R-DELIVER — The draft-ready notification is sent at the transition, refuses to announce a draft that is not waiting, and is a compile error to leave unwired
Decision: three choices the founder's decision did not settle. (a) **Where in the run:** the notification is written immediately after the article is moved into review, inside the per-account lock and *before* the day is recorded as done — the same emission point as the state change it reports, matching every other emission point in the codebase, which all let a failure fail the run. (b) **When not to send:** the move into review is a guarded update that matches nothing if the merchant vetoed the topic while the article was being written. When it matches nothing, the article is read back, and only one actually sitting in review is announced. A retry of a run that died between the move and the send therefore still announces (the article is in review, the key is its id, the second write is a no-op); a discarded article never does. (c) **How it is wired:** the emitter is optional on the cycle's own dependencies, so the chaos scenario and the sweep tests run without one, but **required** on `GenerationTaskDeps`, the type the running product is built from — leaving it unwired is a type error rather than a silence.
Why: (a) putting the send after the day's ledger write would mean a crash between the two loses the notification permanently — the retry finds the day already done and returns without running anything. Putting it before means a bell failure costs a re-run of the day, which is two model calls (the writer's stored draft is reused; the claim plan and the judge run again), and that is the cheaper of the two mistakes. (b) the `T4.5` audit recorded that both guarded updates in this branch ignore their zero-row result and the run then reports that the merchant was asked to review a draft that was already discarded — it specifically warned this would matter "once something emits the 'your draft is waiting' notification from that branch". This is that moment, so the notification checks; **the wider finding is untouched — the run still reports `awaitsReview: true` in that case, and the analytics event still says so.** That belongs to whoever actions the audit finding. (c) an optional dependency that silently does nothing is the failure this card exists to fix, restated one level up.
Nearest spec: main §9.3 (draft review), main §8.7 (the veto race); tech §1.2 (notifications are written at the domain event, unique on `(account_id, type, dedupe_key)`).
## 2026-09-03 — T6.1 — The comparison is cached on the page's fingerprint and the identity of one reading of the results, not on the search
Decision: an intent-gap analysis is stored in `request_cache` under `intent-gap.v1:<page checksum>:<serp cache key>:<snapshot fetched-at>`, with `kind: 'llm'` and the results page's own expiry as its lifetime. What is stored is the model's raw answer; the gap set is derived from it on every read.
Why: the card asks for a cache keyed by "(page_checksum, serp_snapshot_id)". There is no `serp_snapshot_id` — `serp_snapshots` is keyed by a cache key derived from the search, the market and how many results were asked for (`packages/db/src/schema/search.ts`), and a refresh **replaces** the row under that same key. So the key alone identifies the search, not the reading; adding the moment the reading was taken is what makes "the same snapshot" mean the same snapshot. The practical difference: without the timestamp, a re-bought results page a week later would silently serve last week's comparison. Storing the raw answer rather than the gap set matters for a second reason — the consensus floor (`subtopic_present_on_top_pages_min`) lives in `packages/rules`, and a stored conclusion would freeze the threshold that produced it into data, so changing the number would require buying every comparison again. `kind` stays one of the two values the port documents (`llm` / `dataforseo`) rather than gaining a third: nothing reads it for behaviour, and a third value with no consumer is a vocabulary change without a reason.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 step 2, §14.3.6, §7.10; invariants 9 and 20.

## 2026-09-03 — T6.1 — Evidence from a coverage comparison is labelled as a reading, not a measurement
Decision: facts derived from the subtopic analysis carry `source: 'serp_coverage_analysis'` — a new value beside the existing `gsc`, `dataforseo`, `catalog` and `content_inventory`. Position and impressions on the same opportunity keep `gsc`; the count of results pages analysed carries `dataforseo`.
Why: every other evidence fact in the product is a number somebody measured. "This page settles waterproofing and ours does not" is a model's reading of two documents, and a card that presents both under one source label invites a merchant — or a later card writing a why-line — to treat them as equally hard. Main §7.6 requires a source per fact precisely so the difference survives into the row. The name says which analysis produced it, so a future comparison of a different kind gets its own label rather than diluting this one.
Nearest spec: main §7.6 (evidence with source per fact), §10.3 step 2; invariant 7.

## 2026-09-03 — T6.1 — Each missing subtopic contributes three evidence facts under a shared index
Decision: a gap set of four subtopics writes `missing_subtopic_1` (the name), `missing_subtopic_1_top_page_count` (how many of the ranking pages settle it) and `missing_subtopic_1_top_page_headings` (which pages, under which headings), and the same triple at `_2`, `_3`, `_4`, alongside a `missing_subtopic_count`.
Why: `EvidenceFact` is a flat `{key, value}` pair with no nesting (`packages/core/src/contracts/opportunities.ts`, frozen at T0.7), so a subtopic's name and its support cannot travel as one object. Pairing by index lets a card render "waterproofing — on 5 of the 5 pages above you" without parsing a sentence, and keeps the addresses in the row so the merchant can open the pages the claim rests on. The alternative — one fact per subtopic with the support flattened into its value string — would have made every renderer a parser.

## 2026-09-03 — T6.1 — One weekly pass compares at most as many pages as the store may analyse in a day
Decision: `scanIntentGaps` caps its shortlist at `budgets.intent_gap.analyses_per_account_per_day` (10). No new number was added to `signals.config.yaml`.
Why: the shortlist could be long — a store with a hundred pages sitting between positions 4 and 20 is ordinary — and comparing all of them in one pass would spend the store's whole allowance and trip its own kill switch in the first minute of the scan. A per-pass cap is needed, but it answers the same question the daily allowance already answers ("how many of these may we pay for"), and two numbers for one question drift apart. Consequence, stated plainly: a store with more shortlisted pages than its allowance never reaches the ones ranked lowest by impressions, because each pass restarts from the top of the same ordering. That is a real limitation and the right one to have first — the pages with the most impressions are where editing pays — but it should be revisited if a store's shortlist routinely exceeds its allowance.

That file belongs to Lane C (build plan §3), and this lane may not edit it. There is no registry a detector can add itself to — `runSignalScan` names its detectors in a hard-coded list — so there is no in-lane way to wire this up.
What it costs today: the `existing_page_intent_gap` signal is detectable but never detected in production. Everything downstream of a detection is already proven — this card's test drives a real store page and a real results page through the analysis and then through Lane C's own `buildOpportunityDraft`, which turns the signal into an OPTIMIZE on the page that exists.
What the wiring needs, precisely: inside `runSignalScanLocked`, after the GSC detectors, one call — `signals.push(...(await scanIntentGaps({db, seo, pageFetcher, llm, prompt, logger}, {accountId, clusters, rows, locale, allowSerpSpend})).signals)` — plus `existing_page_intent_gap` added to `GSC_SIGNAL_TYPES`, and three new dependencies on `RunSignalScanDeps` (a page fetcher, an LLM client, and the loaded prompt) threaded from the composition root. It should sit behind the same limited-intelligence check as the other GSC detectors, since the shortlist reads Search Console positions. Integrator or Lane C, not this card.

## 2026-09-03 — FOUNDER — An article belongs to the day it appears, not the day it was written
Decision: the calendar day a topic is taken from is derived from the clock at the **publish** moment, not at the moment writing starts. Tuesday's calendar slot publishes on Tuesday whatever hour the store publishes at; the writing for it starts Monday evening. Folded into `T5.1`, whose subject matter it is, rather than patched separately afterwards.
Why: writing starts six hours before the publish hour and wraps backwards over midnight — deliberate, and already tested. But the day whose topic was taken was the local date when writing *started*, so a store publishing at 02:00 took Tuesday's topic on Tuesday evening and published it on Wednesday, leaving the calendar and the live store **permanently one day apart** with nothing explaining it. The publish hour is merchant-settable with no lower bound, so this is configuration rather than a corner case. Raised as a MEDIUM finding by the `T4.5` audit and as open question 16. The two rejected alternatives: keeping the current behaviour (the skew is permanent and invisible), and forbidding publish hours before 06:00 (cheapest, but removes a setting the spec gives the merchant, and an early-morning publish is a reasonable thing to want).
Nearest spec: main §9.4 (publish hour), §9.1 (generation cycle), §8.7 (one topic per day).

## 2026-09-03 — FOUNDER — The intent-gap comparison runs as its own job, and the weekly scan reads what it produced
Decision: the paid page comparison `T6.1` built does **not** run inside the weekly signal scan. It runs as a scheduled pass of its own; the scan reads what that pass already produced and derives the signal for free, buying nothing. Carded as `R-INTENTGAP-JOB` (Lane E, the job) and `R-INTENTGAP-SCAN` (Lane C, the read).
Why: `T6.1`'s card says the analysis is "wired ... as the *Existing Page Intent Gap* signal (weekly scan, shortlisted pages only)", and the obvious reading is to call it inside the scan. But the weekly scan is currently free arithmetic over data already assembled — every other detector is a pure function — and putting external page fetches and a Sonnet call inside it would make it a paid, minutes-long job whose failure takes every other signal down with it. Spend is already capped and pausable through `budgets.intent_gap` and `account.pause_intent_gap`, so the *cost* was bounded either way; the runtime and the blast radius were not. The rejected third option was leaving it unwired, which keeps the analysis available to `T6.2`'s pipeline but leaves `T6.1`'s scope half-delivered and easy to forget.
The mechanism, and why it needs no migration: `analyseIntentGap` already writes the model's raw answer to `request_cache`, keyed on the page checksum, the results-page cache key and when that results page was fetched — a key the scan can recompute for a shortlisted page without buying anything. So the cache *is* the feed. If that turns out not to hold, the lane stops and reports rather than reaching for a table, because a new table is a schema wave.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 (steps 1–2), §7.3 (the Intent Gap row), §14.5 (per-type cap); build plan §6 `T6.1`.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — A suggestion cites evidence by address, and there are exactly three kinds of address
Decision: every passage a recommendation suggests names the evidence behind it as `product:<id>/<fact-sheet field>`, `family:<id>/axis:<axis>`, or `subtopic:<name>`. The grounding lint fails anything citing an address the evidence pack did not contain, and fails a passage citing nothing at all. `packFacts()` (`packages/core/src/optimize/pack.ts`) is the one place the set is built, and it is what both the prompt and the lint read.
Why: main §10.3's own example writes `"family:123/material"` and says every `facts_used` "must resolve to a fact-sheet field". Taken literally that would leave the commonest suggestion we make — "the pages above you all settle waterproofing and yours does not" — with nothing citable behind it, because it rests on a reading of competitor pages rather than on a fact the store recorded. So the address space is the two the spec names plus one for the comparison, and the third is deliberately a different word: anything rendered from it can say that it is a reading of other people's pages, not a measurement, which is the same distinction `T6.1` drew for evidence sources. **The consequence to be aware of**: a section may be grounded entirely in `subtopic:` addresses, which means the store's own facts are not necessarily behind every suggestion — the grader's grounding criterion is what catches copy that then asserts something the store never recorded.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 steps 3–4; invariant 7.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — The evidence pack is not stored, and the download rebuilds only the labels it needs
Decision: `optimize_recommendations` holds the recommendation, the grader's scores and the stamps, and not the evidence pack it was made from. The Markdown/HTML download takes the plain-language labels as an argument, and the route rebuilds them from the store's families and products at download time. An address whose label has gone is still shown — a subtopic as the phrase it names, anything else as the address itself.
Why: the pack is large and almost all of it is a copy of rows that have their own home in the database — the page, the fact sheets, the results page. Keeping a copy would mean a second, staler answer to every question those tables already answer, and there is no column for it (schema wave 4 is closed to this card). What the merchant actually needs from the pack when they open the download days later is one label per citation, and those come back from the store's own rows for the price of two indexed queries and no vendor call. The cost, stated plainly: if a product is deleted after the recommendation was made, its citation renders as the raw address rather than as "Fell Walker — material". Never dropped, because a citation the merchant cannot see is a claim with nothing behind it.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 step 1, §10.4; invariant 20.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — The one re-ask is spent on the free checks; a grader failure ends the run
Decision: a recommendation failing the lints is generated once more with the failures attached. If the second attempt also fails, or if the grader marks either criterion below its floor, the run stores a `failed_validation` record and stops. The grader is never asked about output the lints already refused.
Why: main §10.3 step 4 allows exactly one regeneration and step 5 adds the grader without saying what a grader failure does. The two failures are not alike: a lint failure is objective and local — "you cited an address nobody gave you" — and a model can act on it, whereas a grader failure is a judgement about the whole artefact, and asking again with "it was not grounded enough" attached is paying to talk a recommendation past its own quality bar. Invariant 22's posture (degrade to pause, never to lower quality) points the same way. What this costs: a merchant whose page produces a weak recommendation twice sees one sentence and has spent a generation from their daily allowance — deliberate, because the alternative is showing them the parts that passed, and they have no way to know what was dropped.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 steps 4–5, §14.4; invariant 11 (one repair loop), invariant 22.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — Intent match is held at 4, which the shared grader's own floors would not do
Decision: `LlmJudgeLite` (Lane D's seam) makes the model call and returns the scores; the pass/fail decision for OPTIMIZE is made in `evaluateOptimizeFloors` (`packages/core/src/optimize/grading.ts`) against two new numbers in `signals.config.yaml`, `gates.optimize_recommendation.grounding_min` and `intent_match_min`, both 4. The verdict's own `passed` is deliberately not read.
Why: main §10.3 step 5 says the two criteria have floors of 4. The shared grader computes `passed` from the *article* floors, where only information gain and grounding sit at 4 and everything else — search-intent match included — passes at 3. Consuming its verdict as-is would silently drop the OPTIMIZE bar by a point on the criterion that decides whether the edits address the search at all. The seam is still used for what it is for (a separate, blind grading call on a model that is never the cheap tier); only the floors are ours.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 step 5, §8.4, §7.10; invariants 9 and 11.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — The daily cap is counted in generations, not in model calls, and the two meters disagree
Decision: the in-request cap counts recommendations written today plus generations currently running for the account (`countOptimizeGenerationsSince`, `packages/db/src/repositories/optimize.ts`), against `budgets.optimize.generations_per_account_per_day`. The third request in a day is refused with 409 `optimize_daily_cap_reached`.
Why: main §10.2 caps *generations*, and one generation may make two model calls when the first output fails a lint — charging a merchant's allowance for our own re-ask would take a day away from them over our mistake. The in-flight half is needed because a generation asked for a minute ago has written no row yet, and without it two quick clicks both pass. **Flagged, not fixed**: the nightly auto-trip sweep (`packages/jobs/src/sweeps/auto-trips.ts`, Lane G's file) counts the same allowance in `optimize_reco` *model calls*, trips at used ≥ cap, and the flag it raises is sticky until an operator clears it. So a store that legitimately uses both its generations today — or one whose single generation needed a re-ask — has its OPTIMIZE calls paused indefinitely from then on. That is a real defect reachable for the first time now that anything makes these calls, and it belongs to the sweep's owner: either the trip should fire above the cap rather than at it, or the account flags need a daily expiry.
Nearest spec: main §10.2, §14.5, §7.10; invariants 16 and 17.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — Generation happens in a job, and the route only records that the merchant asked
Decision: `POST /api/recommendations` checks entitlement, the cap and the switches, moves the opportunity to `executing` with a guarded update, and queues `optimize_recommendation_generate`. The work — a results-page read, up to five competitor fetches and two model calls — runs in the worker under the account's advisory lock. On completion the opportunity goes back to `accepted` with the recommendation attached, and `optimize_recommendation_ready` is emitted.
Why: the frozen API contract answers this route with `ok` rather than with a recommendation, and its detail response has a `generating` state, so an asynchronous generation is what the contract already describes. It is also the only shape that works: a minute-long request would be cut off by any proxy in front of the app long before it finished. No notification is emitted when a generation fails its checks — the only notification type available says the recommendations are ready, and they are not; the card carries the failure instead.
Nearest spec: main §10.2, ui §5.4; tech §3; `packages/core/src/api/routes.ts`.

Decision: the routes are `POST /api/recommendations`, `GET /api/recommendations`, `GET /api/recommendations/{id}/download` and `POST /api/recommendations/{id}/apply`, as the card's scope line and the lane's directory list say.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — The applied-detection prompt is a live read, not a stored flag, and it is exact rather than fuzzy
Decision: "Looks like you applied this — confirm?" is computed on every read of a recommendation, by comparing the stored suggestions against the page as the last inventory sync found it (`detectApplied`, `packages/core/src/optimize/applied.ts`). A suggestion counts as applied only when the page's search-result title or description matches it exactly once whitespace and case are levelled, or when a suggested heading is now present. Nothing is stored, and nothing is ever marked applied without the merchant saying so.
Why: main §10.4 asks for detection "at the next content-inventory sync". The sync itself is Lane C's job and outside this lane, but the question the prompt answers — "is this suggestion on the page now?" — is a question about the world at the moment somebody looks, so a live read gives the same answer at the same time without a cross-lane seam and without a stored flag that would keep asking after the merchant had said no. It is also what invariant 26 asks for: attention items are live queries. **Exact rather than fuzzy** because a wrong guess here tells a merchant they did work they did not do; a merchant who retyped the suggestion in their own words is missed, and the only cost of that is the absent prompt.
Nearest spec: main §10.4, §12.3; invariant 26.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — Marking a recommendation applied books the measurement as a queued job, because there is no outcomes table
Decision: "Mark all as applied" completes the opportunity, stamps `applied_at`, and enqueues `opportunity_outcome_measure` with `run_at` set to `applied_at + learning.outcomes.maturity_days` (28). No handler for that task exists.
Why: the card's done-when asks that mark-applied "schedules an outcome row at +28 d". `opportunities.outcome_json` and `outcome_measured_at` are the columns an outcome eventually lands in, and they stay null until there is something honest to put in them (main §9.6.13's "no verdict before 28 days"), so there is no row to write today — what can be written is the *appointment*, and the queue is where appointments live. Writing it at the moment the merchant marks the work applied, rather than having a later sweep go looking for applied opportunities, makes "we will look at this page again on 1 October" a fact in one place from the moment the promise is made. A queued job whose task no worker knows about is not picked up and not lost. **What it costs**: the learning loop (`T7.1`) is deferred out of v1, so these jobs accumulate unrun until it ships; whoever builds it inherits a queue of real appointments rather than an empty table.
Nearest spec: main §10.4, §9.6.10; build plan M7 (deferred).

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — Ranking-page content is read once, by the comparison, and not fetched again for the writing call
Decision: the evidence pack carries the ranking pages' addresses, domains and positions, and their *content* only as the subtopic comparison's output — what each page settles, under which heading. The pages are not fetched a second time to put their text in the writing prompt.
Why: main §10.3 step 1 lists "the top-5 ranking pages' extracted content" in the pack and step 2 then spends that content on the coverage comparison. Fetching them again would double the page-fetch bill and the SSRF-guarded fetcher's work for information the comparison has already distilled into exactly the form the writer needs — and on a cache hit the comparison does not fetch them at all, so a second fetch would also be the only thing making a cached comparison cost money. The writer therefore sees "three of the five pages above you settle sizing, under these headings", not five pages of competitor prose.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 steps 1–2, §14.3.6; invariant 20.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — Keyword stuffing is measured across the suggested prose, and never over the title or description
Decision: `gates.optimize_recommendation.keyword_density_max` (0.05) is read against all the recommendation's sections, answers and headings taken together, excluding the suggested search-result title and description.
Why: measured per passage the number is meaningless — one mention of a four-word search in a sixty-word section is already 7%, so every correct suggestion would fail — and measured including the title it is worse, because naming the search in the title is the thing a title is *for*. Main §10.3 says only "no keyword stuffing" and names no figure, so both the scope and the number are ours; the scope is the part that decides whether the check is real.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 step 4, §7.10; invariant 9.

## 2026-09-04 — T6.2 — This lane wrote outside its directories in three places, all of them additive
Decision: besides `packages/core/optimize`, `packages/jobs/optimize` and `apps/web/app/api/recommendations`, this card added `packages/db/src/repositories/optimize.ts` (a new file, plus one line in the union-merged repositories barrel), the thresholds above in `packages/rules` (`signals.config.yaml`, its JSON schema, its TypeScript view and the committed snapshot), one contiguous block of copy in `packages/ui/strings/en.json`, and two new prompt files in `packages/llm/prompts/`.
Why: recorded so a reviewer sees it rather than discovers it. The repository file is where the constitution puts table access — `packages/db` holds the repositories and `packages/core` may not import a database driver — and it touches no existing file except a barrel that is `merge=union` for exactly this reason. The thresholds are in `packages/rules` because no threshold literal may live anywhere else, and the strings are in the one catalogue all user-facing copy lives in. Nothing else in any of those packages was edited.
Nearest spec: CLAUDE.md code-structure rules; build plan §3 (append-only files); invariant 9.

## 2026-09-04 — R-INTENTGAP-JOB — The pass runs on the store's own Sunday, the day before the scan that reads it
Decision: the paid page comparison is queued for each store on its own local Sunday, by an hourly sweep that asks per store whether it is Sunday there — the same shape the weekly signal scan already uses for its Monday. One job per store, keyed on the store and that date, so the other 23 hours of the day queue nothing.
Why: the founder's split makes the comparison a producer and the weekly scan a consumer, and the scan runs on each store's local Monday. Something has to decide which day the producer runs on, and the day before is the only one that puts an answer on the shelf before the scan reaches for it. It is not tight timing: a comparison stays usable for as long as the results page it was made against, which is seven days (`discovery.cache.serp_snapshot_ttl_days`), so Sunday's answers are still there for Monday's scan and for the six days after it. Same-day was the alternative and was rejected because nothing orders two hourly sweeps against each other — on a bad week the scan would run first every time and find nothing. Hourly rather than a single weekly moment for the reason the crontab file already states: a crontab names a fixed UTC time, and no fixed time is Sunday everywhere at once, so a store far enough west would go permanently uncompared rather than merely late.
Nearest spec: main §7.5 (the cadence table), §10.3; DECISIONS 2026-09-03 FOUNDER (the intent-gap comparison runs as its own job).

## 2026-09-04 — R-INTENTGAP-JOB — Only stores with Search Console connected are swept, and the pass never rebuilds their clusters
Decision: the sweep considers a store only if it has a live Search Console connection, and the pass reads the store's query clusters — the groups of near-identical searches it is shown for — as the weekly scan last wrote them, rather than rebuilding them itself.
Why: two halves of the same point, which is that this pass must shortlist the same pages the scan will later come looking for. The shortlist is a filter over search positions, so a store without Search Console has nothing to shortlist and a pass for it would be a walk that buys nothing and finds nothing. And a cluster's head search is half of the key the scan recomputes to find a comparison — if the pass rebuilt the clusters and produced even a slightly different head, the scan would look under a key nothing was ever stored under. Rebuilding is also a write into another lane's table on a second schedule, which is the sort of thing that races. **The consequence, stated plainly:** a store that has never been scanned has no clusters, so this pass does nothing for it until its first scan has run. That is the right order — there is nothing to compare it on yet — but it does mean the pass is silent rather than merely empty for a brand-new store.
Nearest spec: main §6.7, §7.11 (Limited Intelligence), §10.3; DECISIONS 2026-09-03 T6.1 (the cache-key entry).

## 2026-09-04 — R-INTENTGAP-JOB — The pass has no cursor, because the cache it writes is the checkpoint
Decision: a pass that runs for minutes keeps no record of how far through the shortlist it got. A killed pass restarts from the top of the same shortlist.
Why: the constitution requires anything that can run past a minute to checkpoint, and this can — ten pages, each a bought results page, five page reads and a model call. Progress is already durable without a cursor: the results page is written to `serp_snapshots` when it is bought and the model's answer to `request_cache` the moment it arrives, both before anything is done with them. A restarted pass therefore replays each finished page for four indexed reads and pays for none of it again; the test that kills a pass half-way and resumes it measures exactly one model call, five page reads and no results page bought. A separate "this page is done" marker would be a second record of the same fact, and the way the two would disagree is the damaging one: an entry that expired while its marker survived would leave that page silently never compared again, and the scan finding nothing where it was told to look.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.2–14.3.4 (effectively-once, checkpointing), §14.3.6 (billable reads cached, written before processing); invariants 18 and 20.

## 2026-09-04 — R-INTENTGAP-JOB — A pass stopped by the store's daily allowance is not recorded as finished
Decision: the pass writes its completion to the idempotency ledger — the record of paid work already done, which a redelivered job reads instead of re-running — only when it actually reached the end of the shortlist. Stopping because the store's daily allowance of analyses ran out mid-walk records nothing.
Why: a completion record is a promise that there is nothing left to do for that store on that date, and after a part-way stop that is untrue. Recording it would mean the pages below the cut-off are never reached, not even once the allowance resets, because every later attempt for the same date would short-circuit on the record. `T6.1` already decided the remainder is left rather than squeezed in; this is what makes "left" mean "still available" rather than "dropped". The cost is that a retry re-walks the pages that did get compared, which is four indexed reads apiece and no money.
Nearest spec: main §14.5 (per-type cap), §14.3.1; invariants 17 and 18.

## 2026-09-04 — R-INTENTGAP-JOB — The pass runs for a store whose subscription has lapsed, exactly as the weekly scan does
Decision: no billing, vacation or deletion check was added. The pass is stopped by the operator kill switches and by the store's own daily allowance for this call type, and by nothing else.
Why: this is detection, not generation, and invariant 16 is explicit that billing state gates generation and publishing only. The weekly signal scan — the sibling job, which also buys results pages — reads the kill switches and no lifecycle gate, so adding one here would make two jobs doing the same kind of work answer to different rules with nothing in the specs asking for the difference. **Flagged rather than hidden:** the practical effect is that a lapsed store still costs money on Sundays. It is the posture the product already has, not one this card introduced, and changing it is a decision about both jobs at once.
Nearest spec: main §4.2, §14.4, §14.5; invariant 16.

## 2026-09-04 — R-INTENTGAP-JOB — FLAGGED: nothing schedules the pass and nothing registers it, and both are deliberate
Decision: **none taken.** `registerIntentGapTasks` (`packages/jobs/src/optimize/intent-gap-tasks.ts`) is built, typed, exported and tested, and no code path calls it. `intent_gap_scan_weekly` is not in `packages/jobs/src/runtime/crontab.ts`. Until both land, this pass never runs in production.
Why: two separate holds, both instructed. The schedule is switched off by the founder's decision (open question 4) until the last handlerless crontab entries land, and this card was told in as many words not to be the thing that quietly turns paid work on. The composition root, `apps/web/instrumentation-node.ts`, is reserved for the integrator by the build plan, and `T6.2`'s `registerOptimizeTasks` is already waiting there for the same reason — this is the second entry of the same shape, not a new kind of gap.
What the wiring needs, precisely. In `startServerRuntime()`, alongside the other `register*Tasks` calls: `registerIntentGapTasks({ getDb: db, getPool: dbPool, seo: seoProvider(), pageFetcher: new GuardedPageFetcher(), llm: <the process's Anthropic client>, prompt: loadPrompt('intent-gap', 1) })`. The LLM client is the one thing that is not already built in that file — the generation lane memoises its own inside `apps/web/app/api/articles/_lib/config.ts` and does not export it, so either that factory grows an export or the composition root builds the process's one client itself and hands it to both. And in `crontab.ts`, one entry: `{ task: 'intent_gap_scan_weekly', schedule: '0 * * * *', why: … }` — hourly for the local-Sunday reason above, and only when the founder switches the schedule back on. A crontab entry naming a task nobody registered is refused at worker start, so the two have to land together or the registration first.
Nearest spec: build plan §3 (lane ownership), §6 `R-INTENTGAP-JOB`; DECISIONS 2026-09-04 T6.2 (nothing calls the OPTIMIZE task registration).
## 2026-09-04 — T5.1 — The day an article belongs to is read at the publish moment, not at the writing moment
Decision: the daily generation cycle now derives "which day's topic is this" from the store's local clock at the moment the article is due out — `now` plus the writing lead — rather than from the clock when the writing starts. `publishDayFor(now, timezone, leadHours)` in `packages/core/src/generation/cycle.ts` is that derivation, and both the hourly sweep that queues the job and the run itself use it.
Why: authorised by the founder ahead of this card, from a MEDIUM audit finding. Writing starts a fixed six hours before each store's publish hour and wraps backwards over midnight, so a store publishing at 02:00 starts at 20:00 the previous evening. Reading the date at the writing moment took Tuesday evening's date and published the result on Wednesday, leaving the calendar and the shop permanently one day apart — every planned day delivered late, for ever, on every store whose publish hour is earlier than its lead. The article belongs to the day it appears. Real hours are added and the sum then formatted in the store's zone, rather than a date string being shifted, so a daylight-saving change does not move the answer.
Consequence, stated: for the default 09:00 store nothing changes at all (03:00 + 6h is the same date). It changes behaviour only for a publish hour earlier than the lead — 00:00 to 05:00 — which is precisely the case that was broken.
Nearest spec: main §9.1 (one pass per account per day, anchored to the persona timezone), §9.4 (the publish hour); CLAUDE.md invariant 14.

## 2026-09-04 — T5.1 — One article is handed over per publish hour, oldest first
Decision: the delivery run publishes at most one article per pass, choosing the oldest of those cleared. A merchant with three approved drafts gets one a day for three days.
Why: main §9.4 gives the reason for a fixed hour as "predictable for the merchant, and naturally spaced at ≤1/day so publishing never looks like an algorithmic burst". Handing over everything that happens to be ready would produce exactly that burst the first morning after a merchant worked through a review backlog. Oldest first so nothing waits for ever behind newer work. Nothing in the specs states this explicitly, which is why it is journalled: it is a reading of the pacing sentence rather than a rule quoted from one.
Consequence: a store that accumulates finished drafts drains them at one a day. The count is never shown to the merchant as a backlog figure — invariant 23 forbids denominators — so this is invisible except as articles appearing on consecutive mornings.
Nearest spec: main §9.4; CLAUDE.md invariants 14, 23.
