## 2026-09-04 — R-PUBLISH-2 — The store's own domain reaches the publisher one call at a time
Decision: the claimed domain — the address a merchant typed when they signed up, which is the one their shoppers visit — travels **as a field on each call to the publishing client** (`storefrontDomain`, beside the blog's name, which was already carried this way for the same reason), rather than the client holding one or being given a lookup function. It is read from the `domains` table beside each publish by one helper, `storefrontDomainFor` in `packages/jobs/src/publish/address.ts`, which the first publication, the recovery sweep and a repair all call. No change to the database and no new column.
Why: the client that writes to Shopify is created once for the whole process and serves every store, so it cannot hold one store's domain; but everything else per-store — the shop handle, the token, the blog's name — already arrives per call, and adding a lookup callback would have been a second, different way of doing the same thing. The alternative considered and rejected was widening the existing one-query read of a store's publishing settings (`readPublishTarget`) to join the domain in: it saves one small indexed query per publish but edits a repository file several lanes append to, for a job that runs once a day per store.
Also decided, because the code must do something and no document says what: when an account somehow has no claimed domain the address falls back to the `myshopify.com` host, which is exactly today's behaviour. That state should be unreachable — an account holds a claimed domain before it can hold a Shopify connection — and the alternative, refusing to publish, would invent a new way for a merchant's article not to appear.
Nearest spec: main §12.2 (attribution), §9.5, §2; founder decision "A store's own claimed domain is the address we record" (2026-09-04).

## 2026-09-04 — R-PUBLISH-2 — Articles published before today keep the address they were published under
Decision: nothing rewrites the recorded address of an already-published article. The new address applies to articles published from now on. No backfill.
Why: the recorded address is what a merchant clicks and what the product will match Search Console rows against, and we have no evidence that an article published last week was ever *served* at the claimed domain — only that it will be from now on. Silently moving it would change where a merchant believes their article lives, with no message and no way for them to notice. It is also what the code already guaranteed: the address is written only by the first publication, whose database update is guarded on the article still being a draft, so a repair cannot reach it. A test now holds that: a repair of an article whose stored address is the old `myshopify` one leaves it untouched.
Nearest spec: main §9.5, §12.2.

## 2026-09-04 — R-PUBLISH-2 — A revision has no field for the merchant's own choices
Decision: the update sent to Shopify is described by its own type rather than by "a create with an id added to it". `UpdateArticleInput` carries the title, the body, the summary and our hidden marker, and has **no field at all** for the article's address, its tags or its published state — so no caller can send one by accident, now or later. The create keeps all three.
Why: the founder's decision is that a repair sends only the words we wrote. Enforcing that by leaving keys out of one function body would survive exactly until the next person copied the create's shape; making it inexpressible in the type means the compiler refuses. The load-bearing test asserts on the request actually put on the wire — the keys of the JSON body of the `PUT` — and not on what the code intended: it lists the five keys a revision may carry, so a sixth added later fails rather than quietly overwriting something of the merchant's.
Nearest spec: main §9.5, §14.3.7; invariant 21; founder decision "A repair sends only the words we wrote" (2026-09-04).

## 2026-09-04 — R-PUBLISH-2 — The fake shop now holds tags, so the promise about them is testable
Decision: the test double that stands in for a merchant's Shopify store keeps a `tags` list on each article, which we never write and a revision never clears.
Why: the double is what every publishing job test runs against, and it could not previously show the difference between "we left the merchant's tags alone" and "there were no tags". The end-to-end test of a repair — the merchant renamed the post, tagged it and took it down — needs the shop to be able to hold all three, or it proves only two of them.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.7; tech §2 (every provider behind an interface with a test double).

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — A suggestion that cannot name its search is still shown, and says why
Decision: when the product refuses to improve a page because it cannot tell which search that page competes for, **the merchant is told, in the product**. Two parts: (a) the suggestion is still shortlisted and still appears, marked as needing Search Console connected rather than silently un-actionable; (b) a new machine-readable refusal code is added to the frozen contract, with a sentence in the copy catalogue along the lines of "We don't yet know which search this page competes for, so there's nothing we can safely improve it against."
Why: `R-NOQUERY` stopped the product buying a search-results page for a web address, which was right — but it left a store with **no Search Console connection** holding suggestions whose button can only ever refuse, and refusing in silence. That is not an edge case: Search Console is optional and the Limited Intelligence mode exists precisely for stores without it. The founder chose to turn a dead button into a reason to connect. Not shortlisting them at all was rejected because the merchant would lose a real signal — that a page's Google listing text is missing or duplicated — which is true whether or not we know its search. Reusing the nearest existing refusal code would have shown them "This one has already moved on — refreshed", which is untrue, because the screen maps codes to its own copy and ignores our message.
Nearest spec: main §7.11 (Limited Intelligence), §10.1; invariant 22 (degrade to a visible pause), 24 (canonical copy).

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — Saying "not interested" also calls off an article already booked
Decision: dismissing a suggestion cancels the calendar topic that suggestion produced, if one has been booked or is being written. Today the suggestion disappears and **the article still appears**.
Why: the button already dismisses a suggestion whose article is in flight; the calendar simply never hears about it, because the daily cycle works off the topic row and never looks at the suggestion's status. So the product tells the merchant the suggestion is gone and then publishes it anyway. The founder chose the reading that matches what a merchant just said rather than treating dismissal and the calendar's own veto as two separate acts. **This reaches into the calendar's state machine from the opportunities side**, which is why the lane that found it stopped rather than doing it.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §8.7; invariant 15 (guarded transitions), 14.

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — The published address should use the shop's primary storefront domain
Decision: carded. A store's claimed domain is stored bare (`acme.com`), but its real storefront may be `www.acme.com` or `shop.acme.com`. Shopify knows each store's primary domain and we can read it with the scope we already hold; that is the address Search Console reports under, so it is the one to record.
Why: `R-PUBLISH-2` moved the recorded address from the `myshopify.com` host to the claimed domain, which was the founder's decision and is a large improvement. But recording a host the storefront only redirects *from* risks the same attribution mismatch one level down — and the symptom is the expensive one this whole thread has been about: a ranking article that appears to have earned nothing. The lane recorded it and did not invent a lookup, correctly.
Nearest spec: main §12.2 (attribution), §2 (the claimed domain), §6.2 (Shopify scopes).

## 2026-09-07 — R-HOLD — The domain's release deadline is honoured by the claim itself
Decision: the week-long hold on a deleted account's domain is enforced by the date already written on that domain's row, and it is the claim that acts on it: before a claim inserts, it removes any row for that domain whose recorded release date has passed. Nothing else changes — the insert underneath is untouched, so the unique index still decides which of two racing claims wins. The nightly clean-up still removes released rows, but it is now tidying up rather than keeping a promise: if it never runs again, a domain still becomes claimable the day its week is up.
Why: three shapes were possible and only this one keeps both halves of the brief. Taking the leftover row over in place (an upsert that rewrites its owner) would have made a *read* of that row part of deciding who wins, and it hands a new merchant a row with somebody else's history on it. Treating an expired row as invisible to every reader instead would have meant changing every place in the product that asks whether a domain is claimed, for one case. Removing the row is the same act the clean-up already performs, performed by whoever first has a use for it, and it leaves the claim path — the product's identity rule — literally unchanged.
Two consequences worth stating. The deadline is compared against the *database's* clock, so two web servers disagreeing about the time cannot disagree about whether a hold has ended. And a merchant who already holds a different domain, and who types a released one, will free that released row as a side effect of being told "you already have a domain": the hold had expired, so nothing that was still protected is lost, but the row goes a little earlier than the sweep would have taken it.
Supersedes: the 2026-09-01 `T1.4` entry "`domains.release_after` is a deletion-sweep deadline, not a modifier on uniqueness", which decided the claim ignores that date entirely and named the resulting exposure — "if the sweep never runs, the domain stays blocked forever" — as knowingly accepted. That is the exposure this card closes, on the founder's word. The test that pinned the old behaviour is rewritten rather than deleted: it still holds the half that has not changed, that a hold which has not yet expired refuses everyone.
Nearest spec: main §2, §5, §14.6; invariant 1; founder decision "The seven-day domain hold stays, and becomes reliable" (2026-09-04).

## 2026-09-07 — R-HOLD — The account's deletion stamp is not a second source of the deadline
Decision: the claim consults only the release date on the domain row. It does not also work the deadline out from the owning account's deletion stamp.
Why: those two would be two rules for one thing, and they could disagree. Deletion writes both in a single transaction, so a deleted account that held a domain always has the date on it; a row with no date belongs to a live account and is untouchable. The known gap is a domain row whose date somehow never got written — it would stay blocked, which is the old behaviour and the safe direction to fail in.
Nearest spec: main §5, §14.6.
## 2026-09-07 — R-REVOKE — What is stored for a session is a digest of the browser's cookie, not the cookie
Decision: the `sessions` table's primary key holds a SHA-256 digest of the value the browser presents, in hexadecimal. The browser keeps the original; nothing we store can be presented to sign in. The lookup hashes what it is handed and compares digests, so the read is the same single index probe the table was shaped for. This is the choice `T-WAVE5` deliberately left open, and it needed no migration, as that entry predicted.
Why: a session cookie is a bearer credential — whatever presents it *is* the merchant. Stored verbatim, any copy of that table is a set of working sessions for every merchant signed in at that moment: a backup on somebody's laptop, a support export, a read-only replica whose connection string leaked. Stored as a digest it is a set of useless strings, because a digest cannot be turned back into the cookie it came from and presenting the digest itself matches nothing. The cost is one hash per signed-in request, which is microseconds. Plain SHA-256 with no salt and no stretching is deliberate and is not the mistake it would be for a password: the input is a 128-bit random value the sign-in library generates and nobody ever types, so there is nothing to guess and nowhere else it is reused — and a deliberately slow hash would spend its cost on exactly the request path this feature was priced at one read.
Nearest spec: main §4.1; tech §3, §4 (secrets at rest); DECISIONS 2026-09-04 T-WAVE5 ("A session is a token, an account and an expiry").

## 2026-09-07 — R-REVOKE — A session lasts a month, and its lapse date never moves once set
Decision: the session lifetime goes from 24 hours to 30 days, fixed at sign-in. It is not extended by use: a merchant who signs in today is asked to sign in again in a month whether they visit daily or once.
Why: the day was chosen *because* a session could not be ended. Lapsing was the only thing that ever stopped a leaked cookie, so it had to come round quickly, and the price was making every merchant sign in again every morning. Revoking is now the answer to a leaked cookie — immediate, and it reaches every browser — so the lifetime stops being a security control and goes back to being about how often somebody is made to sign in. A month is the sign-in library's own default for stored sessions. **Fixed rather than sliding is the load-bearing half.** A sliding window extends the row as it is used, which puts a database *write* on the read path on a schedule; the founder priced this feature at one read per signed-in request, and a periodic write is not that. The cost of fixing it is that a merchant using the product every day still signs in again once a month — a link or a Google click. Implemented by setting the library's `updateAge` equal to the lifetime, which is the setting that decides when it extends a session: equal, the moment never arrives while the session is live.
Nearest spec: main §4.1 — silent on session lifetime; build plan §6 `R-REVOKE` ("revisit the 24-hour session lifetime in the same card").

## 2026-09-07 — R-REVOKE — Signing out ends every session the account has, not only the browser that pressed it
Decision: pressing sign out revokes all of that account's sessions. The sign-in library ends the one that pressed the button; a sign-out event then deletes the rest.
Why: the card's done-when says signing out in one browser ends the session everywhere, and the reason is what a merchant means by it. Somebody signs out because a laptop went missing, or because they think a cookie of theirs is loose — and a sign-out that leaves the copy working answers a different question from the one they asked. The cost is that signing out on a phone also signs the desktop out; that is visible, undoable in one click, and the safe direction to be wrong in. The fan-out lives in the sign-out event rather than in the adapter's own delete, deliberately: the library also calls that delete when clearing a lapsed cookie, and when somebody follows a sign-in link for a *different* account in a browser already signed in — widening it there would sign a stranger out of their other devices.
Nearest spec: main §4.1; ui §9 (Settings) — neither says what sign-out reaches.

## 2026-09-07 — R-REVOKE — Asking to be deleted signs every browser out at once, a week before the rows go
Decision: `requestAccountDeletion` — the half of account deletion that runs while the merchant waits — now revokes every session the account has, immediately after the deletion is stamped and before anything that can fail. A new `revokeSessions` port on the account-lifecycle store carries it.
Why: deleting an account here is a stamp, not an erase: the account row survives seven days so nobody can re-claim the domain early, and the sweep erases it on the day the hold ends. The foreign key that takes sessions with the account therefore does not fire for a week — so without this, a "deleted" account keeps working sessions in every browser it was ever signed in on for another seven days, including the one that just clicked delete. Relying on the cascade would have been reading the schema and calling it done. Proved by presenting a session afterwards through the same lookup a signed-in request uses, against a real database.
Nearest spec: main §14.6 (deletion and the seven-day domain hold); main §4.1.

## 2026-09-07 — R-REVOKE — The session endpoint stops echoing the session's own token
Decision: the object returned by `GET /api/auth/session` is built explicitly — the account id and the address, and the expiry — rather than by passing on what the sign-in library hands the callback.
Why: with sessions in the database, what the library hands that callback is the stored row itself, which carries the session token. Passing it on would publish the session's own credential in a JSON body any script on the page can read, undoing the fact that the cookie carrying it is marked unreadable to scripts. Nothing in the product read anything but the account id from that object. A test asserts the token does not appear in it, because this is the kind of thing a later "just spread the object" tidy-up would quietly reintroduce.
Nearest spec: tech §3 (session-cookie auth); main §4.1.

## 2026-09-07 — R-REVOKE — This card edits Lane A's sign-in directory, on the card's own authority
Decision: `R-REVOKE` is a Lane G card and its work is almost entirely in `apps/web/app/api/auth`, which the lane table gives to Lane A. Done as assigned, and recorded here rather than negotiated, because there is no version of "sessions become revocable" that does not change how a session is read.
Why: the build plan divides directories; the founder's card assignment for this wave divides work. Where they disagree the assignment is the newer instruction. Files touched outside Lane G: `apps/web/app/api/auth/_lib/{adapter,config,provisioning}.ts` and their suites, plus two added session tests in `apps/web/app/api/account/delete`. No integrator-resolved file was touched.
Nearest spec: build plan §3 (lane ownership); CLAUDE.md prime directive 5.
## 2026-09-07 — R-RECO-QUALITY — The rationale sentence is written in English whatever language the page is in
Decision: the writing prompt asks for the recommendation's `rationale` — the one sentence saying why a suggested title or description beats the current one — in English, whatever language the store's page is written in. The suggested title and description themselves are unchanged: those are still written in the page's own language, because the merchant pastes them into their shop.
Why: nothing in the founder's decision said which language, and the sentence is read on our own screen, surrounded by our own English wording, rather than on the merchant's page. A Danish sentence between English labels is the "mixed-language sentence" the founder rejected two days earlier for the quality judge's justification ("The judge's own sentences may reach a merchant", 2026-09-04), which is the same situation: model prose shown to a merchant inside our interface. Applied the same answer rather than inventing a second one. **This is user-visible and was not dictated — flagged in the session report.**
Nearest spec: main §10.4; ui §5.3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-RECO-QUALITY — Recommendations stored under the old field name keep working
Decision: `rationale_key` is renamed to `rationale` in the model's response schema and in the stored recommendation, and everything that reads a stored recommendation back accepts both spellings. Rows written before today are not rewritten and no migration is added.
Why: the recommendation is stored as one JSON document per generation, so the rename would otherwise blank the explanation on every recommendation a merchant already has — silently, since the field is allowed to be empty. A migration is not this card's to add, and rewriting merchants' stored model output to fit a rename is worse than reading both names. The prompt version stamped on each row (`optimize-reco.v1` versus `v2`) is what tells the two shapes apart in the record.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 step 3, §10.4.

## 2026-09-07 — R-RECO-QUALITY — The model-written label goes where the merchant actually downloads from
Decision: the "A model wrote this line." label is added to the drawer and to the Markdown and HTML files the drawer's download buttons produce. The separate server-rendered download at `GET /api/recommendations/{id}/download` is left alone, because it never printed the rationale at all and adding it there would be new content rather than a label.
Why: there are two download implementations. The one a merchant reaches is built in the browser from what the drawer already has, and it prints the rationale as an unattributed quote — which is exactly the surface the founder's decision is about. The server route renders from the stored recommendation and omits the field entirely, so there is nothing there to mislabel. Adding the sentence to it would be building something nobody asked for. **Flagged in the session report**: the two documents differ in what they contain, which is a pre-existing divergence this card did not create.
Nearest spec: main §10.4; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-07 — R-RECO-QUALITY — The scheduled shortlist ceiling is its own number, not the allowance minus something
Decision: `budgets.intent_gap.scheduled_shortlist_max` is a threshold of its own in `packages/rules`, set to 8 against a daily allowance of 10, rather than computed as "the allowance minus the day's generations".
Why: a computed ceiling would silently follow the OPTIMIZE generation cap wherever that moved, which is the coupling the founder rejected in a different shape — a merchant's button behaving differently because of something a background job did. Writing it down means someone changing either number sees both. The relationship is not left to a comment: a test runs a full scheduled pass on a store with more candidates than it could ever pay for, then presses "improve this page" as many times as the allowance permits, and fails if any of those presses is refused. A companion case proves the same test refuses when the pass shortlists the whole allowance, so it cannot pass vacuously.
Nearest spec: main §10.3, §14.5; invariant 9 (no threshold literal outside `packages/rules`).
## 2026-09-07 — R-STRANDED — The sweep for interrupted days runs inside each store's own daily pass
Decision: there is no new scheduled job. Every store's daily generation pass — the one that already runs once a day, at that store's own writing hour — now also looks behind it for days whose writing started and never finished. Today's own article is written first; the catching-up happens after it.
Why: the only thing that can strand a day is that store's own daily pass dying, so the same pass is the natural place to notice — it already holds the per-account lock, already knows the store's timezone and its publish day, and already read every reason not to write. A separate hourly sweep would find a stranded day sooner (within an hour instead of within a day), but it needs a recurring-schedule entry, which is integrator-resolved in this build, and it would take the account lock outside the store's own writing window for work that has already missed its day by hours. Ordering: today's article is what the store is owed today, a recovery can wait a pass, and a recovery that fails must never be the reason today's article did not go out.
Nearest spec: main §8.7, §9.1, §14.3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-STRANDED — "Furthest along" means the most money already spent, and the more recent day breaks a tie
Decision: among interrupted days, the one finished is the one whose article already has a stored draft; failing that, the one that at least has an article row; failing that, any of them. Two that got equally far are separated by date, most recent first.
Why: the writer's model call is by far the most expensive step in the pipeline and its output is stored before anything grades it, so a run that reached that point can be finished for the price of the checks alone — that is the work worth rescuing. The tie-break is about staleness rather than cost: a run stranded three weeks ago was written against search results and a catalogue that have since moved, and grading it now grades it against evidence that no longer describes the store.
Nearest spec: main §9.1, §14.3.6.
Class (filled by audit):

## 2026-09-07 — R-STRANDED — An interrupted day is recognised by never having been graded, not by its calendar state
Decision: a day counts as interrupted when its calendar entry is still `generating`, its date has passed, and no Gate 3 decision was ever recorded against it.
Why: the calendar state alone cannot answer the question. Nothing in the product moves a calendar entry out of `generating` when its article is published — both publishing paths update the article row and leave the calendar entry alone — so a perfectly healthy article waiting its turn to go out is, on state alone, indistinguishable from one nobody ever came back for. Sweeping on state would have written those stores a second article for a day they already had one for. Reaching Gate 3 is the moment a day is actually decided, and a run that reached it has either resolved already or resolves down a path that is not this one. (**That the calendar entry never leaves `generating` is a separate defect, reported rather than fixed here** — see the session report.)
Nearest spec: main §8.7 (the calendar's state machine), §8.4.

## 2026-09-07 — R-STRANDED — Both finishing and giving up are recorded under the interrupted day's own idempotency key
Decision: the sweep keys everything it does on `(account, "daily_generation", topic + the topic's own scheduled date)` — the same key the run that died would have recorded had it finished. Giving up writes that key with the outcome `abandoned_stranded`.
Why: it is the one derivation that makes the sweep and the day it is recovering the same piece of work rather than two. A day the killed run somehow did finish is never re-entered; a day the sweep finishes is never finished twice; and a day given up on is never rediscovered the following morning, dead-lettered a second time, and left occupying the single place the sweep has for finishing something. This also tidies an inconsistency: the day's key was previously derived from the *publish date the pass computed*, which is always equal to the topic's own scheduled date for a topic the pass may take, so nothing changes but the derivation now says so.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.1–14.3.4.

## 2026-09-07 — R-STRANDED — A stopped store is not swept at all
Decision: when an operator brake, an unpaid subscription, a merchant on holiday or a lost Shopify connection stops a store's day, the sweep does not run either. A day with nothing planned on it is not one of those reasons — that is the ordinary quiet day, and it is where the sweep gets its room.
Why: finishing an interrupted run is writing an article, and every one of those reasons says do not write. The cost is that a store on a three-week holiday holds its dead letter for three weeks; that was preferred to spending a stopped store's money, and to filing an operator alert about work the product is deliberately not doing.
Nearest spec: main §14.5, §14.6; invariant 16.

## 2026-09-07 — R-STRANDED — A recovery that fails for a fixable reason is left to the next pass; one that cannot be fixed is given up on
Decision: if finishing an interrupted day throws, the failure is classified by the runtime's existing rule. A retryable one is re-thrown and the day is found again by the next pass. A terminal one — a topic whose own inputs cannot be resolved, say — is dead-lettered and closed.
Why: the two failures deserve opposite answers. An outage that ends in an hour should not permanently cost a store a day it had already paid for; a topic that can never be generated should not be retried every morning for ever with nobody told. The runtime already classifies every failure this way and defaults an unrecognised one to retryable, which is the safe side here.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.5, §14.4.

## 2026-09-07 — R-TESTDB — Suites are stamped out of one already-migrated database instead of each running every migration
Decision: the test harness builds one database with every migration applied, once per run, before any test file starts, and each suite's own database is created as a copy of it. Suites no longer run migrations themselves. The copy is identified by a fingerprint of the migration files, so adding or editing a migration builds a fresh one automatically; the old one is left behind and is harmless.
Why: running the full migration set once per suite — about a hundred times per run — was the largest single cost in the harness, and it is what made the gate unreliable rather than merely slow. Two consequences. The setup step routinely took longer than the ten seconds a test file's setup is allowed, which fails the *file* while every assertion in it passes. And the volume of writing it produced made every later clean-up slow, because deleting a database in Postgres makes the whole server flush what it is holding to disk and wait; measured under three simultaneous test runs, single deletions took up to forty-two seconds. Copying a ready-made database is a file copy and costs a fraction of the same work.
Building it up front rather than lazily in the first suite that needs it is deliberate: only one process may build it, so a lazy build makes every other suite wait for it inside its own ten-second setup budget and fail for something that is not its fault. Before any suite starts, nobody is waiting.
Rejected: giving each suite a schema inside one shared database instead of a database of its own. It would have removed the cost entirely, but advisory locks, `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` and the job library's own tables are all per-database, so suites would have started interfering with each other in ways that look exactly like product bugs.
Nearest spec: tech §6 (CI); no spec section governs the test harness.

## 2026-09-07 — R-TESTDB — A suite that leaks a connection is now named, instead of tripping up whichever suite ran next
Decision: closing a suite's database checks whether anything is still connected to it, and fails that suite by name, listing what is attached. It re-checks for two seconds first, because a connection the suite did close takes a moment to disappear from the server's list.
Why: the previous behaviour caught leaks by accident. The clean-up deletes the database with a flag that force-disconnects whoever is attached, and the killed connection then raised an error with no test and no file attached to it — so it landed on whichever suite happened to be running at that instant, and the suite that actually leaked was never mentioned. This replaces an accidental, misattributed signal with a deliberate, attributed one. Proved by writing a suite that deliberately leaks a connection, watching it fail with its own name, and deleting it again.
Nearest spec: none.

## 2026-09-07 — R-TESTDB — The local test database stops making throwaway data crash-safe
Decision: `docker-compose.yml` starts the local Postgres with `fsync`, `synchronous_commit` and `full_page_writes` off. The container must be recreated for this to take effect.
Why: this is the one change that makes the difference between a gate that fails for its own reasons and one that does not, and it is a setting rather than code because the cost is in Postgres itself and nothing in our code can avoid it. Deleting a database forces the whole server to flush everything it holds to disk and wait for it; the suite deletes about a hundred databases per run. Measured, three simultaneous runs: with these settings on, 65 to 68 test files failed per run while every assertion passed; with the harness changes above but the settings unchanged, 15 to 16; with the settings off as well, zero.
The trade is crash-safety this server does not have any use for. It holds throwaway suite databases and a local development database that `pnpm db:migrate` and `pnpm db:seed` rebuild. A crash can leave it unreadable, and recovering means recreating it. **This is reversible and is the founder's to keep or drop** — without it the harness changes still cut failing files by roughly four fifths, but not to zero.
Also measured and rejected: raising the server's connection limit from 100. It is not needed once the harness stops wasting connections (peak use fell to 78 of 100), and on its own it made matters *worse* — 36 to 37 failing files, against 15 to 16 without it — because the old limit was accidentally throttling how many deletions could pile up at once.
Nearest spec: tech §2 (local architecture).

## 2026-09-07 — R-TESTDB — The harness holds one server connection per worker process, briefly, instead of three per suite
Decision: the reachability probe, creating a database and deleting it all share a single connection per test process, capped at one, handed back within half a second of going idle. Suite connections are also handed back after half a second rather than ten. The shared connection is kept on the process, not in the module, because the test runner reloads the module for every file.
Why: the server accepts a hundred clients at once and several build sessions share it. Each suite used to open three separate connection sets to the server itself, and each lingered ten seconds after its last use, so most of the server's capacity was spent on connections doing nothing. Once the limit is reached the server refuses everything, which shows up as unrelated test files failing. Measured: refusals across three simultaneous runs fell from 135 to zero, and peak connection use from 100 of 100 to 78.
Nearest spec: none.

## 2026-09-07 — R-TESTDB — A database that is there but will not take a connection stops counting as "no database"
Decision: a suite skips only when nothing is listening on the port at all. Every other answer — out of connection slots, still starting, password refused — now fails the suite, in CI and locally alike.
Why: the harness skips database-backed suites when there is no Postgres, so the unit tests can be run without Docker. But any error counted as "no Postgres", so a server that was merely overloaded silently removed whole suites from the run and the run still reported green. Measured on the unfixed harness: one run left 49 of 279 files skipped and 574 tests unexecuted, and reported nothing wrong about them. That is a worse failure than a red one, because nobody goes looking. This is also what makes the ten-run measurement for this card honest: no run can now reach green by quietly not running.
Nearest spec: none. Same reasoning as the CI guard already in that function.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SESSION-PRUNE — A lapsed session goes by its own date, and the sweep clears it last
Decision: the nightly retention sweep gains one step — delete every row in `sessions` (one row per signed-in browser) whose own lapse date has passed. It is written as the last of the sweep's prunes, deliberately, and the code says so.
Why: the step is the sweep's only piece of pure housekeeping. Nothing is promised to anybody about when a lapsed session's row disappears — a lapsed session already cannot sign anyone in, because the lookup checks the date. The two steps that run before it are promises with deadlines: erasing an account a merchant asked to have deleted a week ago, and honouring a store's redaction request. The sweep's steps are plain sequential awaits and none of them catches its own failure, so ordering is what decides who pays for a failure; last means a broken `DELETE` on this table costs the night nothing that was owed to anyone. Proved by a test that makes that delete throw and then checks the deleted account was erased anyway. Wrapping it in a `try`/`catch` instead was rejected: it would be the only step in the file that swallows its own error, and a session prune that fails silently every night is a table growing with nobody told.
Deleting by the row's own date rather than by age is forced, not chosen: a session lasts a month from sign-in, so "older than N days" would sign merchants out with days still to run. Tested from both sides — one that lapsed a minute ago goes, one that lapses tomorrow stays.
Nearest spec: main §14.6 (retention).

## 2026-09-07 — R-SESSION-PRUNE — The delete lives beside the other prunes, not with the session repository
Decision: `pruneExpiredSessions` is added to `packages/db/src/repositories/lifecycle.ts`, alongside the prunes for sign-in links and cached vendor answers, rather than to the sessions repository that `R-REVOKE` created.
Why: that file is where every retention delete already lives, including the one for sign-in links, which has its own repository file for exactly the same reason and is not in it. The sessions repository is the code a signed-in request runs; a nightly table-wide delete is not that, and the split keeps the every-request file to the every-request query. No behaviour turns on this.
Nearest spec: none.
## 2026-09-07 — R-GATE-LANG — Removing the four word lists also removes the two other checks that were built on them
Decision: the whole `CheckableLexicon` goes, not just the four lists the founder named. `lexiconFor`, the English word lists and every branch that asked "do we have a list for this language?" are deleted. Three checks change as a result, and only the first was the founder's subject:
(a) **The citation check** stops requiring a citation on a superlative, an absolute, an attributed statement or a comparison. Its figure-based half — numbers, measurements, percentages, durations — is untouched and still refuses an uncited figure. This is the decided change.
(b) **The assertion-strength check** loses its absolute-language half: "always sheds water" resting on a middling claim, and an absolute stated about a piece of advice, are no longer refused for free. What survives is the rule that a specific figure may not rest on a low-confidence claim, which is found by shape and needed no list.
(c) **The self-contradiction pass** now extracts only figures. Advice pointing two ways in two places ("we recommend the Alpha" early, "we would not recommend the Alpha" late) is no longer extracted, so a pair like that is no longer put to the arbiter. Contradictory *figures* — the case that pass was built for — are unaffected.
Why: (b) and (c) both read the same English absolutes/recommendation-verb lists, so they could not survive the removal; keeping either would have left exactly the branch the card's done-when forbids ("nothing anywhere still branches on whether a lexicon exists for a language"), and would have kept an English store held to a bar a Danish store never was — the asymmetry the founder chose to end. The alternative — keep the lists for (b) and (c) while dropping them from (a) — was rejected as reintroducing the same problem under a different name. Both (b) and (c) already did nothing at all for a non-English store, recorded in the 2026-09-03 T4.4 entry, so this levels down to what every non-English store already had rather than inventing a new gap. The strength rule (b) survives as an instruction in the writing prompt, which already carried it; nothing replaces (c).
Nearest spec: main §8.3, §8.4; `docs/content-pointers.md` §3, §8; founder decision "The citation word lists go" (2026-09-04); invariant 11.

## 2026-09-07 — R-GATE-LANG — The prompt describes each kind of claim and gives English examples, rather than listing words to avoid
Decision: `draft.v2.md` names the four kinds of claim that need a citation — superlative, absolute, attributed statement, comparison — says what each one *does* rather than which words spell it, and says the rule applies "whatever language you are writing in". English examples are given, explicitly labelled as illustration of the category rather than as the set to match. The existing absolute-language paragraph, which was a bare list of thirteen English words, is rewritten the same way.
Why: the founder's instruction is to move the rule into the prompt, and the failure being fixed is that a rule expressed as English vocabulary only works in English. A prompt listing words would reproduce that: a model told to avoid "always, never, must" has been told about English, whatever language it is writing. Describing the category and marking the examples as examples is what makes the instruction carry across. Examples were kept rather than dropped because a category named with nothing concrete beside it is read loosely; the risk they carry — a model treating them as the whole set — is what the "rather than looking for the English examples" clause is there to head off. This is not a deterministic list reintroduced: nothing in the product matches against these words.
Nearest spec: main §8.3; founder decision "The citation word lists go" (2026-09-04).

## 2026-09-07 — R-GATE-LANG — Which version of the writing prompt the product asks with is named in one place
Decision: `DRAFT_PROMPT_MAJOR_VERSION` lives in `packages/jobs/src/generation/prompts.ts` and is used by the web app's composition root, by every pipeline test and by both chaos scenarios that build a generation run. It replaces the literal `1` those eight call sites each held.
Why: `draft.v1.md` stays on disk for ever, so a bump that misses a call site does not fail — it quietly leaves that caller writing with the old prompt, and a test or chaos scenario exercising a prompt the product no longer ships proves nothing about the product. It sits in the jobs package rather than beside the web config (where the equivalent constant for the recommendation prompt sits) only because the tests and chaos scenarios that need it cannot import from `apps/web`.
Nearest spec: tech §1.4 (prompts are versioned files, every artefact stamped); `packages/llm/prompts/README.md`.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SIGNOUT — The sign-out lives in the app frame's account menu, not in Settings
Decision: the control that signs a merchant out sits in the toolbar at the top of every signed-in screen, in a small account menu beside the notification bell. It is not on any Settings screen.
Why: ui §9 opens by saying its own list of settings controls is exhaustive — "if a control isn't here, it doesn't exist" — and it does not name a sign-out. A test transcribed that list from the spec by hand and asserts the Settings screens render exactly it, so adding a sign-out there would have had to break that test to land, and the test is right. §1, which describes the frame around every signed-in screen, is not written as a closed list, and the frame's toolbar already exists for exactly this ("the bell, the avatar and anything else a screen wants in the top strip"). The string catalogue has also carried an unused `shell.account` — "Account" — since the shell was built, which is where that label now goes. **This is a placement decision the specs do not make, and it is user-visible.**
Nearest spec: ui §1 (the shell), ui §9 (Settings, exhaustive).

## 2026-09-07 — R-SIGNOUT — The panel says sign-out reaches every browser, before the button is pressed
Decision: the account menu opens onto one sentence and then the button: "Signing out ends your session in every browser you are signed in on, not only this one." New copy, in `packages/ui/strings/en.json`, proposed by this card — the specs write no wording for it.
Why: `R-REVOKE` decided yesterday that pressing sign out ends every session the account has, which is not what a sign-out button usually does. A merchant signing out on a phone is also signing their desktop out, and told nothing, would discover that by accident later. Saying it afterwards in a toast is too late to be a choice, so it is said before. Deliberately plain rather than reassuring: it is a capability ("my laptop is gone — stop") as much as a warning.
Nearest spec: main Appendix A holds no string for this; ui §9.4 and main §4.1 are silent on sign-out entirely.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SIGNOUT — The menu opens with no JavaScript; only the sign-out itself needs scripts
Decision: the account menu is a native `details`/`summary` disclosure rather than a panel opened by React state. The sign-out button inside it does need scripts.
Why: the same reason the navigation rail's "More" control gives — a control that is invisible until a bundle loads is worse than one that opens and does nothing. It also means the sentence above is in the page's markup whether or not the panel is open, so a test can read it without a browser, which matters here because this repository has no browser-DOM test environment. The sign-out is two requests (fetch the anti-forgery token, then spend it), so it cannot be a plain form post; a merchant whose scripts never arrived sees the explanation and an inert button.
Nearest spec: ui §1.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SIGNOUT — The two sign-out requests are ours, not the sign-in library's browser helper
Decision: `packages/ui/src/shell/signout.ts` performs the exchange itself — `GET /api/auth/csrf`, then `POST /api/auth/signout` with the token — instead of calling `signOut()` from `next-auth/react`.
Why: the library's helper needs a `window` and the global `fetch` before it can be called at all, which makes the exchange impossible to drive in a test, and it would put the sign-in library inside the shared component package that every screen imports. Fifteen lines against those two costs. The addresses and the shapes are still entirely the library's; nothing here decides anything about them.
Nearest spec: tech §3 (session-cookie auth); main §4.1.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SIGNOUT — A refused sign-out is detected by where it says to go, not by its status
Decision: `requestSignOut` reports failure when the library answers with a destination inside its own `/api/auth/` routes, as well as on a bad status or a dead network.
Why: Auth.js does not use an error status when it rejects a sign-out — an anti-forgery token that does not match its cookie produces **200** and names its own error page as where to go next. Code that trusted the status would tell a merchant they had been signed out of every browser while every session still stood, which is the worst possible thing to be wrong about here. A sign-out that actually happened never lands back inside the sign-in routes. (The library's own browser helper has this blind spot; ours does not.) Two tests hold it: one against a canned answer, one against the real handlers with a tampered token, which also asserts the session survives.
Nearest spec: none — library behaviour.

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — Two free checks were lost with the word lists, and the loss is accepted
Decision: removing the English word lists also removed two checks that read them — the assertion-strength check no longer refuses an absolute like "always sheds water" resting on a middling claim, and the self-contradiction pass no longer catches an article that recommends a product early and advises against it late. **Accepted.** Neither is rebuilt and neither is added to the prompt.
Why: the founder was shown the consequence, which their original decision text did not mention. Both checks already did **nothing at all** for a non-English store, so removing them levels English down to what every other language already had rather than opening a new gap. Drafts that used to fail those checks for free now reach the paid judge instead — slower and costlier per rejection, not less safe. The lane surfaced this rather than quietly absorbing it, which is why it could be decided.
Nearest spec: main §8.3, §8.4.

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — The writing prompt must name the fields its own answer schema demands
Decision: carded. The article-writing prompt never mentions four fields its schema requires — the meta description, the sections, and two product-reference fields — so the model fills them with nothing told to it about what they are for.
Why: **this is the same defect that produced an unreviewed model-written sentence on the recommendation card**, in a different prompt, and it was found the same way: a lane wrote the test that holds a prompt against its schema, watched it fail, and **removed the test rather than smuggle in the fix**, because telling the writer more changes the articles it produces. That was the right call and it is why this is a decision rather than a repair.
Nearest spec: main §9.2; invariant 25 (prompts as versioned files).

## 2026-09-07 — INTEGRATOR — A fifth reporter failing towards "fine", found by a peer session and verified here
Decision: recorded, and added to `T10.2`'s named work. `pnpm stubs:report` lists three stand-ins. **One is stale bookkeeping** — `LlmJudgeLite` is constructed in production at `apps/web/app/api/recommendations/_lib/config.ts:152` and its line in the report script was never removed. **The other two are real and serious**: `apps/web/instrumentation-node.ts:63` calls `registerOpsTasks(db, { analytics })` and passes neither a judge nor a publishing counter, so the automatic trips for judge rejection rate and publish failure rate report "unmeasurable" and **cannot fire in a deployed process**.
Why it belongs on the list: the stale entry and the two real ones sit in the same report, in the same shape, and **nothing distinguishes them** — so a reader who dismisses one dismisses all three. Verified independently by the integrator before recording; the peer session (`sortiva-a8`) found it while compiling a deploy-readiness report and reported it read-only.
Nearest spec: main §14.5 (auto-trips); build plan §6 `T10.1`, `T10.2`.
## 2026-09-07 — R-DISMISS-CALENDAR — Dismissal calls the calendar's own cancel operation rather than writing to the calendar's rows
Decision: saying "not interested" to a suggestion runs the same operation the calendar's own "delete this day" button runs. Both live in one function in the calendar's own module (`packages/jobs/src/generation/veto-topic.ts`), and the Opportunities route calls it; nothing on the opportunities side updates a calendar row itself.
Why: the founder's decision says dismissal and the calendar's veto are one act rather than two, and the code should say the same thing. The calendar's veto already dismissed the suggestion behind the day, so the two operations were half-merged already — only the other direction was missing. Building a second, quieter cancellation path on the opportunities side would have given the calendar two sets of rules for the same act, which is how the original defect happened. The practical consequence: dismissing a suggestion now also records its search term on the not-interested list, which is what stops replenishment booking the same article again next month. That is not a widening of dismissal — without it the cancellation is only a delay.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §8.7; invariant 15.

## 2026-09-07 — R-DISMISS-CALENDAR — Cancelling a day is one transaction, and a publication landing at the same moment takes the whole thing with it
Decision: the four steps of a cancellation — the day's state, the draft, the not-interested record, the suggestion's own status — are one database transaction. If the draft cannot be discarded because something moved it, or a publication of that article is already claimed and unconfirmed, nothing at all happens and the caller is told it lost.
Why: the window being raced is real and is the expensive one. A publication writes a claim row *before* it sends anything to the merchant's shop and only writes the article down as published *after* the shop confirms, so for that stretch the post can be live on the merchant's site while our own row still calls it a draft. Applying half a cancellation across that window produces exactly the thing this card exists to remove: the suggestion gone, the calendar saying "called off", and the article on the blog. Previously the four steps were four independent writes and the second one's zero-row result was read as "there was no draft", which is indistinguishable from "somebody published it a millisecond ago".
Cost: a cancellation is refused while a publication of that same article is unconfirmed. A worker that dies mid-publish leaves such a claim behind, and the recovery sweep resolves it within about fifteen minutes; until then the merchant is told to try again rather than told something untrue.
Nearest spec: main §8.7 (lock semantics), §14.3.1, §14.3.7; invariant 15, 19.

## 2026-09-07 — R-DISMISS-CALENDAR — A day whose article has already gone out is not "still booked", and dismissal is not refused for it
Decision: the lookup that asks "has this suggestion booked a day we can still call off" excludes a day whose article is already published. Such a suggestion is dismissed on its own, with nothing said about calling anything back.
Why: nothing in the product moves a calendar day out of `generating` when its article publishes (`R-STRANDED` reported the same gap). So on the day's state alone, one that published a fortnight ago looks identical to one being written right now. Without this distinction, every suggestion that had ever produced an article would refuse to be dismissed for ever — the merchant could never clear it off their list. The article's own row is what separates the two, and it also keeps the refusal narrow: what is refused is the *race*, not the past.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §8.7.

## 2026-09-07 — R-DISMISS-CALENDAR — An article written by a run that was already cancelled is never delivered
Decision: the query the publish hour uses to find articles ready to go out skips any whose calendar day was called off.
Why: cancelling discards the draft that exists at that moment, but a run already under way can create its article *after* the cancellation — the writing pipeline creates the article row minutes in, once the research and the evidence check are done. That article would then pass the quality bar and be published, on a day the merchant had cancelled. Discarding at the moment of cancellation cannot cover it, because there is nothing there yet to discard. One exclusion at the single point where anything is handed over covers both orderings. It also matches main §8.7 exactly: cancelling stops the *publication*; the generation cost is already spent and we absorb it.
Cost: such a run leaves a draft row nobody delivers. It is a record of spend we chose to absorb rather than a stranded piece of work — the interrupted-day sweep does not look at it either, because that sweep only looks at days still in `generating`.
Nearest spec: main §8.7, §9.1.

## 2026-09-07 — R-DISMISS-CALENDAR — A lost race is reported with the dismissal route's own conflict code, not a truer one
Decision: when a publication wins the race, `POST /api/opportunities/{id}/dismiss` answers 409 `opportunity_not_open`.
Why: the frozen route table gives this endpoint two conflict codes, `opportunity_already_updated` and `opportunity_not_open`, and neither names a publication. `opportunity_already_updated` would be actively wrong — the screen renders it as "updated by the latest scan", which is untrue. `opportunity_not_open` is the closer of the two: the suggestion is no longer something we can act on. **Flagged for the integrator**: the truthful code is `topic_already_published`, which exists in the shared enum but is not declared for this route, and amending the frozen contract is the integrator's by rule (`R-CONTRACT`).
Nearest spec: main §7.9; tech §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SIGNIN-CSRF — Signing in with Google is two requests from a button, not a form post
Decision: the "Continue with Google" control on `/signin` is a button that runs an exchange — `GET /api/auth/csrf` for the anti-forgery token, then `POST /api/auth/signin/google` spending it — and then sends the browser to the address the library names. It is no longer a `<form>` that posts to the library directly. The exchange lives in `packages/ui/src/public/signin-exchange.ts`, apart from the component, so it can be driven against the real sign-in handlers without a browser.
Why: the form did not work. The sign-in library refuses a post carrying no anti-forgery token, so every press on a deployed server landed the visitor on the library's own error page and nobody could get into the product at all. A form submission cannot fetch a token first, so the control has to be a button. This is the identical shape `R-SIGNOUT` chose two entries above, for the identical reason, and its entries there give the fuller argument against reaching for the library's own browser helper instead.
Cost, stated plainly: a visitor whose scripts never arrived now presses a button that does nothing, where before they pressed one that failed visibly. That is not a regression in what works — signing in without scripts did not work either — but it is a change in how the failure looks. The alternative that would preserve a no-JavaScript sign-in is rendering the token into a hidden field from the server, which is a second, different mechanism for the same job; the card ruled that out explicitly.
Nearest spec: main §4.1; ui §2 (the sign-in screen) writes no wording or mechanism for this.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SIGNIN-CSRF — The sign-in exchange is its own module rather than shared with sign-out
Decision: `signin-exchange.ts` repeats the two-request shape that `packages/ui/src/shell/signout.ts` already has, rather than both calling one shared helper.
Why: the two exchanges answer differently — signing out succeeds by staying on our own site, signing in succeeds by leaving it for Google — so a shared helper would be a function with the interesting part passed in, which is not obviously smaller than two readable modules. Weighed against that: factoring one out means editing a file another card landed hours ago, and this card was told to change nothing that landed with it. **Flagged, not settled**: if a third such exchange appears, the shared helper is the right answer and this note is the reason to do it then.
Nearest spec: none — code organisation.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SIGNIN-CSRF — Two new sentences on the sign-in screen
Decision: new copy in `packages/ui/strings/en.json` — "Taking you to Google…" while the handshake starts, and "We could not start sign-in. Please try again." when it does not. Proposed by this card; the specs write no wording for either.
Why: the press now does something that takes a moment and can fail, where a form post either navigated or did not. Without the first the button looks unresponsive; without the second a failure is completely silent, which is what the old broken behaviour effectively was. Wording follows the sign-out control's failure line rather than inventing a register.
Nearest spec: main Appendix A holds no string for either; ui §2.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SIGNIN-CSRF — The fixture-backed sign-in stub answers in JSON, because the real library's refusal is a destination
Decision: the browser-flow mock server (`apps/web/e2e/mock-api-server.ts`) now answers `POST /api/auth/signin/google` with `{ url }` when the request asks for an answer rather than a redirect, and keeps its old redirect for anything that does not.
Why: the mock stands in for Google, which this repository has no credentials for. The screen now has to read *where* the library says to go in order to know whether the press worked — a refusal is a 200 naming an error page — so a stub that only ever redirected would leave the screen unable to tell success from failure. That would be a difference from the real thing rather than a shortcut past it.
Nearest spec: none — test fixture.

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — R-PAGE-GONE-WRITE — The walk stamps every page it sees, rather than gaining a column for it
Decision: the store-page walk records that it saw a page by writing `store_pages.last_synced_at` for every page the store served it, changed or not. No new column.
Why: the walk deliberately writes only pages whose content moved (`writeChanged`, `packages/core/src/inventory/sync.ts`) so an unchanged page does not look edited to everything watching its checksum and does not re-run the paid analyses hanging off one. That left `last_synced_at` meaning *last changed*, not *last seen* — and the obvious implementation of this card, marking whatever the walk did not restamp, would have marked **every unchanged page in every store as deleted**, plausibly and silently. Something had to record "seen" separately from "changed", and this is the only shape that needs no migration.
Rejected: a separate `last_seen_at` column — the correct separation, but a feature card may not add a migration, so the card would have waited for a schema wave while the product went on recommending improvements to pages merchants had deleted. Also rejected: recording each walk's full list of addresses, which needs a new table and has to survive a walk resumed across many job runs.
Cost the founder accepted: one extra timestamp update per batch, and `last_synced_at` changes meaning. That second half is a repair rather than a cost — the Products screen already shows this column to merchants labelled "Last synced" (`packages/ui/src/products/ProductsScreen.tsx`, `products.table.col.lastSynced`), which is what it will now actually hold. **Anyone later "fixing" the stamping as a stray write would reopen this card's defect.**
Nearest spec: main §12.3 (content inventory), §14.1 (the reconciliation sweep); `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-03 "A deleted store page gets a status field".

## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-WRITE — Only a walk that reached the end of the store may mark anything gone, and it judges by when that walk began
Decision: `syncInventoryBatch` marks pages gone only on the batch where the source reports no further cursor, and it compares against the moment the *walk* started, carried forward in the cursor under `walkStartedAt`. A batch that hands back a cursor marks nothing; a webhook re-read (`syncInventoryRecords`, `resyncInventoryTargets`) marks nothing ever.
Why: this is the founder's own condition from 2026-09-03, which rejected inferring deletion from a walk because an interrupted one would mark live pages gone. The completion signal already existed and was thrown away — `runInventorySync` distinguishes `more`, `done` and `disconnected` and reports it only to a log line. Judging by the walk's start rather than its end matters because a large store is walked over many job runs across more than a day: a page read correctly on the first batch would look stale by the last one and be marked gone. The start time rides in the cursor because that is the only thing that survives between runs; the source ignores keys it does not know and rebuilds its own cursor, so it is re-attached each batch.
Proved by mutation, not by assertion: pointing the sweep at the finish time, sweeping on an unfinished walk, and stamping only changed pages each fail a named test. The third is the trap above.
Nearest spec: main §14.1; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-03 "A deleted store page gets a status field".

## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-WRITE — A page the walk finds is live again, and our own articles are never marked gone
Decision: recording a page as seen also returns it to `live`. And `markStorePagesGoneNotSeenSince` skips rows of type `article_ours`.
Why: two holes that would otherwise be permanent. A page deleted and then restored carries the checksum it always had, so nothing would upsert it and it would stay marked gone for ever — being served is what makes a page live, so the same write that records seeing it is the right place. And our own published articles are our record of what we delivered: a store on export delivery has them nowhere the walk can look, so the walk not finding one is evidence of nothing. Nothing writes `article_ours` rows today, so this guards a hole before anything can fall into it rather than fixing a live fault.
Nearest spec: main §9.5 (export delivery), §12.3.

## 2026-09-07 — INTEGRATOR PLACEMENT — R-PAGE-GONE-WRITE was built from the Lane B worktree in Lane C's inventory files
Decision: the card was dispatched to Lane B, but every file it changes belongs to Lane C under build plan §3 (`packages/core/inventory`, `packages/jobs/inventory`). The integrator authorised the cross-lane touch explicitly, scoped to `core/inventory/{sync,ports}.ts` and its test, `jobs/inventory/tasks.ts`, and `db/repositories/inventory.ts`, after checking that Lane C's uncommitted work touched none of them.
Why: recorded because the constitution calls touching another lane's directory a review failure, so an authorised exception must be visible rather than inferred from a diff. The lane assignment was a slip at card-writing time; the sibling card `R-PAGE-GONE-READ` stays Lane C's and was not touched. It also surfaced a real gap: `packages/db/src/repositories/*` is absent from the §3 ownership table altogether, and the integrator is adding the rule that a repository file belongs to the lane owning the domain it serves.
Nearest spec: build plan §3; `CLAUDE.md` rule 5.
## 2026-09-07 — R-OVERRIDE-STATE — The publish hour stops asking about the override flag, and asks the state instead
Decision: `articlesReadyForDelivery` — the one query that answers "which finished articles go out today" — now has two arms, both naming a state. An article in `cleared_to_deliver` goes out, full stop; an article in `draft` goes out only if the quality bar's own pass is recorded against its calendar day. The two things it used to also accept are gone: the permanent `published_via_override` flag on the article, and a gate decision whose outcome is the string `overridden`.
Why: the flag's meaning is "keep this article out of the data we tune the quality bar against". It never meant "cleared to publish", and reading it as though it did was a workaround for there being no state that said so — the third arm was added for the same reason, as a placeholder for an override route that has never been built. Now that the state exists, one of the two must be the answer, and leaving both means two ways to make an article deliverable that can disagree with each other. The state is the one a person actually sets.
Consequence worth knowing: writing an `overridden` gate decision no longer makes anything deliverable on its own. `OVERRIDE_GATE_OUTCOME` is kept as the audit-trail string it always was; when the "publish anyway" route is built it should record that decision *and* move the article, and only the move decides delivery.
Nearest spec: main §8.6, §9.3; invariant 12; DECISIONS 2026-09-04 FOUNDER "An overridden article gets its own state".

## 2026-09-07 — R-OVERRIDE-STATE — No rows are migrated, because no row outside a test can exist
Decision: existing articles sitting in `draft` with `published_via_override` set are left exactly where they are, and no data migration was written.
Why: not a judgement call about risk — there are none. The only code in the product that ever sets that flag is `markArticleOverridden`, and nothing calls it outside its own tests: the route a merchant would press, `POST /api/articles/{articleId}/publish-anyway`, is declared in the frozen route table and has no implementation behind it. So no merchant has ever overridden anything, and the set of rows a migration would move is empty. Had any existed, they would now be undeliverable, which is why this is stated rather than assumed.
Nearest spec: build plan §6 `R-OVERRIDE-STATE` ("do not migrate existing rows unless you can argue it").

## 2026-09-07 — R-OVERRIDE-STATE — Both hand-over writes accept the new state; the move into review deliberately does not
Decision: the two guarded updates that turn a cleared article into a published one — `markArticleDelivered` (export) and `markArticleAutoPublished` (posting to the merchant's shop) — now match `draft` **or** `cleared_to_deliver`. `markArticleInReview` stays guarded to `draft` alone.
Why: the read decides *whether* an article goes out; these two writes are only the hand-over, and a guard that still said `draft` would find nothing and report a lost race every time a merchant overruled the gate. The review guard is the opposite case and is load-bearing: it is what makes "an overruled article never reaches a review queue" true of every future caller rather than of the one code path that exists today. The founder's reasoning is that a merchant who has just overruled the quality bar has already made the decision review exists to ask for.
Nearest spec: main §8.6, §9.3; invariant 15.

## 2026-09-07 — R-OVERRIDE-STATE — An article approved after review still lands in `draft`, unchanged
Decision: `approveArticleGuarded` — the merchant saying "keep it" about a draft they were shown — continues to move the article back to `draft` rather than to `cleared_to_deliver`, even though that state's name fits it too.
Why: the card is one half of one founder decision, about articles published over a quality rejection. An approved article's calendar day carries a recorded pass from the quality bar, so the delivery read can already tell it apart from an un-graded row and nothing is ambiguous. Moving it as well would be a second behaviour change nobody asked for, in the path that carries almost all normal traffic.
Nearest spec: main §9.3; build plan §6 `R-OVERRIDE-STATE`.

## 2026-09-07 — R-OVERRIDE-STATE — FLAGGED: the frozen API contract and the frontend's article type do not know the new state
Decision: `articleSummarySchema.state` in `packages/core/src/api/schemas.ts` and `ArticleState` in `packages/ui/src/content/types.ts` still list five values and were left alone.
Why: neither is Lane D's to change — the first is the frozen route contract (`R-CONTRACT` is the integrator's), the second is Lane F's. Nothing breaks today: no route serialises an article summary, so the schema is declared and unconsumed, and the articles screen renders from fixtures. But an article in `cleared_to_deliver` would fail that schema's validation the moment somebody builds the list endpoint, and the screen's state filter would have no row for it. Whoever builds the articles list needs both widened first, or needs a deliberate decision to map the state to something else at the boundary.
Nearest spec: ui §7; tech §3; build plan §6 `R-CONTRACT`.

## 2026-09-07 — R-OVERRIDE-STATE — FLAGGED: the export download serves any article with a body, graded or not
Decision: left as found, and reported rather than fixed.
Why: `buildBundleForArticle` — what runs when a merchant presses download on an export-mode store — looks up the article and refuses only if it has no body. It never asks whether the article was cleared to go out, so a half-written draft from a run that died before the judge can be downloaded by article id. This predates the card and is not "which articles go out today" (it is the merchant naming one article rather than the publish hour choosing one), so fixing it here would be a behaviour change outside the card. It is the one remaining path to a finished article that does not consult `articlesReadyForDelivery`.
Nearest spec: main §9.5; invariant 21.
## 2026-09-07 — R-JUDGE-COPY — The judge's model is decided in code, and the environment is ignored rather than refused
Decision: `ANTHROPIC_MODEL_SONNET` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL_HAIKU` — the two variables that pin a model per environment — no longer reach the draft judge. A new `resolveModelForCallType` in `packages/llm/src/models.ts` is now the only place the client resolves a model, and it hands the judge the id from the registry without looking at the environment at all. Setting the variable is silently ignored for that one call, not turned into an error.
Why: the founder's decision says the override mechanism stays for every other tier, and refusing outright could not have delivered that. The variable is per *tier*, not per call, and the judge shares its tier with the writer, the persona, the seed keywords and the claim plan — so throwing when it is set would have taken down five legitimate uses to protect one. Ignoring it for the judge alone leaves the legitimate use working and makes the dangerous one a no-op. The visible consequence is deliberate: pinning the strong tier now moves the writer and leaves the grader where it is, which is the safe direction — a grader that thinks *harder* than the writer is still a check.
Cost: an operator who sets the variable expecting the judge to move gets no error, and would only find out by reading `.env.example` or the resolver. The comment in `.env.example` now says which calls the variable reaches and that no variable moves the judge.
Nearest spec: main §8.4, §14.4; invariant 11.

## 2026-09-07 — R-JUDGE-COPY — The English rule lives in the grading prompt, at a new version, and nothing checks the answer afterwards
Decision: a new prompt file `packages/llm/prompts/judge.v2.md` — v1 plus one instruction: write the per-criterion explanations in English, always, including when the article being graded is in another language; grade the article itself in its own language and never translate it first. `JUDGE_PROMPT_MAJOR_VERSION` in `packages/jobs/src/generation/prompts.ts` names the version the product asks with, replacing the literal `1` its eight call sites each held, exactly as `DRAFT_PROMPT_MAJOR_VERSION` did for the writing prompt. Nothing inspects the sentences that come back.
Why: prompt files are never edited in place, so the change is a new version. And there is no second place the rule could be enforced: the grader's sentence is passed on word for word, and a check that rejected a Danish one would have to either pause the article (punishing the merchant for our prompt) or quietly translate it (inventing text and attributing it to the grader). Neither is better than asking once, clearly, in the only instruction the grader receives. The judge's criteria, its floors and what it is shown are untouched.
Cost: the sentences the grader sends back to the writer as revision instructions are now English about a draft in the store's language. That is a change from before and it is not obviously wrong — the writing prompt already works across languages — but it is a behaviour nobody asked for and it is recorded here rather than left to be noticed.
Nearest spec: main §8.4, §8.6; invariant 8 (which the founder's decision deliberately excepts for this one sentence).

## 2026-09-07 — R-JUDGE-COPY — The grading eval set moves to the version the product ships
Decision: `packages/llm/eval/judge.eval/eval.json` now names `judge.v2`, so `pnpm eval` grades the prompt the product actually asks with.
Why: the eval exists to measure what the real model does with the real prompt, and the twenty hand-scored cases include Danish drafts precisely because language matters here. Leaving it on v1 would have left the quality gate's own measurement pointed at a prompt nobody ships — the same failure the writing prompt's version constant was introduced to prevent. The gold scores are unaffected by the change, which touches the language of the explanation and not the scoring; **this was not re-measured, because `pnpm eval` calls the vendor and is not part of this session's gate.**
Nearest spec: main §8.5 (calibration); tech §1.4.

## 2026-09-07 — R-JUDGE-COPY — This card edits Lane D's directories, on the card's own authority
Decision: `R-JUDGE-COPY` is assigned to a Lane G session and its work is in `packages/llm`, `packages/jobs/src/generation`, `packages/core/src/gates/gate3` and `apps/web/app/api/articles/_lib/config.ts` — Lane D's and the platform packages'. Done as assigned and recorded here rather than negotiated, following the precedent `R-REVOKE` set on 2026-09-07: where the lane table and a founder card assignment disagree, the assignment is the newer instruction.
Why: there is no version of "the judge cannot be downgraded and answers in English" that does not change the model client and the grading prompt. Files touched are listed in the session report. No integrator-resolved file and no migration was touched.
Nearest spec: build plan §3 (lane ownership); CLAUDE.md prime directive 5.
## 2026-09-07 — R-CREATE-COMPLETE — The suggestion and the calendar day are two cards, and only the suggestion half is done here
Decision: publishing now finishes the *suggestion* on the Opportunities screen. It still does not move the *calendar day* out of "Generating", so the Content calendar keeps reading "Generating" for past published days. Not fixed here, reported instead.
Why: they look like one defect and share one cause, but the calendar half needs an answer nobody has given. The state it would move to (`published`) does exist in the calendar's own state list, so contrary to the card's note **no migration and no new state are needed for the ordinary case** — the blocker is a different one. A merchant may overrule a quality rejection and publish anyway; that day is sitting in `rejected_by_gate`, and main §8.7 draws `rejected_by_gate` and `published` as two *alternative* endings rather than a path from one to the other. So closing the calendar half means deciding what an overridden day says it is — and the product's rule that override-published work is shown segregated from the rest (invariant 12) is exactly what makes that a founder's answer rather than a lane's. On top of which the calendar's state machine is another lane's, and the pattern set a day earlier by `R-DISMISS-CALENDAR` is that the opportunities side calls an operation the calendar owns; no such operation exists — nothing in the product has ever written a topic's state as `published`.
Cost: the sibling defect stays. The shape it needs is a guarded move from `generating` and `in_review` to `published` at the same two places this card writes to, plus an answer for `rejected_by_gate`.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §8.7; invariant 12, 15.

## 2026-09-07 — R-CREATE-COMPLETE — The completion happens inside the two writes that publish an article, not at the places that call them
Decision: `markArticleDelivered` (the article becomes downloadable for a store that publishes it itself) and `markArticleAutoPublished` (the post is confirmed on the merchant's own Shopify blog) each now run their own guarded update and the suggestion's completion in one transaction.
Why: those two are the only places in the product where an article's state becomes `published`, and four different routes reach them — the daily publish hour, the post to the shop, the recovery sweep re-sending a post the shop said it never got, and the same sweep adopting a post it found already there. Attaching the completion to the call sites would have covered whichever ones were noticed and left the rest with the original defect; a lane a month from now adding a fifth route gets it for free. One transaction rather than two writes because the gap between them is the defect in miniature: a worker dying in it leaves the article on the merchant's site with the suggestion still saying it has not been written.
The trade: `markArticleDelivered` and `markArticleAutoPublished` return more than an article row now (the article, plus the suggestion they closed or `undefined`), so their callers say out loud when a suggestion had already moved on rather than the repository swallowing it. That rippled into two of another lane's tests, which used the hand-over as a way to *stage* a published article and now stage it with a direct write instead.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §14.3.1; invariant 15, 18.

## 2026-09-07 — R-CREATE-COMPLETE — A publication finishes a suggestion in any status it is still open in, and stops silently if it is not
