Decision: the completion is guarded on the same "still open" set the two existing completions use, and a zero-row answer is logged and otherwise ignored. It never fails the publication.
Why: the row is normally `scheduled` when its article goes out, but it need not be — a merchant can dismiss it, a scan can expire it, while the article is in the writing pipeline. Naming the whole open set rather than `scheduled` alone means the completion states the truth main §7.9 states ("`completed` — content published") for every row a publication can legitimately find, and refuses by construction for the three it must not touch: `dismissed`, `completed` and `expired` are all outside the set and none of them has a drawn edge to `completed`, so the graph would throw if this ever tried. Not failing the publication is the important half: the article is on the merchant's site by the time this runs, and unwinding that to protect a status would be the worse of the two wrongs.
The moment is stamped in `applied_at`, matching what the other two completions do, so a finished row says when it finished. Both existing readers of that column filter to OPTIMIZE work, so nothing counts a published article as advice a merchant applied.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §9.6.2; invariant 15.

## 2026-09-07 — R-CREATE-COMPLETE — `R-DISMISS-CALENDAR`'s carve-out for an already-published day now only ever applies to old rows
Decision: left in place, and its test now stages its published article with a direct write rather than through the publish hand-over.
Why: that card decided a suggestion whose article has already gone out is dismissed on its own rather than refused, precisely because nothing closed such a suggestion and a merchant would otherwise have been stuck with it on their screen for ever. With publication closing it, the merchant is never offered the button in the first place — the card is gone from the screen — so the carve-out can now only be reached by a row published *before* this change. Removing it would strand exactly those rows, which is the situation it was written for.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §8.7.

## 2026-09-07 — INTEGRATOR — Six screens have no server, and the contract keeps declaring the endpoints rather than dropping them
Decision: found while building `R-CONTRACT`. Ten endpoints are declared in the frozen route table, called by live screens, and **built nowhere** — the articles library and article page, the override-publish button, both Performance screens, the Products screen, the opportunity detail drawer, and `GET`/`PATCH /api/settings`. The route table **keeps** all ten entries rather than being trimmed to what exists, and four cards (`R-API-ARTICLES`, `R-API-PRODUCTS`, `R-API-PERFORMANCE`, `R-API-SETTINGS`) build the servers behind them, one per owning lane. `R-CONTRACT` itself is narrowed to what the founder actually delegated: moving the entries whose endpoints exist at a different address, and adding the ones that were built without ever being declared.
Why: trimming the table to what exists is the tempting reading of "amend the contract to the built addresses", and it would be wrong. Those entries are the record of what six screens need; deleting them would turn a visible gap into an invisible one, and the fake server the frontend is built against is generated from that table, so the screens would break in tests as well as in production. Keeping them costs one thing — a future routes-on-disk check has to distinguish "declared and not built yet" from "declared and lost" — and that check does not exist yet; it lands with `T10.2`, which can be told about these four cards.
The reason this went unseen for the whole build is worth recording separately, because it is a pattern and not an accident: the fake server answers every **declared** address whether or not anything was built, `contracts:check` compares the table only to a generated document and never to the routes on disk, and `getJson` (`apps/web/app/(app)/_lib/api.ts:38`) returns `null` on any failure by deliberate design, so a 404 from a route that does not exist looks exactly like an account with no data. Three mechanisms, each defensible alone, and together they make a missing server render as an empty state with nothing red anywhere. **Eighth of the reporters that fail towards "fine".**
Nearest spec: build plan §3 (contracts change only through the integrator), §6 `M9` ("starts Wave 1 on MSW mocks; integration cards follow backends" — for these six the integration card never followed); tech §3.
## 2026-09-07 — R-SCANCOPY — Both screens stop naming Monday; the monthly email keeps it, deliberately
Decision: the founder's reword reaches the two sentences a *screen* shows — the Opportunities screen's empty state and the dashboard's growth card — and does not reach `email.monthlySummary.nextNone`, the equivalent sentence in the monthly summary email, which still reads "Nothing new is waiting. Your next scan runs Monday."
Why the dashboard was included though the card named one sentence: three shipped strings named Monday, and the card's own done-when is that the empty state and the header "can never contradict each other". Two of the three are screens with the same falsehood — a store is scanned on its own local Monday, and a re-queued or paused account moves even that — and fixing one screen while the other still promised Monday would have been the same defect with a smaller blast radius. Both had the next-scan timestamp already in the response they render from.
Why the email was not: an interval is computed at one moment and true only at that moment. A screen is drawn when the merchant looks at it, so "in 3 days" is correct as they read it. An email is composed when we send it and read whenever it is opened — this one is a monthly retention email that can sit unread for a week — so "in 3 days" would become newly untrue in the inbox in a way "Monday" never does. The founder's stated reason for the change was the contradiction between the Opportunities screen's header and the line beneath it; an email has no such header, so the reason does not carry across. And the facts the email is built from (`MonthlySummaryFacts` in `packages/core/src/email/summary.ts`) carry no scan timestamp at all, so making it relative would mean widening an interface another lane fills, outside this lane's directories.
**Left open for the founder, not resolved here:** the email still tells some merchants the wrong day. Making it day-agnostic without making it relative — "at your next weekly scan", say — is new quoted copy nobody has approved, so it was not invented. A test pins this sentence as the single remaining weekday in the whole catalogue so the exemption stays visible.
Nearest spec: main Appendix A; ui §5.1; tech §1 (email); invariant 24.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SCANCOPY — Four forms per surface, and the one that promises nothing
Decision: each of the two screens gets four sentences rather than one: `{days}` days out, `tomorrow`, `today`, and an `unscheduled` form that stops after "nothing open" and says nothing about timing. The `unscheduled` form is used when no next-scan date is known **and** when the date we hold has already gone by.
Why: "in 1 days" is broken English, so a singular form was unavoidable the moment the founder chose an interval; "today" is needed because a scan due later the same day is nought days away. The fourth is the important one. Guessing a next scan from the weekly cadence would have put us straight back to promising a day we do not control, and stating an interval to a date that has already passed is simply false. Saying nothing about timing is the only honest answer, and the note already rendered underneath ("The calendar keeps running underneath…") means the merchant is still not left reading it as "nothing to do", which ui §5.1 forbids.
Nearest spec: ui §5.1.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SCANCOPY — The interval counts to the date the header prints, in the server's day
Decision: the day count is a whole-calendar-day difference between two UTC dates — the day the page was drawn and the day of the next scan — not a count of 24-hour blocks. The day the page was drawn is decided by the server and threaded down as a `YYYY-MM-DD` string (`today`), the convention the dashboard already used, rather than read from the browser.
Why: the header on the same screen already prints the next-scan date, and it formats that timestamp in UTC. If the sentence below counted in any other clock the two could name different scans, which is the exact contradiction this card exists to remove. Reading the current day from the browser instead would have meant a client component rendering one sentence on the server and a different one after hydration whenever the two straddled UTC midnight.
Consequence worth stating plainly: for a store far from UTC the interval can be a day out from what their own calendar says. That is the same approximation the header has always had, and keeping the two consistent was judged more important than making either one locally exact — a merchant reading two different answers on one screen is a worse failure than a merchant reading one answer that is a day generous.
Nearest spec: ui §5.1.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SCANCOPY — Nothing computes a next-scan time, so the sentence a merchant actually reads today has no timing in it
Decision: not fixed here, recorded because the visible outcome of this card depends on it. `/api/opportunities` returns `nextScanAt: null` unconditionally (`apps/web/app/api/opportunities/_lib/handlers.ts`, with a comment saying null is the honest answer because nothing schedules a next-scan prediction anywhere). So in the live product both empty states now render the `unscheduled` form — "No open opportunities right now" and "Nothing new to act on right now." — and the day count, though built and tested, reaches no merchant until something computes that timestamp.
Why it was still worth doing: removing a sentence that is false for some stores every week is worth doing on its own, and the interval is ready the moment a real next-scan time exists. Building that prediction is Lane C's territory (the weekly scan and `signal_runs`) and was not this card's to take.
Nearest spec: main §7.5 (the weekly scan's cadence); ui §5.1.
## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-READ — Four signal inputs read only the pages the store still serves; the existing-target check deliberately reads all of them
Decision: `assembleMetadataInput`, `assembleFamilyCoverageInput`, `pageFacts` (all in `packages/jobs/src/scan/assemble.ts`) and the intent-gap shortlist (`packages/jobs/src/scan/intent-gap.ts`) now call a new `listLiveStorePages` instead of `listStorePages`. `existingTargetInputFor` keeps reading every row, including deleted ones, and a comment there says why.
Why: the split looks inconsistent and is not. Those four ask "what does this store cover?", and a page the merchant deleted is not coverage — leaving it in makes the product suggest improving a page nobody can visit, and makes a product range read as already covered so it stays quiet about writing a replacement. The existing-target check asks the opposite question, "is there a page I must not compete with?", and it answers it by reading a presence flag off the row. **Filtering deleted rows out of that one would silently undo this whole card**: a page it holds no row for is a page it has no opinion about, which it treats as still published, so every deletion would read as live again. Proved by mutation rather than argued — reverting either half fails a named test.
Rejected: making `listStorePages` itself exclude deleted pages. It would have fixed Lane E's three call sites too, but it changes what another lane's code returns while that lane is not present, and account deletion legitimately wants every row.
Nearest spec: main §7.7 (the existing-target check), §12.3 (the content inventory), §10.3 (intent gap); invariant 6.

## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-READ — A new repository read rather than a filter at each call site
Decision: `listLiveStorePages` is added to `packages/db/src/repositories/inventory.ts` beside `listStorePages`, rather than each caller filtering the rows it gets back.
Why: there were four call sites and a fifth is likely, and a filter a caller must remember is one a caller will forget — the failure would be silent and would look like a suggestion the product simply chose to make. Two named reads make the choice visible at the point of asking, and make "every page, including deleted ones" a deliberate thing to type. No behaviour turns on this beyond that.
Nearest spec: none; build plan §3 as amended today (a repository file belongs to the lane owning the domain it serves, so this file is Lane C's).
## 2026-09-07 — T7.2 — A rewrite the merchant asked for is recorded as a freshness opportunity
Decision: a request to rewrite one of our own published articles — whether the merchant pressed "Request refresh" or an improve-this-page press landed on a page we published — is written as a piece of work of type `freshness_opportunity`, pointing at the **article** rather than at the address it is published at.
Why: everything that reaches the calendar has to be a piece of work on the Opportunities list, because the calendar's own table requires one and there is no other way in. The list of work types is a fixed set in the database, only a schema-wave card may add to it, and this is a feature card. Of the types that exist, `freshness_opportunity` is the only one whose stated meaning is "an older page could become competitive again with an update" and whose stated action is a rewrite — which is exactly what a merchant pressing the button is asserting. The alternatives were both worse: reusing the striking-distance type would claim a measurement nobody made, and rewriting the existing improve-this-page suggestion's own action would change which button its card offers, which is user-visible behaviour belonging to another lane. Pointing at the article rather than the address means two presses on the same article are one piece of work rather than two rewrites of it, and that the record survives the page moving.
**This needs two sentences from the copy catalogue that do not exist yet** — `freshness_opportunity.requested` and `freshness_opportunity.our_own_article` — and a missing key renders as blank, so it is named in the session report.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.5, §10.5, §7.3 (Freshness Opportunity row), §7.9; invariant 10.

## 2026-09-07 — T7.2 — The merchant's own request is not refused for ranking too low
Decision: the weekly scan proposes a rewrite only for an article ranking in the configured band and shown at least as often as the store's middle article. A merchant pressing "Request refresh" is **not** refused for either of those. The three rules that protect them from us — the article is not live, they published it over our quality objection, a factual correction is already queued — apply to everybody, as does the cooldown.
Why: the band and the traffic floor exist to rank candidates the product proposes unprompted, out of a store's whole back catalogue, because a calendar day spent revisiting an article is a day not spent covering something new. A merchant who has gone to the article and pressed the button has already answered the question those two rules are asking. Refusing them because the article sits at position 30 would be the product overruling the person who owns the shop about their own page, with no way for them to act on the disagreement.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.5 (the scan's eligibility), §10.5 ("the 60-day cooldown and the not-override-published exclusion apply"), ui §6.3.

## 2026-09-07 — T7.2 — The cooldown starts when the rewrite reaches the merchant
Decision: the sixty-day cooldown is recorded when the rewrite is actually published or handed over, not when it is requested or scheduled — and it is recorded against the article that was **rewritten**, named by the piece of work, rather than against whichever article row the writing pipeline produced.
Why: the cooldown exists because Google takes weeks to re-read a page and form a new opinion of it. A request that the merchant then vetoes, or a draft held back for quality, must not lock an article out of being rewritten for two months on the strength of work that never reached anyone. Until this, nothing wrote that history at all: the rule was correct in tests and could never have been true in production, with no way to tell from the outside. The write reads from the articles table rather than trusting the reference, so a piece of work naming an article that no longer exists records nothing instead of failing a key check and rolling back a publication that has already happened on the merchant's shop.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.5, §14.3.7.

## 2026-09-07 — T7.2 — "Not eligible" is a 422 with its own code, not a conflict
Decision: the refresh endpoint answers a press inside the cooldown with the frozen 409 code the contract already names, and the other refusals — not live, published over our objection, correction queued — with a 422 carrying `refresh_not_eligible` and the reason. No new code was added to the frozen conflict vocabulary.
Why: that vocabulary is deliberately exactly the set of codes a mutation returns when it *loses a race*, and the screen maps each to specific copy. None of these three is a race: pressing again in a moment changes nothing, and the state that refused is not one somebody else moved the row into. The 404 for an unknown article already sets the precedent that a route may answer outside that enum at a status other than 409.
Nearest spec: tech §3; `packages/core/src/api/errors.ts`; ui §6.3.

## 2026-09-07 — T7.2 — An admitted request is ranked against the batch it arrives in, which is one
Decision: a rewrite admitted to the pool has its impact ranked over a batch of one, the same thing the daily repair pass already does when it raises a single drifted article.
Why: impact is a percentile rank within a store's own candidates of the same action, and a single request has no batch to be a percentile of. Reading every open rewrite candidate to rank against would make admitting one request a scan of the store's whole pool, and it would still be a different comparison from the one that decides anything: which rewrites actually get days is settled later, by the replenishment pass, over the whole pool at once and under the cap. See the identical treatment in the drift sweep.
Nearest spec: main §7.6, §9.6.4, §9.6.5.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PRODUCTS — The merchant's checklist is recomputed on every visit, because the scan never recorded which products fell short
Decision: `GET /api/products` builds each merchant task by repeating the scan's own reasoning against today's catalogue — which of the store's product groups the held search is about, which of their products fail the "is this product described well enough to write from" floor, and which of the ten extractable fields each one is missing — rather than reading a stored list.
Why: there is no stored list to read. A HOLD opportunity (an opportunity we believe in and will not act on, because the store's product pages do not say enough) records `products_needing_detail: 9` as an evidence fact and nothing else; the per-product shortfall exists only inside the scan's own working memory and is discarded. The alternative was to ask for a column in the next schema wave and ship the screen with an empty checklist until then.
The recomputation turned out to be the better behaviour anyway, not merely the available one: a merchant who fills in a product's material sees it leave the list on their next page load instead of waiting for the weekly scan. A test proves that specific movement rather than asserting the list's contents once.
Cost worth knowing: the two reads it needs (the store's groups, and the distilled products behind the ones the search maps to) run on every page load. Both are indexed reads on one account and neither calls a vendor or a model.
Nearest spec: main §6.3, §7.3 (the catalog richness gap row), §7.4 (HOLD); ui §7.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PRODUCTS — Only a catalogue-richness hold gets a product checklist
Decision: every open HOLD becomes a task card, but the list of products underneath it is built only for the one signal that means "the product pages do not say enough" (`catalog_richness_gap`). Any other hold renders with an empty product list.
Why: the checklist is derived from the opportunity's own reference, and for this signal that reference is the search phrase — which is what makes mapping it back to product groups possible. A future hold about something else would carry a different kind of reference behind the same field, and running the same mapping over it would produce a confident list of the wrong products. Showing none is the honest answer to "we do not know what this hold is about". Today this branch is unreachable: nothing in the product produces a HOLD from any other signal.
Nearest spec: main §7.4, §7.8.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PRODUCTS — A product nothing has read yet is shown as sparse, and it is counted
Decision: the products table lists every product in the store, including ones with no fact sheet. Such a product shows no facts, all ten fields missing, and the band `sparse`. It is counted in "products" but not in the store's own richness figure.
Why: two separate judgements, deliberately not merged. The table is the merchant's catalogue and leaving rows out of it would quietly shorten their product count to "the products we happened to have read". The richness figure is a measurement, and measuring products we have not read would drag a store's band down for our own queue depth — so it stays computed from distilled products only, which is exactly what the confirmation screen already shows.
Cost: the three bands have no fourth word for "not analysed yet", so a product still queued for distillation reads as sparse. Calling it rich would be the worse of the two errors, and the merchant sees a fact count of zero beside it.
Nearest spec: main §6.3 (richness); ui §7.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PRODUCTS — The whole catalogue is returned in one answer and the cursor is always null
Decision: `GET /api/products` returns every product with `cursor: null`, rather than a page.
Why: the contract has a cursor field but declares no query parameter to hand one back in, so nothing can ask for a second page. Worse, the screen's only filter — "show me the products we know too little about" — runs in the browser over whatever it was given, so any cap would silently hide the very products that filter exists to surface. That is the same shape of failure this card exists to repair: a screen that looks fine while it is not showing you everything.
Cost: a very large catalogue is a large response. If that becomes real, the fix is a declared query parameter and a server-side sparse filter, not a silent cap.
Nearest spec: ui §7; tech §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PRODUCTS — FLAGGED: nothing records when a merchant task was finished, so the "completed" section can never fill
Decision: `completedAt` is always null. Only open holds are returned.
Why: a hold that the merchant resolved leaves as an expiry whose recorded reason is "the evidence no longer holds" — the same reason produced when the search simply lost its volume, or the keyword was removed. Reading that as "you completed this" would congratulate merchants for work they never did. The screen's completed-tasks section (ui §7: "Completed tasks collapse with the date and, once the opportunity proceeds, a link to what it became") therefore stays empty in the live product.
What it would take: something at expiry time that distinguishes "the catalogue improved and this can now proceed" from every other reason the evidence stopped holding, plus a stamp for when. That is the scan's own territory, not this card's.
Nearest spec: main §7.9; ui §7.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PRODUCTS — A store with no Shopify connection gets an empty admin link rather than a guessed one
Decision: each product on a task card carries a deep link into the merchant's Shopify admin, built from the shop handle on their live connection. With no connection — or a handle that does not look like one — the link is the empty string.
Why: the screen already refuses to render any address that is not an HTTPS Shopify admin one and falls back to a plain row, so an empty string lands exactly where it should. Guessing an address for a store we are not connected to would be inventing somewhere to send them.
Nearest spec: main §6.2; ui §7.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PRODUCTS — The test that seeds a quarantined product description is added to the quarantine allowlist
Decision: `apps/web/app/api/products/_lib/products-read.test.ts` joins the seven files permitted to name `raw_body_html` — the merchant's own marketing copy, which is stored but never allowed to flow into anything we write.
Why: the test stores a description on a product and then asserts that none of it appears in the bytes `GET /api/products` sends back. Proving the description never reaches a merchant-facing response requires putting one there first, which is the same reason the distillation test and the chaos scenario are already on that list. The allowlist exists to make each such addition a visible decision rather than an inferred one.
Nearest spec: main §6.3; invariant 3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PRODUCTS — The Products routes read through a store, so no route file holds a database handle
Decision: a new `makeProductsStore` in `packages/db` answers the four questions the Products screen asks (the catalogue, the family list, the still-open opportunities, the shop's Shopify handle). The route's composition file builds that store and never names the raw database handle.
Why: a lint rule forbids reaching the database outside `packages/db`, and the several route folders that do it are each individually exempted in `eslint.config.mjs` — a file only the integrator edits. Following that pattern would have meant asking for an eighth exemption. The profile screen's own store already sets the alternative precedent one directory over, and it costs nothing: the handle is still resolved on the call rather than at construction, which is what keeps a build with no database configured from producing a server whose every route answers 500.
Consequence: the store returns only the shop's handle, never the connection row, so the encrypted access token has no path to a response serialiser.
Nearest spec: tech §3; CLAUDE.md code-structure rules (route handlers parse → call core → serialise).

## 2026-09-07 — R-CONTRACT — The frozen contract now describes the endpoints that exist, and names the seven that are deliberately outside it
Decision: applying the founder's delegated ruling of 2026-09-04. Five endpoints move to the addresses that were actually built — the blog picker and the delivery toggle to `/api/publish/*`, recommendation generation and reading to `/api/recommendations`, and "restore a dismissed suggestion" to the name it was built under, `undismiss`. Seven endpoints that were built and never declared are now declared: the two publishing settings, the write-permission grant, the article export download, the scan progress poll and its stream, and the three recommendation routes. The table goes from 56 routes to 62.
Also: **the opportunity path parameter becomes `{id}`**, following the directory that was built, rather than renaming two route directories inside a lane that is mid-card. A parameter's *name* is not an address — both spellings resolve to the same URL at runtime — so this is the table describing reality at no cost to anyone.
And: **`POST /api/opportunities/{opportunityId}/tasks/{taskId}` was not unbuilt, it was built somewhere else** — marking one task applied is `POST /api/recommendations/{id}/apply` with the task named in the body. It is a move, not a gap, and was nearly mis-carded as one.
Why the parameter rename rather than moving the code: the founder's ruling was that addresses chosen by the lanes read better than addresses chosen by a table written in milestone 0, and nothing is deployed, so no external caller depends on either spelling.
Nearest spec: build plan §3 (contracts change only through the integrator); tech §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-CONTRACT — Seven endpoints are listed as outside the JSON contract rather than left silently absent
Decision: a new exported list, `UNCONTRACTED_ROUTES`, names every endpoint that exists on disk and is deliberately not in the route table, each with its reason: Auth.js's own routes, the three OAuth callbacks the vendor redirects a browser to, the one-click unsubscribe link (both methods), and the recommendation download, which answers with the document itself as an attachment.
Why: the table describes JSON request and response shapes, and giving a redirect or a file download a zod response schema would state something untrue in order to look complete. But leaving them merely absent is what has cost this project a whole build: **"not in the table" and "nobody built it" have looked identical the entire time**, which is exactly how ten endpoints came to be called by finished screens with no server behind them. `T10.2` adds the check that compares the table against the routes on disk; that check needs to be able to tell a deliberate exclusion from a hole, and this is what it will read. Adding a path to the list is meant to be a decision someone makes in the open — it says *this is not JSON*, never *this has no contract yet*.
Nearest spec: tech §3; build plan §6 `T10.2`.

## 2026-09-07 — R-CONTRACT — The two scan-progress routes sit before the opportunity detail route, and the reason is in the file
Decision: `/api/opportunities/scan-status` and `/api/opportunities/scan-stream` are placed ahead of `/api/opportunities/{id}` in the table, with a comment saying why.
Why: found by a failing test rather than by reading. A consumer that matches routes in table order — the frontend's mock server does exactly this — reads `scan-status` as an opportunity id and answers the detail shape for a progress request. Next.js itself prefers the fixed segment over the dynamic one, so the real server was never wrong; only order-sensitive consumers are, and the mock is the one the whole frontend is built against. The ordering is load-bearing and would look like tidiness to anyone rearranging the file, which is why the comment is there rather than just the order.
Nearest spec: tech §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-CONTRACT — The article export's 409 stays outside the conflict-code enum
Decision: `GET /api/articles/{articleId}/export` declares no `conflicts`. Its 409 — the article names a product the store no longer sells, so handing the file over would publish a hole — carries an error class in the generic envelope, the same way its 404 already does.
Why: the conflict enum exists for *lost races*, where the UI needs a machine-readable code to decide which of several outcomes to show. Nothing about a missing product is a race; it is a refusal with a reason. Widening the enum to cover refusals would make "409 with a code" mean two different things, and the frontend would have to tell them apart by knowing which route it called.
Nearest spec: main §9.4, §9.5; tech §3; invariant 15.

## 2026-09-07 — R-REFUSAL — The refusal happens at the press, and the card's two halves were three
Decision: the improve-this-page press now resolves the page's search *before* enqueueing anything, and refuses on the spot with a new machine-readable code, `optimize_no_target_query`. The card assigned "the contract" to the integrator and "the words" to Lane F; **it named nobody for the part that actually refuses.** The refusal existed only inside the generation step, which runs after the press has already answered "generating" — so the button spun and came back with nothing changed, and no code could reach the merchant no matter what the contract said. The judgement the step makes is now made at the press too, from the same function, which is exported for the purpose and narrowed to take only the database rather than the whole generation dependency set.
Why the integrator did it rather than carding a third lane: the contract change and the code that returns the code have to land together or the table declares an outcome nothing produces — which is precisely the defect found across ten endpoints earlier today, and it would have been indefensible to create a fresh instance of it while carding the others. The file is Lane E's ground and Lane E held no session; the change is one guard clause and one export, both additive, and neither alters a response shape.
Cost, stated: two database reads now happen on a press that used to enqueue immediately. That is the price of telling the merchant at the moment they are looking at the button rather than never.
Nearest spec: main §7.11, §10.1; invariant 22 (degrade to a visible pause, never silently).

## 2026-09-07 — R-CONTRACT — Correcting this journal: the conflict enum is not only for lost races
Correction to the entry above dated today, "The article export's 409 stays outside the conflict-code enum", which justified itself by saying the conflict enum "exists for *lost races*". **That is not true of the enum as it stands and was wrong to write.** `service_paused`, `write_scope_required`, `target_blog_unresolved`, `refresh_within_cooldown` and `competitor_limit_reached` are all in it and none is a race; they are outcomes the screen needs its own sentence for. The enum is better described as **the outcomes a merchant must be shown specific copy for**, which is exactly why `optimize_no_target_query` belongs in it.
The export's 409 still stays out, but for the narrower reason that was always the real one: that route answers with a file, its 404 already carries an error class rather than a code, and adding one code to a route whose other failure is shaped differently would leave the frontend telling them apart by knowing which route it called.
Why record the correction rather than edit the entry: the wrong sentence was load-bearing for two hours and could have been read by another session in that window, and a journal that quietly rewrites itself is worth less than one that shows where it was wrong.
Nearest spec: tech §3.
## 2026-09-07 — R-REPAIR-COPY — FLAGGED: the card said "renders blank"; it renders an admission, and the same admission is on almost every Opportunities card
Decision: recorded, not fixed here. Two corrections to the premise the card was written on.
First, nothing rendered blank. Every one of the fourteen places that turns a reason key into a sentence goes through one renderer, and that renderer already answers a key it has no sentence for with "The reasoning for this one isn't available yet." A merchant saw that line, not an empty space. The practical effect was the same — no explanation — and the fix is the same, so the card stands.
Second, and much larger: the repair path's four were not the only gap. **Sixteen of the twenty explanations an opportunity can carry had no sentence**, and twelve of those are the weekly scan's own signals — striking distance, low CTR, decay, cannibalization, uncovered query (both forms), competitor gap, family coverage gap, weak metadata, intent gap, indexing. Those are the ordinary cards on the Opportunities screen, the product's central surface, so in the live product nearly every card explains itself with the admission line.
How it hid: the mock data, the browser-test fixtures and the screen contract all use two keys — `striking_distance.page_one_intent_mismatch` and `uncovered_commercial_query.no_suitable_url` — that the catalogue holds and **the engine never produces**. The screens were built against the catalogue and the engine was built separately, so every screenshot and every fixture-driven test showed a working why-line while the real engine produced keys with no words behind them.
Not fixed because writing twelve signal explanations is not this card's scope. They are named in `REASON_KEYS_AWAITING_COPY` (`packages/ui/src/strings/reason-copy.ts`) and a test fails if anything joins that list or is left on it after being written.
Nearest spec: main §7.1 (the why-line is rendered from the scoring record), §7.3 (the signal catalogue); ui §5.2; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-07 — R-REPAIR-COPY — The loudness for a missing explanation is in CI, and runtime behaviour is left exactly as it was
Decision: a missing sentence fails tests by name. At runtime the renderer keeps doing what it already did — showing "The reasoning for this one isn't available yet." and carrying on. It does not throw, log, or emit an event.
Why: the two audiences want opposite things. A missing key is a copy oversight, and the person who can fix it is reading a build, not a merchant's screen; a merchant who meets one should lose one sentence of explanation, never the card, the screen, or their trust. Making the renderer throw would turn a copywriter's omission into a blank Opportunities page. The renderer already returns a `known` flag saying it gave up, and nothing anywhere read it — that flag is now what the tests assert on, which is the smallest change that turns a silence into a failure.
Cost worth knowing: a key that goes missing between releases is invisible in production. Closing that would mean an event on the fallback path, which is a telemetry change and a different card.
Nearest spec: main §7.1; invariant 8, invariant 26 (events carry ids and aggregates only).

## 2026-09-07 — R-REPAIR-COPY — The repair explanations carry no numbers
Decision: all four repair sentences are count-free, even though the repair path hands the renderer a count of broken references.
Why: that count is one in the ordinary case — a single withdrawn recommendation — and zero for the two drifts that are about a range rather than a product, and the catalogue has no machinery for singular versus plural. "1 products" on the most common path is worse copy than no number, and "0 products" would be wrong. The number is not lost: the card's evidence row already carries `affected_references` with its source, which is where the interface spec puts numbers anyway — the why-line is the plain "why" and the evidence line is the measurements.
The one number that is offered, the article's id, is a UUID and belongs in no sentence; the card's own title is already the article.
A test asserts that no repair sentence asks for a placeholder the repair path does not supply, because an unsupplied one prints literally — a merchant would read the words "{product_title}".
Nearest spec: ui §5.2 (card anatomy: evidence line vs why-line); invariant 23.

## 2026-09-07 — R-REPAIR-COPY — A wordless drift kind fails, because the list of them is read from the policy table rather than typed
Decision: the set of repair explanations the test checks is computed from `driftPolicies()` — the table in `packages/core/src/repair/drift.ts` that says what can go wrong under a published article — mirroring the key the opportunity builder composes.
Why: a hand-typed list of keys is the same shape of thing as a hand-maintained catalogue, and would go stale the same way. Reading the policy table means a fifth kind of drift added tomorrow produces a fifth key with no sentence and fails a named test, which is the whole point of the card. The mirror of the builder's key expression is held in place from the other side by the repair suite, which pins the key a deleted product produces.
Rejected: calling the real builder instead of mirroring it, which would remove the duplication entirely. It needs the scoring configuration, which lives in `packages/rules` — a package `packages/ui` does not depend on. Adding that dependency for one test is a bigger change to the package graph than the duplication is worth, and the duplication is one line under two named tests.
Nearest spec: main §14.1 (the drift table); §7.3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-REPAIR-COPY — `collection_deleted` gets a sentence although nothing produces it yet
Decision: an explanation was written for the drift kind "a collection this article was built from was deleted", even though the daily drift pass never raises one — it detects deleted products, long-unbuyable products and ranges whose attributes moved, and nothing else.
Why: it is a row in the policy table, so the opportunity builder will produce that key the moment a detector reaches it, and a card whose only reason for existing is that a key went unnoticed should not leave a known key unwritten. The alternative — writing it when the detector lands — is exactly the sequencing that produced this card.
Nearest spec: main §14.1 ("Collection deleted → re-run family grouping for member products only").

## 2026-09-07 — INTEGRATOR — The clean negatives from the producer-side audit, recorded so nobody re-runs them
Decision: recording two results that are *absences*, because an audit that finds nothing is worth as much as one that finds something and is otherwise invisible to the next session.
**Scheduled jobs versus registered handlers: no mismatch, in either direction.** Eighteen scheduled entries against thirty-three registered handlers, resolved through their constants rather than by matching names. The one apparent mismatch, `subscription_reconciliation_nightly`, is registered at `apps/web/app/api/webhooks/stripe/_lib/tasks.ts:15` — outside `packages/jobs`, which is why a jobs-only scan misses it. `intent_gap_scan_weekly` is registered and deliberately unscheduled, documented where it is registered. **This matters because a schedule entry naming a task nobody registered once disabled all seventeen recurring jobs silently**, and that check has now been run properly.
**Email keys the code can build: none missing.** Ten emailable types across subject, body, preview and call-to-action, plus the generic fallback each parameterised type can reach.
Also recorded: four candidate findings were discarded before reporting, and one of them is a method note worth keeping. `email.opportunitiesReady.subject.generic` looks missing and is unreachable, because that spec sets `parameterised: []` and the builder returns before it can construct the key. **A check that ignored that field would have produced a real-looking finding about copy that no merchant can ever see.** The lesson generalises: for this class of defect, resolving what the producer can actually emit is the whole job, and the declaration side always looks fine.
Nearest spec: main §14.3, §14.7; tech §1, §5.
## 2026-09-07 — R-ARTICLE-OURS — A page is recognised as ours by its address, not by the id the shop gave it
Decision: the store walk decides whether a page it just read is an article we published by comparing the address the store served against `articles.published_url` — our own record of where each article of ours went. Both sides go through the same normalisation (`canonicalStoreUrl`) before they are compared, because the walk builds an address out of a handle while the address on an exported article was typed by a merchant and can carry a trailing slash or a tracking parameter that means nothing.
Why: the address is the only key that covers both ways we deliver. For an article we posted to the merchant's shop ourselves, we hold Shopify's own id for it on the publication claim (`publish_intents.shopify_article_id`), and matching on that would be exact and would survive the merchant renaming the post. But we hold no such id for an article the merchant downloaded and published themselves — and per main §9.5 export delivery is the **default** and is available to Shopify stores, so those merchants can and do paste our articles onto their own Shopify blog, which this walk reads every night. Matching by id would have left every one of those permanently unrecognised. Matching by address costs a comparison and covers both.
What it costs, stated plainly: if the merchant renames the post on their shop, its address changes, our record still names the old one, and the page stops being recognised until somebody corrects the address. Nothing in the product corrects it today — see the flagged item below.
Rejected: matching on Shopify's article id (misses every export-delivered article); matching on the article's title or slug (a merchant may retitle either, and two stores' articles can share a title).
Nearest spec: main §12.3 ("plus our own published articles"), §9.5 (delivery modes), §14.1.

## 2026-09-07 — R-ARTICLE-OURS — Recognition is a write of its own, run after the page write, on every page the walk sees
Decision: the marking is written by a new `markStorePagesOurs`, called once per batch for whichever of that batch's addresses matched, after the content write and before the deletion sweep. It is not part of the row the content write inserts.
Why: this is the same rule `R-PAGE-GONE-WRITE` established for "we saw it", and for a sharper version of the same reason. The content write (`writeChanged`) runs **only for pages whose words moved**, and one of our own articles never moves again after the night it appears — so recognition riding on it would happen at most once and could never happen at all for the case that matters most: an export-delivery merchant confirming the address days or weeks after the walk has already filed the post as one of their own. Running it after the content write rather than before is what lets a page seen for the very first time be recognised on that same walk: there is no row to mark until the write has made one. Running it before the sweep means a page we have just recognised is one the sweep already knows to leave alone. Like the "we saw it" stamp, it leaves the checksum untouched, so being recognised is not an edit and does not re-run the paid analyses hanging off one.
Proved by mutation rather than asserted: pointing recognition at the changed rows, dropping the normalisation, letting the nightly write demote a recognised row, and dropping the sweep's exclusion each fail a named test.
Nearest spec: main §12.3, §14.1; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 "The walk stamps every page it sees".

## 2026-09-07 — R-ARTICLE-OURS — The walk marks, and never un-marks
Decision: a page the walk does not recognise is left exactly as it is. Nothing demotes an `article_ours` row back to an ordinary blog post, and nothing clears its article id.
Why: for the same reason our own articles are never marked gone. A store on export delivery may publish our articles somewhere this walk cannot look at all, so the walk failing to recognise a page is evidence of nothing whatever — and the marking is our record of what we delivered. The nightly page write already refused to demote such a row; this extends the same refusal to the new write rather than introducing a second, quieter way to lose the record.
Nearest spec: main §9.5, §12.3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-ARTICLE-OURS — The lookup reads the store's whole published list each batch, and the comparison happens in our code
Decision: `publishedArticleAddresses` returns every published article of the account that has an address, oldest first, and the walk intersects that with the batch's addresses in memory. It does not narrow the query to the batch's addresses.
Why: narrowing in the database would mean an exact string comparison, which is precisely what the normalisation exists to avoid — the address a merchant typed and the address the walk built are the same page written two ways. The read itself is bounded by the product's own cap of at most one article a day per store, returns two short text columns, and runs once per batch of a walk that already makes a paid vendor call per page. Where two articles somehow claim one address, the walk keeps the first, and the oldest-first ordering is what makes that the same answer every night instead of alternating.
Nearest spec: none; invariant 20 (nothing here is a billable read).

## 2026-09-07 — R-ARTICLE-OURS — The inventory's repository reads the articles table
Decision: `publishedArticleAddresses` lives in `packages/db/src/repositories/inventory.ts` — Lane C's file — and selects from `articles`, which belongs to the article pipeline's domain.
Why: recorded because the repository-ownership rule added on 2026-09-07 assigns a repository file to the lane owning the domain it serves, and this one now reads across that line. It is a read of two columns with an account scope on it and no write of any kind; putting it in the articles repository instead would have made the inventory's own question live somewhere the inventory does not own, which is the worse of the two.
Nearest spec: build plan §3 as amended 2026-09-07.

## 2026-09-07 — R-ARTICLE-OURS — FLAGGED: a merchant renaming our article on their shop breaks the link, permanently
Decision: not fixed, and not in this card. Naming it because it is now reachable.
What happens: the marking is by address. If the merchant edits the post's handle on their Shopify blog, the shop starts serving it at a new address. The walk files that as a **new, unrecognised** page, and the old address's row keeps the marking — and because a recognised row is never marked gone, that stale row stays `live` for ever. The product would then hold one page it believes is our article at an address nobody can visit, and one page it believes is the merchant's at the address our article is actually at. An improve-this-page press on the real one would get a list of edits for a page we wrote, which is the exact thing `T6.3` refuses.
Why it is not fixed here: correcting it means noticing a rename, which means either matching on Shopify's article id as a second key (we hold it only for articles we posted ourselves) or re-reading the address after a rename webhook. Both are their own card, and both are product decisions about what our record of "where we published" means.
Nearest spec: main §9.5, §12.3, §14.1.
## 2026-09-07 — R-API-ARTICLES — An overridden article is reported to the screens as a draft, because they have no word for the state it is in
Decision: the articles list and the article page report an article in `cleared_to_deliver` — the storage state meaning "a person has decided this goes out" — as `draft`. The override flag beside it is what says how it got there.
Why: the frozen response contract names five article states and the database has six. The sixth landed with `R-OVERRIDE-STATE`; the contract, the copy catalogue and the screens were all written before it and know nothing about it, and the fake server the frontend is built against is generated from that contract. Widening the contract is not this card's to do and would be a change every lane consumes. Of the five words available, `draft` is the honest one: it is already where an approved article waits for the publishing hour, and it already means "delivery may take this" everywhere else in the build. The alternative — inventing a sixth word for the browser only — would put one fact in two vocabularies with nothing keeping them in step.
Cost worth stating: an overridden article and an approved one read identically on the screen except for the override badge. That is what the badge is for, and it is the only place the two differ.
Nearest spec: main §8.6 (the override and its flag); ui §6.2 (the state column); DECISIONS 2026-09-04 FOUNDER "An overridden article gets its own state".

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-ARTICLES — FLAGGED: no article carries a performance figure, because nothing measures one
Decision: `performance` is always null on every article, in the list and on the page.
Why: the table that would hold a per-article performance window (`article_labels` — clicks, impressions, mean position and a winner/neutral/underperformer label against the store's own median) exists in the schema and is written by nobody and read by nobody. The learning loop that fills it is deferred. Null is the value the contract already allows and the screen already draws as "too new to judge" rather than as a failure, so the column renders honestly rather than emptily.
Visible consequence: the library's "has performance" filter matches no article in the live product, and the ui §6.2 clicks/position/trend columns stay blank for every store. That is not this card's to fix — it needs the learning loop and a Search Console read per article.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.2 (labels relative to the store's own median), §13 `article_labels`; ui §6.2; invariant 13.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-ARTICLES — An article whose product has left the store still loads, with an empty body
Decision: `GET /api/articles/{articleId}` answers 200 with `html: ''` when the article's words cannot be rendered — the writer has not finished, a referenced product has been deleted from the shop, or the body carries a marker no reference explains. It does not refuse.
Why: the page carries the quality report and the "publish anyway" decision as well as the article. Refusing the read takes both away — the screen's loader turns any failure into a missing page — at the one moment a merchant most needs them. The download route (`/export`) still refuses properly and says which product broke, so the honest refusal exists where a merchant is actually being handed a file.
Cost worth stating plainly: the download buttons on both Content screens build their files from this response rather than from `/export`, so an article in this state downloads as a title and nothing else. Making that right means either pointing the buttons at `/export` (another lane's screens) or rendering from the last recorded values (a renderer nobody has asked for). Named here rather than fixed.
Nearest spec: main §9.3 (the read-only review surface); ui §6.3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-ARTICLES — A quality report with no grader recorded is shown as no quality report
Decision: the article page returns `qualityReport: null` when the gate-3 decision behind it carries no prompt version or model id, even though it carries scores and justifications.
Why: the judge's written objections are the one place in the product where a merchant reads a model's own prose rather than a template, and the founder allowed that on condition it is labelled as model-written wherever it is seen. The screen builds that label out of the model id and prompt version. A report with neither would put a model's sentences in front of a merchant with nothing on the page saying so. Showing none is the smaller loss, and the case is not reachable from Gate 3 as it stands — Gate 3 records both.
Nearest spec: main §8.5 (a stored score has to be attributable to the prompt and model that produced it); invariants 8 and 11; DECISIONS 2026-09-04 FOUNDER on the judge's justification.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-ARTICLES — The whole library comes back in one answer and the cursor is always null
Decision: `GET /api/articles` returns every article the store has, with `cursor: null`.
Why: the same reasoning as the Products screen one card over, and for a smaller list — a store writes at most one article a day. The screen's own filters run in the browser over whatever it was handed, so any cap would silently hide the very rows a filter exists to find, which is the same shape of failure this card exists to repair. The contract does declare a `cursor` query parameter, unlike the Products one, so paging is expressible; nothing sends it, and building a page boundary nothing asks for would only make the silent truncation possible.
Nearest spec: ui §6.2; tech §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-ARTICLES — The audit row keeps the gate's account of what failed and the merchant's separately
Decision: the `gate_decisions` row an override writes records the failed criteria as *the gate itself* recorded them, and keeps the criteria the confirmation dialog restated in a field of its own (`acknowledged_criteria`).
Why: the confirmation body is written by the browser, and an audit trail whose account of what was overruled comes from the thing doing the overruling is not an audit trail. The gate's own row is authoritative. The merchant's list is still worth keeping — it is the record of what they were actually shown before they decided — so it is kept beside it rather than instead of it, and the two can be compared if they ever disagree.
Nearest spec: main §8.6 ("every override is logged, `gate_decisions` outcome `overridden`"); invariant 12.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-ARTICLES — Drawing the article page no longer writes
Decision: building an article's rendered body was split into a read-only render and the recording of what a merchant was handed. The download route still records; the page does not.
Why: the recording exists so the app can show the same figures between downloads and so the daily repair pass has something to compare the store against. A page view is neither a hand-over nor a download, and letting one move that baseline would make the repair pass compare the store against whatever was true the last time somebody happened to look at the page.
Nearest spec: main §14.1 (drift and repair), §9.5 (export).

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PERFORMANCE — Nothing on the Performance screen carries a verdict, because nothing in the product computes one
Decision: every row of the results table comes back labelled `unrated` — the word the screen renders as "too new to judge — we wait 28 days" — for articles and for improved pages alike, unless a measurement has actually been recorded against the opportunity.
Why: a verdict on an article ("winner", "neutral", "underperformer") is supposed to be computed weekly against the store's own median clicks. The table that would hold those verdicts, `article_labels`, is declared in the schema and **written and read by nothing**: the learning loop that fills it is deferred out of v1 by the founder. There is therefore no verdict to report, and the vocabulary the screen speaks has no fourth word for "nobody has looked yet". Of the words available, `unrated` is the only one that is not a judgement; calling every article "neutral" would be the product pronouncing on work it never measured. `R-API-ARTICLES` met the same wall on the same day and returned null for the same reason.
Consequence worth stating plainly, because it is what a merchant actually sees: the screen hides the clicks, impressions and position of any row with no verdict — a deliberate rule of its own, so that a nought is never read as "nobody came" — so the results table renders as a list of titles with dashes beside them until something computes labels. The figures behind those dashes are real and are already in the response, so the table fills in the moment a verdict exists. The chart above it, which is the screen's main content, is drawn from real data throughout.
For opportunities the picture is slightly better: `opportunities.outcome_json` is a column this endpoint reads, so an outcome recorded there is shown. Nothing writes that column either today.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.2 (the maturity gate and store-relative labels), §9.6.10 (per-opportunity outcomes); ui §8.1; invariant 13.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PERFORMANCE — A store whose Search Console grant died keeps its chart
Decision: the Performance screen treats a *broken* connection as connected. Only a store that never granted Search Console, or granted without ever choosing which property is theirs, gets the full-page connect card.
Why: this is not a new rule, it is an existing one applied. `packages/core/src/search/connection.ts` already draws exactly this line for the Limited Intelligence badge, and says why in the file: a dead grant means we cannot fetch anything new, but the sixteen months we already synced are real and still worth reading. Showing the connect card instead would erase a merchant's whole history from the screen on the day a token expired, and would tell someone who has connected to connect. The prompt to reconnect belongs on Settings → Connections, which is where the same connection reads `broken`.
Nearest spec: main §7.11, §12.2; ui §8.1, §9.3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PERFORMANCE — Every window ends on the last day we hold, not on today
Decision: the chart stops at the newest day the store has any search data for, and both Search Console tables compare a window ending on that same day against an equally long window immediately before it.
Why: Google reports about two days late. A window ending today would always carry two empty days, and comparing that against a full period behind it would make every store in the product look like it was declining by roughly a fifteenth, every day, forever. Ending at the last day we hold is also what makes the note already printed under the tables true — "Changes compare like periods only — never a partial period against a full one". The lag itself is not hidden: the screen carries a fixed sentence saying Search Console data arrives about two days late.
Second half of the same decision: days *inside* the range with no data stay null rather than becoming noughts, so the chart breaks its line, and the screen counts them and says how many there were.
Nearest spec: main §12.2 (the ~2-day lag); ui §8.1 ("Gaps render as gaps, never interpolated"); main §14.4.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PERFORMANCE — The Search Console tables answer 250 rows at a time, and the screen has no way to ask for more
Decision: each table returns its busiest 250 rows with a cursor for the next page. The cursor names the table it came from, so one kept across a change of dimension or time range is ignored rather than applied to a different set of rows.
Why: a twelve-month range on a large catalogue groups to tens of thousands of distinct searches. Returning all of them would make the screen that exists to be a way *into* Opportunities the slowest page in the product, and it is rendered on the server, so the merchant would wait for every one. Rows come back busiest first, so a page holds what somebody would actually look at.
**The cost, named rather than buried:** the screen has no "show more" control, so today the rows past the first page are unreachable from the browser even though the API will serve them. That is the same shape of failure this card exists to repair — a screen that looks complete while it is not showing everything — so it is flagged for the integrator rather than resolved here, because adding a control is frontend work in another lane's directory. The alternative, returning everything, was rejected as the worse of the two: a page that never finishes loading hides *all* the rows.
Nearest spec: ui §8.2; tech §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PERFORMANCE — A row is badged only by an opportunity keyed on that exact page or that exact search
Decision: a page row carries the badges of open opportunities whose stored reference is the same address; a search row carries those whose stored reference is the same search text. A search that is merely a *member* of a cluster an opportunity was raised on carries no badge.
Why: the reference is the identity the dedupe index is built on, so matching on it cannot point a merchant at work about something else. Expanding through cluster membership would badge every search in a cluster with the same opportunity — plausible for cannibalization, which is genuinely about a whole cluster, and misleading everywhere else. The card asked for badges that link into Opportunities; badges that are certainly right is what it got. If the head-query-only behaviour proves too thin in use, the expansion is one read of `query_clusters` away.
Nearest spec: ui §8.2; main §7.9 (the dedupe key); §7.3 (cannibalization).

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PERFORMANCE — The drawer's history is three stamped moments, not an audit trail
Decision: `GET /api/opportunities/{id}` returns history entries only for moments the opportunity row itself has a date for — when the scan detected it, when the merchant marked it applied, and when a scan expired it. Each entry's `from` status is null, and each entry's reason is null.
Why: **no table records a status change.** There is no audit log anywhere in the schema, so a complete history is not something this endpoint could tell the truth about; the three stamped columns are the only transitions with evidence behind them. `from` is null because the status a row moved *out of* was never written down, and naming one would be the product inventing its own past. The reason is null because the row records *why* it expired but the copy catalogue holds no sentence for any expiry reason — and a template key nobody has written renders as a blank line, which is worse than an entry with no reason under it.
What it would take to do better: a small append-only table written by the same guarded updates that already move the status. That is a migration, so it belongs to a schema wave, not to a feature card.
Nearest spec: main §7.9 (the lifecycle); ui §5.3 §7 (History); invariant 8.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PERFORMANCE — The drawer never buys a results page, and refuses a stale one
Decision: the drawer shows who else Google ranks for a search-shaped opportunity only from an unexpired snapshot we already hold. An expired snapshot is reported as no snapshot; nothing here calls the search-data vendor.
Why: a drawer opening is a merchant clicking "Details", and a click that costs money is a click somebody will make a hundred times. And a decision shown against last month's results page is the one degradation the product refuses outright — it pauses rather than continue on stale data. The freshness check is inside the query the repository already runs, so a stale snapshot cannot be read by accident.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.6 (billable reads are cached), §14.4 (degrade to pause); §12.6; ui §5.3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PERFORMANCE — Two new database reads live in this lane's own files, and the recommendation mapping was copied rather than shared
Decision: the per-day and per-key Search Console totals were added to `packages/db/src/repositories/search.ts` and the applied-opportunities read to `repositories/opportunities.ts` — both files this lane owns. The mapping from a stored recommendation to the shape the drawer reads was written fresh in `packages/core/src/opportunities/recommendation-view.ts` rather than shared with the almost identical mapping inside `apps/web/app/api/recommendations/_lib/handlers.ts`.
Why the copy: that file belongs to another lane and its mapping function is not exported, so sharing it would have meant editing a directory this card does not own while that lane may be mid-card. About thirty lines are now written twice, and the two must not drift — the recommendations route's download and the drawer are supposed to show the same advice. Worth the integrator's attention as a candidate for one shared function later; not worth reaching into another lane to fix today.
Nearest spec: build plan §3 (repository ownership, as amended 2026-09-07); CLAUDE.md code-structure rules.

## 2026-09-07 — R-API-PERFORMANCE — An export-mode article whose address nobody confirmed is left out of the results table
Decision: an article delivered by export whose final published address the merchant never confirmed does not appear in the results table at all.
Why: without the address there is no way to tell its Search Console rows from anybody else's, so it can neither be measured nor honestly shown. Listing it with noughts would read as an article nobody found, which is a verdict — and the spec is explicit that absence of data is not failure. The screen has an answer for this case — such articles are meant to be listed greyed out with a "confirm URL" action — but the frozen response shape carries no field to say a row is in that state, so there is nothing this endpoint could send that the screen would draw correctly. Named for the integrator rather than solved by inventing a field.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.7 ("absence of data is not failure"), §12.2; ui §8.1.

## 2026-09-07 — INTEGRATOR — Plurals go in the renderer, not in sibling keys, and the guard is the point
Decision: `R-PLURALS` takes **plural support in the renderer** — `Intl.PluralRules`, which is in the runtime, so no dependency — rather than giving each affected sentence a `.one` sibling chosen by the caller. **And the card is not done until a guard fails when a sentence carries a countable placeholder without plural handling.**
Why: the survey found twelve sentences that read wrong at one, not the two the card named — `{days}` reaching 1 happens the day before every scan. The sibling-key approach is the pattern the product already uses (`publishedLine` in `packages/core/src/email/summary.ts:76`, which reads well and ships today), and it would work. It was rejected because **its twelfth fix and its thirteenth omission are the same event**: nothing stops the next sentence forgetting, and "a thing that is right until someone forgets" is the defect class this project has now found nine times in one day. Putting correctness in one place and a guard around it is the only version that cannot rot.
Cost accepted, and it is real: this changes the catalogue's *syntax*, which every lane writes into, and it makes `publishedLine` a second way to do one thing — the same shape as `R-SETTINGS-ONE-PATH`, which was carded today for exactly that. **Migrating `publishedLine` onto the renderer is part of this card, not a follow-up**, so the second way does not survive the change that makes it redundant.
Who decided and on what authority: the integrator. The user-visible outcome is identical either way — the merchant reads correct English — so this is an engineering choice rather than a product one, and the founder has been told in one line that it was made and can be reversed. **English is currently the only catalogue**, so the multi-language argument for the renderer is future-facing and was not the deciding one; the guard was.
Nearest spec: main Appendix A; invariant 8 (templates over the record, never a model), 24 (canonical strings verbatim).

## 2026-09-07 — INTEGRATOR — A canonical string reads "1 ways" and only the founder can change it
Decision: **escalated, not taken.** `appendixA.opportunityHeadline` — *"We found {count} ways to grow your store organically"* — is in the spec's canonical copy table (main Appendix A), pinned verbatim by a snapshot test, and rendered on the dashboard and the onboarding activation header. **At a count of one it reads "We found 1 ways to grow your store organically", on the merchant's first real screen**, which the spec itself calls the core value proposition.
Why it is not the integrator's: invariant 24 says canonical strings are used verbatim, and Appendix A is the founder's text. No plural machinery can fix this sentence without rewording it, so **the choice exists regardless of which shape `R-PLURALS` takes** and should not ride on that decision. The guard added under `R-PLURALS` renders and pins it exactly as it stands, so nothing changes until the founder answers.
Verified 2026-09-07 before escalating: `packages/ui/strings/en.json:6`, pinned at `packages/ui/src/strings/strings.test.ts:24`, rendered at `DashboardScreen.tsx:108` and `ActivationHeader.tsx:86`, and in the spec's Appendix A table.
Nearest spec: main Appendix A; invariant 24.

## 2026-09-07 — CORRECTION — `listStorePages` stays unfiltered, but not for the reason given
Correction to the `R-PAGE-GONE-READ` entries of today and to the `R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE` card, both of which said the shared page read must keep returning deleted rows because "one caller — account deletion — legitimately wants every row." **There is no such caller.** Account deletion erases those rows with a direct delete statement (`packages/db/src/repositories/lifecycle.ts:241`, `purgeStoreDerived`) and never reads them first. Found by `R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE`'s lane while working from that claim.
**The conclusion is unchanged and the real reason is better**, and it was already written down in the same entry: the existing-target check decides by reading each row's status, so a page missing from its list is one it holds no opinion about and treats as still published — filtering there would turn every deletion back into a live page and silently undo the feature.
Why this is worth a correction rather than a quiet edit: **the wrong reason was load-bearing.** It was repeated in the repository's own comment and in two lane briefs, and it named a caller that does not exist. Somebody checking it later would find no such caller, conclude the guard was obsolete, and remove it — reaching the opposite of the right answer by way of a fact nobody had verified. The comment now carries the real reason and says explicitly that the old one was wrong.
Nearest spec: main §7.7, §12.3, §14.6; invariant 6.
## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE — Three reads of the store's pages, three different answers, only one of them a filter
Decision: of the three unfiltered reads the card names, only one becomes `listLiveStorePages`. The weekly page-comparison pass (`packages/jobs/src/optimize/scan.ts`) filters. The recommendation run (`generate.ts`) and the evidence pack (`pack.ts`) keep reading every row and refuse on the row's status instead.
Why: a filter there would have been the wrong shape and would have made the defect worse rather than better. Both of those look the page up by address and behave differently when they cannot find it — `generate.ts` treats "no row" as "carry on" (it is only asking whether the page is one of our own published articles), so filtering the deleted page out would have hidden it from the check and let the run go on to buy a results page and a model call for it. The filtered read cannot express "we hold this page and the merchant has taken it down", which is exactly the thing being refused. `pack.ts` has the same problem in reverse: a page we have never held and a page the merchant deleted are two different answers to the merchant, and one read cannot produce both.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 (the evidence pack), §12.3; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-PAGE-GONE-READ (the same split, decided the same way for the existing-target check).

## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE — A deleted page is also never offered as somewhere to add a link
Decision: the list of the store's other pages the evidence pack offers the model as internal-link candidates is drawn from the live pages only. This is a second, independent change inside `pack.ts`, not a consequence of the first.
Why: nothing else in the product could catch it. Every other read here is about the page being improved, and this one is about the pages around it — a recommendation carrying a deleted page as a link target tells the merchant to add a link that breaks the page they add it to, and it would pass every check the pipeline runs, because the address is genuinely in our inventory. Main §10.3's own lint list requires internal-link targets to exist in the inventory; the inventory keeping a row for a deleted page is what makes that lint no longer mean what it says.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 (lints); §12.3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE — Two more call sites than the card named, and only one of them was fixed
Decision: the card names three reads; there are seven. Four are in `apps/web/app/api/recommendations/_lib/handlers.ts`. One gained the refusal (the improve-this-page press), one is now filtered (the FIX recommendation's link realignment), and two were deliberately left alone and are flagged instead.
Why, one by one. **The press** reads every row on purpose — it has to tell a deleted page apart from a page we hold nothing for, and it is the only place a person is waiting on the answer. **The FIX recommendation** hands the merchant a list of pages to go and edit so a link points at the right one of two competing pages; a deleted page on that list is an instruction that cannot be carried out, and the filter is the whole fix. **The "looks like you applied this" check** compares the stored recommendation against the page's current title and headings, and a deleted page still holds both, so the product can offer to confirm that advice was applied to a page that is gone — confirming stamps the row applied and starts a 28-day measurement on nothing. Left alone because it is not a recommendation being produced, which is what this card's done-when is about. **The download's label lookup** reads the page only to find which product families to name; filtering it would strip the labels out of a document the merchant is downloading about advice they already have, which is worse, not better.
Nearest spec: main §10.4 ("mark as applied", the heuristic detection); §11 (the FIX layer).

## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE — The press answers 422 with a code the frozen conflict vocabulary does not hold, and the integrator is asked for it
Decision: pressing "improve this page" on a deleted page answers HTTP 422 with `optimize_page_gone` and the sentence "This page is no longer in your store, so there is nothing to improve." The code is **not** added to `CONFLICT_CODES`; `packages/core/src/api/errors.ts` and `routes.ts` were not touched.
Why: the vocabulary of conflict codes is the integrator's, and a route answering with a code the contract does not declare is the same defect, in reverse, as a contract declaring an outcome nothing produces — so the two halves cannot land separately from a lane session. Reusing an existing code was rejected on the record set by `optimize_no_target_query` this afternoon: the screen picks its sentence from the code and ignores the message, so the nearest existing code (`opportunity_not_open`) would tell the merchant the suggestion had moved on, which is untrue — it is still open and will work again the moment the page comes back. 422 rather than 409 follows the article refresh route, which today answers its own out-of-vocabulary refusals that way; the client reads `error.code` off any failing response regardless of status, so the merchant is told either way.
**What the integrator has to decide, and it is one line either way:** whether this belongs in the enum. Recommended yes — the corrected reading of that enum recorded today is "the outcomes a merchant must be shown specific copy for", and this is one; every other refusal on this route is a 409 with a code, and a single 422 among them is an inconsistency the drawer will have to know about. Promoting it means adding `'optimize_page_gone'` to `CONFLICT_CODES`, adding it to this route's `conflicts` list, and replacing the `pageGone()` helper's body with `conflict('optimize_page_gone', …)`.
Nearest spec: tech §3; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-REFUSAL and the R-CONTRACT correction to the conflict-enum entry.

## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE — A page put back in the store is eligible again with nothing else run, and four tests say so
Decision: nothing was built to re-admit a restored page. Each of the four places that now refuse a deleted page has a paired test that deletes the page, has the walk find it again, and asserts the refusal has stopped.
Why: the whole mechanism is that the row keeps its checksum and its body while it is marked deleted, so the walk seeing the page again is all it takes — and that is precisely the property a later reader would break by tidying the row away or archiving it. Tests are the only thing that makes it visible, since no code says it.
Nearest spec: main §12.3; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-PAGE-GONE-WRITE ("A page the walk finds is live again").

## 2026-09-07 — R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE — FLAGGED: nothing closes the suggestion when its page goes
Decision: reported, not fixed. A suggestion to improve a page stays open on the Opportunities screen after the merchant deletes that page. What this card changed is that pressing the button now refuses instead of spending; the card itself is still there, still saying the page could be improved, and the merchant can press it as often as they like.
