Why not fixed here: expiring or closing an opportunity is the lifecycle another lane owns (main §7.9), the row's status is guarded by transitions written there, and invariant 10 says expiry never deletes — so which status a deleted page's suggestion should move to, and whether it comes back if the page does, is a decision rather than an implementation. The refusal is the safe half and it is complete.
Nearest spec: main §7.9 (the opportunity lifecycle); invariant 10.

## 2026-09-07 — R-APPLIED-ON-GONE — The refusal is inside the detector, not at its one call site, because the second caller is one the spec already promised
Decision: the check that notices "your page now says what we suggested" (`packages/core/src/optimize/applied.ts`) refuses a page the store no longer serves *itself*, and the page's status is now a required part of what a caller hands it. The API route that asks the question was not otherwise changed; it still reads every page row, deleted ones included, and passes the status through.
Why not the filtered read this lane used elsewhere today: a filter at the call site would have produced exactly the right behaviour — the deleted page falls out of the list, is not found, and no prompt is offered, because "no row" already means "say nothing" here. That is the criterion this lane used two cards ago to decide filter-versus-refuse, and it points at the filter. It was rejected on a different ground. **Main §10.4 asks for this detection at every content-inventory walk, and that job does not exist** — the drawer's read is the only implementation today. Whoever builds the walk version will call this function, and with a filter at the other call site nothing would tell them. Making the status part of the argument means the compiler stops them: a page cannot be described to this function without saying whether the store still serves it. The check is in one place and the guard is un-forgettable, which is the shape `R-PLURALS` was decided into this morning for the same reason.
Cost accepted: `CurrentPageState` gained a required field, so every future caller writes one more line. Only this lane's code calls it.
Nearest spec: main §10.4 (notice, then ask); §12.3 (the inventory row a deleted page keeps); invariant 13.

## 2026-09-07 — R-APPLIED-ON-GONE — "We cannot measure this" and "this never happened" are different sentences, so mark-applied still works on a deleted page
Decision: pressing "mark as applied" on a page the merchant has since taken down **succeeds**. The suggestion completes, `applied_at` is stamped, and every open task is marked — exactly as before. The only thing withheld is the 28-day outcome measurement, which is no longer booked; the response simply carries no `outcomeDueAt`, which the frozen contract has always allowed to be absent (`applyRecommendationResponseSchema`, `packages/core/src/api/schemas.ts:784`). Nothing was added to the conflict vocabulary and no contract file was touched.
Why not refuse the press: a merchant who applied our advice and *then* deleted the page did the work. Refusing them would leave the product asserting they never acted, on a screen where they can see it, in order to protect a measurement we were going to skip anyway. The measurement is the only thing that is genuinely impossible — the comparison is Search Console's figures for the 28 days before against the 28 after, and for an address that stopped serving it would read as a collapse our advice caused. So the mark is a record and it stands; the promise is a promise and it is not made.
What this leaves for the founder, and it is copy rather than code: the drawer's sentence for an applied suggestion with no result yet is `opportunities.drawer.outcomePending` — *"Nothing measurable yet. We read the result 28 days after this is applied."* — and for these rows it is untrue, because no read is coming. A second sentence is needed and it lives in the frontend lane's file. Reported to the integrator with a proposed key and text; nothing renders wrongly until one of these rows exists.
Nearest spec: main §10.4 ("mark as applied"), §9.6.10 (the 28-day anchor and what it measures); invariant 13 (no verdict before 28 days).

## 2026-09-07 — R-APPLIED-ON-GONE — Measurements already booked against pages since deleted are left exactly where they are
Decision: nothing was deleted, cancelled or swept. Any `opportunity_outcome_measure` job already queued for a page the merchant has since taken down stays in the queue.
Why, and this is verified rather than assumed: **nothing runs that task.** No `registerTask('opportunity_outcome_measure', …)` exists anywhere in the tree — the handler belongs to a later card, and Graphile only ever fetches tasks the running worker knows about — so an already-queued row is inert today and cannot produce a false verdict. Deleting them would destroy the only record that a promise was made, which is the principle behind invariant 10 (expiry never deletes), and it would do so to prevent something that cannot currently happen. The right place for the check is that handler when somebody writes it: a page can be deleted at any point during the 28 days a measurement is waiting, which no check in the request path can prevent.
Residual race, stated rather than closed: the page's status is read immediately after the mark and immediately before the queue write. A walk that deletes the page between those two statements leaves one queued job. Serialising the request under the account lock was rejected as disproportionate — the consequence is a queued row for a task nobody runs, and the handler has to make this check regardless.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.10; §14.3 (idempotency and queues); invariant 10.

## 2026-09-07 — R-APPLIED-ON-GONE — Marking one task applied is left alone, deliberately
Decision: the per-task half of the same route — "mark this one thing applied" — was not changed. It still succeeds on a page the store no longer serves.
Why: it books nothing. The 28-day measurement is started only by marking the whole recommendation applied, and a task mark is purely the merchant's own record of what they did, which this card is not in the business of overwriting. Changing it would have cost the merchant a true statement and bought nothing.
Nearest spec: main §10.4.

## 2026-09-07 — R-APPLIED-ON-GONE — FLAGGED: the product still nudges merchants about advice for pages they deleted
Decision: reported, not fixed. `unappliedOptimizeRecommendations` (`packages/db/src/repositories/notifications.ts:235`) raises an attention item — *"Recommendations you haven't marked as applied."* — for any recommendation old enough and unmarked. It has no opinion about whether the store still serves the page, so a merchant who deleted a page is nudged to go and apply advice to it.
Why not fixed here: it is the same defect family as this card but it is not this card's subject — nobody is asked to confirm anything and no measurement is booked — and the file belongs to the ops-and-notifications lane by the repository-ownership rule added to the build plan today. The fix is a status check of the kind this card just wrote, and it is one line in somebody else's file.
Nearest spec: tech §1 (attention items are live queries); main §10.4.
## 2026-09-07 — R-NEXTSCAN — The next scan is the sweep's own next matching wake-up, worked out from the store's clock
Decision: `GET /api/opportunities` stops answering `nextScanAt: null` unconditionally. The date now comes from a new function, `nextWeeklyScanAt` (`packages/core/src/signals/next-scan.ts`), which reproduces the question the weekly scan itself asks. That scan is a sweep that wakes every hour and takes every store whose *own* calendar says Monday; so the prediction walks those same wake-ups forward and returns the first one at which this store's calendar says Monday. For a UTC store mid-week that is next Monday 00:00 UTC; for a Berlin store it is 22:00 the Sunday before; for one in Auckland, 12:00 the Sunday before; for one in Kolkata, whose midnight falls on a half hour the sweep does not wake on, 19:00 the Sunday before — the first wake-up that is genuinely inside their Monday.
Why not "last scan + 7 days", anywhere: the founder's reword removed "the next scan runs Monday" because a fixed weekday is a promise we cannot keep — stores are scanned on their own local Monday, and a store that was skipped, paused or re-queued moves even that. Adding seven days to the last scan is that same untrue sentence computed somewhere else: it is wrong by a day for most of the world, and wrong by a week for any store whose last scan did not happen when it should have. Deriving the answer from the sweep's own rule cannot be wrong in that way, because it is the rule.
What was changed to keep it that way: `sweepWeeklyScans` (`packages/jobs/src/scan/weekly.ts`) no longer has its own copy of "what day is it there" or its own run-id format — it reads both from the same core module. Two copies of that question would let the promise and the work drift apart with neither side failing.
Consequence worth stating: the prediction is only as fine as the sweep's wake-up interval, which is hourly. If that schedule is ever made coarser the answer becomes early by the difference rather than wrong about the day. Nothing was added to or changed in the crontab.
Nearest spec: main §7.5 (the weekly scan's cadence — "every Monday, persona-country clock"), §7.11; ui §5.1; invariant 22.
Class (filled by audit):

## 2026-09-07 — R-NEXTSCAN — Three kinds of store are told nothing, and that is quieter than the machinery actually is
Decision: `nextScanAt` stays `null` — the screen renders in full and simply carries no timing line — when a kill switch is up (the product as a whole, or this account), or when the account's engine is stopped: deletion requested, not paid up, or vacation mode switched on. The API asks those two questions by calling the very functions the scan calls (`mayAccountWorkRun` and `accountLifecycleGate`, `packages/jobs/src/runtime/gate.ts`) rather than re-deriving either answer.
**Flagged, because the second half is deliberately not what the machinery does.** The weekly sweep consults the kill switches but *not* the lifecycle gate: today an unpaid store and a store on vacation are still scanned every Monday. So this makes the screen quieter than the truth for those merchants — they will be scanned, and are told nothing about it. That direction was chosen on the card's instruction and because it is the safe error: silence costs a merchant a sentence, whereas telling someone we have stopped working for that work is scheduled is a promise the product may not keep, and the moment billing ever does gate the scan the screen would be lying rather than quiet. Read access is untouched by any of this (invariant 16) — every opportunity, count and last-scan date still renders.
**Left open for the founder:** whether the weekly scan itself should skip a store nobody is paying for. It is a real question about cost — a scan is free of vendor spend by design (main §7.5, steps 1–5) but not free of database work — and it is not a scan-timing card's to take.
Nearest spec: main §7.5, §14.4 (degrade to a visible pause rather than a plausible guess); invariants 16, 22.

## 2026-09-07 — R-NEXTSCAN — A Monday already scanned is answered with next Monday, not with today
Decision: when the store's current local date is a Monday, the API looks for a *finished* weekly run recorded against that exact date — the same `weekly-<accountId>-<local Monday date>` id the sweep derives — and, if it finds one, moves the answer on a week.
Why: without it a merchant reading the screen on Monday afternoon, hours after their scan finished, would be told a scan is coming that has already been and gone. The lookup is one indexed read on the pair the `signal_runs` table is already unique on, so it costs nothing, and it uses the run id rather than a date comparison because the id is the thing the sweep's own idempotency turns on — a scan that ran and a scan we think ran can never disagree.
Consequence: a Monday whose scan has *not* run yet is answered with the next wake-up, which is later the same day. That is correct — it is genuinely still coming — and the empty-state sentence renders its "today" form for it.
Nearest spec: main §7.5, §14.3.1 (derived idempotency keys); ui §5.1.

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — R-OVERRIDE-TOPIC — The calendar says what happened to the day; the article page keeps the fuller story
Decision: once a merchant overrules a quality refusal and the article goes out, the calendar draws that day as **published** and shows no rejection. The article page continues to show both facts — that we objected, and that the merchant published anyway.
Why: the two surfaces have different jobs, and the founder chose to let them differ rather than reconcile them. The calendar answers "what happened on this day", and what happened is that an article went out; drawing a refusal there contradicts the merchant's own store. The article page answers "what is the story of this piece", where being overruled does not undo having been objected to — `R-OVERRIDE-JUSTIFICATION` deliberately kept both events in that history for the same reason.
What it rests on, verified rather than assumed: the calendar serialiser attaches a rejection only while the topic is still `rejected_by_gate` (`apps/web/app/api/calendar/_lib/handlers.ts`), so moving an overruled topic to `published` removes the rejection card without any change to that code. The decision was put to the founder on that basis and the behaviour was checked before it was written down.
Held by a test rather than by memory: `calendar.test.ts` asserts a delivered, overruled day reads `published` with a null rejection. The neighbouring case — an overridden article that has *not* yet gone out — still asserts the refusal is named, because that day genuinely is still held.
Nearest spec: main §8.6 (the override and its audit row), §8.7 (the calendar's states); ui §6.1, §6.3; invariant 12.

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — R-REWRITE-PLACE — A rewrite replaces the article in place
Decision: when the product rewrites one of its own articles, it updates the existing post — same address, same post, new words — rather than publishing a second one. Confirmed by the founder directly, matching the answer relayed through the `sortiva-a8` session earlier the same day, so the two paths agree and this entry is the decision of record.
Why: a second post competing with the first for the same search is cannibalization, which the existing-target check (invariant 6) exists to prevent, arriving by the one route that check does not guard. Updating in place also keeps the article's accumulated search history. The cost the founder accepted: a rewrite overwrites words a merchant may have edited themselves.
The boundary, carried from `R-PUBLISH-2` and not automatic: a republish sends title, body and summary only. A rewrite does the same. It does not touch the post's address, the merchant's own tags, or their choice to unpublish it. The accepted cost is that our words are replaced, not that everything around them is.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.5, §14.3.7 (the two-phase publish's conditional update, which already exists and never falls back to create); invariants 6 and 19.

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — R-HANDLE-RENAME — We follow a rename by listening for it, not by guessing
Decision: when a merchant renames one of our published articles on their shop, we learn it from Shopify's notification rather than by matching on title or on the marker metafield. The alternative — a second recognition key — was declined.
Why: a second key costs a lookup and can be wrong, and being wrong here means claiming a merchant's own writing as ours.
What this rests on, verified after the decision and cheaper than the question implied: **`articles/update` is already a topic the app subscribes to** (`packages/core/src/catalog/webhooks.ts`) and already arrives as an `article_updated` event. So this is not a new subscription, a new scope or a new failure mode — it is teaching an existing receiver to notice that the address moved and to write the new one down.
What it does not cover, and this is a real limit rather than a caveat: an export-mode store, where the merchant pastes our article into their own blog, never gives us a Shopify article at all. There is no notification and no id for those, so recognition there stays by address and a rename still detaches. Export is the default delivery mode, so this answer fixes the auto-publish half only.
Nearest spec: main §9.5, §12.3, §14.3.7; tech §4.

## 2026-09-07 — FOUNDER — R-GONE-SUGGESTION-CLOSES — A suggestion goes when its page goes
Decision: when a merchant deletes a page, the suggestion to improve that page stops being offered as work.
Why: it cannot be acted on, and leaving it on the screen asks the merchant to keep deciding about something that no longer exists.
Two things the answer does not state, taken as follows and flagged in the session report so they can be reversed cheaply: the row moves to a closed status rather than being deleted, because invariant 10 says expiry never deletes and the row is the only record that we ever suggested it; and a page the nightly walk finds again brings its suggestion back, matching what `R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE` already decided and tested for the improve-this-page button, where a restored page is eligible again with nothing else run.
Nearest spec: main §7.9 (the opportunity lifecycle), §12.3; invariant 10; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE.

## 2026-09-07 — R-RECO-VIEW-ONE — The one recommendation mapping lives with the lane that owns the recommendation, and the old address becomes a forwarding line
Decision: the mapping from a stored improve-this-page recommendation to the version a merchant reads now exists once, in `packages/core/src/optimize/recommendation-view.ts` — Lane E's own core directory, beside the recommendation type it reads. It produces the **full** view: the fields, the sections, the questions, the links, the note, and the row's own id, address and time. The opportunity drawer's shorter version is **cut from that full view** by a function that only drops fields, so the two can no longer say different things. The file the previous copy lived in, `packages/core/src/opportunities/recommendation-view.ts`, is now nothing but a re-export of the same names, so the opportunities barrel and the drawer's own handler — another lane's files — did not have to change at all.
Why: the thing that changes is the *recommendation's* shape, and the lane that changes it is Lane E. Leaving the shared mapping in Lane C's directory would mean every future change to what a recommendation contains is made by a lane reaching into a directory it does not own — which is exactly the reason the copy was made instead of shared in the first place, so keeping it there would leave the cause in place while removing this instance of the effect.
The alternative, stated because it is a fair one: keep the whole mapping where it was, in `core/opportunities`, and have this lane import it from there. Fewer files, no forwarding line, and it would have satisfied the card. It was rejected for the reason above, and because publishing the new full-view names from that directory would have meant editing another lane's barrel file anyway — so the "cheaper" option was not actually cheaper in files touched outside this lane.
Cost accepted: a five-line file that holds no logic. **It can be deleted by the integrator whenever it is safe to edit `packages/core/src/opportunities/index.ts`** — move the seven names it forwards onto the `optimize` barrel and delete the file. This card did not do it because that barrel is not this card's to touch and Lane C may be mid-card.
Who decided and on what authority: this lane. No user-visible behaviour differs either way — the merchant reads the same two screens — so it is an engineering choice, and it is reversible by moving one file.
Nearest spec: main §10.4 (the recommendation output and its download); build plan §3 (lane ownership); CLAUDE.md code-structure rules.

## 2026-09-07 — R-RECO-VIEW-ONE — What "the same advice" is proved against
Decision: one test, in this lane's directory, stores a single recommendation and then calls **both** real endpoints — the opportunity drawer and the recommendation card — against a real database, and asserts the drawer's answer equals the card's field for field, for a recommendation that succeeded and for one that was refused. The two older tests that each checked one screen's mapping on its own are left in place.
Why: the defect this card removes is *disagreement between two screens*, and a test that checks one screen cannot see it — that is what the two existing tests were, and adding a third of the same kind would have measured nothing new. Driving both screens from one stored row is the only shape of test that fails when they diverge; it was checked by breaking the shared mapping deliberately and watching it go red. The older single-screen tests stay because they also cover things this one does not (whether the store page looks already changed, what the download contains), and one of them lives in another lane's directory.
Nearest spec: main §10.4; ui §5.3.
## 2026-09-07 — R-CALENDAR-PARAMS — A calendar day's explanation is rebuilt at read time, from the rows that persist
Decision: a new `topicWhyLine` (`packages/core/src/calendar/why-line.ts`) works out the values a day's sentence needs from the day's row and the opportunity behind it, and all three calendar routes go through it. The move/pin response and the add-a-topic response each pay one extra query to read that opportunity back.
Why: a topic stores only the *key* of its explanation — `why_line` is a single text column and there is nowhere beside it for the values — so every screen showing a day has to put them back, and none of them did. Rebuilding is possible because the planners choose the key from things that are stored: the scheduler stores the opportunity's own reason key, and the opportunity row holds that key's values beside it as a matched pair. Rejected: adding a column for the values, which is a migration and this is not a schema-wave card; and filling them in each route, which is how the three drifted apart in the first place. The two extra queries were accepted rather than leaving those two responses with a placeholder, because both re-render the chip on screen — a merchant dragging a day would have watched its sentence go blank.
Nearest spec: main §8.7, §9.6.8; ui §6.1; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-07 — R-CALENDAR-PARAMS — A sentence whose values were never recorded is replaced, never printed with the blank showing
Decision: when a day's stored key names a sentence that cannot be filled, the day falls back to the reason its opportunity carries; failing that, to the screen's own line ("We planned this one from your growth opportunities." / "You added this topic yourself."). It never renders the unfillable sentence.
Why: one line genuinely cannot be rebuilt. The replenishment planner explains some days with "Similar to your best-performing articles, going by {dimension}", and that axis was worked out against a table of learned patterns which has since moved on — nothing persists it, and re-deriving it at read time would answer a *different* question than the one the day was planned on. A second case is a stored key that has drifted from its opportunity's current reason, which re-detection can cause because it updates an opportunity in place rather than making a second one. In both, the merchant loses a more specific sentence and gains a true one; the alternative was the literal text `{dimension}` on screen, which is the defect this card exists to remove. The fallback chain is the planner's own: its last resort is already "use the opportunity's reason".
Cost, stated: a merchant whose day was chosen because it resembles their winning articles will now read the underlying opportunity's reason instead. Recoverable only by storing the values, which needs a column and therefore a schema wave.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.8; ui §6.1; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-07 — R-CALENDAR-PARAMS — The no-blanks guarantee is proved by rendering, and the old template-level check is left alone
Decision: `apps/web/app/api/calendar/_lib/why-line.test.ts` renders every sentence a calendar day can show — from every opportunity reason, every Gate 1 verdict, each of the planner's four lines, the two the calendar writes itself, an empty column, and a key nobody has words for — and fails on a surviving brace. The values it renders with come from what each producer declares it sends, not from reading the sentence. The template-level guard `R-GATE-COPY` left in `packages/ui/src/strings/reason-copy.test.ts` is **not** changed.
Why: the card's own point is that a check over the template cannot see this fault — the calendar's tests asserted a key and a params object were present, which was always true, while the screen showed the braces. Rendering is the only check that sees what a merchant sees.
The guard was left alone because its premise is only half retired. It forbids a number in the eleven Gate 1 / Gate 2 / calendar sentences, for three stated reasons: the calendar sent nothing (fixed here), Gate 1 buries its measurements a level down in the audit column, and Gate 2 records none. A held day shows **two** sentences — why it was planned, filled from the opportunity, and why it was stopped, filled from the gate's own decision — and only the first is fixed. A number added to a Gate 1 sentence today would render on the first and print a brace on the second. So the guard still bites, and `R-GATE-PARAMS` is what retires it. The rendering test above covers that second surface too, so the failure is named there as well.
Nearest spec: main §8.2, §8.5, §8.6; ui §6.1; invariant 8.
## 2026-09-07 — R-HANDLE-RENAME — A rename is followed only where the shop's own id says which post it is
Decision: the walk decides that one of our own articles has moved by matching the post's Shopify id — the id the shop gave us when we made the post, kept on the publication claim (`publish_intents.shopify_article_id`) — against the id on the post the shop has just handed back. Nothing else counts as a rename. A post whose id we do not hold is left entirely alone.
Why: the founder declined a second recognition key precisely because being wrong here means claiming a merchant's own writing as ours. This is not a second key: it is our own paperwork from the moment we made the post, exact, and it exists only for posts we made. A title match or a nearest-address guess would put our article's address onto a page the merchant wrote.
What it costs, and the founder's answer already states it: only auto-publish delivery produces such an id. An export-mode store — the default — pastes our article onto its own blog, the shop believes the merchant wrote it, and a rename there still detaches the article from its page. A test asserts that limit rather than leaving it to be inferred.
Nearest spec: main §9.5, §12.3, §14.3.7.

## 2026-09-07 — R-HANDLE-RENAME — The address the shop has abandoned is marked gone, and keeps its marking
Decision: when a rename is followed, the inventory row at the old address is marked `gone`, and it keeps both its `article_ours` marking and its link to the article. It is not deleted and not demoted.
Why: our own articles are exempt from the nightly deletion sweep, so nothing else would ever retire that row — it would sit `live` for ever at an address nobody can open, and everything reading the live inventory would go on counting it as coverage. The exemption exists because a walk failing to find an export-delivered article is evidence of nothing; a shop telling us the same post now has a different address is evidence of something, and is the one case where absence has a cause we know.
Keeping the marking follows the rule `R-ARTICLE-OURS` set — the walk marks and never un-marks. The row is our record that we delivered an article to that address, and the shop moving the page does not make that untrue. `gone` rather than deleted is the same reason store pages are never deleted: the walk can find an address again and put it straight back to live.
Nearest spec: main §12.3, §14.1; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-ARTICLE-OURS "The walk marks, and never un-marks", R-PAGE-GONE-WRITE.

## 2026-09-07 — R-HANDLE-RENAME — Only a rename is followed; an article we hold no address for is left alone
Decision: the walk corrects an address it already holds. It never fills in a missing one — an article we posted to the shop as an unpublished draft has no public address and we hold none for it, and this leaves it that way.
Why: filling one in is a different behaviour from correcting one, with its own question behind it (does a post going from draft to live on the shop count as us having published it?), and nobody has asked it. The card asked for a rename to be followed.
Consequence worth naming: such an article stays unrecognised until it is published and something records its address. Nothing about that is new; this card simply does not change it.
Nearest spec: main §9.5.

## 2026-09-07 — R-HANDLE-RENAME — The inventory's repository reads the publication claims and writes the article's address
Decision: `shopPostsWePublished` and `followOurArticleRename` live in `packages/db/src/repositories/inventory.ts` — Lane C's file. The first reads `publish_intents` and the second writes `articles.published_url`, both of which belong to the publishing pipeline's domain.
Why: recorded because the repository-ownership rule of 2026-09-07 assigns a repository file to the lane owning the domain it serves, and these two cross that line — further than the read `R-ARTICLE-OURS` already journalled, because one of them writes. The alternative was to put the inventory's own question and the inventory's own correction inside another lane's file, which is the worse of the two and is what the earlier entry decided for the same reason. The write is guarded to a published, auto-delivered article whose stored address is the one being moved from, so it can only ever correct an address we ourselves posted to.
A related placement, in the same spirit: a publication claim is named after the article it was made for and nothing else joins the two, so `packages/jobs/src/inventory/tasks.ts` unpacks the name with the article pipeline's own reader (`articleIdFromIntentExternalId`) rather than a query being taught the shape of the name in a second place.
Nearest spec: build plan §3 as amended 2026-09-07; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-ARTICLE-OURS "The inventory's repository reads the articles table".

## 2026-09-07 — R-TOAST-CODES — The refusal check is derived from the route table, so the two codes outside the conflict enum are covered by it
Decision: the exhaustiveness check behind the Opportunities screen's refusal copy (`packages/ui/src/opportunities/conflict-copy.test.ts`) no longer walks the conflict enum. It walks the route table: every conflict code, plus the lapsed-subscription code wherever a route declares it needs an active subscription, plus the rate-limit code wherever a route declares limits. A refusal with no sentence fails a test that names the code.
Why: the browser reads the short machine-readable refusal code off **any** failing response, not only a 409 (`httpOpportunitiesApi.post`). Two contract codes sit outside the conflict enum deliberately and correctly — `entitlement_inactive` (402, the subscription lapsed) and `rate_limited` (429) — so a check over that enum passed while both still reached the merchant as "This opportunity was updated by the latest scan." The route table already declares which routes carry each, so the browser can derive the whole refusal surface instead of keeping a second list; a hand-kept list is how these two survived the card that gave every other refusal its words.
Rejected: widening the conflict enum to hold them, which would be a contract change (the integrator's), and would also destroy what that enum means — the set of codes a guarded state change returns.
Nearest spec: tech §3; ui §5.4; main §4.2 (billing gates new work, never read access).

## 2026-09-07 — R-TOAST-CODES — A rate limit says here what the preview screen already says, rather than getting a second sentence
Decision: `rate_limited` maps to `preview.rateLimited` — "Too many requests — try again in a minute." — the sentence the public preview screen already shows when it meets the same 429.
Why: only the preview route declares rate limits today, so this is defensive rather than live; a limit put in front of any other button would otherwise arrive as a scan conflict. Reusing the existing sentence rather than writing a near-identical one keeps one set of words for one event, which is the same reasoning that already points `service_paused` at the pinned outage wording. The cross-namespace key looks odd at the call site and is commented for that reason.
Rejected: a new `opportunities.toast.rateLimited` saying the same thing, which is two sentences to keep in step for no gain.
Nearest spec: ui §5.4; main §14.5 (the preview's limits); invariant 24 (canonical strings are not reworded — this is not one of them, but the same one-sentence-one-event posture).

## 2026-09-07 — R-TOAST-CODES — FLAGGED: a merchant whose subscription lapsed is still told their opportunity was re-scored
Decision: left without a sentence, on purpose, and now recorded by name in `REFUSAL_CODES_AWAITING_COPY` (`packages/ui/src/opportunities/actions.ts`) with a test that holds the list honest in both directions — a code that is given words has to leave the list, and a code no route can return any more has to leave it too.
Why not fixed: what a lapsed subscriber should read is billing copy, and billing copy is the founder's. Six routes answer this code and two of them are buttons on the Opportunities screen — "Schedule" on a CREATE or REFRESH card, and the recommendation generator — so the merchant presses, is told their opportunity was updated by the latest scan, and is not told the one thing they could act on. That is untrue rather than merely unhelpful.
The behaviour is deliberately unchanged rather than quietly redirected to a different generic line. Routing it to "That didn't go through — nothing was changed." would be less wrong and is a one-line change, but choosing what a lapsed subscriber reads is a product decision, and making it silently is how the original defect happened. **Recommendation, for the founder: one sentence that says the subscription is not active and that published work and read access are untouched (main §4.2), and it closes.**
Nearest spec: main §4.2; tech §3; ui §9.4.

## 2026-09-07 — R-TOAST-CODES — Two comments corrected in passing, and one adjacent gap left alone
Decision: two comments in `packages/ui/src/strings/reason-copy.ts` and `reason-copy.test.ts` said the calendar sends an empty bag of values with every chip's why-line. That stopped being true when the calendar's routes were fixed earlier tonight. Both now say what is still true — a *held* day renders two sentences, why it was planned and why it was stopped, and only the first is fed, because Gate 1 files its measurements where the read-back does not look and Gate 2 files none — which is why the guard those comments justify still bites. One test's name changed with it, since the old name named the retired half. No behaviour changed.
Left alone and flagged instead: `SCAN_REASON_PARAMS` in the same file omits `freshness_opportunity.requested` and `freshness_opportunity.our_own_article`, though both are on the list of keys the guard checks. The guard iterates the map, so it silently skips them — the exact blind spot it exists to close. It is not a one-line fix: both sentences interpolate `{article_title}`, and nothing in `packages/core` produces either key, so there is no producer to mirror. Establishing who emits them and with what values is somebody's card, not a correction made in passing.
Nearest spec: ui §6.1; main §7.1; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-07 — R-TOAST-CODES — FLAGGED: three of the five addresses the Opportunities screen posts to do not exist, and the browser test invents them
Decision: found while proving the new sentences reach the screen, verified against the frozen route table and against every `route.ts` on disk, **not fixed** — it is a different card and touches another lane's ground.
`httpOpportunitiesApi` (`packages/ui/src/opportunities/actions.ts:225`) posts five paths under `/api/opportunities`. Two are real: `/{id}/dismiss` and `/{id}/schedule`. Three are not, anywhere:
- `/{id}/restore` (`actions.ts:211`), the Undo on a dismiss toast. The contract and the server both call it `undismiss` (`packages/core/src/api/routes.ts:355`, `apps/web/app/api/opportunities/[id]/undismiss/route.ts`). **Live effect:** the merchant presses Undo, is told "That didn't go through — nothing was changed", and the card disappears again when the list re-reads.
- `/{id}/recommendations` (`actions.ts:240`), the "Generate recommendations" button. The real route is `POST /api/recommendations` (`routes.ts:382`, `apps/web/app/api/recommendations/route.ts`) — **which is the route that returns `optimize_page_gone` and `optimize_no_target_query`.**
- `/{id}/tasks/{taskId}` (`actions.ts:244`), "mark applied" in the drawer. The nearest real route is `POST /api/recommendations/{id}/apply` (`routes.ts:390`).
Why nothing goes red: the browser test's stand-in server implements the invented addresses (`apps/web/e2e/mock-api-server.ts:233` and `:248`), so the end-to-end flow passes green against a server that answers what nobody built. That is the same shape as the day's other findings, one layer further out — and it is the reason the mock server is not evidence about wiring.
**Consequence for this card, stated plainly:** the two new sentences are correct and are proved to be what the merchant reads once the code arrives; on the deployed product the code cannot arrive from that button, because the button asks an address that 404s. Closing this needs the button pointed at the real routes, which is a wiring card in the shape of `R-EXPORT-WIRE`.
Nearest spec: ui §5.4; tech §3; build plan §6 (the "screens call addresses that have no route file" family and its missing routes-on-disk check).
## 2026-09-07 — R-GONE-SUGGESTION-CLOSES — The nightly walk closes the suggestion, not the weekly detection pass
Decision: a suggestion about a deleted page is taken down by the store walk, on the batch that reached the end of the store, immediately after the walk has marked the missing pages gone. The weekly signal scan — which already has an expiry pass and already has the analytics handle this would want — was the alternative and was not used.
Why: the walk is the only thing in the product that can conclude a page has gone, and it runs every night; the scan runs weekly. Putting the closing in the scan would mean a merchant looking at a card they cannot act on for up to a week after deleting the page, which is most of what the founder's answer was about. The walk already holds the account's advisory lock when it gets there, so this needs no new serialisation.
What that costs, and it is the one thing worth reversing if it turns out to matter: the walk's dependencies carry no PostHog handle, so this pass emits no `opportunity_status_changed` event and the expiry dashboards will not count these closures. Wiring one in means adding a dependency to the inventory job and changing `apps/web/instrumentation-node.ts`, a file the build plan reserves for the integrator, so it was not done here. Every closure is logged (`opportunity_closed_page_gone`, with the account, the row, the signal and the status it came from).
Nearest spec: main §7.9 (expiry), §12.3, §14.1 (the nightly sweep), §14.7 (events).

## 2026-09-07 — R-GONE-SUGGESTION-CLOSES — The closed row is `expired`, stamped `entity_deleted`
Decision: the status is `expired` and the reason is the existing `entity_deleted`. No new status and no new reason was invented, and no migration was needed.
Why: main §7.9 defines `expired` as "the evidence no longer holds at a later scan" and gives "product deleted" as one of its own examples, and says in the same breath that expiry never deletes the row. `entity_deleted` was already in the list of expiry reasons the code allows ("the product or page the opportunity was about no longer exists") and had no writer until now — this is the case it was written for. The distinct reason matters downstream: `evidence_no_longer_holds` says a measurement moved, which is something the learning loop can draw a conclusion from, while `entity_deleted` says the merchant took the subject away, which it must not.
Nearest spec: main §7.9; invariant 10.

## 2026-09-07 — R-GONE-SUGGESTION-CLOSES — Only rows nothing else has taken over are closed
Decision: the pass closes a suggestion sitting at `new`, `accepted` or `blocked`, and leaves `scheduled` and `executing` alone. It also only looks at rows whose subject is a page address; a suggestion keyed on a search, a range of products or an article is not something an address can answer for.
Why: the same boundary the weekly scan's own expiry already draws. A `scheduled` row has a calendar day, and an `executing` one has a recommendation being generated; both belong to machinery in another lane, and expiring the row from under it would strand that work. Neither state is a dead end — they come back to one of the three above when the work finishes or refuses — so the next night's walk closes them then. In practice a page-keyed suggestion rarely reaches either, because the calendar's rows are keyed on searches and product ranges rather than on pages.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §8.7; build plan §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-GONE-SUGGESTION-CLOSES — Expiry can now be told which statuses it may expire from
Decision: `expireOpportunity` takes an optional set of statuses to move the row out of, defaulting to every open one, which is what it did before. The new pass names its three.
Why: invariant 15 wants the guard on the update to be the state the caller actually expects. Filtering in the caller's own code and then issuing an update that would accept any open status is not that: between reading the rows and writing one, another worker can have moved it into a status this pass was deliberately keeping its hands off, and the wider update would silently overwrite that. Naming the statuses turns it into a zero-row answer the caller stops on. The weekly scan's own expiry pass has the same shape and was left as it is — changing it is a fix to code this card was not sent to change, and it is written up in the session report instead.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §14.3.1; invariant 15.

## 2026-09-07 — R-GONE-SUGGESTION-CLOSES — Nothing was built to bring a suggestion back, and two tests say so
Decision: a page the walk finds again gets its suggestion back with nothing built for it: the row goes back to live, and the next detection pass proposes it again on its own, as a new row. The closed row stays closed. Two tests hold that — one that a restored page is suggested again, and one that there is exactly one open suggestion about it afterwards.
Why: the same answer `R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE` reached for the improve-this-page button, and for the same reason: the mechanism is that a deleted page keeps its row and its contents, so the walk seeing it again is all it takes. Reviving the *closed* opportunity instead was rejected — main §7.9 says a signal detected again after expiry is a new row, the partial unique index is written so that an expired row cannot block one, and the closed row is the record of a suggestion the merchant was actually shown and never acted on, which the learning loop reads as it was.
The consequence to know: a restored page waits for the next detection pass, so the suggestion can be up to a week coming back, where the improve-this-page button starts working again the moment the walk finds the page.
Nearest spec: main §7.9; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-PAGE-GONE-OPTIMIZE "A page put back in the store is eligible again with nothing else run".
## 2026-09-07 — R-PUBLISH-DEADLOCK — One order for the three rows of a calendar day, taken up front, rather than a per-account lock on the merchant's own click
Decision: a calendar day is three rows — the article, the day itself, and the suggestion the day came from — and every transaction that writes more than one of them now takes all three first, through a single function that owns the order (`lockDayForWrite`, `packages/db/src/repositories/day-lock.ts`): article, then day, then suggestion. The three callers are the daily hand-over (`markArticleDelivered`), the write-down of a post that went to the merchant's shop (`markArticleAutoPublished`), and calling a day off (`cancelDay`, which serves both the calendar's veto and the merchant's "not interested").
Why not the per-account advisory lock invariant 18 names, which would have made ordering irrelevant: **it is a worker facility and one of these two paths is a merchant's click.** The lock is taken in `withAccountLock` (`packages/jobs/src/runtime/lock.ts`), on a dedicated database connection, with a wait budget of ten minutes deliberately sized to queue behind a full catalogue sync. The publish hour is a worker step and already holds it; the dismissal is a Next.js request handler and holds nothing. Putting the same lock in the request would make "not interested" hang for as long as whatever background work that store happened to be doing — up to those ten minutes — on a button whose entire promise is an instant answer. The non-blocking variant would answer "your store is busy, try again", which is a new refusal a merchant has never been shown and is not this card's to invent. Two further facts, verified rather than assumed: the worker's lock is *session*-level on its own connection (the substitution journalled 2026-08-27 T0.4), so a transaction-scoped `pg_advisory_xact_lock` on the same key taken from a pooled connection inside a worker step would wait on the step's own lock for ever; and a second, separate lock namespace for publication would serialise only the paths that remember to take it — exactly the same discipline the row order needs, with an extra concept to explain.
What the row order buys that a mutex would not: it also orders these transactions against every *other* transaction that touches the same rows, present and future, rather than only against the ones that opt in.
Cost accepted: three extra `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` statements per publication and per cancellation. Both run once a day per store, or once per merchant click. A cancellation now also queues on the suggestion's row slightly earlier than it did, which is waiting we wanted.
Where the rule lives, because this is the second time it has been got wrong the same way: at the function every such transaction has to call, with each call site pointing at it. The previous attempt reasoned correctly about the two rows in front of it and did not notice which row its own transaction was already holding from further up; with all three taken at the top, a write added below cannot reintroduce the inversion, because there is nothing left to acquire.
Nearest spec: main §8.7, §9.4, §14.3.1; invariants 15 and 18.

## 2026-09-07 — R-PUBLISH-DEADLOCK — The auto-publish route was fixed with the export route, not left for a second card
Decision: `markArticleAutoPublished` — the paperwork after a post has gone to a merchant's own shop — takes the same up-front lock as the daily hand-over, though the card named only the hand-over and the cancellation.
Why: it is the same defect, the same three rows and the same merchant path, and a test added here proves it deadlocked in exactly the same way. The reason it is reachable at all is worth recording: cancelling a day refuses outright if a publication of that article is still claimed (`hasPendingPublishForArticle`), which looks like it would stop this race — but the claim is *confirmed*, in its own earlier transaction, before the article is written down as published. So during the transaction that races the cancellation there is no pending claim left to refuse on, and the two meet. Fixing one route and leaving the other would have left the card's own done-when — a publish racing a dismissal never deadlocks — false for every store that has auto-publish turned on.
Nearest spec: main §9.5, §14.3.7.

## 2026-09-07 — R-RULES-OVERRIDES — A store judged by an override stamps a version that says so
Decision: `rules_version` — the string stamped on every opportunity and gate decision so a decision can later be explained by the numbers behind it — stays exactly what it is today for a store on the repo file's numbers: the sha256 of `signals.config.yaml`. A store carrying an override stamps `<that same hash>+ov.<16 hex characters>`, where the 16 characters are a hash over the key/value pairs that actually won the fold.
Why: the file hash covers the file, which holds the global numbers and the per-language ones. A row in `rules_overrides` is not in that file, so a store carrying one and stamping the plain hash would be claiming it was judged by numbers it was not judged by — in the one record the learning loop and every audit read. Three properties were wanted and this shape has all three: a store on the defaults is unchanged, so nothing already stamped becomes wrong; the base hash stays at the front, so the version is still legible and still sorts and groups with the file it came from; and two stores given the *same* override stamp the *same* string, so the weekly calibration review's breakdown by `rules_version` groups a cohort rather than scattering into one bucket per store. Hashing the rows (with their account ids and timestamps) instead would have scattered it.
Alternatives rejected: a second column saying "overridden" needs a migration, and schema waves are closed; leaving the version alone was the thing the card exists to prevent.
The known limit, stated because it is the obvious next question: a store's *locale* still does not appear in the stamp, and two stores in different languages have always stamped the same version despite being judged by different numbers. That is pre-existing — the locale layers are inside the hashed file, so the hash identifies the document rather than the layer — and this card did not change it. If it matters, the fix is the same shape as this one.
Nearest spec: main §7.10; invariant 9.

## 2026-09-07 — R-RULES-OVERRIDES — A malformed override stops the store's scan rather than being skipped
Decision: an override row that cannot be applied — a key naming no threshold, a key naming a whole group instead of one number, a value of the wrong kind, or a value that leaves the merged set of numbers failing the config schema — throws. In the scan that means the run for that one store fails and retries into the dead-letter queue; other stores are unaffected, because a row is refused at the store it aims at.
Why: the card's own done-when. A threshold that quietly fails to apply is worse than one that was never set, because the operator believes it is in force and only the store's behaviour says otherwise. Falling back to the defaults and logging was the alternative and is the same failure with a paper trail nobody reads.
What makes this safe to do: `pnpm rules set` runs the identical check before writing anything, so reaching a broken row needs someone to write SQL by hand. `pnpm rules list` re-checks every row it prints and marks the bad ones, so the state is visible without running a scan.
Nearest spec: main §7.10; invariant 9.

## 2026-09-07 — R-RULES-OVERRIDES — The thresholds are read from the table on every scan, with no cache
Decision: no cache. `readRulesOverridesForAccount` runs once per scan of one store, and the numbers are folded fresh each time. The repo file itself stays cached process-wide as it was.
Why, and what it costs: one indexed lookup against a table that holds a handful of rows, next to the dozens of far heavier queries a scan already makes — the cost is not measurable at this scale. The thing bought is that there is no window in which the product is running on numbers the table no longer holds, and no invalidation to get wrong. The answer to "when does my change take effect" is "that store's next scan", with nothing else to explain.
What would change this: if a threshold read ever moves onto a request path — a screen resolving thresholds per page view — this needs revisiting. It is a per-scan read today and nothing else calls it.
Nearest spec: main §7.10; tech §2 (cost disciplines).

## 2026-09-07 — R-RULES-OVERRIDES — Only the weekly signal scan reads the table; the gates and the other jobs still read the file directly
Decision: the reader is wired into `packages/jobs/src/scan/run.ts`, which is where opportunities are detected, scored and written. Every other caller of the config — the topic-admission gate and the draft gates (`packages/jobs/src/generation`), the OPTIMIZE passes (`packages/jobs/src/optimize`), the keyword and catalogue jobs (`packages/jobs/src/ingestion`) — still calls `rules().forLocale(...)` and is unaffected by an override.
Why: those directories belong to Lanes B, D and E, and the build plan's ownership table is explicit. Wiring them is a one-line change each in shape, but each one also has to answer for the version it stamps on what it writes, which is the substantive half of this card and not a thing to do in someone else's directory without their card.
The consequence, stated plainly so nobody assumes otherwise: an override on a gate threshold — `gates.demand_floor.monthly_search_volume_min`, `gates.draft_grading.*` — can be set today and will **not** be applied by the gate. It is applied wherever the scan reads it. This is a real gap between what the operator command will accept and what the product currently honours; closing it is a card per lane.
Nearest spec: main §7.10, §8.2–8.4; build plan §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-RULES-OVERRIDES — A row's language is matched exactly, and the reader's declared shape changed
Decision: two smaller choices in the same area.
A row aimed at a language matches the store's recorded language exactly. A row for "da" does not reach a store recorded as "da-DK" — unlike the locale layers inside the config file, which resolve a full tag through its language subtag. Why: the table read and the fold have to agree about what "applies" means, and an exact string comparison is the one rule that is the same in SQL and in TypeScript. The subtag walk is a fold-time concept and putting half of it in a query is how the two drift apart. An operator who wants both writes both rows, and `pnpm rules list` shows them.
`RulesOverrideRow` — the shape the reader returns — used to carry `patch`, a partial layer already assembled. It now carries `key` and `value`, the two columns as they are in the table, and the patch is assembled during the fold. Why: the validation that refuses a malformed row has to name the key that is wrong, and by the time a row is a partial layer the key is gone. Nothing consumed the old shape — the interface had no implementation but the null one — so this breaks no caller.
Nearest spec: main §7.10, §6.5 (locale).

## 2026-09-07 — R-RULES-OVERRIDES — Setting an override replaces by deleting first, and wants a unique index it cannot have
Decision: `setRulesOverride` deletes the rows at the same aim with the same key and then inserts, inside one transaction, rather than being an insert-with-conflict.
Why: there is no unique index on `(account_id, locale, page_type, key)` and adding one is a migration, which only a schema-wave card may write. The transaction is what stops a crash between the two steps leaving the store with no override at all, and two operators setting the same threshold at the same moment still leave exactly one row, because the delete takes the row lock.
**A request for the next schema wave:** a unique index on those four columns, with the three nullable ones handled — Postgres treats nulls as distinct in a plain unique index, so it needs `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` or an expression index over `coalesce`d values. Until it exists, a row written by hand in SQL can duplicate one written by the command, and the fold will apply whichever sorts last rather than refusing. The command itself cannot produce that state.
Nearest spec: main §7.10, §13 `rules_overrides`; CLAUDE.md (migrations are added only by schema-wave cards).

## 2026-09-07 — R-RULES-OVERRIDES — A row aimed at every store needs two named people
Decision: `pnpm rules set` and `pnpm rules clear` require `--actor`, refuse `auto` as that name, and additionally require `--second` — a different named person — when the row is aimed at no store, no language and no page type, and therefore changes the numbers every store is judged by.
Why: the card sends this tool to follow `scripts/kill-switch.mjs`, and those are that file's two rules: a change is made by a named person, and a change that affects everybody takes two of them, so an incident is not closed because it was inconvenient. A global threshold row is the most dangerous thing this command can do — it changes the whole product's judgement, with no deploy and no review. An aimed row needs one name, as raising a switch on one account does.
This is my choice, not the founder's: the card said follow the house style and this is what following it means here. Reverting it is deleting one branch in `reviewWrite`.
Nearest spec: main §14.5; `scripts/kill-switch.mjs`.
## 2026-09-07 — R-GATE-PARAMS — Gate 1 writes its measurements twice rather than moving them
Decision: `admit-manual-topic.ts` keeps `scores_json.reasonCard` exactly as it was and adds `reason_params` beside it, holding the same values. Gate 2 gains the same key in `generate-article.ts`. Both now match the shape Gate 3 already wrote.
Why: the reason card is more than the values — it also records whether a held topic can resolve itself when the merchant changes something, and a page we can send them to. Nothing reads either yet, but they are the audit trail main §8.5 asks the gate to keep, and moving the card out to flatten it would have thrown them away to fix an unrelated read. Duplicating four small scalars in a free-form JSON column costs nothing measurable and leaves both readings intact. The alternative, giving the table a column of its own for these, is a migration and this is not a schema-wave card.
Nearest spec: main §8.2, §8.3, §8.5, §8.6.

## 2026-09-07 — R-GATE-PARAMS — The proof runs the real gate and reads the words, not the template
Decision: `apps/web/app/api/calendar/_lib/gate-reason-params.test.ts` drives the real Gate 1 and Gate 2 writers against a real Postgres, asks the real calendar route for the response a browser would get, and renders the sentence. Four of its five checks fail if the writers are put back the way they were, which was confirmed by doing exactly that.
Why: the fault this pair of cards closes is invisible to any check over a template — the calendar's own tests asserted that a key and a bag of values were present, which was true, while the screen showed the braces. The strongest check is that a hand-added topic Gate 1 stopped renders its two sentences — why the day was planned, from the opportunity, and why it was stopped, from the gate — to the same words. Those two rows are written from the same verdict, and before this card the first was full and the second empty, which is the precise reason the eleven sentences were written with no numbers in them.
Stated limit: the half that asserts a number appears in the rendered text can only bite once a sentence has a blank to put it in, and none of the eleven do yet. It is written to go live the moment one does, rather than needing a second card.
Nearest spec: main §8.2, §8.3, §8.6; ui §6.1; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-07 — R-GATE-PARAMS — The no-numbers guard is narrowed to the two lines nothing measures, not deleted, and this edits another lane's file
Decision: the guard `R-GATE-COPY` left in `packages/ui/src/strings/reason-copy.test.ts` — which failed if anyone put a `{blank}` in any of the eleven gate and calendar sentences — now covers only `topic.auto` and `topic.manual_addition`. Its sibling in `apps/web/app/api/calendar/_lib/why-line.test.ts` is narrowed the same way, and now renders the other nine with the values their producer sends instead of with nothing.
Why: the guard's premise was that no screen could fill these blanks, for three named reasons — the calendar sent nothing, Gate 1 buried its measurements, Gate 2 recorded none. All three are now fixed and the premise is retired, which is what this card was for. It is narrowed rather than removed because two of the eleven are the calendar's own words about the calendar ("We planned this one from your growth opportunities."), with no measurement behind them at all — a blank there could never be filled by anything, so that part of the guard is permanent rather than temporary.
**`packages/ui` is Lane F's directory and this is a deliberate crossing, flagged for the integrator.** Only the test and a stale explanatory comment are touched; no sentence a merchant reads is changed, and the sentences themselves (`packages/ui/strings/en.json`) are left entirely to Lane F. Leaving the guard standing would have blocked the copy edit this card exists to unblock, and the build plan records that stepping over it is the signal the work is done.
Nearest spec: main §8.2, §8.6; build plan §3 (lane ownership); `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-GATE-COPY and R-CALENDAR-PARAMS.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SLEEPY-RACE — The race is forced onto one branch rather than made true of both
Decision: the test "loses to a publication that commits underneath it" now waits until the dismissal is *observably queued behind* the article row the publication is holding — a poll of `pg_stat_activity` on the suite's own database — and only then commits the publication. Its assertions are unchanged: the dismissal loses, refuses with `topic_resolved`, and every part of it rolls back.
Why not the other option the card offered, asserting what is true of both branches: the two branches disagree about the only things worth asserting. When the dismissal reads the calendar day before the publication commits, it loses everything and refuses; when its first read lands after the commit, there is no day left to call off, so it dismisses the suggestion on its own and succeeds. `result.ok`, the suggestion's status, the day's state and the not-interested list all differ. What is left in common is "the article ends up published and nothing is half-applied", which is a far weaker statement than this test exists to make — and it is already made, unforced and twenty-five times over, by `packages/jobs/src/publish/complete-opportunity.test.ts`. The second branch also already has a test of its own ("dismisses a suggestion whose article has already gone out"), so weakening this one would have left the losing branch with no assertions anywhere.
What the wait is really asserting, stated because it is not obvious: a dismissal that is already blocked on that row has, by definition, already read the calendar day, and it can only have read it while the publication was uncommitted. Being blocked *is* the proof that we are on the branch the assertions belong to. A sleep could only hope for it.
Nearest spec: main §8.7, §14.3.1; invariant 15; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-PUBLISH-DEADLOCK.

## 2026-09-07 — R-SLEEPY-RACE — The lock-wait helper is copied into the second test file rather than shared
Decision: the "wait until a connection is queued on a lock" helper now exists twice in `packages/jobs` — in `publish/complete-opportunity.test.ts`, where `R-PUBLISH-DEADLOCK` wrote it, and in `generation/dismiss-opportunity.test.ts`. It is about fifteen lines. The two copies differ: the publish one waits for a given number of waiting connections, this one for at least one, and this one carries a failure message about the article row specifically.
Why: the natural home for a shared version is `packages/db/src/testing.ts`, which the build plan names as one of the files no lane owns and the integrator resolves by hand, precisely because merging both sides of it can be silently wrong. Putting a helper there to save fifteen lines is not worth a hand-resolved merge on a night with several lanes running. A third home invented inside `packages/jobs` would be a new structure this card was not sent to create.
The cost, so nobody is surprised: if the way we detect a blocked connection ever has to change, it changes in two places. Both are test-only. If a third caller appears, that is the moment to hoist it — with the integrator, not around them.
Nearest spec: build plan §3 (files no lane owns).

## 2026-09-07 — R-SLEEPY-RACE — The waiting budgets are set far above the work, on purpose
Decision: the forced race gets 120 seconds for the test and 30 seconds to observe the dismissal blocking. It takes about a tenth of a second when the machine is idle.
Why: this is the same reasoning `R-PUBLISH-DEADLOCK` applied to its own race tests, and this card exists because the suite went red for a reason that was not a defect. The two things that can make this test slow are a loaded machine and a broken ordering, and they must never be confused; a budget close to the real cost turns the first into the second. Thirty seconds rather than the publish tests' ten because the failure being guarded against here is a Node process starved of CPU by thirty test workers, which is exactly the condition under which this test misbehaved in the first place.
What a red still means: the 30-second wait fails with a sentence saying the dismissal never queued behind the held article row, which is true only if the dismissal stopped taking that row before it writes — a real change to `lockDayForWrite`'s contract, not noise.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.1; `docs/agent-work-plan.md` R-TESTDB.
## 2026-09-07 — R-OPPS-WIRE — Marking work applied costs a read first, because the id it is addressed by is published nowhere else
Decision: "mark this task applied" and "mark all as applied" each read `GET /api/recommendations?opportunityId=…` first, take the recommendation's own id out of the answer, and then post to `POST /api/recommendations/{id}/apply`. Two requests where the screen used to make one.
Why: the route that records work as applied is addressed by the *recommendation*, not by the opportunity the merchant is looking at — `findOptimizeRecommendation` looks the path parameter up in the recommendations table. The drawer's main read, `GET /api/opportunities/{id}`, does not carry that id: the contract's detail response describes the recommendation's fields, links and state and gives it no identifier at all. The one answer that does publish it is the recommendations read, which returns the stored view including its id.
Rejected, and it is the better fix: adding `id` to the recommendation object in `opportunityDetailResponseSchema`, which would let the drawer's existing read carry it and cost no second request. That is a change to the frozen contract and to a route in another lane's directory, so it is not this card's to make. **Flagged for the integrator**: if that field is added, this read can go.
Cost, stated plainly: one extra round trip per press, and a press made while the recommendation is being regenerated finds nothing and says "That didn't go through — nothing was changed." rather than marking something that has been withdrawn.
Nearest spec: ui §5.3; main §10.4; tech §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-OPPS-WIRE — "Mark all as applied" is one request against the recommendation, not one per task
Decision: the footer button posts to the apply route with no task named, which is what that route means by the whole recommendation. It used to fire one request per open task.
Why: the two are not the same thing on the server. Naming a task marks that task; naming none marks the opportunity applied, stamps the moment, marks every remaining task, and books the measurement of whether the advice worked for 28 days later. Marking each task in turn left the opportunity itself unapplied, so nothing was ever measured — the outcome the whole learning loop reads would simply never have arrived for a merchant who used that button. Nobody would have noticed for 28 days, and then only as an absence.
Nearest spec: main §9.6.2 (no verdict before 28 days), §10.4; ui §5.3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-OPPS-WIRE — FLAGGED: "Skip this task" is removed, because no route has ever recorded a skip
Decision: the Skip control beside each open task in the drawer is gone, and the screen's mark-a-task action narrows to "applied". The strings stay in the catalogue, and a task already sitting in the skipped state still renders as skipped.
Why: it posted to `/api/opportunities/{id}/tasks/{taskId}` with `{state: 'skipped'}`, an address that has never existed. `R-CONTRACT` moved marking-applied to `POST /api/recommendations/{id}/apply`, and that route takes only a task id — it marks applied and nothing else. The request schema for the old address, `markTaskAppliedRequestSchema`, is still in `packages/core/src/api/schemas.ts` and is now referenced by no route at all. So on the deployed product this button has always answered "That didn't go through — nothing was changed."; the card's done-when is that no press sends to an address nothing serves, and removing a control that only ever failed is the way to meet it inside this lane.
Rejected: mapping Skip onto the apply route, which would record a task the merchant declined as one they did. And leaving the button in place disabled, which needs new copy explaining a limitation nobody has decided to have.
**This is a user-visible removal and wants a decision rather than my judgement**: if skipping a task should exist, it needs a route and a line in the contract, and both are outside Lane F. The screen half is one small revert.
Nearest spec: ui §5.3; tech §3; build plan §3.

## 2026-09-07 — R-OPPS-WIRE — The check is a recorder on the real client, not a reader of the source
Decision: the new check (`apps/web/app/(app)/_lib/screen-addresses.test.ts`) drives every press through the same HTTP client the browser uses, records the addresses that come out, and holds each one against two things: the frozen route table, and the route files actually present under `apps/web/app/api`. The two halves fail separately and name the offending address.
Why: a check that reads `/api/…` strings out of the source would have caught none of the three. Every one of them was assembled at run time from a base path and a fragment, so the string a reader can see is `/api/opportunities` and the address the browser sends is something else. Recording what the client emits is the only view that matches what a merchant's browser does.
Both halves are needed because the two failures are different and this project has had both: ten endpoints were declared in the contract and built nowhere (screens rendering their empty state against a 404), and three addresses were sent by a screen and declared nowhere. Contract-only or disk-only would have missed one of those.
The check also names, as its own proof, the three exact addresses this screen used to send, and asserts the full list of presses rather than only their verdicts — so a press that quietly stops sending anything cannot make the check pass over a shorter list.
Nearest spec: tech §3; build plan §6 (`T10.2`, the routes-on-disk check, which is still the integrator's and covers the whole product rather than the screens).

## 2026-09-07 — R-OPPS-WIRE — The browser suite's stand-in server declares its addresses against the route table
Decision: every answer `apps/web/e2e/mock-api-server.ts` gives from run state is now registered through `declare(method, contractPath, handler)`, which throws at start-up if the frozen route table holds no such address. The hand-written path regexes are gone; the matcher is built from the contract's own spelling. The suite's control surface — resetting state, reading back what the screens sent, standing in for a vendor's redirect — is registered through `scaffolding()` and must live under `/api/_e2e/`.
Why: this server implemented two of the three invented addresses itself, so the screen was checked against a server built to agree with it and every browser flow passed green. Fixing the three strings and leaving the server hand-written would have left the next wrong address just as invisible. A stand-in that cannot answer an address the product does not have is a stand-in that can be evidence about wiring.
One thing left exactly as it was, and worth knowing before somebody tidies it: the answers are matched in declaration order, so `/api/opportunities/{id}` is declared last and would swallow a request for `/api/opportunities/scan-status`. That is the ordering hazard the route table itself carries a comment about, and it is unchanged by this card.
Nearest spec: tech §3; build plan §6 (the "checked against its own idea of itself" family).

## 2026-09-07 — R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES — Options are asked for in the field list; metafields are a request of their own, made only for a product we have not seen or that changed
Decision: the catalogue walk and the nightly sweep add `options` to the Shopify product field list, which costs nothing. Metafields are fetched with a separate `products/{id}/metafields.json` request per product, and only for a product whose row we do not hold or whose content fingerprint has moved. Both walks now count their run budget in requests rather than pages.
Why: no version of Shopify's REST Admin API returns a product's metafields alongside the product, so there is no cheaper shape available short of introducing GraphQL, which nothing else in this codebase speaks. At one paced request a second, asking for every product every night would turn a two-minute sweep into an eight-minute one per store for an answer that has not changed; gating on the fingerprint is the same discipline distillation already uses ("re-run only when the product's `updated_at` changes", main §6.3). The budget change follows from it: `PAGES_PER_RUN` promised "about eight minutes at one request a second", which stopped being true the moment a page of 250 products could cost 251 requests.
The consequence, stated plainly because it is the cost: a product whose metafields we have never read stays empty until the merchant next edits it. "We never asked" and "this store has none" are indistinguishable from our side, and telling them apart would need a column recording when we last asked — which is a migration, and schema waves are closed.
Nearest spec: main §6.2 (the catalogue read, which names metafields), §6.3; DECISIONS 2026-09-03 T4.0 (`products.options` / `products.metafields`).

## 2026-09-07 — R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES — Neither column joins the content fingerprint
Decision: `productContentChecksum` is unchanged. A merchant who renames an option axis or edits a metafield without touching anything else does not cause a re-distillation.
Why: the fingerprint is what distillation, the drift sweep and the family step's idempotency key are all keyed on. Adding two fields to it would give every product in every existing store a different fingerprint on the first pass after deploy, which reads as `product_updated` for the whole catalogue: a model call per product per store, a change-stream event per product, and a family regrouping for everyone, all at once. That is a cost decision with a blast radius, not a detail — so it is left for the founder rather than taken here. What is lost meanwhile is small: family grouping reads the option and metafield columns live from the database rather than through the fact sheet, so an edited axis is picked up by the next grouping run without any fingerprint moving; only the fact sheet's `variant_axes` waits for a re-distillation.
Nearest spec: main §6.3 (distillation cache key), §6.4.

## 2026-09-07 — R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES — A write that did not read a column leaves it alone, rather than reporting "none"
Decision: `ProductInput.options` and `.metafields` are optional, and `undefined` means "this caller did not read it". `upsertProducts` splits its batch by which of the two each row carries and gives each group its own conflict clause, so a column nobody read is not in the `SET` list at all. An empty list still means "the store states none" and is written.
Why: three paths write a product and they know different amounts. The full sync has both, the nightly sweep has options always and metafields for changed products, and a webhook delivery has options and never metafields. Without the distinction, every price edit a merchant made would arrive as a webhook and silently erase the metafields the sync had gone and fetched — the kind of loss nothing would report, because an empty column is exactly what an unconfigured store looks like.
Nearest spec: main §6.2, §14.1; DECISIONS 2026-09-03 T4.0 (the column defaults to `'[]'` so every reader's code is one shape).

## 2026-09-07 — R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES — Shopify's placeholder option is dropped where an option becomes an attribute, not where it is stored
Decision: the `Title: Default Title` option Shopify invents for a product with nothing to choose is stored verbatim with the rest and filtered out at the point an option is turned into an attribute or an axis name.
Why: T4.0 settled that the column holds what Shopify returns and that normalising it is the family-grouping code's job. The filter itself is not optional: family similarity is the fraction of attribute names two products share, so a placeholder every product in every store carries and agrees on would make two entirely unrelated products score a perfect match on it — the exact failure the sparse-product guardrail exists to prevent, arriving through a different door.
Nearest spec: main §6.4 (guardrails); DECISIONS 2026-09-03 T4.0.

## 2026-09-07 — R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES — Only two metafield types become attributes, with a length cap and a per-product ceiling
Decision: a metafield becomes an attribute only if the store declared its type as `single_line_text_field` or `list.single_line_text_field`, its value is at most 60 characters and holds no newline, and at most twelve per product are taken, in the merchant's own order. Everything else is stored and ignored. A metafield with no declared type is skipped rather than guessed at.
Why: a metafield value can be a document (`json`), an object (`rating`, `dimension`, `weight`), a formatted tree (`rich_text_field`) or an internal id (`*_reference`), and only the type says which. An axis name and value are shown to a merchant as a comparison-table heading and as a family tag, so reading an untyped value would put `{"value":4.7,"scale_max":5}` or `gid://shopify/Product/12` on their screen — the failure `packages/core/src/families/attributes.ts` already names ("an axis called `option_2` would be worse than no axis at all"). The length cap is the same argument as excluding `verifiable_claims` from axes: a sentence is true, unique to one product, and useless to compare. The per-product ceiling exists because similarity is a fraction over names, so a store keeping fifty metafields on every product would swamp the handful of facts read from its descriptions and every product would look like every other. All three numbers are UNCALIBRATED and named in one place; they are not opportunity thresholds and do not belong in `packages/rules`.
Flagged for the founder: this is the judgement in this card most likely to want revisiting once a real store's metafields have been looked at.
