Nearest spec: main §6.4; main §6.3 ("supplementary structured data … is merged in without distillation").

## 2026-09-07 — R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES — Option axes are set aside in the split-variant comparison, metafields are not
Decision: `withoutVariantTokens` now drops attributes sourced from the product's own options as well as from variant words in the title. Metafield-sourced attributes stay in the comparison.
Why: the split-variant check merges two rows that are one product published twice, and it does that by requiring their attributes to agree everywhere *except* the axis they vary along. An option is that axis by definition — "Trailblazer — Red" carries `Colour: Red` and "— Blue" carries `Colour: Blue` — so counting it as disagreement would make the check reject exactly the case it exists to recognise, and stores with options would have merged less than they do today. A metafield is not a variant axis by definition, and the file's own reasoning says which way to err: merging two genuinely different products is the worse failure, so evidence that they differ is kept.
Nearest spec: main §6.4 (split-variant detection).

## 2026-09-07 — R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES — A failed metafield read is "not read", and only a dead token stops the walk
Decision: any failure fetching one product's metafields is logged and treated as unread, leaving the stored value untouched and the walk continuing. A `shopify_token_invalid` is re-thrown.
Why: the product itself has already been read and is about to be written, so the metafields are an enrichment on top of work that succeeded. A product deleted between the list read and the metafield read answers 404, which Shopify's client classifies as non-retryable — so without this, one vanished product would fail a whole store's onboarding sync permanently. Treating it as unread rather than as empty is what makes the next sync try again. The token exception is the one failure that is the store's rather than the product's: it routes the merchant to the reconnect screen, and swallowing it would leave the walk grinding through a catalogue it can no longer read.
Nearest spec: main §6.2 (token revocation), §14.4.

## 2026-09-08 — T-WAVE6 — The claim staleness column is dropped, and the override table gets the index it always wanted
Decision: migration `0012` drops `article_claims.staleness` and its enum `claim_staleness`, and adds a unique index over all four scope columns of `rules_overrides` with `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. Authorised by the founder on 2026-09-07, who was shown what each of four unused storage things was for and answered "finish the first three, drop the fourth". Schema waves are otherwise closed; this is a mini-wave in the shape of `T4.0a`, `T4.0b` and `T-WAVE5`.
Why the column goes rather than gets built: it would have marked each claim an article makes as stable, seasonal or volatile, so the repair sweep knew which articles rot fastest. Nothing ever set it, so every claim was filed as "stable" by its own default. **The cost accepted: re-checking a published article stays time-based rather than content-aware.** The surrounding table is real and working and is untouched — every article we write still stores its plan of assertions and the evidence behind each.
Why the index is written in raw SQL rather than declared in the schema: this version of the schema builder has no `nullsNotDistinct()` on a unique index, and the clause is the whole point rather than a detail. Three of the four scope columns are null for a broader scope — a global override has no account, no locale and no page type — and Postgres counts two nulls as different values, so the ordinary unique index would accept the exact duplicate this one exists to refuse. The schema file carries a comment saying the index exists and where, because nothing in it would otherwise show that.
Held by a test rather than by memory: `constraints-t-wave6.test.ts` asserts the column and type are gone, that a claim still stores, that a second override at the same scope is refused globally and per store, that the same threshold at four *different* scopes is still allowed, and that the index really carries `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. **Mutation-checked:** with the index statement removed from the migration, three of those fail; with it restored, all seven pass.
Left for a lane: `pnpm rules set` still writes by delete-then-insert inside a transaction, which was correct when nothing stopped a duplicate. It can now be a single upsert. That is Lane C's file and not this wave's to change.
Nearest spec: main §6.3, §7.10; CLAUDE.md (migrations are forward-only and added only by schema-wave cards).

## 2026-09-08 — R-NUL-BYTE — The unmergeable-row key prefix becomes an ordinary space, and git is told source files are text
Decision: `packages/core/src/families/splitVariants.ts` no longer contains a literal NUL byte. The key that keeps an unmergeable row out of every bucket is now a named constant, `UNMERGEABLE_KEY_PREFIX`, whose value is a single space. `.gitattributes` marks `*.ts` and `*.tsx` with git's `diff` attribute.
What the byte was doing: split-variant detection groups product rows by their *residual title* — the title with colour, size and material words taken out of it, so "Trailblazer — Red" and "Trailblazer — Blue" both reduce to "trailblazer" and can be recognised as one product published twice. A title that is *nothing but* variant words reduces to nothing, names no product, and so must never share a bucket with anything. It was given a private key of its own product id behind a prefix, and that prefix has to be something no real residual title can start with.
Why an ordinary space is enough, and is in fact stronger than the NUL: the prefix is compared against a residual title, not against a raw merchant title, and a residual has had its whitespace collapsed and trimmed before it is ever used as a key. So a non-empty residual provably cannot begin with a space — in any language, any script, any alphabet. The guarantee comes from a normalisation five lines away in the same file, not from a belief about what merchants type, which is why it does not fail on a German or Arabic store. The NUL had no such guarantee: a title *can* carry a NUL and keep it through stripping, and when it did, the old code mistook that product's real residual for the private prefix and reported its title as empty. Verified: 40,000 random product sets built from Latin, CJK, emoji and whitespace-only fragments produce byte-identical grouping before and after; the only inputs that differ are titles containing a literal NUL, where the old behaviour was wrong.
Why `.gitattributes` as well, when the byte is gone: git calls a file binary when it finds a NUL and then prints a byte count where the diff should be. That is what happened here — a merge showed this file as `Bin 9457 -> 9930 bytes`, so nobody could review a change to it. Setting the `diff` attribute makes git render TypeScript textually whatever bytes it holds, which keeps the failure from recurring and, immediately, makes *this* commit readable: without it the diff is still binary, because the version being replaced is the one carrying the NUL.
Costs and limits: `diff` is set rather than `text` on purpose — `text` would also switch on line-ending normalisation, which is a separate decision nobody has asked for. A future edit that stops `stripVariantTokens` trimming would silently break the collision guarantee; the constant's comment says so, and a test now pins it.
Nearest spec: main §6.4 (split-variant detection); CLAUDE.md (a comment earns its place by saying what the code cannot show).

## 2026-09-08 — R-NUL-BYTE (addendum) — The mutation check the entry above promised, and one correction to it
This card was picked up after the session that wrote the entry above was killed mid-sentence, with the work uncommitted and its mutation check never run. The work was committed unchanged first, then checked. Both findings below are from running it, not from reading it.
The mutation check, now run: the new test was confirmed to fail when the guarantee it describes is deliberately broken, three separate ways. (1) Emptying the prefix, so an unmergeable row's private key is just its product id: the row whose title is `   p1` then lands in the same bucket as the row whose id is `p1`, and they merge — the exact collision the prefix exists to prevent. (2) Making the title stripper preserve original spacing, so a residual title *can* begin with a space: the private key becomes reachable and a real title is reported as empty. (3) Pointing the reader at a different prefix from the one the writer wrote, so the two uses drift apart. Each mutation failed that one test and left the other 43 passing, so the test is both load-bearing and narrow. Reverted after each.
The correction: the entry above, and the comment on the constant, said the guarantee comes from trimming, and warned against removing the trim. Trimming is only half of it. `stripVariantTokens` builds a residual out of words it obtained by splitting on whitespace and discarding empties, so no piece of a residual can carry a leading space before the trim is ever reached — mutation (2) went green until *both* were abandoned. The guarantee is therefore stronger than claimed, and the warning was pointed at one of two supports; the constant's comment now names both. Verified separately at runtime: a NUL passes through the stripper untouched (it is not whitespace, so neither the split nor the trim removes it) while a leading space cannot survive it, tested with ASCII space, tab, newline and the ideographic space U+3000.
Not verified: the entry above cites 40,000 random product sets producing byte-identical grouping. That run was not reproduced here and no fixture or script for it was left behind, so it is recorded as the predecessor's claim rather than as a checked fact. The evidence relied on instead is that all 43 pre-existing tests pass against the new code **untouched** — the test file's diff is 17 added lines and no deleted or altered ones — which is what shows behaviour did not move.
Shared file, flagged for the integrator: `.gitattributes` is not this lane's to own, and the two lines added to it change how git renders **every** `.ts` and `.tsx` file in the repository, not just this one. Kept deliberately: the setting only affects how diffs are displayed, never file content or checkout, and without it this very commit would have been unreviewable, since the version being replaced is the one holding the NUL. It needs an integrator's eye because it is repo-wide and every lane shares the file.
Nearest spec: main §6.4; CLAUDE.md (a comment earns its place by saying what the code cannot show).
## 2026-09-08 — R-CONTRACT-2 — The recommendations read is declared as what it answers, which is four shapes rather than one
Decision: `GET /api/recommendations` now declares `readRecommendationResponseSchema`, a union of the four answers the handler actually gives: advice that exists; advice being written right now; a technical fix, which is a different shape entirely and carries no recommendation; and nothing at all. It previously declared the opportunity-drawer shape, which this endpoint has never returned — the declaration required an `opportunity`, a `serpSnapshot` and a `history` the handler does not send, and omitted the `looksApplied` and `appliedAt` it does.
Why a union rather than one object with everything optional: the four cases are genuinely different answers, and a client that cannot tell them apart renders the wrong thing. An all-optional object would have been easier to write and would have described nothing.
Why nothing was red: `contracts:check` compares the declarations to each other and to the routes that exist on disk — never to what a handler returns. **That limit is now stated on the card rather than left to be rediscovered.** Two lanes found this independently on 2026-09-07, which is what made it worth doing rather than noting.
Also removed: `markTaskAppliedRequestSchema`, referenced by no route since the skip address it belonged to was removed with the button that had never worked.
The task shape is declared twice on purpose. This endpoint sends a task's `kind` and the opportunity drawer does not, so the richer shape is declared here rather than added to the shared one — widening the shared schema would have declared a field one of its two endpoints omits, which is the fault this correction exists to remove. **That the two endpoints disagree about a task's shape is left as found**; unifying them is a lane's call, not a contract correction.
One consequence handled rather than left: `packages/ui/src/msw/fixtures.ts` answered the old, wrong shape, so correcting the contract turned its guard red. That fixture is Lane F's file and the integrator edited it, because a contract change that breaks a fixture has to carry the fixture with it or `main` goes red. The fixture now answers the richest of the four real shapes, which is the one a screen is built against.
Not done here, and carded: the opportunity drawer's own read still does not carry the recommendation's id, so marking a task applied costs a second read. Adding the field is easy; **populating it is a lane's work, and declaring a field nothing fills is the exact pattern this whole day has been about.**
Nearest spec: main §10.4; tech §3; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 `R-CONTRACT`, `R-OPPS-WIRE`, `R-RECO-VIEW-ONE`.
## 2026-09-08 — R-GATE-NUMBERS — Six of the eleven gate sentences gain their measurements; three values stay out and why
Decision: `gate1.rejected_zero_volume`, `gate1.rejected_not_winnable`, `gate1.rejected_off_catalog`, `gate1.admitted_pinned_despite_zero_volume`, `gate1.converted_existing_target_refresh` and `gate2.held_thin_pack` now carry `{placeholders}` in `packages/ui/strings/en.json`. Three values their producers send are deliberately not printed: `winnability` and `boilerplate_ratio`, and `via`.
Why: the first two arrive as fractions on a 0–1 scale — a store's chance of ranking comes through as `0.09`, the share of repeated product copy as `0.83` — and a merchant reading "0.09" learns nothing. Turning them into "9%" is the producer's job, not the copy's: `product_family_coverage_gap` already does exactly that (`Math.round(share * 100)` in `packages/core/src/opportunities/reasons.ts:90`), and its sentence prints a plain "%". Dividing in the sentence would put a number rule in the copy layer, which is the one place the project has decided numbers never live. `via` names which of our data sources found an existing page — `gsc`, `content_mapping` or `limited_intelligence` — and is machine vocabulary, not English; showing it needs a sentence per value.
Nearest spec: main §8.2 ("every failure has a precise user-facing reason"), §8.3; invariant 9.

## 2026-09-08 — R-GATE-NUMBERS — Gate 2's sentence states what it counted without claiming that count is what stopped it
Decision: `gate2.held_thin_pack` reads "What came back held {distinct_claims} distinct point(s) — we look for at least {distinct_claims_min}, and for points that belong to individual products rather than repeating across all of them." It names the measured count and both requirements, and does not say which of the two failed.
Why: the gate holds a topic when **either** requirement fails — too few distinct facts, or too many of them repeated across every product (`packages/core/src/generation/gate2.ts:104`). A sentence reading "fewer than the 6 we need" would therefore be plainly false for the store held on repetition alone, whose count may be well above the floor. The sentence still gives the merchant the one number they can act on.
Nearest spec: main §8.3, §8.6.

## 2026-09-08 — R-GATE-NUMBERS — "We could only find about N searches a month" is what an unmeasured keyword says too
Decision: `gate1.rejected_zero_volume` prints the volume the gate recorded, which is `0` both for a keyword measured at zero and for one nothing measured at all — Gate 1 collapses "no reading" to zero before storing (`packages/core/src/gates/gate1.ts`, `demandFloorReason`). The sentence is worded "We could only find about {n} …" rather than "{n} people search for this" so it describes our reading rather than asserting the world.
Why: the alternative is a second sentence for the unknown case, which needs the gate to stop collapsing null to 0 — another lane's file and outside this card. The hedged wording is honest under both readings today. **Flagged for the integrator**: if the gate ever distinguishes them, this sentence should split in two.
Nearest spec: main §8.2 (demand floor); §8.6.

## 2026-09-08 — R-GATE-NUMBERS — The catalogue's placeholder reader was counting the words inside a plural form as values somebody had to send
Decision: `placeholdersIn` (`packages/ui/src/strings/reason-copy.ts`) now skips over a `{n, plural, one {…} other {…}}` block and reports the block's own number, instead of reporting the words inside it.
Why: it matched any `{word}`, so the first sentence to state both forms of a count made the copy checks fail with "asks for {search}, which its producer does not supply" — `search` being a word in the sentence, not a value. It also silently missed the one name that really does have to arrive, the number the block chooses on. Every check that asks "does this sentence only want things its producer sends" runs through this function, including the one in another lane that renders the gate's real output, so it had to be right before any sentence could state both forms.
Nearest spec: ui §6.1; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-08 — R-GATE-NUMBERS — Two sentences are left alone because giving them numbers means rewording approved copy
Decision: `gate1.held_insufficient_substance` and `gate1.converted_existing_target_optimize` gain nothing. They are aliases onto two Appendix A sentences, and their values now arrive — the held topic knows how many facts it found, how many it needed and how many products are short of detail.
Why: an alias has no wording of its own, so putting a number in one means either editing a canonical string (forbidden — invariant 24, and a snapshot test holds both character for character) or giving these two keys sentences of their own, which is a change to what a merchant reads and the founder's call. Main §8.6 asks a rejection card for "add material/dimension details to these 3 products and we'll retry this topic", which is precisely the sentence the values would allow, so the case for asking is strong.
Nearest spec: main Appendix A, §8.6; invariant 24; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-GATE-COPY ("Two of the eleven point at approved wording").
## 2026-09-08 — R-WRONG-GATE-REASON — A held day with no recorded reason gets its own key rather than a borrowed one
Decision: when a gate decision row carries no `reason_user_facing` of its own, `apps/web/app/api/calendar/_lib/handlers.ts` now sends the template key `gate.reason_unrecorded` with an empty parameter bag, instead of falling back to `gate1.held_insufficient_substance`.
Why: the fallback was a guess dressed as a measurement. `gate1.held_insufficient_substance` resolves, through an alias, to the Appendix A sentence saying the store's product descriptions do not yet carry enough detail to write from — a specific factual claim about the merchant's own catalogue. A Gate 2 or Gate 3 row missing its reason therefore showed that claim under a heading naming a different check ("Stopped at: Evidence check"), and nothing on the screen distinguished a reason we measured from one we borrowed. Admitting we did not record it says less and is true, which is the posture main §8.6 asks for when it requires a plain-language reason beside the gate that produced it.
Why a new key rather than reusing an existing sentence: the catalogue has no sentence for it yet, so the renderer answers with its own admission — "The reasoning for this one isn't available yet." (`renderTemplatedLine`, `packages/ui/src/opportunities/why.ts`, which catches the missing-string throw). That is already the right words. Giving the key purpose-written words later is then a copy edit inside Lane F, with no second change to this route. The response contract types `templateKey` as a plain string, so no schema or route change is needed.
The parameters are deliberately dropped: a sentence admitting we recorded no reason has no blanks, and the values the row did measure belong to the sentence that was never written rather than to this one.
Stated limit, and the thing another lane has to close: the CI guard that fails when a producible key has no sentence (`packages/ui/src/strings/reason-copy.ts`) works from hand-kept lists in Lane F's directory. `gate.reason_unrecorded` is not on them, so nothing fails today and the key could stay wordless indefinitely. Reported to Lane F rather than added here, because that file and `packages/ui/strings/en.json` are theirs. Note for whoever writes it: `gate.` is not one of `CATALOG_NAMESPACES` (`gate1.`, `gate2.`, `gate3.`, `topic.`), so the lookup resolves this key to `template.gate.reason_unrecorded` unless the namespace list gains `gate.`.
Nearest spec: main §8.6; ui §6.1; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-08 — R-WRONG-GATE-REASON — The proof asserts on the key and on the words, and pins neither the admission nor a future sentence
Decision: three tests in `apps/web/app/api/calendar/_lib/calendar.test.ts` drive the real route against a real Postgres for a gate 2 and a gate 3 row with no recorded reason. They assert the key is not Gate 1's, that the rendered sentence is not the Appendix A richness sentence, that the parameter bag is empty, and that the heading still names the check the row itself recorded. Confirmed to fail — all three — by putting the fallback back.
Why they do not assert today's admission text: Lane F will eventually write real words for this key, and a test pinning "The reasoning for this one isn't available yet." would go red on the day the product got better. Asserting what the sentence must *not* be survives that; asserting what it currently *is* would not.
The shared `held` helper gained a gate parameter, defaulting to 3 so its three existing callers are unchanged.
Nearest spec: main §8.6.

## 2026-09-08 — R-EXPIRY-GAPS — A store whose search data has stopped arriving has nothing search-driven retired
Decision: before the weekly pass retires anything, it asks for the newest day of search data the store holds. If that day falls before the window the pass just measured, no opportunity of a search-driven kind is retired on this pass, and the pass logs how many rows it held back (`signal_scan.expiry_held_open_no_search_data`). Inherited from an earlier session on this card, checked against the card and kept.
Why: retiring an opportunity says the evidence stopped holding, and we may only say that while we can still see the evidence. A store whose Google grant died, whose sync stalled, or which never connected produces exactly the same reading as a store where every page came right at once — and acting on it would take a merchant's whole board down on the strength of a broken pipe. This is the "degrade to pause, never to lower quality" posture (invariant 22) applied to expiry.
What it replaces: the old code held these cards open only when the connection itself was gone. A store with a live connection whose data simply stopped arriving had every search-driven card retired at once, which is the more likely failure of the two and was not covered.
The bar is the whole window rather than a fraction of it, because a fraction is a number and numbers live in `packages/rules`. The cost of the coarse bar: a sync that stopped part-way through the window still allows expiry, on thinner data than usual.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §7.11, §14.4; invariants 10 and 22.

## 2026-09-08 — R-EXPIRY-GAPS — FLAGGED: a store that never reconnects keeps its search-driven cards indefinitely
Decision: the card called the old behaviour "accidental immortality" and asked for a stated fate. The fate is now stated and it is still that the cards stay: nothing ages them out. That is deliberate and it is not complete.
Why nothing was built to age them out: §7.11 promises that connecting Search Console later re-scores the existing opportunities rather than duplicating them, which needs them to still be there; and how long a card may outlive its evidence before it is retired anyway is a number and a product judgement, not something a fix to an expiry pass may invent. **For the founder: the open question is whether a card whose evidence we have not been able to see for N weeks should be retired, and what N is.** Until that is answered, the log line above is what makes such a store visible instead of merely quiet.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §7.11; invariant 9 (no threshold outside `packages/rules`).

## 2026-09-08 — R-EXPIRY-GAPS — An intent-gap card retires when Search Console stops placing the page in the band the signal is defined over
Decision: the "this page answers less than the pages above it" card now has two ways out instead of one. Either a stored comparison was replayed for the page and reported nothing missing, or Search Console no longer places the page between the two positions the signal is defined over. Inherited from an earlier session, checked and kept.
Why: the paying pass that buys these comparisons shortlists inside the band only, so a page that has left the band will never be compared again — and under the old rule, which required a fresh comparison, its card could never be retired at all. §7.9 names "page moved to #2" as its own example of evidence no longer holding, so this is the spec's own case rather than a new one. The reason stamped is `evidence_no_longer_holds`, which is what a measurement moving means.
A page that has left the store is excluded from this route on purpose: the nightly walk retires that one under `entity_deleted`, and the two reasons mean different things to the learning loop — one says a measurement moved, the other says the merchant took the subject away.
The coupling this creates, and it is now commented at both ends: the free reader and the paying pass have to build the band the same way, or the scan retires cards for pages the paying pass deliberately admitted from outside it. They agree today because neither supplies the competitor-gap targets `shortlistIntentGapPages` will accept — nothing supplies them anywhere.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §7.3; invariant 10.

## 2026-09-08 — R-EXPIRY-GAPS — A renamed post takes its open suggestions with it, rather than losing them
Decision: when the shop tells us a post we published has a new address, the open suggestions about the old address move to the new one, in the same transaction that follows the rename. The founder's card recommended moving; nobody had decided, so this records the choice.
Why: following a rename marks the old address gone, and marking an address gone is exactly what the nightly walk reads to conclude a suggestion has lost its subject. So before this, renaming a post silently took down the advice about it, filed as `entity_deleted` — a reason that tells the learning loop the merchant removed the page. The page is the same page and the merchant never answered the advice. Doing the move inside the rename's own transaction means the walk never sees a gone address with live cards pointing at it, so no ordering between the two passes has to be arranged.
What is deliberately not moved: a suggestion the calendar or a recommendation run has taken over (`scheduled`, `executing`). That is the same boundary both expiry passes already draw, and moving the subject out from under running work is the hazard those passes were narrowed to avoid. Such a row keeps the old address until that work finishes and the walk closes it then — the residual, stated rather than discovered.
And a suggestion of a kind already open at the new address is left where it is and counted, because only one open suggestion of a kind may exist per subject (invariant 10) and the one already there was written against the page as it now is. The walk takes the stranded row down and the merchant has a live card about the real address either way.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §12.3, §14.1; invariants 10 and 15; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 R-HANDLE-RENAME "The address the shop has abandoned is marked gone", R-GONE-SUGGESTION-CLOSES "The nightly walk closes the suggestion".

## 2026-09-08 — R-EXPIRY-GAPS — FLAGGED: the not-interested marker stays at the address the merchant left behind
Decision: found while moving the open suggestions, not fixed, because it is about rows this card was not sent to touch.
When a merchant says "not interested" we write a marker keyed on the signal and the address (`dismissed_opportunities`, unique on `(account_id, signal_type, entity_ref)`), and the detector checks it before writing a new row. That marker is not moved by a rename. **Live effect:** a merchant who dismissed advice about a post, then renamed the post, is offered the same advice again at the new address. Moving the marker is not symmetrical with moving an open row — the marker is the record of an answer the merchant gave, and whether that answer travels with the page is a product question rather than a mechanical one.
Nearest spec: main §7.9; `packages/db/src/schema/opportunities.ts:213`.

## 2026-09-08 — R-EXPIRY-GAPS — The mutation check the card's tests had never been put through, and the one that was passing for free
Decision: every new test was run against the old behaviour before being kept. Four of the five in `packages/jobs/src/scan/expiry.test.ts` failed as they should. The fifth — "is left alone when the page left the store rather than the band" — passed either way and was rewritten.
Why it was passing for free: it wrote the page's last-seen time from the wall clock and then asked the walk to mark gone everything not seen since the test's own clock, which is the earlier of the two. The page was never marked gone, so the test proved nothing about a deleted page. It now writes the page on the test's clock and asserts that one row was actually marked gone before drawing any conclusion from the page being absent. With that fixed it fails against an implementation that does not exclude a deleted page, as it should.
The four tests added for the rename move were put through the same check: removing the move, ignoring the one-open-suggestion-per-subject rule, and widening the write guard past `new`/`accepted`/`blocked` each turn exactly one of them red.
Nearest spec: tech §6 (CI); `CLAUDE.md` (tests live beside code).
## 2026-09-08 — R-OPTIMIZE-AXES — A product's option axes stay out of citable evidence, now for a reason that is true of a field with values in it
Decision: `variant_axes` remains excluded from `CITABLE_FIELDS` in `packages/core/src/optimize/pack.ts`. The old reason — written when the field was hard-coded empty — was that it is "structured data the storefront already shows and that a pasted paragraph would go stale against", which was really an argument about `price_range` standing in for both. That half is rewritten; the price and the marketing flag keep their own reasons, which are unchanged and still correct.
What the field is, plainly: a fact sheet is the ten-odd things we know about one product with the marketing removed, and a recommendation may only suggest copy that cites one of them by address. `variant_axes` holds the merchant's own names for the choices on a product — "Size", "Colour" — read out of Shopify's option definitions by `R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES` on 2026-09-07. It is the most trustworthy attribute data we hold, because no model touched it.
Why it is still not evidence: **the sheet keeps the axis name and throws the values away, on purpose** (`axisNames`, `packages/core/src/distill/distill.ts:170` — a sheet describes one product, and listing values would say a shoe is black *and* tan). And an option becomes an axis whether the merchant filled it with twelve values, with one, or with none at all: `namedOptionAxes` drops only Shopify's `Title: Default Title` placeholder and deliberately keeps an axis a merchant defined and never filled in. So "Colour" is what a shop selling one black shoe and a shop selling five colourways both store, and from inside the pack the two are the same string. It reads as "this product comes in a choice of colours" and it means "this shop has defined a Colour option". Suggested copy is written to be pasted onto the merchant's own page in their own voice; a sentence promising their customers a choice that may not exist is the exact failure the grounding rule exists to prevent. The judge-lite would not catch it either — `gradingEvidence` hands the grader the whole fact sheet, so it is misled by the same half-fact rather than able to check the claim against it.
What this costs, stated because it is real: a store whose products carry a "Width: Regular/Wide" option gets no recommendation grounded in that, even where the ranking pages settle fit and sizing and the store's own answer is sitting in a structured field. A family's *differentiation* axes — what tells the products in one family apart — are separately citable as `family:<id>/axis:<name>` and unaffected, but they are a comparison across products: an axis every product in a family shares is not a differentiation axis, which is precisely the "every shoe here comes in wide" case this exclusion also loses.
What would let it be lifted, so this is a decision rather than a wall: the axis **values** reaching the pack, not a change to the citable list. Then `Colour: black/tan` is a complete assertion, and a one-value or empty axis is filterable. Two verified routes, both outside Lane E: extend `productSubstanceForFamilies` (`packages/db/src/repositories/distill.ts:132`), which today selects only the fact sheet, to carry `products.options` — the column exists and `productsForGrouping` already reads it; or add the values to the fact sheet itself, which is Lane B's call and would change what every downstream reader sees. **Recommended if a founder wants this: the repository read, because it takes the live column rather than a sheet that only moves on re-distillation** (per this card's sibling entry, an edited axis does not move the content fingerprint). Not built here — it is a new evidence source with its own shape, prompt and staleness questions, and this card asked for a judgement on the field as it stands.
Held by tests rather than by the comment alone: `packages/core/src/optimize/pack.test.ts` asserts no address is offered for the field, that a populated field yields a fact list identical to an empty one (so a store that publishes nothing there is exactly where it was), that the axis names never reach the writing model at all, that a suggestion citing one fails the grounding lint, and that family axes stay citable. Mutation-checked: adding `variant_axes` to the citable list fails four of the five.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 (the evidence pack and the grounding lint), §6.3 (`variant_axes`); DECISIONS 2026-09-07 `R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES`, 2026-09-02 T2.3.
## 2026-09-08 — R-INCIDENT-NOTES — A note outlives the incident, because lowering a switch updates the row rather than replacing it
Established, not chosen — the card asked for this to be checked before anything was designed. Lowering a kill switch is `UPDATE ops_flags SET reset_at = now(), reset_by = … WHERE … AND reset_at IS NULL` (`resetGlobalFlag` / `resetAccountFlag`, `packages/db/src/repositories/system.ts`). The row keeps its primary key, so `incident_findings.ops_flag_id` still names the incident it was written about, and a note survives the incident closing. Nothing anywhere deletes an `ops_flags` row. So no schema change and no different attachment point are needed, and the table is not write-only in the way the card feared.
A second fact that follows from the same read, and shapes the command: the two unique indexes on `ops_flags` are partial — they cover only rows where `reset_at IS NULL`. Raising a switch that was lowered last week therefore inserts a *new* row with a new id rather than reopening the old one. Each trip is its own incident, and notes stay attached to the occasion they explain rather than accumulating against the switch's name. This is why the note command addresses an incident and not a flag.
The one case where a note does disappear, stated rather than fixed: `ops_flags.account_id` cascades from `accounts`, and `incident_findings` cascades from `ops_flags`. Deleting an account therefore removes its account-scoped incidents and any notes on them. That is the GDPR hard-delete of main §14.6 working as intended — an operations note naming one store is store-derived data — and global incidents, which are the ones an investigation is usually about, are untouched. Changing it would mean keeping a record about a merchant who asked to be forgotten, so it is left alone.
Nearest spec: main §14.5 — "every auto-trip creates an incident record"; silent on what happens to the record afterwards.

## 2026-09-08 — R-INCIDENT-NOTES — `pnpm switch history`, because `list` deliberately shows only what is stopped now
Decision: a new subcommand, `pnpm switch history [<flag>] [--account <id>] [--limit <n>]`, printing incidents newest-raised first including closed ones, each with its notes and its id. Backed by `listRecentFlags` in the system repository. `pnpm switch list` is unchanged in what it selects and now prints the notes and the id under each open incident.
Why it is not scope creep: the card's done-when is "record a finding against an incident **and read it back later**". `listActiveFlags` answers "what is stopped right now" and says so in its own comment — it is the operator's incident board, and widening it to closed incidents would spoil the answer it exists to give. Without a second read, a note becomes unreadable the moment the incident it explains is closed, which is the write-only failure this card was raised to end, in a different place.
The id is now printed on every incident line-up. It is the only handle on a closed incident: a name resolves to the switch that is up, and once it is down nothing but the id names that particular occasion.
Nearest spec: main §14.5; silent on operator tooling. Follows the T8.4 precedent that a manual switch nobody can flip is not a manual switch.

## 2026-09-08 — R-INCIDENT-NOTES — A finding takes one name, deliberately weaker than the four-eyes rule beside it
Decision: `reviewFinding` (`packages/core/src/ops/kill-switches.ts`) requires a non-empty author and a non-empty finding, and refuses `auto` as an author. One name is enough even on a global incident, where lowering the switch needs two.
Why: four eyes exists because declaring an incident over has consequences for everybody — a single person deciding it is over is how an incident gets closed for being inconvenient. Writing down what you saw is not that decision, and a note that cannot be written without a colleague present is a note that does not get written. `auto` is refused for the reason it is refused as an operator lowering a switch: the product does not investigate itself, and a note in its name would read as though somebody had looked when nobody had.
Nearest spec: main §14.5 — "every flip is logged with actor + reason", written about flips; silent on notes.

## 2026-09-08 — R-INCIDENT-NOTES — Naming a switch that is not up is refused, not resolved to its last incident
Decision: `pnpm switch note <flag> …` attaches only to the incident currently open on that switch. If none is open, the command refuses and names the two ways forward — `pnpm switch history <flag>` to see the closed ones, and `--incident <id>` to note one of them.
Why: "the most recent incident on this switch" is a guess about which occasion the operator meant, and the wrong guess files a finding about last month's outage under this month's. Refusing costs one extra command and cannot put a note on the wrong incident. It also matches how the rest of this script behaves — it refuses an unknown flag, a missing reason and a missing account rather than filling anything in.
Nearest spec: none; this is operator-tool behaviour the specs do not describe.

## 2026-09-08 — R-INCIDENT-NOTES — Findings take a `SystemScope` even when the incident is about one store
Decision: `addIncidentFinding`, `listIncidentFindings`, `listFindingsForFlags`, `findFlagById` and `listRecentFlags` take a `SystemScope`; only `findActiveAccountFlag` takes an `AccountScope`, matching `isAccountFlagActive` next to it.
Why: `incident_findings` has no `account_id` column, and the switches it hangs off are already read under `SystemScope` (`listActiveFlags`). A note about a store's spend trip is an operations record about the product, read by the people running it and never by a merchant, so there is no tenant to scope it to. The scope is still explicit and greppable, which is what the rule in `packages/db/src/scope.ts` is for.
Nearest spec: CLAUDE.md code-structure rules — every repository method takes a scope.

## 2026-09-08 — R-INCIDENT-NOTES — Nothing edits or deletes a note; the schema permits it and no command offers it
Decision: the command writes and reads findings and does nothing else. The table has no append-only guard — its schema comment says correcting a typo in your own note is not the hazard that revising a financial record is — but no code path updates or removes a row.
Why: the card asks for recording a finding and reading it back, and an edit command is a feature nobody asked for. Recorded here so the next person finds out the absence was deliberate rather than overlooked: the door is open in the schema, and `pnpm switch note … --replace <id>` or a delete would be a small addition if an operator ever wants one. Until then a correction is a second note, which is also how an investigation reads.
Nearest spec: none; the schema comment on `incident_findings` in `packages/db/src/schema/jobs.ts` states the intent.
## 2026-09-08 — R-UNRECORDED-KEY — The "we didn't record why" key gets purpose-written words rather than a place on the known-gap list
Decision: `gate.reason_unrecorded` now has its own sentence in `packages/ui/strings/en.json` — "We stopped this one at the check named here, but didn't record why. That's a gap in our own records rather than anything we found in your store." The alternative the card offered, listing it in `REASON_KEYS_AWAITING_COPY` so the guard counts it while it stays wordless, was not taken.
Why: the two options do not read the same on screen. Listed as a gap, a merchant reads the renderer's generic line — "The reasoning for this one isn't available yet." — which is what every key with no copy shows, so it says nothing about *this* day and hints the reasoning might yet appear. It never will: the row that stopped the day recorded nothing and is not going to. The written sentence says the true thing, and says the one thing worth saying beside it — that the silence is ours, not a finding about the merchant's catalogue. That distinction is the whole point of `R-WRONG-GATE-REASON`, which stopped this case borrowing Gate 1's claim about thin product descriptions; leaving the generic line in place gets most of the way there and stops short.
Why it does not regress the gap list: `REASON_KEYS_AWAITING_COPY` is empty and its comment says the honest thing to do with a wordless key is to name it there. Naming a key we can write words for today would have made the list a parking space rather than a record of real gaps.
Nearest spec: main §8.6 (a rejection card carries a plain-language reason beside the gate that produced it); ui §6.1; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-08 — R-UNRECORDED-KEY — `gate.` becomes a catalogue namespace of its own, not a fifth `gate3.`
Decision: `catalogKeyFor` (`packages/ui/src/opportunities/why.ts`) gains `gate.` alongside `gate1.`, `gate2.`, `gate3.` and `topic.`, so the sentence lives under its bare key rather than under `template.gate.reason_unrecorded`. `packages/ui/src/strings/reason-copy.ts` gains `UNRECORDED_REASON_PARAMS`, a one-entry table folded into `GATE_REASON_KEYS`, so the CI guard that fails when a produced key has no sentence now counts it.
Why a namespace of its own rather than filing it under one of the gates: it is the only explanation on a held day that no gate wrote — the calendar composes it when the row is silent, and it appears under a heading naming gate 1, 2 or 3 alike. Filing it as `gate3.something` would make the next reader take it for that gate's finding, which is the exact confusion this key was created to end.
Why a separate table rather than a row in `ADMISSION_REASON_PARAMS`: that table mirrors the keys `runGate1` and `runGate2` build, and a test pins its contents key for key so a new gate outcome cannot slip in unnoticed. Adding a key no gate builds would have blunted that check.
Nearest spec: main §8.6; ui §6.1; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 R-WRONG-GATE-REASON (which named the namespace problem in advance).

## 2026-09-08 — R-CRITERIA-LABELS — The criterion names are mapped in the why-line renderer, and the gate is left alone
Decision: `renderTemplatedLine` (`packages/ui/src/opportunities/why.ts`) — the one function every explanation in the product passes through — now maps the value of `failed_criteria` through the criterion label catalogue before filling the sentence. A merchant whose article was held by the quality bar reads "didn't meet our bar on Information gain" instead of the grader's field name `informationGain`. Nothing was asked of Lane D and nothing outside `packages/ui` changed except one test assertion (entry below).
Why in the renderer rather than at either end: the gate that records the criteria and the route that serves them have no idea which language the store reads, so words cannot be chosen there without putting copy outside the catalogue — the reason `R-REJECTION-REASON` left this alone. A screen doing it for itself is the other failure already demonstrated: the article page and the override dialog have named these correctly since they were built, and the calendar, which came second, did not. The renderer is where both problems stop.
What it costs: a one-entry table naming the parameters that carry a name rather than a measurement. A second such value later is a line in that table.
Nearest spec: main §8.4, §8.6; ui §6.1, §6.2; invariant 8; CLAUDE.md code-structure rules (copy lives in `packages/ui/strings` only).

## 2026-09-08 — R-CRITERIA-LABELS — The label lookup moves to the copy layer, because three surfaces need it and only one had it
Decision: `criterionLabel` moves from `packages/ui/src/content/articles.ts` to a new `packages/ui/src/strings/labels.ts`, beside the catalogue it reads, and gains a sibling `criteriaNamed` that names a whole set. Its two existing callers now import it from `../strings`. It is not re-exported from its old home: both `./strings` and `./content` are star-exported from the package barrel, so the same name exported twice would be ambiguous to anything importing `@sortiva/ui`.
Why moved rather than imported where it stood: the why-line renderer lives in `opportunities/`, which nothing under `content/` may import *from* in reverse without inverting the package's own layering — `content/` already reaches into `opportunities/` in six files. Putting a pure catalogue lookup in the copy layer, which both may depend on, avoids that.
Stated limit, and the thing that would let a line of this go: the gate records the failed criteria as one string with the names already joined (`packages/core/src/gates/gate3/gate3.ts:253` and `:321`, `.join(', ')`), so `criteriaNamed` splits it back apart on commas to name each one. Nothing depends on the joining — a single name reads correctly today and a list would need only the split removed — but the split is a workaround for a shape, not a design. Lane D owns that file; asked for in the session report rather than changed here.
Nearest spec: ui §6.2; CLAUDE.md code-structure rules (lane ownership; copy in `packages/ui/strings` only).

## 2026-09-08 — R-CRITERIA-LABELS — One assertion in Lane D's calendar test pinned the defect and had to move with it
Decision: `apps/web/app/api/calendar/_lib/calendar.test.ts:438` asserted that the held-day sentence contains the literal `informationGain` — the exact thing this card removes — so the branch would have gone red with the fix in. The assertion now expects the catalogue's name for that criterion and refuses the field name. Nothing else in that file changed; the four other mentions of `informationGain` there are stored data and API fields, which are right to stay as identifiers.
Why edited rather than reported and left: `apps/web/app/api/calendar` is Lane D's directory and this is the one line of it touched. Leaving it would have handed the integrator a red suite whose failure is the card working. Flagged in the session report so the ownership crossing is visible rather than discovered in review.
Nearest spec: CLAUDE.md prime directive 5 (lane ownership).

## 2026-09-08 — R-GRADER-SEES-MORE — The grader's evidence is now the writer's evidence, assembled once instead of twice
Decision: `gradingEvidence` (`packages/core/src/optimize/grading.ts`) no longer walks the pack for itself. Its store-facts section comes from `citableStoreFacts`, a new function in `packages/core/src/optimize/pack.ts` that is also what renders the same facts into the writing prompt (`recommendation.ts`, `factsBlock`). One list, read from two places, instead of two lists nobody compared.
What was wrong, plainly: a recommendation is suggested copy for a merchant's own page, and it may only say things that point at a fact the store itself recorded. The writer is shown a filtered list of those facts; three fields are deliberately kept off it — the product's price range, a flag saying whether marketing language was thrown away during distillation, and the merchant's names for the option axes ("Size", "Colour"). The grader that decides whether every sentence is traceable was handed each product's **whole** fact sheet. So the grader held the price range and the writer never did. A sentence the model invented about price — "from £120" — could be marked well-grounded against a figure that was never in front of it, and go to a merchant to paste onto their page. Live today; the axis half was dormant only because nothing showed those to the writer either.
Why this is not the "judge is blind to the writer's context" rule, and how both are kept: main §8.4 says the judge "sees draft + evidence pack + top-3 ranking competitors' content, never the writer's conversation". That rule keeps the judge independent by giving it **less** — no earlier attempt, no reasoning to grade instead of the result. This was the opposite failure: **more**. Nothing withheld was returned. The grader is still not shown the page's body text, the Search Console numbers, the store's voice profile, the internal-link candidates, the ranking pages' excerpts, or any part of the writing call. Independence comes from the withholding; grounding comes from the parity; the two are not in tension because a grader that holds *less* can never wrongly confirm a claim.
A second, smaller over-share went with it: the grader was also sent every product's title and every family's name directly. A product whose only recorded fact is its price, or a family with no differentiation axes, reached the grader while never reaching the writer at all. Deriving from the same list removes that without a separate rule.
What the grader's section looks like now: the same address/label/value triples the writer is given (`product:<id>/<field>`, `family:<id>/axis:<name>`), which is also strictly better for the question being asked — the recommendation cites those addresses, so the grader can check a citation against the thing it names rather than against a loose object.
Held by tests: `packages/core/src/optimize/evidence-parity.test.ts`. It takes every primitive value the grader is sent and requires each to appear in the text the writer was actually sent, so a leak through *any* route fails — a new key, a nested object, a field added to the fact sheet later. It is written against values, not field names, and the withheld fields carry sentinel values supplied through a mapped type, so a new non-citable field on the fact sheet fails to compile until somebody gives it one. A fourth test asserts the reverse direction — page body, persona, search numbers and link candidates stay out — so nobody closes a future drift by handing the grader everything.
Mutation-checked: restoring the old line (`storeFacts: pack.products.map(… product.factSheet)`) turns three of the four red, naming the price sentinel and the axis sentinel. Separately, adding the page body, the persona and the query numbers to the grader's evidence turns exactly the independence test red and leaves the parity tests green — which is the split they were designed for, since the writer did see all three.
Nearest spec: main §10.3 step 5 (judge-lite on grounding and intent-match) and §8.4 ("factual grounding — every product claim traceable to the pack"); invariant 11. DECISIONS 2026-09-08 `R-OPTIMIZE-AXES`, which found this.

## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH — The gates stamp the version the resolver hands them, not a scheme of their own
Decision: the topic-admission gate and the two draft gates resolve their thresholds through one small helper, `resolveRulesForGate` (`packages/jobs/src/generation/rules-for-gate.ts`), and stamp whatever version string that call returns. No gate composes a version itself. The scheme is the weekly scan's, unchanged: a store on the repo config file's numbers stamps the bare hash of that file, and a store carrying an override stamps the same hash with `+ov.` and sixteen characters over the values that actually won.
Why: `rules_version` — the string recorded beside every gate decision so a decision can later be explained by the numbers behind it — is only useful if it means the same thing everywhere it appears. A second scheme invented here would split the learning loop's breakdown into two vocabularies for one idea, and a store moved between the scan's and the gates' readings of "which numbers judged this" would be unexplainable. Reusing the resolver is also what keeps the property that made the scan's scheme worth having: two stores given the same override stamp the same string, so a cohort of overridden stores stays visible rather than scattering into one bucket per store.
Nearest spec: main §7.10, §8.2–8.4; invariant 9.

## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH — Three gate decisions, three places that stamp; no single writer was introduced
Decision: this lane writes gate decisions from three call sites — Gate 1 in `admit-manual-topic.ts`, Gate 2 and Gate 3 in `generate-article.ts` — and they stay three. Each now resolves its store's numbers and stamps the version it was given. A fourth site, `override-article.ts`, records a merchant publishing over a refusal, and it deliberately stamps **nothing**.
Why, and the risk it leaves: a single writer that every gate had to go through would make it impossible for one of them to drift back to the config file, and that is a real advantage. But the three sites differ in more than the version — different gates, different audit contents, one of them nested inside a branch that runs before any model call — so the shared thing would either be a wrapper so thin it guarantees nothing, or a rewrite of how three gates record their work, which is a bigger change than this card. What is shared instead is the *resolution*: all three take their numbers from the one helper, so a site that forgot to stamp would also have had to fetch its thresholds from somewhere else, which is visible. `gate-rules-overrides.test.ts` covers Gate 1 and Gate 2 by name and `generate-article.test.ts` covers Gate 3; a fourth gate added later with no stamp would pass CI, and that is the residual risk, stated rather than hidden.
Why `override-article.ts` stamps nothing: that row records a person overruling the gate, not a threshold judging anything. No number produced it, so a version claiming numbers did would be the same kind of false record this card exists to prevent. The row is already distinguishable by its outcome, and overridden articles are excluded from calibration anyway (invariant 12).
Nearest spec: main §8.5, §8.6; invariant 9.

## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH — The gates read overrides for the locale they already judge by, and no page type
Decision: the override read passes the same language the gate was already using — the one handed to it by its caller — and never a page type. It does not go and read the store's recorded language for itself.
Why: `resolve()` folds the config file's own per-language layer and the table's rows in one call, and it refuses rows aimed somewhere the caller did not ask about, so the two have to agree about which language is in play. Using a different language for the table read than for the config layer would make a store's numbers depend on which of the two answered first. Going the other way — having the gate look up the store's language itself — would change which config layer applies to stores in every non-English market, with no override anywhere in sight, and that is a behaviour change well outside this card. Page type is not a thing a gate knows: gates judge a topic and a draft, so a row aimed at a page type reaches none of them, exactly as it reaches none of the scan.
**The gap this leaves, and it is pre-existing:** `POST /api/calendar/topics` passes no language at all (`apps/web/app/api/calendar/topics/_lib/add.ts:78-93`), so a hand-added topic is judged by the global defaults whatever market the store sells into — and now, by the same token, an override row aimed at a *language* will not reach it either. A row aimed at the store, or at every store, does reach it. Reported rather than fixed: supplying that language is somebody's card, not a line to slip into this one.
Nearest spec: main §7.10, §6.5, §8.2.

## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH — A threshold read now happens inside an HTTP request, which the no-cache decision named as its own trigger to revisit
Decision: the uncached read stays uncached. The topic-admission gate runs inside `POST /api/calendar/topics` — a merchant pressing "add" and waiting — so from today the overrides table is read while a request is open, which the decision that chose no cache (2026-09-07, `R-RULES-OVERRIDES`) named as the one circumstance that would make it worth revisiting.
Why it is still the right answer here, stated so the next person does not have to re-derive it: the read is folded into the batch of queries that gate already makes in parallel, so it adds no round trip to the request's wall time; it is one indexed lookup against a table holding a handful of rows; and the same request already makes a model call to work out what the merchant's typed title is about, which is orders of magnitude more expensive. The thing a cache would cost — a window in which a store is judged by numbers the table no longer holds, and an invalidation rule to get wrong — is worth more than the microseconds it would save.
What would change this: a *page view* resolving thresholds, or any read not already sharing a round trip with other work. The condition to watch is "a read that adds a round trip", not "a read in a request".
Nearest spec: main §7.10; tech §2 (cost disciplines).

## 2026-09-08 — R-TASK-DONE — A finished merchant checklist gets an expiry reason of its own
Decision: `EXPIRY_REASONS` gains `catalog_now_sufficient`. The weekly scan stamps it when it retires a `catalog_richness_gap` hold whose mapped families now clear the substance floor — the same measurement, taken in the same pass, that decides whether to raise the hold in the first place. Every other way a hold stops being detected keeps `evidence_no_longer_holds`.
Why: a hold is the only work in this product the merchant does rather than us, so it is the only expiry that can mean a person acted. `R-API-PRODUCTS` correctly refused to infer that at read time, because reading `evidence_no_longer_holds` as "you completed this" would also congratulate a merchant for a keyword losing its search volume. Recording the distinction where the measurement is taken is the fix that flag asked for.
Consequence: `expired_reason` is a `text` column, so this needed no migration. The reason is written by the scan alone; nothing infers it later.
Nearest spec: main §7.9 (expiry is automatic, logged with the reason, and never deletes); ui §7.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TASK-DONE — The moment a task was finished is the expired row's `updated_at`
Decision: `completedAt` on a merchant task is the expired opportunity's `updated_at`, not a new column.
Why: expiry is the last write a row ever takes. The partial unique index that dedupes open opportunities covers only the open statuses, so a signal detected again after expiry inserts a fresh row and never reaches back to the expired one — which makes `updated_at` on an expired row exactly the moment it was retired. A dedicated `completed_at` would be more legible and would need a schema wave; schema waves are closed and this reads the same value.
Risk, stated rather than discovered: if a future card ever writes to an expired row, this date silently becomes that write's date instead. The repository function carries that warning where a caller will see it.
Nearest spec: main §7.9; ui §7.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TASK-DONE — A merchant who did the work is credited even if the search went quiet
Decision: `keywordsClearingSubstanceFloor` ignores the demand and winnability floors that gate detection. A keyword whose products now clear the substance floor is named as cleared whether or not the search is still worth writing about.
Why: the two facts are independent. The merchant was handed a checklist of product details and filled it in; marking that undone because Google's volume estimate moved in the meantime is the more dishonest of the two answers. The card the checklist was blocking does not come back either way — it expires — so nothing is over-promised by saying the work was done.
Nearest spec: main §7.9, §6.3; ui §7.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TASK-DONE — The completed section is capped at the twenty most recent, newest first
Decision: `listCompletedMerchantTasks` returns at most 20 rows, ordered by when they were retired.
Why: ui §7 collapses completed tasks behind a summary line, so the screen never needs the full history, and an uncapped read grows without limit for a store that has been going for years. Nothing is deleted — the rows stay for the learning loop, they simply stop being sent to a fold nobody has opened. The number is a page size for a collapsed list, not a threshold on any measurement, so it does not belong in `packages/rules`.
Nearest spec: ui §7; invariant 10 (expiry never deletes).

## 2026-09-08 — R-FIXTURE-KEYS — Each orphaned fixture key is replaced by the key the engine really builds for that card
Decision: `striking_distance.page_one_intent_mismatch` and `striking_distance.page_one_reachable` become `striking_distance.optimize`; `uncovered_commercial_query.no_suitable_url` becomes `uncovered_commercial_query.create`.
Why: each fixture already carries exactly the numbers its replacement asks for — the striking-distance ones send `position` and `impressions`, the uncovered ones send `volume` — and each already carries the matching recommended action, `OPTIMIZE` and `CREATE`. So the fixtures now describe a card the engine can actually make, rather than one it never could, and no fixture had to be reshaped to get there.
Consequence: the fake server the frontend develops against now serves a real sentence where it previously served "the reasoning for this one isn't available yet". That is the intended behaviour and no test asserted on the old admission.
Nearest spec: main §7.1; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-08 — R-FIXTURE-KEYS — The guard is repo-wide and carries a named list of what is still broken
Decision: `apps/web/app/api/opportunities/_lib/fixture-keys.test.ts` reads every source file under `packages/` and `apps/`, finds every explanation key written as a literal, and asserts the catalogue can answer it. Two short lists carry the exceptions: keys deliberately absent (four, used to prove the renderer's fallback) and keys with no sentence anywhere that sit in another lane's files (ten). Three further assertions stop either list rotting: a key that acquires a sentence must leave, a key nothing names any more must leave, and a run that finds no keys at all fails rather than passing vacuously.
Why: the card asked for the check and the check cannot be scoped to five files without leaving the same hole open everywhere else. Scanning everything found nine more orphaned keys the card's list did not name. Fixing all of them would mean editing test files across four other lanes mid-run, which is how merges get lost; naming them makes the debt visible and makes a *new* one fail immediately, which is what the card is for.
Consequence: the outstanding list is a debt register, not an escape hatch. Its comment says so, and the two hygiene assertions mean an entry cannot be added and then forgotten.
Nearest spec: invariant 8.

## 2026-09-08 — R-FIXTURE-KEYS — "Resolves" means the catalogue holds the key, by either route
Decision: a key passes the guard if the renderer's own mapping finds a sentence for it (prefixing `template.`, following the aliases) **or** the key is already a catalogue key in final form.
Why: the email templates and a few pinned Appendix A lines are written as finished catalogue keys and are not reason keys at all; judging them by the reason-key mapping alone would fail three correct call sites. The second route is deliberately forgiving and it conceals a real, separate fault — several keys a producer emits exist in the catalogue under their bare name while the renderer only looks under `template.`, so the sentence exists and the merchant never reads it. That is a fault in the mapping, not in the keys, it belongs to the lane that owns the renderer, and it is reported rather than recorded here as though the keys were wrong.
Nearest spec: invariant 8, invariant 24.
## 2026-09-08 — R-CONTRACT-PROVE — Every endpoint's answer is now parsed with the shape that endpoint declares
Decision: `apps/web/app/(app)/_lib/route-answers.test.ts` drives each route in the frozen route table through its **real `route.ts`** against a real, seeded Postgres, takes the JSON that comes back, and parses it with the response schema that route declares. 54 of the 62 routes are proved this way; seven are named as ones that cannot be driven here, each with its reason; two server-sent-event streams are excluded by the table itself.
Why the real route file rather than the handler behind it: every route's handler is built by a small factory that a test can call with substitutes, and several suites already do that. Calling the factory proves the factory, not the endpoint — the wiring between the route file and the factory is exactly the layer that has been wrong before, and a hand-written map from route to factory would be one more thing kept in step by hand. The module to import is derived from the contract's own path (`/api/opportunities/{id}` → `opportunities/[id]/route`), so a route file that moves or stops exporting its method fails here by name.
The one thing replaced is the session: `withAccount` reads the signed-in account from the sign-in library at request time, and booting that library performs a live discovery call to Google before any handler could run. Everything else — the dependency wiring, the SQL, the guarded updates, the queue — is the production path.
Nearest spec: tech §3; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-CONTRACT-2`, which states the limit this closes.

## 2026-09-08 — R-CONTRACT-PROVE — A route that cannot be driven is named with its reason, and the list of names is derived
Decision: `UNDRIVABLE` in the same file names seven endpoints and says why each cannot be exercised: the three Stripe routes (the plan card reads live prices, checkout and the customer portal are calls into Stripe), two Shopify publishing routes (they list or create a blog on the merchant's real store), the Search Console property list (it asks Google), and the public preview (a bot-challenge check, a fetch of a stranger's website and a model call). Two more — the ingestion and scan streams — are excluded by reading `sse` off the table rather than by anybody listing them.
Why it is derived rather than maintained: a test asserts that every route in the table is either driven or named, so a route added tomorrow makes this file red until somebody says which it is. The seven entries in `UNCONTRACTED_ROUTES` set the precedent that "not covered" and "nobody thought about it" must not look the same.
A second guard came out of writing it: a reason shorter than a phrase fails its own check, because naming a route without saying why is the same as skipping it.
Nearest spec: main §14.7 (a check that cannot fail proves nothing); `packages/core/src/api/routes.ts` `UNCONTRACTED_ROUTES`.

## 2026-09-08 — R-CONTRACT-PROVE — The two endpoints that fail their own declaration are recorded, not corrected, and the record is checked
Decision: `KNOWN_MISMATCHES` records the two endpoints whose answer their own declaration rejects, each with the exact complaint parsing produces. The check asserts the complaint is **still** exactly that: if the endpoint and its declaration come to agree, the file goes red asking for the entry to be deleted; if they disagree differently, it goes red saying so.
Why not simply fix them: the route table is frozen and belongs to whoever integrates, and a handler belongs to the lane that owns its directory — neither is this card's to change. Why not simply leave the suite red: a red suite with no explanation is reverted by the next person who sees it, and this whole week has been about faults that nobody wrote down. Recording the mismatch and asserting it holds keeps the finding alive without asking anyone to ignore a failure.
Nearest spec: `CLAUDE.md` (one card per session; a lane owns only its directories).

## 2026-09-08 — R-CONTRACT-PROVE — Search Console's "connect" button answers a field name nothing agreed on
Finding, not fixed here: `POST /api/gsc/oauth/start` answers `{ redirectUrl }`. The contract declares `{ url }`, and the Shopify install route beside it answers `{ url }`. **The Settings screen's "Connect Search Console" button reads `body.url`, finds nothing and throws** (`packages/ui/src/settings/ConnectionsSettings.tsx:63-65`), so on a deployed server that button fails. The onboarding step survives only because it was written to accept either name (`packages/ui/src/onboarding/SearchConsoleStep.tsx:97-98`) — a screen hedging between two spellings is itself the symptom.
Where each piece lives: the handler is `apps/web/app/api/gsc/_lib/handlers.ts:42` (Lane C's directory); the declaration is `packages/core/src/api/schemas.ts:125`, used at `packages/core/src/api/routes.ts:210` (the integrator's). Both consumers are Lane F's. The weight of evidence — the contract, the sibling route and both screens — says the handler is the odd one out, but the call is not this card's.

## 2026-09-08 — R-CONTRACT-PROVE — The article export answers a list of files where its declaration says one object
Finding, not fixed here: `GET /api/articles/{articleId}/export` answers `{ files: [{ filename, content, … }] }` — the bundle's own shape (`packages/core/src/publish/bundle.ts:58`), and what the handler sends at `apps/web/app/api/articles/_lib/delivery.ts:70`. The contract declares `files` as one object mapping name to contents (`packages/core/src/api/schemas.ts:901-903`, used at `packages/core/src/api/routes.ts:502`). Nothing is broken on screen, because the code that reads it was written against the list; the declaration has simply never described this endpoint. The handler is Lane D's directory, the declaration the integrator's.

## 2026-09-08 — R-CONTRACT-PROVE — The suite's own configuration is real values, not stand-ins
Decision: the suite sets the configuration the routes refuse to start without — the app's public address, the token-encryption key, the Shopify and Google client credentials, the webhook signing secrets — with real, locally generated values rather than by making the code that reads them optional. The three webhook receivers are driven with signatures this file computes with the same schemes the vendors use, so the signature check they run is the real one and not a bypass.
Why it is worth saying: a receiver whose signature check is switched off in tests is a receiver nobody has tested. The Stripe **secret key** is set only so the client object can be constructed for the webhook path; no route driven here calls Stripe, which is why the three billing routes are named as undrivable rather than pointed at a fake key.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.7, §14.7; tech §4.

## 2026-09-08 — R-CONTRACT-3 — The article export is declared as the list of files it has always answered
Decision: `articleExportResponseSchema` declares a list of files, each carrying its own name, type and contents, rather than one object mapping name to contents. Nothing on any screen changes: everything that reads this endpoint was built against the list, and the map has never been served by anything.
Why now: `R-CONTRACT-PROVE` found it within an hour of existing, by sending the endpoint a real request and parsing the answer with its own declaration — the check that declaration had never faced in the months it was wrong.
Why a list is also the right shape rather than merely the true one: each file carries a name because the merchant saves it under that name, and a type because the browser needs one to hand it over. A map from name to contents would have to invent the type at the point of use.
Held by the new check rather than by memory, and the mechanism deserves recording because it is the reason this was fixed rather than filed: the finding was carried as a named record asserting the *exact* complaint the mismatch produces, so the suite stayed green and the finding could not be forgotten — and the moment the declaration was corrected the suite went red asking for its own record to be deleted. It was, in the same commit.
Nearest spec: main §9.4, §9.5; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-CONTRACT-2` (the same fault, found by eye rather than by a check).

## 2026-09-08 — R-SCAN-DATE-ZONE — The opportunities response carries the store's calendar, so a date can be named rather than guessed
Decision: `listOpportunitiesResponseSchema` gains `timezone`, always present and never null — the store's own timezone, defaulting to `UTC` for a merchant who has never chosen one. This is the contract half of the card; formatting the two dates in that calendar is Lane F's and is not done here.
What was wrong: the response carried two instants — when the last scan finished, when the next one falls — and nothing that could turn either into a day. A Berlin store's next scan is `2026-09-13T22:00Z`, which is their Monday the 14th and reads as **Sunday the 13th** to anything formatting it in UTC. Both surfaces that print it, the Opportunities header and the Dashboard's quiet state, were therefore a day early for every store east of us, always, in one direction.
Why not nullable, and why not a separate "scan timezone": the account column is not-null with a `UTC` default, so there is always a real answer, and an optional field is exactly the hedge that let the Search Console field-name fault survive — a consumer that has to cope with a missing value is a consumer that will silently cope with a wrong one. The name matches `settingsSchema.timezone`, which is the same fact about the same store.
Why the field is sent even to a store that is told no next scan: the *last* scan still has a date, and that one is withheld from nobody. A store on vacation, unpaid, or paused reads its header in its own calendar like everyone else.
Held by three tests in `apps/web/app/api/opportunities/_lib/next-scan.test.ts`, one of which formats the same instant twice — once in UTC, once in the store's zone — and asserts the two disagree by a day, so the test states the defect rather than describing the fix. Mutation-checked: hardcoding `UTC` in the handler fails two of the three.
The mock the frontend builds against now carries `Europe/Berlin` rather than UTC on purpose, so a screen that formats without the field shows the wrong day in development instead of only on a real merchant's account.
Nearest spec: main §6.5 (locale and timezone), §9.4; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-07 `R-NEXTSCAN` and `R-SCANCOPY` (which journalled the UTC approximation as acceptable **while `nextScanAt` was always null** — it is live now).

## 2026-09-08 — R-STUB-REPORT — A stand-in running inside the product is now a test failure, not a silence
Decision: `seams-wired.test.ts` gains the direction it never had. It already refused to let a stand-in be *removed* from the wired-stub report without a real implementation to point at. It now also refuses to let one be *built by shipping code*: for every `Stub*` class, the set of production files constructing it must be empty, unless recorded in `WIRED_IN_PRODUCTION` by the exact file that does it.
What that found immediately: `StubNotificationEmitter` — recorded since 2026-09-02 as replaced, which was true of the Shopify path where it was checked — is still constructed by the Stripe webhook receiver, where it drops the payment-failed email on the floor. Carded as `R-DUNNING-DROPPED`. That entry is the record; repairing the wiring turns the suite red asking for it to be deleted, the same mechanism `R-CONTRACT-PROVE` established.
Why a record rather than an exception list: an exception says "this is allowed". A record says "this is a defect, here is exactly what it is, and the check will tell you when it stops being true". The difference is that nobody has to remember.
Nearest spec: main §14.7; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-CONTRACT-PROVE` (the pattern being reused).

## 2026-09-08 — R-STUB-REPORT — The report's first entry was stale, and a report a reader discounts is a report they ignore
Decision: `StubJudgeLite` is no longer constructed by `scripts/stub-report.mjs`, and its real implementation is recorded. `pnpm stubs:report` was announcing that "the quality bar is not actually applied" to recommendations. It is applied: `LlmJudgeLite` is built unconditionally in the improve-this-page worker's dependencies and those are registered in the composition root, so a merchant's click really is graded. The line was simply never removed when the seam was filled.
Why it is worth a journal entry rather than a quiet deletion: the report had three entries, one false and two true, and nothing distinguished them. The two true ones say that both of the product's rate-based safety brakes cannot fire. A reader who correctly learns to discount the first entry discounts those as well.
Checked end to end before removing, to the standard the file's own earlier notes set — two previous removals from this report were made on claims that turned out to be false, which is why that standard exists.
Nearest spec: main §14.4, §14.7.

## 2026-09-08 — R-STUB-REPORT — A guard that assumed the product would never be finished
Decision: the sanity check asserting the report still constructs at least one stand-in is replaced by one that proves the parser works on a sample. With the judge entry retired, no `Stub*` is on the report at all — and the old assertion read that as a broken check rather than as the goal being reached, failing the moment the last stand-in was replaced.
