Worth recording because the shape recurs: a guard that proves it is looking at something real by requiring an outstanding defect to exist will fail on the day the defect is fixed. Prove the mechanism against a sample; assert the absence separately.
Nearest spec: main §14.7.
## 2026-09-08 — R-GSC-URL-FIELD — The handler is the one that moves, and it keeps the internal name it always had
Decision: `POST /api/gsc/oauth/start` now answers `{ url }`. The core function behind it still returns `{ redirectUrl }`; only the JSON the browser receives changed. Nothing else was touched: the declaration stays as it was, and the Shopify install route beside it was already right.
Why the handler rather than the declaration: four things already said `url` — the frozen contract, the sibling route that starts the Shopify install, the Settings screen, and the onboarding screen's preferred branch — and one thing said `redirectUrl`. Changing the declaration would have meant changing the two screens and the sibling route to match a name only this handler used.
Why the internal name stayed: `startGscConnect` returns `redirectUrl` and is used by tests inside `packages/core`. Renaming it would have spread a wire-format fix into domain code for no gain; the handler is where the wire format is decided, so that is where the translation lives.
Nearest spec: tech §3 (API conventions); main §6.7.

## 2026-09-08 — R-GSC-URL-FIELD — The handler's own test parses with the contract's schema instead of naming the field
Decision: the connect-button test in `apps/web/app/api/gsc/_lib/gsc.test.ts` looks the endpoint up in the route table, asserts the table still declares it as a plain redirect answer, and parses the response with that declaration rather than reading a field name written out in the test.
Why: the fault this card fixes was a field name that existed correctly in four places and wrongly in one, and the endpoint's own test was the fifth place — it read `redirectUrl` and passed, which is how a broken button reached a deployed server with a green suite. A test that restates the name it is checking cannot catch the name being wrong. Parsing with the declaration means the endpoint's test fails the moment the endpoint and the contract disagree, without waiting for the whole-repo contract suite to run.
Nearest spec: tech §3; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-CONTRACT-PROVE` (the suite that found this).

## 2026-09-08 — R-GSC-URL-FIELD — The onboarding step reads one field name, and a wrong answer now shows the merchant a failure
Decision: the onboarding Search Console card no longer accepts either `url` or `redirectUrl` from the connect endpoint. It reads `url`, and anything else lands in the step's existing "couldn't start" state.
Why: accepting two names meant the one screen that would have reported the broken endpoint reported nothing instead, so the Settings screen — which never hedged — was the only place the fault was visible, and it is the place a merchant reaches later. Verified before removing it: the handler now answers `url`, the browser-test fixture for this endpoint already answered `url`, and the Settings screen already read only `url`.
What it costs: if this endpoint ever regresses, onboarding shows a visible failure rather than quietly working. That is the intent — a silent success on a wrong answer is what hid this for months.
Nearest spec: main §6.7 (the step is skippable, and a failure to start is not a dead end); tech §3.

## 2026-09-08 — R-INDEXING-SPLIT — The machine word picks the sentence instead of being offered to one
Decision: the weekly scan now emits `indexing_issue.fix_not_indexed` or `indexing_issue.fix_canonical` and sends no parameters at all, replacing the single key `indexing_issue.fix` that carried the machine word `not_indexed` / `canonical_mismatch` as a value. The code that chooses is a `switch` over the two codes with a compile-time exhaustiveness guard, so a third code cannot be added without someone writing its sentence.
Why not one sentence with a parameter: the value is a machine token, so a sentence that printed it would say "canonical_mismatch" to a merchant. That is why the copy card wrote one sentence covering both conditions, and why it could go no further from its own side.
Why two sentences rather than a richer single one: a page Google has never indexed and a page Google is folding into another of the merchant's own are different problems with different remedies — the first is "find out why Google will not take this page", the second is "decide which of your pages should be the main one". The task text under the card already split on exactly this distinction; only the explanation did not.
Nearest spec: main §7.3 (the taxonomy carries these as two rows), §11 (the technical layer's two remedies), §7.1 (the why-line renders from templates, never from a model).

## 2026-09-08 — R-INDEXING-SPLIT — The split is proved from the merchant's side, because the params guard cannot see it
Decision: a new test in `apps/web/app/api/opportunities/_lib/indexing-reason.test.ts` drives the engine's own reason function with both conditions and renders each answer through the real catalogue, asserting the two read as different sentences, that neither falls through to "the reasoning isn't available yet", and that no machine word or unfilled placeholder reaches the text.
Why it exists on top of the guards already there: the existing guard compares the numbers a sentence asks for against the numbers the scan sends. Both of these sentences ask for nothing, so that guard passes whether or not the two keys are actually different sentences — the exact thing this card changed is invisible to it. The check also cannot live in `packages/core`, which never sees the words.
Why it sits in the web app rather than in `packages/ui`: it needs both sides at once, and the endpoint directory is where this lane's cross-side checks already live.
Nearest spec: main §7.1; invariant 8.

## 2026-09-08 — R-INDEXING-SPLIT — Two files outside this lane were changed, and here is the reason
Decision: the sentences (`packages/ui/strings/en.json`) and the hand-kept list that mirrors the engine's keys (`packages/ui/src/strings/reason-copy.ts`) were edited from this lane, although `packages/ui` belongs to the front-end lane.
Why: the card's done-when requires the two conditions to "read as two different sentences", and the catalogue is the only place in the repository a sentence may live. Leaving them would have landed two keys with no words behind them — the precise fault this week has been spent closing — and would have left the mirror list naming a key the engine no longer emits. Neither file is among the ones the concurrently running front-end lane was told to work in. Flagged in the session report for the integrator rather than assumed.
Nearest spec: `CLAUDE.md` (a lane owns its directories; copy lives in `packages/ui/strings/*.json` only).
## 2026-09-08 — R-TEMPLATE-PREFIX — The renderer learned the four families of key, rather than the producers being renamed
Decision: `catalogKeyFor` (`packages/ui/src/opportunities/why.ts`) now recognises `optimize.`, `appendixA.`, `fix.` and `email.` alongside the gate and topic families as keys already written in their finished catalogue form. No producer was renamed and no sentence moved.
Why the renderer and not the producers: the eight keys were never wrong. Each names a sentence that already sits in the catalogue spelled exactly that way, and each was written where it was for a reason that still holds — `appendixA.outage` is one of the sentences the product may not reword, so it is keyed by its row in the canonical-copy table and is read by a second consumer (the "service paused" toast) that looks it up directly; the six `fix.consolidation.*` lines sit beside three headings the screen will look up directly, so both halves have to share one spelling. Renaming any of them into a `template.` namespace would have moved a canonical string away from its canonical key to satisfy a lookup, which is the wrong way round.
What a merchant now reads, where they previously read "The reasoning for this one isn't available yet": the sentence explaining that a page recommendation failed our own grounding checks, and the outage line when a topic they typed in could not be classified. The six consolidation lines have no screen yet and will be correct when one arrives.
Nearest spec: main Appendix A; ui §5.3; invariants 8 and 24.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TEMPLATE-PREFIX — The repo-wide key guard now asks the renderer alone, and the forgiving second route is gone
Decision: `resolves()` in `apps/web/app/api/opportunities/_lib/fixture-keys.test.ts` is deleted. Every hand-written key found in the tree is now judged by `hasCopy`, which is the renderer's own resolution and nothing else. A key that exists in the catalogue under its bare name but in a family the renderer does not know now fails the guard by name.
Why: the second route — "or the catalogue holds the key in final form" — is what let this fault ship. `R-FIXTURE-KEYS` recorded it as deliberately forgiving and reported the fault separately rather than recording it as a key problem, which was right at the time; closing it needs the renderer to answer for every family first, which is the entry above. Three call sites depended on the forgiving route and now resolve properly: the two monthly-summary reasons and the one Appendix A reason a summary email names.
Consequence: the guard is now a real seam check rather than a spelling check. A producer writing `products.something` as an explanation key fails immediately, naming the key and the file and line it was written on, instead of a merchant reading the admission.
Nearest spec: invariant 8, invariant 24.

## 2026-09-08 — R-COMPLETED-LINK — OPEN QUESTION, NOT DECIDED: what a merchant should reach from a task they finished
Status: **stopped for the founder.** Nothing was changed. All three answers below show the merchant something different, so picking one is a product decision rather than a repair.

What exists now, in plain terms. The Products screen has a section called "Knowledge gaps": each entry is a piece of advice we cannot give yet because the merchant's own product pages do not say enough — no material, no dimensions — and it lists which products and which fields. When they fill those in, the weekly pass notices, retires the entry, and it drops into a collapsed "Completed tasks" fold with its subject, the date, and a link labelled **"See what it became"**.

The fault. That link points at the finished task's *own* record on the Opportunities screen (`packages/ui/src/products/ProductsScreen.tsx:124`). Two things make it dead rather than merely odd. The record was retired when the work was done, and `GET /api/opportunities` only ever serves records still open (`listOpenOpportunities`, `packages/db/src/repositories/opportunities.ts:237`) — so nothing on that screen can show it, under any filter. And even if it could, it would show the chore the merchant just finished, which is not "what it became".

What the interface spec asks for (ui §7): completed tasks collapse with the date "and, once the opportunity proceeds, a link to what it became". So the affordance is spec-named and the words on it are right; only its destination has never existed.

What "what it became" would actually be. The finished task is about one search term. Once the catalogue says enough, a later weekly pass can raise a *new* piece of advice about that same search — a different record, with a different identity, and only if the search is still worth writing about. Nothing today records that the second came from the first, and the response the screen reads carries only the finished task's own identity.

The three answers, and what each costs:
1. **Drop the link.** The fold keeps the subject and the date. Costs nothing, ships today, and the merchant simply gets no route onward. It also means the screen stops offering something the interface spec names.
2. **Link to the successor** — the advice now standing for that same search. This is the spec's intent read literally. It needs the Products endpoint to look for an open record about the same subject and send its identity, which is a field added to a frozen response shape and work in the lane that owns opportunities; and it needs an answer for the common case where there is no successor, because a search that stopped being worth writing about produces none.
3. **Link back to the finished task itself and make that work**, relabelling it honestly ("See the task you finished"). This needs the opportunities endpoint to serve retired records, which is a change to what an endpoint returns and affects more than this screen.

Recommendation if one is wanted: (1) now and (2) as its own card, because a dead link is worse than an absent one and (2) is not small.

Related, found while reading and left alone: the Opportunities screen offers filter chips for **completed, dismissed and expired** records (ui §5.1 asks for all three, and the dismissed one is meant to offer "restore"), and the endpoint behind it serves only open records — so none of the three chips can ever show anything. Same root cause as this link. Carded separately in the session report.
Nearest spec: ui §7; ui §5.1; main §7.9 (expiry never deletes).
## 2026-09-08 — R-JUDGE-SEES-MORE — The judge's store facts are the writer's own facts, enumerated once instead of twice
Decision: the article judge's "what the store actually knows" block (`packages/core/src/gates/gate3/judge.ts`) no longer walks the fact sheets for itself. It is built from `citableProductFacts`, a new function in `packages/core/src/generation/evidence-pack.ts` that is also what the claim plan the writer works from is built from (`claims.ts`, `deterministicMerchantClaims`). One list, read from two places, instead of two lists nobody compared.
What was wrong, plainly: an article may only state things that trace back to something the store itself recorded. What the store recorded is a "fact sheet" per product — the distilled facts from its own product description. The writer never sees a fact sheet; it sees an approved claim list built from the ten fields a description can support. The judge, whose job includes deciding whether every product claim is traceable, was rendered **every** non-empty field of the sheet — including four the writer never had: the price range and the option-axis names (merged from the store's variant data, not from any description), the flag saying marketing language was dropped, and our own count of the facts. So a sentence the model invented about price could be marked well-grounded against a figure that was never in front of it. The card named two of those four; the flag and the count are the same fault and went with them.
On "harmless today": the price range reached the judge as the literal text `[object Object]`, because the renderer called `String()` on a `{min, max}` object. No figure was exposed — by accident, not by design, and the accident ends the moment that shape changes. It is fixed rather than noted.
Why this is not the "judge is blind to the writer" rule, and how both are kept: main §8.4 says the judge is a separate call, blind to generation — it sees the draft, the evidence and the ranking pages, never the writer's conversation. That rule keeps the judge independent by giving it **less**: no instructions, no claim list, no earlier attempt. This was the opposite failure, **more**. Nothing withheld was returned: the judge still cannot see the claim plan, the writing instructions, the length target, the internal links or a repair attempt. Independence comes from the withholding; grounding comes from the parity; the two do not conflict, because a judge that holds *less* can never wrongly confirm a claim.
Where this departs from a literal reading of the spec, stated rather than buried: §8.4 says the judge sees "draft + evidence pack + top-3 ranking competitors' content", and §8.3 says the article is written from the evidence pack. Our build interposes a claim plan between the pack and the writer, so the writer never sees the pack — which is what created the gap. Narrowing the judge to the citable part of the pack is the reading that keeps grounding meaningful; handing the writer the whole pack would be the other way to close it, and it is not one this card may take.
Held by tests: `packages/core/src/gates/gate3/evidence-parity.test.ts`. It takes the store-facts section apart **out of the built judge call** — not out of the list behind it — and requires every value in it to appear in the text the writer was really sent, and every field in it to be one of the ten. The four withheld fields carry distinctive sentinel values supplied through a mapped type, so a new non-citable field on the fact sheet fails to compile until somebody gives it one. A fifth test asserts the reverse direction, so nobody closes a future drift by handing the judge everything.
Nearest spec: main §8.4 (blind separate call; factual grounding — every product claim traceable to the pack); invariant 11. `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-GRADER-SEES-MORE`, the identical fix on the recommendation path, which this follows deliberately rather than inventing a second scheme.

## 2026-09-08 — R-JUDGE-SEES-MORE — The judge is no longer told which product families exist or what they differ by
Decision: the "product families and how they differ" block is removed from the judge's call. It listed each family's name and its differentiation axes — the attributes a range varies along, e.g. capacity or width.
Why: the writer is shown those axes only when the article's shape expands a section per axis, which is three of the seven shapes; for the other four (sizing, how-to, troubleshooting, informational-commercial) the axes never reach it. The family's *name* never reaches the writer under any shape. So for four shapes in seven this block was the same over-share as the fact-sheet fields, and no rule inside the judge could tell which case it was in — the judge is not told the shape.
Why nothing is lost where it mattered: for exactly the three shapes whose writer did see the axes, the axes are written into the article's own section headings ("Selection criteria: by capacity"), and the judge reads the article. So the axis context survives wherever it was legitimately available.
The alternative, not taken, and what it would cost: pass the judge the axes the writer was actually shown, which means threading the article's shape or the writer's section list through `JudgeInput`, `gate3.ts`, the generation job and the eval runner, and making the judge's evidence depend on the shape. More moving parts for information the headings already carry. If a later card wants the family *name* in front of the judge, that is the shape of the change.
Nearest spec: main §8.4, §9.2 (axis-derived sections).

## 2026-09-08 — R-MANUAL-TOPIC-LOCALE — A hand-added topic is judged by the store's own market, read from its profile
Decision: `POST /api/calendar/topics` (`apps/web/app/api/calendar/topics/_lib/add.ts`) now reads the store's profile and passes its language down to Gate 1. The parameter has existed all along on both functions below the route — nothing in `packages/jobs` changed.
What was wrong, plainly: the minimum monthly search volume a topic must clear before we will write about it is set per language, because thirty searches a month is a real subject in Danish and nearly nothing in English. The scheduled path passes the store's language and always has. The route a merchant types a topic into passed none, so every hand-added topic in every market was measured against the English bar — and, because that number is printed into the sentence explaining the decision, a Danish merchant was shown an English figure as the bar they had missed. The same omission meant an operator's threshold change aimed at a *language* never reached this gate, while one aimed at the store or at every store always did, which is what made the failure partial and easy to miss.
Where the language comes from: `personas.language`, the profile row written during onboarding and confirmed by the merchant — the same field the scheduled generation path already uses, so the two agree by construction rather than by coincidence.
A store with no profile yet keeps the global defaults, rather than being refused. That is exactly today's behaviour for such a store, and adding a topic is not the moment to discover onboarding is unfinished. It is a fallback, not a preference: any store that has completed onboarding has this row.
Cost: no extra round trip. The read is folded into the same parallel batch as the "is this day free" check, which already runs, and it happens after the entitlement check so an unpaid request never pays for it. This is the same reasoning as the uncached override read recorded under `R-OVERRIDE-REACH`: the condition to watch is a read that adds a round trip, not a read inside a request.
Held by tests, in `add.test.ts`: two stores, same typed topic, same stored volume of thirty — the Danish one is planned, the English one is planned with the demand warning and shows its own floor. A second test sets an override aimed at language `da` and proves it now reaches this gate. Mutation-checked: passing `null` for the language again turns both red, the first because the Danish store is warned as if it were English, the second because the gate reads 100 instead of the operator's 500.
Nearest spec: main §8.2 (demand floor, tuned per country), §6.5 (the profile's language), §7.10; invariant 9.
## 2026-09-08 — R-AXES-DESCRIPTION — The `variant_axes` description now says an option exists, not that a choice does
Decision: the doc comment on `FactSheet.variant_axes` (`packages/core/src/distill/schema.ts`) is rewritten.
It said, in full: *"The axes the product's own variants differ along. Merged from the stored variant data rather than extracted, because it is already structured."*
It now says the field holds the merchant's own names for the options **defined** on the product — "Size", "Colour" — copied from the store's option definitions rather than extracted; that the values are dropped on purpose, because a sheet describes one product and listing them would say a shoe is black *and* tan; that a name lands there whenever the merchant defined the option, "whether they filled it with twelve values, with one, or with none at all", with only Shopify's `Title: Default Title` placeholder removed; and therefore that a shop selling one black shoe and a shop selling five colourways both store "Colour", so the field "says an option exists, never that a choice does".
Why: the old sentence described a field the code does not produce. `namedOptionAxes` (`packages/core/src/catalog/products.ts`) deliberately keeps an option a merchant defined and never filled — its own comment says the name "is the half we could not get anywhere else" — and `axisNames` then takes the names and throws the values away. So "differ along" is false for a single-value or empty option, and that exact falsehood is the hinge of `R-OPTIMIZE-AXES`'s judgement to keep the field out of citable evidence. A reader who trusted the sentence rather than the content would reasonably conclude the exclusion was over-cautious and lift it, which would licence suggested copy promising a merchant's customers a choice that may not exist.
Treated as a prompt edit on the card's instruction, and one verified fact against that instruction: **this comment reaches no model today.** `variant_axes` is absent from `DISTILL_SCHEMA` and from `ExtractedFacts`, so the distillation prompt never mentions it; the writer and grader both read `citableStoreFacts`, which excludes it; and nothing in the tree renders a TypeScript doc comment into a prompt (checked by searching the whole repo for the old sentence — it appears only in the source file, the card and this journal). The instruction still holds for the next reader, human or model, which is the audience the card names.
No behaviour changed and no test changed: nothing asserts on this text. The two tests that pin the behaviour it now describes already exist — `distill.test.ts` proves values never enter the sheet and that the placeholder option yields an empty list, and `catalog/products.test.ts` proves a one-value "Colour" option survives.
Nearest spec: main §6.3 (the fact sheet and "supplementary structured data … merged in without distillation"); DECISIONS 2026-09-08 `R-OPTIMIZE-AXES`, 2026-09-07 `R-PRODUCT-ATTRIBUTES`.

## 2026-09-08 — T10.2 (audit) — Three places where the constitution and the code disagree, left open for the founder
Open questions, not decisions. The invariant sweep (`docs/audit-invariants-2026-09-08.md`) found three of `CLAUDE.md`'s numbered invariants describing behaviour the product does not have. Each is a wording-versus-behaviour choice with a real consequence, so none was resolved here.
**One.** Invariant 5 says domains seen ranking in Google search results "may be *suggested* to the merchant, never auto-added" to their competitor list. Onboarding adds them: `proposeCompetitors` (`packages/jobs/src/ingestion/keywords.ts:443`) writes ranked domains into `competitors` marked as ours, before the merchant has looked. This was flagged when it was built (2026-09-03 `T2.6`, which argues the invariant compresses a narrower rule from main §7.2.1) and never reconciled. Nothing enforces either reading. The choice: keep the auto-added draft list and reword the invariant, or make onboarding suggest rather than write.
**Two.** Invariant 22 says "no model substitution". Only the quality judge is pinned; a per-call override and the `ANTHROPIC_MODEL_*` environment variables move every other call type, and that is tested as working behaviour. The choice: narrow the invariant to the judge, or narrow the overrides.
**Three.** Invariant 18 names `pg_advisory_xact_lock`. The lock code deliberately uses the session-scoped `pg_advisory_lock` instead, for reasons journalled under `T0.4`, and an earlier audit (`docs/audits/T0.4.md`) already asked for the wording to be reconciled. This one is a one-line edit rather than a product choice, but it is still the constitution naming something the code does not do.
Nearest spec: main §7.2.1 (competitors), §14.4 (degradation), §14.3.3 (serialisation); `CLAUDE.md` invariants 5, 18, 22.

## 2026-09-08 — R-CLOCK-SILENT — A scheduled job with no handler stops the worker instead of stopping the schedule
Decision: `bootstrapWorker` refuses to start — marking the worker stopped and throwing with the missing names — when any scheduled entry has no registered handler. It previously computed `enableCron = registered.size > 0 && missing.length === 0` and, when that came out false, wrote one `logger.log` line and started anyway with the entire schedule off.
What that meant in practice: everything the product does on its own runs off that schedule — the day's article, the nightly billing reconciliation, the Search Console pull, the five-minute sweep that finishes interrupted publishes. One misspelt name in one entry silenced all eighteen, the web server went on serving pages, and the health check said the worker was running, because it was.
Why the old shape existed and why it expired: through M0 no handlers existed at all, and running with no schedule beat a crontab pointing at nothing. That stopped being true with the first handler and the condition outlived it — the same shape as several findings this week, a reason that expires while the code that depends on it does not.
Why the loud guard already in the tree did not fire: `assertCrontabTasksExist` throws with exactly the right message, and `startWorker` calls it only when cron is enabled — the flag a missing name had just switched off. Unreachable in production by construction. Its two tests called it directly or forced the flag on, so neither exercised the path a deployed server takes.
New option `cronEntries` on `bootstrapWorker`: production never passes it and gets the real schedule. Three existing tests whose subject is liveness or the analytics drain now pass `[]`, which starts a worker with no cron — what they wanted anyway. An empty schedule turns cron off rather than passing an empty crontab string, because Graphile reads a falsy crontab as "go and find a crontab file".
Mutation-checked: disabling the refusal fails two of the three new tests in `cron-required.test.ts`, and the third — the one proving this is not a blanket refusal — still passes, which is the split it was written for.
Verified rather than assumed: the built application still boots and its health check goes green, which under the new rule can only happen if every one of the eighteen scheduled jobs has a handler today. The clock is on; what was missing was anything that would say if it went off.
Nearest spec: tech §2, §5; main §14.7.
## 2026-09-08 — R-DUNNING-DROPPED — The declined-card email follows the status write, and the card's done-when names a different event
Decision: the test that proves the email now sends drives the webhook with **both** events Stripe sends when a card is declined — the invoice one first, asserted to change nothing, then the subscription one that does the work. No code was changed to make the invoice event emit anything.
What the card asked for, and why it could not be met literally: its done-when says "a test drives the receiver with a signed `invoice.payment_failed` event and asserts the row exists". Stripe sends two events for one declined payment: `invoice.payment_failed` (this invoice was not paid) and `customer.subscription.updated` (the subscription is now `past_due`). Our webhook deliberately acts only on the second. Invoice events are stored and then ignored, because the subscription's status has exactly one writer and deciding status from an invoice would create a second one — `processing.ts` says so in a comment and `singleWriter.test.ts` enforces it. The main spec agrees: it says the email is sent **on `past_due`** (main §4.2), which is a status, not an event. So a test that delivered only the invoice event and expected a notification row would have been asking for behaviour the build does not have and the spec does not require.
What the test does instead, and why that is the stronger version: it delivers the invoice event alone, asserts nothing was written and nothing queued, then delivers the subscription event and asserts the bell row and the queued email. A reader now learns which event carries the email, which the card's wording would have hidden.
The option not taken, and its cost: making `invoice.payment_failed` emit the email directly would cover the case where Stripe's subscription event is lost in transit — the merchant would hear sooner. It would also put a second trigger on the same email with a different dedupe key (the invoice event carries no billing period, which is what identifies a dunning episode), so a merchant could get two emails for one declined card. Today a lost subscription event is caught by the nightly reconciliation, which re-reads Stripe and now sends the email itself — up to 24h late rather than never. That is a product choice about how fast the merchant must hear, and it is left for the founder rather than taken here.
Nearest spec: main §4.2 (dunning on `past_due`; webhooks and the single writer); invariant 16.

## 2026-09-08 — R-DUNNING-DROPPED — The rest of the dunning sequence was the same defect, not a second one
Finding, recorded so the next reader does not have to re-derive it. The card asked whether the follow-ups were separately broken. They were not: every message in the sequence is emitted by one function (`announce` in `packages/core/src/billing/processing.ts`), and both of its callers — the webhook drain and the nightly reconciliation — were built with the same dropped-notification stand-in. One wiring change covers all of it, and there are now tests for each caller.
What the sequence actually contains, since "dunning follow-ups" suggests more than exists: one email per dunning episode. Stripe's Smart Retries fires a fresh pair of events on every retry attempt while the status stays `past_due`; the dedupe key is built from the subscription and its billing period, so every attempt after the first writes nothing. There is no second or third dunning email, and a final cancellation sends no email at all — the notification matrix has no type for it and main §4.2 does not ask for one. If the founder wants a "last chance before cancellation" email, that is a new notification type and a new card, not a repair.
Nearest spec: main §4.2; tech §1.2 (the `(account_id, type, dedupe_key)` triple).

## 2026-09-08 — R-SIGNIN-EMAIL — The email sign-in exchange lives beside the Google one, in the shared component package
Decision: `requestEmailSignIn` was added to `packages/ui/src/public/signin-exchange.ts`, the file that already holds the exchange the Google button performs. That file belongs to the frontend lane; the integrator's written authorisation for this card covers the sign-in screen and its test, so this is a third file of that lane's, named here and in the session report.
Why not somewhere in this lane's own directories: the file exists precisely so a button's whole behaviour can be run against the real sign-in handlers without a browser, and that is the property this card needed most — the defect being repaired is a test that could not see the screen. Putting a second, differently-shaped exchange elsewhere would have left the two halves of one screen in two packages with two conventions, and the end-to-end test would still have had to reach into the component package to find the function the button calls.
The one thing that is genuinely different between the two exchanges, recorded because getting it backwards is silent: **success is read the opposite way round.** A Google press that worked leaves our site, so a destination still inside our own sign-in routes means it failed. An email press that worked never leaves — the sign-in library names its own "check your mail" page — so success is that one page and everything else, the error page included, is a failure. Both are read from the destination and neither from the status, because the library answers a refusal with `200`.
Nearest spec: main §4.1 ("standard email + OAuth"); ui §2.2 ("standard flows; no invention here").

## 2026-09-08 — R-SIGNIN-EMAIL — Six sentences on the sign-in screen were authored, not taken from anywhere, and one of them makes a claim about how the link behaves
Decision: the email half of the sign-in screen ships with six new strings in `packages/ui/strings/en.json` — `signin.or` ("or"), `signin.emailLabel` ("Email address"), `signin.emailPlaceholder` ("you@yourstore.com"), `signin.email` ("Email me a sign-in link"), `signin.emailSending` ("Sending…") and `signin.emailSent` ("Check your email — we've sent a sign-in link to {email}. It works once."). The failure line reuses the existing `signin.failed`, which already covers a press that did not start a sign-in.
Where they come from: nowhere. Main Appendix A's canonical-copy table has no sign-in row, and ui §2.2 says only "Email + Google OAuth (§4.1). Standard flows; no invention here." So none of these is a string the product is forbidden to reword, and no snapshot pins them. They are authored, in the same position as the sign-in screen's existing words — T9.2 (2026-09-02) recorded "Continue with Google", "Sign in to Sortiva" and the rest as genuinely new for the same reason, and listed them rather than burying them.
Why ship them rather than wait: the screen cannot render an address field with no label and no button text, so holding the copy holds the whole card, and the card is the only way in for a merchant without a Google account. `docs/founder-decisions.md` §E3 makes copy the founder's call, so these five labels are listed here for a review that has a list rather than a diff.
The one worth a second look, because it is a claim and not a label: **"It works once."** It is true — the link's single-use token is spent when it is opened — but it is the only thing on the screen that describes how the link behaves, and it is silent about the other way a link stops working: it lapses after fifteen minutes (`SIGN_IN_LINK_MAX_AGE_SECONDS`). A merchant who opens the message an hour later meets a failure the screen never warned them about. Saying so is a second authored sentence, so it was not written here.
Nearest spec: main §4.1; ui §2.2; main Appendix A (silent on this screen); `docs/founder-decisions.md` §E3.
## 2026-09-08 — R-CHAOS-KILLS — Every chaos scenario must prove it was actually interrupted, and the two obvious stronger assertions are wrong
Decision: the chaos suite asserts `result.kills > 0` for every scenario, unless the scenario declares `selfInterrupting` — a sentence saying what interrupts it instead, checked for actually being a sentence. The harness's own no-work case and `process_death_mid_step`, which starts a real child process and SIGKILLs it, are the two that declare it.
What was wrong: the suite ran each scenario with a budget of three kills and then asserted only that the result named the scenario it asked for. A driver that reaches no checkpoint cannot be killed, so the harness returns having killed nothing, the universal convergence checks run against a pass that ran start to finish undisturbed, and the nightly run reports success. Renaming or removing a scenario's checkpoint calls produces exactly that.
**The audit that found this proposed asserting the full kill budget was spent and that the surviving pass reached a checkpoint. Both are wrong, and the measurements say so.** Running them turned six of ten scenarios red. Three of those six are working correctly: `catalog_sync` converges after one kill, `distill` and `drift_repair` after two, because these pipelines are resumable — the work left after a kill is smaller than the work before it, and by the second or third pass there is genuinely nothing left to interrupt. The pass that finally completes is the one picking up the remainder, and the remainder can legitimately contain no checkpoint at all. Demanding either would have failed a suite that was working, which is how a real check gets weakened back out again.
The fourth and fifth, `empty` and `process_death_mid_step`, are the opt-out cases. The sixth was nothing — a miscount on my part before the numbers were printed.
Why the opt-out lives on the scenario rather than in a list in the suite: a list is maintained; a field is answered. A scenario added tomorrow is asserted unless its author writes down what kills it, and a reason under thirty characters fails, because an opt-out nobody has to justify is a place to hide a scenario that has stopped testing anything.
Mutation-checked both halves: removing the catalogue walk's checkpoint call fails that scenario by name, telling the reader its checkpoints have gone or it must declare what interrupts it; shortening the opt-out reason to "no work" fails the scenario that carries it.
Nearest spec: main §14.3.9; tech §5.
## 2026-09-08 — R-BRAKES-BLIND — The quality brake counts real gate verdicts, and the counting rule is spelled out here
Decision: the automatic brake that stops all writing when the quality gate starts refusing most drafts now reads `gate_decisions`, the table where every verdict on every draft is written. The read is `recentGate3Outcomes` (`packages/db/src/repositories/ops-counters.ts`), a new file rather than an addition to the content engine's own repository, because it exists for the operations sweep and is deliberately unscoped where every content read is per-store. Three choices inside it that the specs do not dictate:
**One — what counts as a refusal.** The gate has one name for a pass and several for a refusal: a failed lint, a self-contradiction, a judge score under the floor, a failed repair. Anything that is not the pass counts as a refusal, including a name nobody has invented yet. Rejected: listing the refusal names, which would silently drop a new one and leave the brake reading a healthier number than the truth. The pass string is typed against the gate's own vocabulary, so renaming it breaks the build here instead of turning every pass into a refusal.
**Two — a merchant's "publish anyway" is not a refusal.** Publishing over a rejection writes a second row on the same draft recording that the merchant overruled us. It grades nothing, so it is excluded: counted as a refusal it would double every override and let a store that overrides often pause writing for every other store. The refusal it sits on top of still counts — the gate really did refuse that draft, whatever the merchant did next. This is narrower than invariant 12, which excludes override-*published articles* from calibration; that rule is about learning from our own judgement, and this is about noticing our judgement has broken.
**Three — all stores at once.** The switch this raises stops writing for everybody, so the rate is measured across every account rather than per store. One busy shop's bad afternoon is exactly what it must not mistake for a broken prompt.
Also decided: the count is measured over the last fifty verdicts with no time limit, which is what main §14.5 says — "the trailing 50 drafts", not a period — and what makes the rule mean the same thing in a quiet week as a busy one. Consequence worth knowing, and left alone rather than invented around: an operator who lowers this switch while the last fifty verdicts still show a bad rate will see it go straight back up, and can only clear it by fixing the cause or by fifty further drafts being graded. Named as a card candidate in the session report rather than fixed here.
Where the counter is built: inside the sweep itself, out of the database handle it already holds, rather than handed down from the process that starts the worker. That is the point of the change — the brake was wired to a stand-in for months precisely because the one place that could have connected it never did, and a default that needs no wiring cannot be forgotten the same way. Tests still override it to hand the arithmetic a rate directly.
Nearest spec: main §14.4, §14.5 (auto-trips), §8.4–8.6 (the gate and the override), §7.10 (the ceilings live in `packages/rules`); invariants 11, 12, 17.

## 2026-09-08 — R-BRAKES-BLIND — OPEN QUESTION: the publishing brake cannot be built without somewhere to write down a failed publish
Not a decision. The half of this card that is blocked, and the reason, so the integrator can decide rather than rediscover it.
**What the brake is for.** If more than a fifth of attempts to post an article onto merchants' shops fail inside an hour, that is Shopify having a bad day rather than us, so posting pauses everywhere while writing carries on (main §14.5: "Publish API error rate > 20% over 1h"). The arithmetic exists and is tested. The count does not.
**Why the table it would read cannot answer.** Posting is guarded by a claim row in `publish_intents`: we write the claim, send the post, then confirm the claim with the id the shop gave back. That row has three ends, and none of them is "tried and failed":
- **confirmed** — the shop took the post. Success.
- **abandoned** — we gave up. Written by the recovery sweep twenty-five minutes after the claim, once three passes have failed to settle it, or when a republish finds the merchant has deleted the article. A real failure, but a rare and heavily delayed one.
- **deleted outright** — and this is the problem. When the shop *refuses* the post, the claim row is removed so the next attempt can take the name back. Refusal covers a dead token, a page that is gone, a permanent rejection, and — the case that matters most here — **a rate limit** (`sendDisposition`, `packages/core/src/publish/failure.ts`). A rate-limit storm is the single likeliest shape of "the platform is failing", and it is precisely the shape that leaves nothing behind.
So a failure rate computed from the rows that survive would read close to zero right through the outage the brake exists to catch — the "query that silently returns zero forever and looks healthy" the counter's own header was written to avoid. Deleting the row is not a bug: the claim's whole job is to be a name only one attempt can hold, and a row left behind under any state would block that publication for ever (`releasePublishIntent`, `packages/db/src/repositories/publishing.ts`).
**Therefore the honest answer needs a durable record of an attempt and how it ended, which is a schema change, which is not a feature card's to make.** The counter stays a stand-in that says out loud it cannot see, and `pnpm stubs:report` still lists it — which is the correct state, not a gap. What is now fixed is the *reason* recorded there: it used to say `publish_intents` did not exist.
**The three ways forward, for whoever decides.**
1. *A new append-only table* — one row per attempt: account, the publication's key, when, and how it ended (took it / refused it / could not tell / gave up). The counter becomes a two-column count over an hour. Leaves the claim's uniqueness rule completely alone, which matters because that rule is the only thing standing between a crash and a merchant getting the same article twice. Recommended.
2. *Add a fourth state to the claim itself.* Cheaper-looking and worse: the claim would have to stop being deleted on refusal, so the unique index that makes the claim work would need a partial form excluding failed rows. That is surgery on the one guarantee we least want to be clever about.
3. *Leave it blind and delete the brake*, accepting that a Shopify outage means every store's morning post fails and nothing pauses. Stated only because it is a real option; the alert on abandoned publishes in main §14.7 would still fire, and an alert is not a brake.
**Not proposed: counting only the abandoned rows.** It is honest about what it measures and dishonest as a brake — the number would almost never reach even the minimum sample of five in an hour, so the brake would look connected and still never fire, which is worse than one that says it cannot see.
Nearest spec: main §14.5 (the trip), §14.3.7 (two-phase publish and the claim), §14.7 (the abandoned-publish alert); invariants 19, 22.

## 2026-09-08 — R-STUB-REPORT-2 — A stand-in is found by what it does, not by what it is called
Decision: the two checks in `seams-wired.test.ts` find stand-ins by scanning every shipping file for a class that either extends the shared stand-in base or calls `registerStub` itself. They used to read one file for classes named `Stub…`.
What that missed, and it was found by the lane that tripped over it rather than by me: the two counters that make the automatic brakes blind live in `core/ops/counters.ts` and are called `Unrecorded…`. Neither check could see them. They appeared on `pnpm stubs:report` only because a line in the report script constructs them by hand — so deleting that one line would have removed the last visible trace of a brake that cannot fire, with nothing anywhere to stop it.
`UnrecordedPublishOutcomes` is now recorded in `WIRED_IN_PRODUCTION` with what a user loses by it, because it is genuinely built by shipping code and deliberately so. Carded as `R-PUBLISH-ATTEMPTS`.
A second fault, mine, found while mutation-checking this: each stand-in gets its own test from the list the scan returns, so **narrowing the scan removed a test rather than failing one** — a smaller number and no other signal, which is the exact shape this file exists to catch, one level up. There is now an assertion that every name written down elsewhere — on the report, or in either record — is a name the scan can see. Mutation-checked: dropping the `registerStub` half of the scan fails it by name.
Nearest spec: main §14.7; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-STUB-REPORT`.

## 2026-09-08 — R-CONTRACT-DISK — The contract check finally compares the contract to the routes, and the walk has one home
Decision: `pnpm contracts:check` now reads the route files under `apps/web/app/api` and compares both ways — a served address the contract does not declare fails, and a declared address no file serves fails. `UNCONTRACTED_ROUTES` still excuses the addresses deliberately outside the JSON contract (redirects, downloads, the identity library's own family), each with its reason.
What was wrong: everything the check did compared the contract to itself — the frozen route table against the document generated from that table, and back. Ten endpoints were once built at addresses the table did not know about while the table declared several nothing had implemented, and this check passed on every run throughout. It is the founder's reporter 2, and it was still open this morning: two tests had since covered the gap from other directions, but the gate runs the script independently of the test suite.
Why the walk moved into `packages/core/src/api/routes-on-disk.ts` rather than being written a second time: `screen-addresses.test.ts` already had one, and a second copy of "what does this application serve" is how the two ends of a check come to disagree without either being wrong — which is the fault this whole week has been about. The test now imports it. **Deliberately not exported from the core barrel:** it reads the filesystem and the barrel reaches browser bundles, so both callers deep-import it.
One behaviour is stricter than the copy it replaced: a directory in parentheses is dropped rather than becoming a path segment. None exists under the API root today; the old copy would have invented an address if one appeared.
A walk that finds nothing now fails rather than agreeing with any contract at all.
Mutation-checked in both directions: a route file at an address nobody declared fails naming it and saying what to do; moving an existing route's directory fails twice, once for the address that appeared and once for the one that vanished. Today it passes with 70 served addresses, all accounted for.
Nearest spec: main §14.7; tech §6; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-CONTRACT-PROVE`.

Deleting them would have left the wiring with no note saying why an optional dependency is pinned at all, which is the thing that was worth writing down.
The correction is only honest because the missing test now exists. Both comments also record what went wrong, in one sentence each: these assertions stayed green for the whole life of a screen that offered a single Google button, because a configuration object cannot see a screen. A future reader tempted to treat "the provider is configured" as "the merchant can use it" meets the counter-example in the same paragraph.

## 2026-09-08 — R-LINT-PROOFS — All seven banned vendor libraries now have a planted proof, not three
Decision: five new cases in `scripts/lint-proofs/` — `resend`, `stripe`, `posthog-node`, `@shopify/shopify-api` and `googleapis`. Each plants a real import of the library outside its wrapper, runs the real lint command, and fails unless the rule rejects it.
What was wrong: every vendor library must be reached through a single wrapper, and importing one anywhere else is a lint error. Seven were banned and three were proved. The other four bans — the ones covering the email vendor, Stripe, Shopify and Google — could have stopped working and nothing would have said so. That matters more than it sounds: the wrappers are where spend is recorded, where responses are cached before use, and where tokens are kept out of logs, so a bypassed wrapper is a bill nobody counted rather than a style problem.
Mutation-checked: deleting two entries from the rule's table fails their two proofs by name — "lint accepted raw resend import outside the email wrapper" — and leaves the other fourteen passing.
Nothing shared was edited, which is the point of the harness: it discovers cases by file, so this added five files and touched no list.
