## 2026-09-08 — R-SCREEN-READS — The walk follows a page that awaits, because the whole steady dashboard sits behind one
Decision: kept from the session that died mid-card, and verified rather than taken on trust. The renderer that drives a screen calls each component and walks whatever it returns. A Next.js server component is an `async function`, so what it returns is a promise of its tree, and the walk treated that promise as a leaf and stopped there.
Why it matters here rather than in the abstract: `apps/web/app/(app)/dashboard/SteadyState.tsx` is one of those, and it is the entire steady-state dashboard — the growth headline, what is next, the month's counts, the search chart and the "needs you" list. The dashboard was being driven as far as the page's first line and no further. Measured both ways before and after: two endpoints and six fields before, six endpoints and fifty-nine after.
Mutation-checked: a component made to throw inside `SteadyState` fails the suite by name, which it could not have done if the walk never reached it.
Nearest spec: `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-CONTRACT-PROVE` (the sibling check, same principle: drive the real thing).

## 2026-09-08 — R-SCREEN-READS — Every screen is driven on the day its answers describe, and that day is asked of the fixtures
Decision: each screen is driven with the clock moved to the moment the mock answers describe. Only `Date` is faked, not timers, because the driver relies on real `setTimeout` to let a screen's effects settle.
Why: the answers describe a store on one particular day, and a calendar or a chart drawn around the real today has no cell for any of it. It draws an empty grid, and every read that would have happened inside a chip that was never drawn simply does not happen — the calendar was recording six field reads and now records twenty-three, and the dashboard gained nine more on top of the ones above.
The day is exported from the fixtures (`FIXTURE_NOW` in `packages/ui/src/msw/fixtures.ts`) and read from there rather than repeated in the test. A literal would let the fixtures move and take that coverage away with nothing going red — a silent loss of coverage is the precise fault this card exists to end.
Kept from the dead session's draft; the derivation replaces a hard-coded date it had left behind.
Nearest spec: main §9.1 (the calendar is drawn around today); `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-CONTRACT-PROVE`.

## 2026-09-08 — R-SCREEN-READS — Where a render stops is stated: nothing on the real answer, a named twelve on the emptied one
Decision: replaces the dead session's debug printing, which listed render failures to the console and asserted nothing. A component that throws returns no tree, so everything below it is never walked and none of its reads are checked. The walk collected those and dropped them, which is a check quietly covering less than it claims.
Two statements now hold that. On the drive against the answer an endpoint really sends, **no screen may stop at all**: all twenty-five render end to end today, and one that starts stopping fails naming the screen and the component. On the second drive — the one that empties every value so that `a.url ?? a.redirectUrl` actually evaluates its second name — twelve screens do stop, because emptying values is something no endpoint does and a component that formats a number or looks a word up by one will throw on the spot. Those twelve are listed in `EMPTIED_PASS_STOPS`, each with what stopping there costs, and the list is held exactly: a new one must be admitted with a sentence, and a fixed one must be deleted.
What that costs, said plainly: on those twelve screens, a hedge between two spellings sitting *below* the named component would still go unnoticed. A field a screen simply reads is covered everywhere; it is only the unreached fallback branch that is not.
Why a register rather than a red suite or a silent skip: this is the same shape `R-CONTRACT-PROVE` established for routes it cannot drive — "not covered" and "nobody thought about it" must not look the same.
The unused `failures` channel on the render pass, which nothing had ever read, is deleted in favour of this.
Nearest spec: main §14.7 (a check that cannot fail proves nothing); `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-CONTRACT-PROVE`.

## 2026-09-08 — R-SCREEN-READS — Stated limit: an open map is a hole this check cannot close
Finding, and the reason the next entry exists. The check asks each endpoint's declaration whether it *could* carry a field, by planting a key and parsing with the endpoint's own schema. Where the declaration says "an object with any keys" — the values a why-sentence fills its blanks from, an article's per-criterion justifications, the identifiers an attention item carries — every key survives that test, so **any name a screen reads there is accepted, including a misspelt one.**
Eight reads across the twenty-five screens land on a field the answer does not carry; seven of the eight are inside such a map. Two of those places are separately guarded — the why-line parameters by `packages/ui/src/strings/reason-copy.test.ts`, which holds each sentence's blanks against what its producer sends. The identifiers on an attention item are not guarded anywhere, and that is where a live fault is sitting today.
Not closed here, because the obvious closure is wrong: comparing against the keys the mock answer happens to carry would fail every legitimately-varying map, starting with the why-line parameters, whose keys differ per sentence by design.

## 2026-09-08 — R-SCREEN-READS — FINDING, not fixed: four of the five dashboard "needs you" links go to the wrong page
Found while auditing what the check above cannot see; it is exactly the fault this card exists to catch, and this check cannot catch it.
The dashboard's "needs you" list gives each item a link, chosen from the identifiers the item carries. The server sends those identifiers under snake-case names — `article_id`, `opportunity_id` (`packages/db/src/stores/notifications.ts:60,69,75` and `packages/db/src/repositories/notifications.ts:222,257`). The screen reads camel-case ones — `item.refs.articleId`, `item.refs.opportunityId` (`packages/ui/src/dashboard/dashboard.ts:210,212`). Neither ever matches.
What a merchant loses: the link never crashes — it falls through to a default by item kind — so a draft waiting for review opens the whole articles library instead of that draft; an unconfirmed export URL and a pending repair both land on the content page instead of the article that needs them; an unapplied recommendation lands on the content page instead of the opportunity it belongs to. Only the merchant-task item, which is routed by kind rather than by identifier, goes where it should. Four of the five kinds are wrong, on the first screen a merchant sees.
Why nothing noticed: the mock server the frontend develops against writes the camel-case spelling (`packages/ui/src/msw/fixtures.ts`, `GET /api/attention`), so the links work in development and only in development. Both spellings are legal against the declaration, which types these as an object with any string keys.
Not fixed here: the fix is one lane's screen or another's store, the choice of which spelling wins is not this card's, and this session owns one card. Carded as `R-ATTENTION-REFS`.

## 2026-09-08 — R-SCREEN-READS — Stated limit: a poll started by one screen can be recorded against the next
The driver lets a screen's effects settle with real timers, so a screen that polls has a `setTimeout` outstanding when its test ends. That callback can fire during a later screen's drive and be recorded against it — which is why the landing page's preview form appears to read the notification bell's answer.
It cannot hide a fault or invent one: the pair that is checked is the endpoint and the field, both of which are still true of the read. It can only put the right complaint under the wrong screen's name. Left alone deliberately: cancelling them means the driver owning every timer a screen starts, which is a larger machine than the confusion is worth.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — The server now has the same declared table of analytics events the browser has, and drops everything else
Decision: `packages/core/src/contracts/analytics-events.ts` lists every event the server may send to our analytics vendor and, for each, the properties it may carry and what kind of value each one is. The wrapper that talks to the vendor (`packages/providers/src/posthog/index.ts`) runs every capture through it — the ordinary one, the model-call one, the search-data one and the crash one — and silently drops anything the table does not name. The test double runs the same table, so a test that asserts "an article title cannot get out" is asserting what production does.
Why: the promise to merchants is that nothing they wrote — product copy, a prompt, a draft article — reaches a third-party analytics vendor; only identifiers and counts. In the browser that was already structural. On the server the capture took an open bag of properties and ran a credential scrubber, which redacts an access token and passes a paragraph of prose through untouched. This journal said so outright ("today the rule is upheld by review alone") and two audits had it open.
Why a copy of the browser's shape rather than a new scheme: there is one rule and it should have one form. The kinds are the browser's four — an identifier, an enumerated name, a count, a yes/no — with the same rule that an identifier has no spaces and stops at sixty-four characters, which is what a headline and a paragraph both fail.
Nearest spec: main §14.7 ("events carry ids and aggregates only — never product content, article text, prompts"); invariant 26.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — A fifth kind, for the one event that reports a set of counts it cannot name in advance
Decision: the server table has a kind the browser's does not: `count_map`, names paired with counts. Exactly one property uses it — `family_grouping_completed.grouping_sources`, which reports how many product families each grouping method produced.
Why it is not a loophole: every key in such a map must satisfy the same shape rule as an enumerated name (no whitespace, sixty-four characters at most, not a credential) and every value must be a number. So it admits nothing an `enum` property would not already admit, and it cannot hold a sentence.
Alternative rejected: declaring the property undeclared and letting the guard drop it, which would have silently removed a number a dashboard reads.
Nearest spec: main §14.7; invariant 26.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — An event the table has never heard of keeps its row and loses every property
Decision: if a capture names an event with no row in the table, it is still sent, carrying only the account (or preview domain) the wrapper itself attaches; every property the call site supplied is dropped. If the event *name* is not even shaped like a name — lower-case words joined by underscores — nothing is sent at all.
Why: the rule is about content, and dropping the properties keeps it completely. Dropping the whole row instead would also hide that the work happened, which is a worse telemetry failure than a row with nothing on it, and both are equally visible to whoever is building the dashboard that needs it. The name is checked as well because a name assembled from a merchant's words would otherwise carry them past a table that only inspects properties.
Nearest spec: main §14.7; invariant 26.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — `null` is allowed under any declared property
Decision: a declared property may hold `null` whatever its kind.
Why: "we had none" is an answer with no content in it, and several events legitimately report one — Gate 1 makes no model call, so it has no model id or prompt version to name. Refusing null would have meant dropping those properties, which loses the difference between "no model was used" and "nobody said".
Nearest spec: main §14.7; invariant 26.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — The guard is at the wrapper only; the compiler still accepts any event name
Decision: `AnalyticsEvent.event` stays a plain string. The table is enforced when an event is sent, not when one is written.
Why, and what it costs: narrowing that field to the list of declared names would make an undeclared event a build failure rather than a silent stripping — genuinely stronger. But `AnalyticsEvent` is a shared interface three other lanes' code builds events against, and narrowing it is the kind of interface change the constitution says to ask about rather than take. Left as a card candidate. Until then, an undeclared event is caught when someone looks at the dashboard, not when they compile.
Nearest spec: main §14.7; CLAUDE.md prime directive 3.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — The table declares what the code emits today, not everything the spec names
Decision: rows exist for the twenty-eight events the product actually sends. The spec's §14.7 taxonomy also names events nothing emits yet — `shopify_oauth_granted` / `_abandoned`, `ingestion_step_completed`, `distillation_completed`, `optimize_recommendation_generated`, `opportunity_outcome_measured`, `publish_intent_created` / `_confirmed` / `_abandoned`. They are not in the table.
Why: declaring permissions for events nobody has built means guessing their properties, and a wrong guess is a permission granted in advance. The card that builds each one adds its row, which is the workflow the table is for. The cost is that the first attempt to emit one of them will find its properties stripped; the fix is one line in one file.
Nearest spec: main §14.7.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — A search phrase from the merchant's own catalogue was being sent, and the call site is fixed as well as guarded
Decision: `StubExistingTargetCheck` in `packages/core/src/contracts/doubles.ts` attached the head term of a keyword cluster — a phrase derived from the merchant's catalogue and search data, with spaces in it — to the `stub_used` event. The new table drops it; the call site no longer offers it.
Why both: leaving the argument in place would have left the code reading as though the phrase were captured, with only a silent drop to say otherwise. This is the one live violation of the rule the guard found in existing code.
Nearest spec: main §14.7; invariant 26.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — "Analytics is told, never asked" is now two checks instead of a shape
Decision: `packages/providers/src/posthog/control-plane.test.ts` asserts two things. First, every method on the analytics port returns nothing — a method that answers a question has to return an answer, so a read cannot be added without failing. Second, the one file allowed to hold the analytics vendor's library never calls any of the vendor's flag or remote-config methods, which are the vendor's own perfectly good control plane and must not become ours.
Why: when we stop spending money or halt a job, that decision is read from our own database, because a brake has to work on the day the vendor is down — which is the day something has gone wrong enough for a brake to matter. Until now the rule rested on the port happening to have no method that returns anything, which is a shape and not a check.
Each half is mutation-checked: adding `isSpendingCapped(): Promise<boolean>` to the port fails the first, and implementing it with the vendor's `isFeatureEnabled` fails the second.
What it cannot see, stated rather than implied: it reads the port and the one file that imports the vendor's library. Somebody who called the vendor's HTTP API directly, from a file importing nothing, passes both — that path is closed by the lint rule keeping the vendor's library inside this directory, and by nothing else.
Nearest spec: main §14.5, §14.7 ("PostHog is telemetry and alerting, not the control plane"); invariant 17.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — The spend-ledger tests no longer claim to cover a rule they never touched
Decision: the comment at the top of `packages/core/src/contracts/spend.test.ts` said those tests covered "the port's own rules" including that analytics is never the control plane. The four tests below it cover which attribution column is set, a negative cost, a cache hit recorded as free, and a ledger outage that must not fail the job. The comment now says that, and points at the file where the control-plane rule is actually checked.
Why: an over-claiming comment is worse than no comment. The audit found this one while looking for the mechanism it described, which did not exist.
Nearest spec: main §14.7; invariant 17.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — CONTRADICTION: "notifications are append-only" is not true of the product, and cannot be made true without changing behaviour
Not a decision. The constitution's invariant 26 says notifications are append-only records. The shipped product updates and deletes them, in three places, all of them deliberate and all of them needed:
1. **Opening the bell writes `seen_at`, clicking an item writes `read_at`** (`markNotificationsSeen`, `markNotificationRead`). Without these the badge never clears.
2. **The nightly retention sweep deletes notifications older than the retention window** (`pruneNotifications`). Keeping them for ever is what the retention policy forbids.
3. **Deleting an account removes its notifications**, through the foreign key's cascade. Required for deletion to mean deletion.
So the property that is actually true, and worth defending, is narrower: **what a notification says is written once and never rewritten, and nothing removes one except retention and account deletion.** That is what the new check enforces. The invariant's wording needs correcting to match, which is the founder's or integrator's call, not mine.
Nearest spec: tech §1 (notifications, retention); main §14.6 (deletion); invariant 26.

## 2026-09-08 — R-TELEMETRY-TEETH — Append-only is enforced by a source check; making it true at the database needs a migration
Decision: `packages/db/src/repositories/notifications-append-only.test.ts` reads every shipping file and fails, by name, on any update or delete against the notifications table that is not one of the three permitted writes above, and on any permitted update that sets a column other than the two read-state timestamps. Each permitted write carries a written reason. The check also asserts it found writes at all, so a rename or a broken walk fails rather than quietly passing over an empty list.
What it cannot do, and this is the part the card asked to be said out loud: it stops code we write. It does not stop anyone holding a database connection — a migration, an admin script, a psql session. Making the database itself refuse an update or a delete means `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE` on the table for the application role, or a trigger, and either is a migration. **Schema waves are closed, so this is the integrator's call and is not taken here.** Note that a plain revoke would also break the two writes the product needs, so the real form is a trigger that permits only the read-state columns and the retention sweep's role — more machinery than a revoke, and worth deciding on rather than assuming.
Mutation-checked twice: a repository function that rewrites a notification's payload fails two of the checks by name, and a raw `DELETE FROM notifications` in an unrelated file fails one.
Nearest spec: tech §1; invariant 26.
## 2026-09-08 — R-CREATE-UNCHECKED — Which of the three ways to propose a new page were actually unsafe, and what the permission slip now does
Decision: all three findings that can end in "write a new page for this" now carry the existing-target check's answer, and the action step refuses to return a new-page recommendation without a permission that only the check can issue. The permission type stays; it acquired three real callers rather than being deleted.

**Established before changing anything, because two of the three might have been safe.**
- **The uncovered-search finding was safe.** Its detector refuses to answer at all for a search nobody ran the check on — it throws rather than treating "not asked" as "nothing found" — and it drops any search where the check found a page that can take the work over. Verified by resolving its one production caller, which does run the real check. It was changed anyway, but only to carry the permission it was already entitled to; its behaviour is unchanged.
- **The competitor-gap finding was unsafe, and this is the one that mattered.** It decided on a search-result position alone: nothing of ours visible in the results meant a new page. A page can serve a subject perfectly and rank nowhere — that is precisely why the check exists — so a store with a collection page for the subject, not yet found by Google, would be told to publish a second page competing with it. Its own comment claimed a middling position (11–30) converted the advice to "improve what you have", which is true and does not cover a page at position 90 or a page at no position at all.
- **The range-coverage finding was unsafe too, and less obviously.** Its comment said the detector "already excludes any family with mapped content that ranks or is ours". Reading the assembly that feeds it: whether a page has ever been shown is hard-coded to false at the only production call site — nothing measures it — so the "ranks" half of that exclusion can never fire. The remaining half only catches articles we published ourselves, and those are blog pages, which the nightly walk gives no ranges to. In practice the exclusion excluded nothing. Its argument was the stronger-looking one and it was the more thoroughly hollow.

**What a merchant sees change.** A competitor gap over a page of theirs that search has not found becomes "improve this page" (or, where the page is an article we published, a rewrite) instead of "write another one". A range whose collection page already serves the subject stops attracting a new article. Where the page found is only a partial match, the new page still goes ahead and now carries the task of linking the two together, so they support each other rather than splitting one search — the permission carries that obligation, so honouring the check and honouring the link cannot come apart.

**Choices the specs do not dictate.**
1. *A range is asked about under its own name.* The check answers "do we already have a page for this intent", and an intent is a search. A whole range has no single search, so its name stands in for one and the permission is checked back against the same name. The alternative — leaving the range finding to a stated guarantee of its own — was rejected because its stated guarantee was the one that turned out to be hollow.
2. *A strong match converts the competitor gap rather than suppressing it.* Invariant 6 says a match converts to improve-or-rewrite, never a competing page; suppressing would have thrown away useful advice the merchant can act on. The page's kind decides which: an article we published is rewritten, the merchant's own page is recommended for edits. That page-kind split did not previously exist on this finding, whose founder-set 11–30 rule is OPTIMIZE-only; the split applies only to a page the check found, never to one found by position alone, where we know nothing about what the page is.
3. *One answer per subject, shared by all three findings, computed once per scan.* The alternative is each finding asking separately, which is three chances to disagree about one store and three times the reads. A subject with no answer raises an error rather than defaulting: "we did not ask" and "we asked and found nothing" look identical downstream and only one is safe.
4. *The store is read once per scan instead of once per search.* The three reads behind the check are per-store; only the last step is per-subject. Without this, widening the question from a few searches to every candidate would have multiplied a full pass over the store's page list and its search history by the number of candidates.

**Mutation-checked, six ways.** Dropping the permission check on the competitor branch fails two tests by name. Adding a fourth finding that proposes a new page fails the test that reads the list of findings off the code. Letting the range finding ignore a page the check found fails one test; faking its answer instead of asking fails three. Blinding the check to the store's page list fails seven. Removing the link obligation from a partial match fails two. One more, worth recording because it found a hole in my own test: forging a permission by copying a real one's fields with a spread *kept working*, because the marker that makes a permission real is a symbol and a spread copies symbols. The forgery in the test is now built field by field, and the test failed correctly afterwards.

**Left alone, deliberately, and named in the session report as card candidates.** Nothing decides what a store page is *for* — `store_pages.intent_class` is null on every real store — so the check can call a merchant's collection page a partial match but never a full one. The consequence today is that the conversion to "improve what you have" fires only where Search Console shows the page ranking; everywhere else the merchant gets a new page plus a link to the old one, which is the safe direction but not the best one. And nothing measures whether a store page has ever been shown for anything, which is the hard-coded value described above.
Nearest spec: main §7.7, §8.2 (the check and Gate 1), §7.3/§7.8 (which finding suggests what); invariants 6 and 7.

## 2026-09-08 — R-ATTENTION-REFS — The dashboard's "needs you" links point at the right thing, and the contract names the keys
Decision: `attentionResponseSchema.refs` stops being an open map and names the four keys an item may carry — `article_id`, `opportunity_id`, `task_id`, `recommendation_id` — each optional, the object strict. The dashboard reads those names. The spelling chosen is the underscored one, because that is the vocabulary the notification record already uses, in rows already written and under a rule of its own (`notifications/refs.ts`) that says to name the thing rather than the words. The screen was two lines; the producer is five call sites and a stored payload shape.
What was wrong, in a merchant's terms: the first screen they see lists what needs their attention, and each row links to the thing. The server sends `article_id`; the screen read `articleId`. Nothing matched, so every row fell through to a default by kind — a draft waiting for review opened the whole articles library rather than that draft, an unconfirmed address and a pending repair landed on the content page rather than the article needing fixing, and an unapplied recommendation landed on the content page rather than its opportunity. **Four of the five kinds.**
Why nothing caught it, which is the part worth keeping: the contract declared an open map, so **both spellings were legal** and neither the route check nor the new screen check could see the difference — before or after a fix. The mock the frontend develops against used the screen's spelling, so the links worked in development and only there. Found by hand by the lane building the screen check, while auditing that check's own blind spot.
Three things came with it. The mock now carries **two** attention kinds rather than one, because a mock describing a single kind let the screen read a name no answer in front of it ever contained. The notification mock's `refs` was underscored to match what the server really stores. And the screen check gained a well-formed identifier among its probe values: it decides "could this endpoint ever send this field?" by planting a value and re-parsing, and with only `'probe'`, `1`, `true`, `null`, `{}` and `[]` to plant, **any field declared as an identifier read as one the endpoint could never send** — my precise declaration turned a real fix into a false alarm, which would have happened to the next person too.
Left open: `notificationSchema.refs` is still an open map with the same hole. Its vocabulary is wider and its renderer resolves names at run time, so tightening it is a card rather than a line.
Cross-lane: the screen, its type, its test and the mock are Lane F's, and the probe change is in Lane F's new check. Taken by the integrator with Lane F idle, because it is a live defect on the first screen a merchant sees and the fix spans the contract, which is the integrator's by rule.
Mutation-checked: pointing the article link at the opportunity key instead fails "sends each item to the surface that can resolve it".
Nearest spec: main §7.12; ui §4; `DECISIONS.md` 2026-09-08 `R-SCREEN-READS`.
## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH-2 — The refresh pool and the drift pass resolve the store's numbers, and pass no language while doing it
Decision: `requestArticleRefresh` (`packages/jobs/src/generation/request-refresh.ts`) and the daily drift pass (`packages/jobs/src/drift/sweep.ts`) now take their thresholds and their version string from `resolveStoreRules`, the helper the three gates already use. Both pass **no locale**, exactly as they behaved before.
Why the locale is left out, since it looks like an omission: neither path has ever applied the config file's own per-language layer — both read `rules().defaults`, the global layer, and not `forLocale(store's language)`. Starting to look the language up here would change which numbers every non-English store is judged by, with no override anywhere in sight. That is a behaviour change well outside a card about reach, and it is the same reasoning the gates recorded on 2026-09-07. The consequence, stated plainly: a `rules_overrides` row aimed at a **language** does not reach these two paths. A row aimed at one store, or at every store, does. This is the same gap already recorded for `POST /api/calendar/topics`.
What changes for a merchant: nothing, for a store with no override row — the numbers are identical and the version string stamped is the identical bare file hash, so nothing already recorded becomes unreadable. For a store carrying a row, a press of "Request refresh" is judged against that store's cooldown and ranking band, the daily check on published articles uses that store's out-of-stock window and substitute-similarity floor, and the piece of work either writes down stamps the version that says an override was in play.
Cost: the refresh read is folded into the same round trip as the article lookup (`Promise.all`), so a merchant pressing the button waits no longer than before. The drift pass takes one extra indexed lookup per store per day, inside the account lock it already holds. This is the condition the no-cache decision named — a read that adds a round trip — and neither adds one.
Nearest spec: main §7.10, §14.1; invariants 7 and 9.

## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH-2 — The gate helper is renamed, because gates are no longer the only callers
Decision: `resolveRulesForGate` in `packages/jobs/src/generation/rules-for-gate.ts` becomes `resolveStoreRules` in `packages/jobs/src/generation/store-rules.ts`. Its behaviour is unchanged. The DECISIONS entry of 2026-09-08 that introduced it names the old file.
Why: the drift pass is not a gate and neither is the refresh pool, and a function whose name says "gate" is the kind of thing a later reader copies rather than calls. The alternative — a second helper doing the same three lines — is how two schemes for one idea start.
The one thing worth noticing: `packages/jobs/src/drift/sweep.ts` now imports from `../generation/`. That direction already exists in the same area (`drift/repair.ts` imports from `../publish/`), and the helper's other home would be `packages/jobs/src/runtime/`, which no lane owns and which would then depend on `../scan/`. Left where it is.
Nearest spec: main §7.10.

## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH-2 — Which numbers an override actually reaches is a table in the repo, not something to be traced through four files
Decision: `packages/rules/src/reach.ts` classifies every number in `signals.config.yaml` as **honoured** (every piece of code that reads it asks for the store's rows first), **partial** (some readers do and some take the repo file's value), or **ignored** (no reader asks for the store's rows, so a row changes nothing at all). Each entry carries a plain-language note naming what reads it. Entries are dotted prefixes and the narrowest one wins, so a group states the common case and the exceptions sit under it.
Why a table rather than something derived: there is no way to compute this. It is a fact about roughly forty call sites, and a hand-kept record is the only honest form. So the file says outright what it is and what it is not: **nothing reads it at runtime, and moving an entry to "honoured" makes no reader honour anything.** Wiring the reader is what does that, and the entry then follows.
What the test beside it can and cannot prove. It proves **completeness** — every leaf in the config file is classified, so a new group of thresholds cannot arrive unclassified — and that every prefix names a real path. It cannot prove a classification is still *true*: that a reader honours what the table says it honours is held by the tests beside those readers. That residual risk is the price of the table and is stated rather than hidden.
Rejected: annotating the YAML file itself. Its bytes are hashed into `rules_version`, the string stamped on every decision the product makes, so adding a word to it would change the version every store stamps and break comparison with every record written before today.
**Outside Lane D, and flagged for the integrator.** `packages/rules` is Lane C's by the ownership table; the integrator authorised the operator script but not this package. It went here because the operator command already imports `packages/rules/src/*` directly, because the completeness test has to run in CI and `scripts/` is not collected by vitest, and because the table is data about the rules layer. Two new files, plus an export block in the union-merged barrel; nothing existing was changed. Move it if that is wrong.
Nearest spec: main §7.10; invariant 9; build plan §3.

## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH-2 — The command refuses a number nothing would read, and takes an extra word for one only half the product reads
Decision: `pnpm rules set` now refuses a key the reach table marks **ignored**, naming what reads it and saying that setting it would change nothing. A key marked **partial** is also refused, saying which half would not move, and `--partial` sets it anyway. A key marked **honoured** is unaffected. `pnpm rules clear` is never refused — a row already in the table must always be removable. `pnpm rules list` marks any row whose key is not fully honoured, so a threshold set before today and quietly doing nothing is visible without running a scan.
Why partial is not simply allowed, and not simply refused. Allowing it silently is the defect this card exists to close: an operator moves the judge's floor believing the whole product now uses it, and only the article gate does. Refusing it outright would take away something that works today — since the gates landed, moving `gates.draft_grading.grounding_min` really does change what gets published — so a flat refusal would be a regression dressed as a fix. An acknowledgement flag is the same shape as the `--second` rule this command already has for a change that affects every store: friction in proportion to how easy it is to be wrong about what you just did.
Rejected: printing a warning and writing anyway. A warning after a successful write is read by nobody, and the whole point is that the operator's belief and the product's behaviour should not diverge silently.
Nearest spec: main §7.10, §14.5; `scripts/kill-switch.mjs` (house style for a named-operator change).

## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH-2 — Found and deliberately left: the calendar's replenishment pass reads seven thresholds from the file
Decision: `packages/jobs/src/generation/replenish.ts` — the pass that decides which of the outstanding work gets a calendar day — reads `learning.replenishment_horizon_days`, `learning.replenishment_target_horizon_days`, four numbers under `learning.patterns`, `learning.refresh.batch_share_max`, both `learning.exploration` numbers and `scoring.create.competitor_gap_source_bonus` straight from the repo file. It is a Lane D file and the card did not name it. Left alone, and recorded in the reach table so the command refuses those keys.
Why it is not the same defect: the two readers this card fixed **stamp a version** on the row they write, so reading the file made their record actively false. Replenishment stamps nothing — it writes calendar days, not a judged record — so the harm is only that an override does not reach it, which the command now says out loud rather than accepting in silence. Wiring it is a card, not a line: two of its numbers (`learning.patterns.multiplier_clamp_min`/`_max`) are also read by the weekly scan, which does honour overrides, so today those two are partial and one pass disagrees with the other about a store's clamp.
Card candidate: **the replenishment pass reads a store's own numbers**, Lane D, and it would move `learning.*` from ignored to honoured in one go.
Nearest spec: main §8.7, §9.6.3; invariant 9.

## 2026-09-08 — R-OVERRIDE-REACH-2 — Found and deliberately left: what the merchant is shown is computed from the repo file
Decision: three readers recompute a confidence band from `scoring.confidence` without consulting the store's rows — the opportunities screen, the performance screen (`apps/web/app/api/opportunities`, `apps/web/app/api/performance`) and the reader that lists accepted work (`packages/jobs/src/scan/opportunity-source.ts`). The weekly scan and the refresh pool do consult them. So a store with a moved confidence threshold has work scored one way and described on screen another. Not touched: two of those are Lane F's and Lane C's, and Lane F and Lane C are both running.
Card candidate: **the screens describe a store's work by the numbers that judged it**, and it is small — the band is already stored on the row in most cases, so the fix may be to stop recomputing rather than to resolve overrides.
Nearest spec: main §7.6, §7.10; ui §4.

## 2026-09-08 — R-REAL-NETWORK-TESTS — Two tests that failed for weeks, and neither was flaky in the way it looked
Decision: both are fixed, and they had different causes, which is why one card was not enough.
**The sign-in test made a live request to Google on every run.** The screen is handed a `fetch` that answers from the real sign-in handlers, so the test looks self-contained — but the sign-in library reads Google's own description of where its endpoints are before it can build a sign-in URL, and it uses the process's `fetch`, not the injected one. That document is now answered from a copy in the test file, captured 2026-09-08. Nothing about the library's behaviour is stubbed; only the document it would have fetched. Anything else the file tries to reach now throws, naming the address — the more useful half, because a file that starts reaching somewhere new should say where rather than hang until the timeout.
The measurements: the request takes about 230 ms from this machine while idle, matching the 414 ms the test took when it passed, and it timed out at exactly five seconds when it did not. **The tests now run in 15 ms rather than 414.** A unit test that cannot run without a vendor being up and quick is not a unit test.
**The rate-limiter's pacing test timed the wrong two moments.** The limiter controls when a request is *sent*; the test measured when two requests *arrived* at a local server. On a busy machine a request sits between those moments, and if the first waits longer than the second the arrival gap comes out shorter than the gap the limiter actually left — 75 ms against a 90 ms floor, twice in a row, while passing every time it ran alone. It is now timed from the caller's side, where delay can only push the number up, so a failure means the limiter really did not wait. What it no longer distinguishes is waiting before the first request rather than between the two; the burst test above it covers that, and the arrival count still proves both requests were made.
Mutation-checked: raising the limiter to a hundred thousand a second fails the pacing test.
Why this is worth an entry rather than a quiet fix: three separate full-suite failures today were shrugged at as load, and the state file carried a note calling one of them "not a load flake" without saying what it was. Both had ordinary causes findable by measuring rather than re-running. **Capture the runner's output to a file** — two of the three failures could not even be named because the output was piped through `grep`.
Nearest spec: main §14.7; tech §6.

## 2026-09-08 — Founder decisions, sixteen at once — how these were taken, and how far they can be trusted

Decision: the sixteen entries that follow record answers Balazs gave on 2026-09-08. **They did not reach me directly.** They were put to him in a different Claude session (`sortiva-98`), which relayed them here with the note "first-hand, not a relay of a relay: I put the questions to him and these are his words."

Why that is written down rather than assumed: this repository has one integrator and one path to `main`, so the journal is the only place these answers exist. A reader in three months has no way to tell a founder's answer from an agent's inference unless the entry says which it is. Every entry below is therefore marked as relayed, and where a relayed answer rested on a fact I could check, I checked it before writing it down — which is how the correction in the next entry was found.

What this does **not** authorise: nothing irreversible or externally visible was taken on the strength of the relay alone. The two entries that change what a merchant sees — the competitor list and the quality brake — are recorded as decided but reach `main` as ordinary cards with tests, reviewable before anything deploys.

## 2026-09-08 — R-DEAD-STORAGE — The card is withdrawn: all four things it proposed to delete are either already gone or in use

Decision: **`R-DEAD-STORAGE` is deleted, not rewritten.** It proposed dropping two tables and two columns as unused. Nothing on its list should be dropped.

- `article_claims.staleness` — **already dropped**, by migration `0012_t_wave6`. Nothing to decide.
- `rules_overrides` — **live**. It is the per-store threshold layer: read by `packages/rules/src/{load,overrides,reach}.ts`, written by `pnpm rules set/list/clear`, given a unique index by that same migration, and being extended by a card that is running right now. Dropping it would have deleted a working feature mid-build.
- `products.metafields` — **written, stored, and read.** Shopify does not send a product's metafields alongside the product, so `packages/jobs/src/ingestion/metafields.ts` fetches them per product; the catalog upsert persists them (`packages/db/src/repositories/catalog.ts`); family grouping reads them back (`packages/db/src/repositories/families.ts` → `packages/core/src/families/group.ts`). The relayed correction called this column unwritten. It is not.
- `incident_findings` — **live, and it is an operator feature.** `pnpm switch note` writes a row and `pnpm switch list` / `history` read them back (`scripts/kill-switch.mjs`), which is how a person investigating a raised brake writes down what they found. The relayed correction named this the one item safe to drop. Dropping it would take the notes out of the incident tool.

Why the card was wrong: it was written from the read-only audit of 2026-09-07, and work landed that same evening the audit never saw. The relayed correction caught two of the four, and applied no fresh checking to the other two — it repeated the same mistake one layer up.

**The lesson, which has now fired three times this week: a finding is a claim about a tree, and a tree older than the finding is a different tree.** Anything carded off the 2026-09-07 audit is re-checked against the working tree before dispatch, and a correction to an audit gets the same treatment as the audit.
Nearest spec: main §7.10, §14.5; build plan §7 (audit schedule).

Decision (founder, relayed): option (b). A new account's business-competitor list is **empty**. Domains found ranking in search results are shown as **suggestions** the merchant may accept; nothing is added on their behalf. The constitution's invariant 5 stands unchanged — the code moves to meet it.

What was wrong: the constitution says domains seen in search rankings may be suggested to a merchant and never added automatically, because a competitor list is a statement about the merchant's own business and the product should not be putting words in their mouth. Onboarding added them anyway.

## 2026-09-08 — R-PUBLISH-ATTEMPTS — A small append-only table records every publish attempt and how it ended

Decision (founder, relayed): option (a). Build a table with one row per publish attempt and its outcome. The safety brake — the thing that stops publishing when too many attempts are failing — then reads it, and the last remaining stand-in leaves `pnpm stubs:report`.

Why nothing could count this before: the two-phase publish machinery deletes its claim row on the commonest failure, deliberately, so that a retry can take the name again. That means the commonest kind of refused publish leaves no trace at all — which is why the brake was built visibly blind rather than built wrong.

The rejected alternative stays rejected: adding a fourth state to the claim row would need surgery on the index that makes the claim safe in the first place.

Consequence: this needs a migration, so it belongs to a schema wave.
